units.la: VANQVAM variæ extent nobilissimæ huius artis institutiones, nullæ tamen, aut paucæ, quod pollicentur, efficiunt. Nam ut omittam quarundam fastidiosam prolixitatem, nonnullæ totæ sunt in controversiis scientiæ naturalis dissolvendis, quas fortasse aliunde hauriri satius esset. Ego vero hoc egi, ut totius Medicinæ (quod ab aliis neglectum est) brevis illa quidem, sed perspicua idea oculis subiiceretur. in qua non Physiofiologiam modò, sed & cæteras partes ita persequor, ut nihil magnopere desiderari putem. Vtrum autem quod volui, assequutus fuerim, viderint alii. Cæterùm ut huic opellæ aliquid lucis accedere patiaris à nominis tui splendore, Illustris Domine, unicè peto. Tibi enim jure, meritóque inscribo. Iure, quia inter tot Reipub. negotia, Academiæ quoque nostræ curam sustines: eoque ad te non publicorum modò studiorum, sed & privatæ diligentiæ rationes quodammodo pertinent. Meritò autem, propter veterem benevolentiam, qua me prosequeris, cuius sanè fructum difficilibus temporibus expertus sum. Accipe ergo hoc à me pignus, non gratiæ tibi referendæ, sed potius publicè testandæ. Vale.
units.tr: Although there are many very noble institutes of this art, none or few achieve what they promise. For, to pass over the tiresome prolixity of some, several are wholly devoted to resolving controversies of natural science, which would perhaps be better drawn from elsewhere. I, however, have aimed to set before the eyes a brief yet clear outline of the whole of medicine, which others have neglected. In it I pursue not only physiology but also the remaining parts in such a way that I think nothing much is left wanting. Whether I have achieved what I intended, let others judge. Meanwhile, I ask only one thing: that you allow some light to fall on this little work from the splendour of your name, Most Illustrious Sir. I dedicate it to you rightly and deservedly. Rightly, because amid so many affairs of the Commonwealth you also bear the care of our Academy, and so the reasons of not only public studies but also of private diligence in some measure pertain to you. Deservedly, on account of the long-standing goodwill with which you favour me, the fruit of which I have indeed experienced in difficult times. Accept therefore this pledge from me, not to repay your kindness, but rather to bear public witness to it. Farewell.

units.tr: Nor is that enough. The same man delights to put his mark on the little books that the divine Aristotle would wish to be his own.

units.tr: Add that, as once Podalirius and Machaon did, he brings countless souls back from the lake of Styx.

units.tr: Now too he brings into the light's shores the works we longed for, works that will please the old man of Cos and the old man of Pergamum.

units.tr: Tell me what rewards of praise this man deserves, who holds together, joined in one, what others scarcely hold singly.

units.tr: The saying of the greatest of physicians, "Life is short, art is long" [Ὁ βίος βραχύς, ἡ δὲ τέχνη μακρή], which the following poem mentions, stands at the beginning of the first book of the Aphorisms; Seneca also mentions it at the start of his De brevitate vitae.

units.la: LOngam artem Hippocrates, medicorum gloria prima, Et pariter VITAM prodidit esse BREVEM. De medica oraclum, quo diû nil certius arte: Cogimur & vitæ de brevitate queris. Cùm medicina volent tot carmina longa per orbem, Nil profecturis carmina structa modis. Irrita neglectis cadunt medicamina CAUSIS. Et Stygijs ager præcipitatur aquis. Nec profligandis sunt comentaria morbis, Vanus & (heu) labor est pharmacopæ tuus. Ipsa nova Asclepî tentatur natio morbo; Heîc ubi nil herbæ, nil & Hygeia potest.
units.tr: Long ago Hippocrates, the first glory of physicians, also declared that LIFE is SHORT. You ask about the brevity of life, and we are compelled to consider the oracle about medicine, which for a long time nothing has been surer than art. Although so many long poems about medicine circulate through the world, poems constructed in these ways bring nothing to those who will profit from them. Remedies fall in vain when the CAUSES are neglected, and the field is plunged into the Stygian waters. Commentaries are no use for beating down diseases; your pharmacopoeia is a vain labour (alas). The new race of Asclepius is itself attacked by disease, where neither herb nor Hygieia can do anything.

units.la: Ipse cubat medicus, cui sola Empirica cordi,
units.tr: The physician himself lies sick, he for whom only the Empirical school is dear,

units.la: Et Methodus, sanum non habet ille caput;
units.tr: and the Methodic school; that man has no sound head.

units.la: Sed tua quod Themison ventosa cucurbita quærat.
units.tr: But your Themison seeks the cupping-glass,

units.la: Juppiter! hoc pereat cum Themisone genus.
units.tr: Jupiter! may that race perish along with Themison.

units.la: Dogmaticusque velit se quivis doctor haberi,
units.tr: Let any doctor who wishes to be considered a Dogmatist,

units.la: Et medicus ferri clara per ora virûm,
units.tr: and a physician famous on the lips of men,

units.la: Cui Logos in pretio. Phryx verò & barbarus esto.
units.tr: for whom Logos [λόγος] is in esteem: let him be a Phrygian or a barbarian indeed.

units.la: Cui vilet magnus (pro pudor!) Hippocrates.
units.tr: For whom great Hippocrates is cheap (what a shame!).

units.la: Natura ingreditur cuius nunc templa minister
units.tr: Whose temples the vigorous minister of nature

units.la: Strenuus; heicque acrem se probat esse virum.
units.tr: now enters, and here proves himself a brave man.

units.la: Ille novos medicos (natta, vappaq, silete) Instituat; vacuo naviget amne Charon.
units.tr: Let him set up new physicians (nattas and vappas, be silent); let Charon sail on his empty river.

units.la: Nec pater ossa legat, nec tot modo funera mater:
units.tr: Let no father gather the bones, and no mother mourn so many funerals;

units.la: Augeat aut censum trux Libitina suum.
units.tr: let savage Libitina increase her own tally.

units.la: Sic fugientem animam poterit revocare Machaon
units.tr: Thus Machaon will be able to recall the fleeing soul,

units.la: Belgicus, & quisquis sit Rationis amans.
units.tr: the Belgian, and whoever is a lover of Reason.

units.la: Sic humana salus toto curabitur orbe:
units.tr: Thus human health will be cared for throughout the whole world:

units.la: Hippocrates dicti dememinensq; sui,
units.tr: Hippocrates, mindful of what he said,

units.la: Gilberto praeunte, BREVEM mox adseret ARTEM;
units.tr: with Gilbert leading, will soon assert that ART is BRIEF;

units.la: Et VITÆ LONGOS adseret ille COLOS.
units.tr: and he will assert that LIFE has LONG COURSES.

units.la: Eidem viro Philosophicis scriptis claro, & nunc demum Medicinos libros feliciter molienti.
units.tr: To the same man, distinguished for his philosophical writings and now at last happily undertaking medical books.

units.la: POstquam beatas Cœlitum petiit domos Ingens Lycei lumen Heurnius pater; Cœloque postquam clarus ille Pavius, Suadæ medulla, fidus additum novum: Nil è cathedris prodiit Galenicis. Apollinare obmutuit collegium. Non scripta cedro digna vendidit Tryphō, Coæ insulæ illa, aut invidenda Pergamo. Manus deorum desiêre pharmacum, Opemque ferre languidis mortalibus. Nemo est, ut ante, sævi ab Orci faucibus Retractus, ipse gaudet umbris Cerberus,
units.tr: After the great light of the Leiden school, Heurnius the father, sought the blessed homes of the heavenly ones, and after that famous Pavius, the marrow of eloquence and a faithful addition, had gone to heaven, nothing came forth from the Galenic chairs. The college of Apollo fell silent. Tryphon sold no writings worthy of cedar oil, those of the island of Cos or those that Pergamum might envy. The hands of the gods ceased to supply medicine and to bring help to sick mortals. No one, as before, is drawn back from the savage jaws of Orcus, and Cerberus himself rejoices in the shades.

units.la: Trino salutans portitorem gutture; Gaudentem & ipsum, & lintre plena turgi- dum. Tandem (heu) misertus, strage motus & gravi Gilbertus, ecce, occurrit, & pugnat stilo, Vsum medendi sex libellis edocens. Belle Herclè, temporique! ne Bataviæ Horrenda Pestis vastitudinem inferat. Iam jam dolentem me videre Cerberum, Puto, atque inanem navigare Porthmea. Hic gravia damna, quæ per Heurnij necem Cineresq; Pauli passa pridem Patria est, Pensabit unus, instar Æsculapij. Rependegrates, Patria; ô! quid restitas? Dubitasne, gallum cui sacrare debeas?
units.tr: Greeting the ferryman with his triple throat, and himself rejoicing and swollen with a boatload. At last Gilbert, moved with pity and stirred by the grievous slaughter, comes forward, and fights with his pen, teaching the practice of healing in six little books. Well done, by Hercules, and well timed! Lest the dreadful plague bring devastation to Batavia. Now, I think, Cerberus sees me grieving and sailing empty across the Porthmeus. This one man will make good the heavy losses which the fatherland has suffered for some time through the death of Heurnius and the ashes of Paulus, like another Aesculapius. Pay back, fatherland! Oh, why do you hesitate? Do you doubt to whom you ought to sacrifice a cock?

units.la: INSTITVTIONVM MEDICARVM Auctore GILBERTO IACCHÆO, CAPVT I. De Medicinæ constitutione.
units.tr: THE INSTITUTES OF MEDICINE by Gilbert Jacchaeus, CHAPTER I. On the constitution of medicine.

units.la: Missis sectis Methodicâ & Empiricâ, consilium est, Rationalis omnium quippe perfectissimæ, institutiones breviter quidem, sed tamen perspicuè tradere. Initium operis à Medicinæ constitutione faciam: qua ignorata, necesse est omnia alia inde dependentia pariter ignorari.
units.tr: With the Methodist and Empiric sects set aside, my purpose is to set out the institutes of rational medicine, which is by far the most perfect of them, briefly but clearly. I shall begin the work with the constitution of medicine, since if that is unknown, everything that depends on it must likewise remain unknown.

units.la: Artis huius constitutio in tribus est posita ; Subiecto (quo revocantur Medicinæ principia) Divisione, & Fine.
units.tr: The constitution of this art rests on three things: the subject (to which the principles of medicine are referred), the division, and the end.

units.la: Subjectum, circa quod versatur Medicus, omnium confessione, est corpus humanum quâ sanabile: Nam quanquanquam homo consideretur ab Ethico, Physico, Theologo; non tamen consideratur cum relatione ad sanitatem, quod facit Medicus: Modus ergo considerandi hominem, distinguit Artem hanc ab aliis. Physica siquidem considerat hominem, quà mobilem. Ethica, quà virtute informandum. Nec refert quod multa sint physicæ cum Medicina communia, ut tota doctrina physiologica; quia Medicina hac parte subiicitur physicæ, sumitque tanquam principia physicorum conclusiones: Quâ de causa factum est, ut hæc Medicinæ pars dicta fuerit speculativa; non quod vere sit speculativa, sed quia à praxi longius abest. Et quanquam stirpes, metalla, & huiusmodi materia medica hîc considerentur, omnia tamen referuntur ad corpus humanum; ad quod etiam eorum temperamenta exiguntur.
units.tr: The subject with which the physician is concerned is, by general agreement, the human body insofar as it is curable. For although man is considered by the ethicist, the natural philosopher and the theologian, he is not considered in relation to health, which is what the physician does. The manner of considering man therefore distinguishes this art from the others. Natural philosophy considers man as mobile; ethics considers him as one to be formed by virtue. Nor does it matter that many things in natural philosophy are common to medicine, such as the whole physiological doctrine; for in this part medicine is subordinate to natural philosophy and takes the conclusions of natural philosophy as its principles. For this reason this part of medicine has been called speculative: not because it is truly speculative, but because it is further removed from practice. And although plants, metals and such materials of medicine are considered here, all are nevertheless referred to the human body, to which their temperaments too are brought to bear.

units.la: Quod ad finem attinet; sciendum, disciplinarum speculativarum finem, non esse distinctum à rerum subje- ctarum cognitione ; quod in Mathe- maticis patet: At disciplinarum esse- ctricium alia est ratio : nam cognitio hic in seipsâ non quiescit, sed ordina- tur aliò , nimirum ad operis alicuius directionem; sicut in artibus mecha- nicis videre est. Iam vero medicina cum sit disciplina factiva , cognitio- nem omnem aliò refert, tanquam ad finem. Finis hic est sanitas; constitu- tio, nimirum, hominis integra , qua omnes functiones animales, vitales, naturales inculpatè obeuntur: proin- de huc omnia in Medicina referun- tur. Præcepta enim aut respiciunt præsentis sanitatis conservationem , aut absentis revocationem. Incum- bit ergo medico non tantum morbũ præsentem debitis auxiliis tollere ; sed ne redeat sedulò cavere, eamque victus rationem instituere quæ sani- tatem maximè conservare possit. Nam, curare, non tantum est summo- vere ea quæ actiones lædunt, sed & mala imminentia præcavere. Quâ de caucausâ ab Hippocrate lib. de Flat. (si modò sit illius Author) Ars ista definitur, ejectio, & detractio. quod fieri non potest sine accurata cognitione, non tantum corporis humani, sed etiam aliorum medicamentorum, tam simplicium, quam compositorū.
units.tr: As for the end, it should be understood that the end of speculative disciplines is not distinct from the knowledge of their subjects, as is clear in mathematics. But the case of factive disciplines is different: for knowledge here does not rest in itself but is directed elsewhere, namely to the direction of some work, as can be seen in the mechanical arts. Now medicine, since it is a factive discipline, refers all knowledge elsewhere, as to an end. This end is health: that is, the integral constitution of the human being, in which all animal, vital and natural functions are performed without fault. Therefore everything in medicine is referred to this. For its precepts either concern the preservation of present health or the recovery of health when it is absent. It is therefore incumbent on the physician not only to remove the present disease with due remedies, but also to take diligent care that it does not return, and to establish that regimen of living which can most of all preserve health. For to cure is not merely to remove what harms the actions, but also to guard against impending evils. For this reason Hippocrates, in the book On Flatulence (if indeed he is its author), defines this art as expulsion and removal. This cannot be done without accurate knowledge not only of the human body but also of other medicines, both simple and compound.

units.la: Quod ad divisionem attinet; quamquam Galenus, finem considerans, duas Medicinæ partes constituat; ὑγιεινὴ, quæ præsentem sanitatē tuetur, & ab imminentibus malis conservat; & θεραπευτικὴ, quæ sanitatem restituit: (quæ, quia in operatione consistunt, à quibusdam Practicę dicuntur) alii tamen non incommodè adjiciunt, Physiologiam, Patheologiam, eamque partem quæ σημειωτικὴ dicitur. Physiologia hic non est cuiusvis corporis naturalis consideratio; sed humani tantum, eorumq; quæ illi secundum naturam insunt; qualia sunt Elementa, temperamenta &c. Patheologia explicat ea quæ homini contra naturam insunt; qualia sunt illa tria, morbus, eius causa, & & symptoma, Σημειωτικὴ ex signis, non tantum de praesenti aut praeteritâ constitutione judicat, sed & futurum morbi eventum praevidet. A quibusdam hae tres, ad illam partem Medicinae quae speculativa dicitur, referuntur. Speculativa ergo has tres sub se continet; sicut & Practica totidem; Διαιτητικὴν, Φαρμακευτικὴν χειρypгικὴν. Prima considerando lex res non naturales, convenientem unicuique dietam praescribit. Secunda convenientibus medicamentis morbum profligat, quo pertinet omnis medicamentorum tam cognitio, quam praeparatio. Postrema denique urendi, secandi, omniumque earum operationum quae manu peraguntur, regulas proponit & tradit. Ex quibus patet, Medicinam esse artem sanitatis humanae Effectricem. Artem dico proprie: nam Scientia non est. Ac proinde Avicenna statim in principio, licet scientiam dixerit, practicam tamen adjecit. Dico sanitatis humanae; ut Medicum à Veterinario Mulo medico distinguam. Efficere, non tantum est absentem sanitatem medicamentis revocare, sed & bonis alimentis præsentem conservare; siquidem & conservare efficere est.
units.tr: As for the division: although Galen, considering the end, makes two parts of medicine, the hygienic [ὑγιεινὴ], which maintains present health and preserves it from impending ills, and the therapeutic [θεραπευτικὴ], which restores health (these, because they consist in operation, are called practical by some), others not inappropriately add physiology, pathology, and the part called semeiotic [σημειωτικὴ]. Physiology here is not the consideration of any natural body whatever, but of the human body alone, and of those things that are in it according to nature, such as the elements, temperaments and so on. Pathology explains those things that are in man contrary to nature, such as the three things: disease, its cause, and its symptom. Semeiotic, from signs, judges not only the present or past condition but also foresees the future outcome of the disease. By some these three are referred to that part of medicine which is called speculative. Speculative medicine therefore contains these three under it, just as practical medicine contains three parts: dietetic [Διαιτητικὴ], pharmaceutical [Φαρμακευτικὴ] and surgical [χειρουργική]. The first, considering the non-natural things, prescribes to each person a diet suited to him. The second overcomes disease with suitable medicines, and to it belongs all knowledge as well as the preparation of medicines. Lastly, the surgical part sets out and teaches the rules of burning, cutting, and all those operations that are performed by hand. From these things it is clear that medicine is the art effective of human health. I say art, properly: for it is not a science. Accordingly Avicenna, at the very beginning, although he called it a science, added practical. I say of human health, so that I may distinguish the physician from the veterinarian (mulomedicus). To effect is not only to recall absent health by medicines, but also to preserve present health by good food; for to conserve is also to effect.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: De Elementis.
units.tr: On the Elements.

units.la: Quanquam Medici cum Galeno triplicem ordinem constituant, Definitivum scilicet, Compositivum, & Resolutivum; nos tamen, quia definitivus non incommodè ad alios referri potest, duos reliquos persequemur. Ordo omnis est habitudo plurium ad unum. Analyticus verò vel Resolutivus docet omnia in arte ad unum finem ordinare, Initium ergo ducens ab ultimo fine, media quibus talis finis obtineri potest, indagat; sicut in Ethicis Aristotelis, & ejusdem lib. de demonstrat. videre est. Quo etiam ordine, disciplinę omnes, tam practicæ, quam theoreticæ traduntur. At Compositivus seu Synteticus ordo, à primis seu simplicissimis fimis causis seu principiis incipiendo, procedit ad ea, quæ inde constant: quod factum est à Philosopho in Libris Acroamat. aliisque sequentibus. Nos itaque, quia omnis ordo nostræ faciliori cognitioni inservit, Physiologiam ordine compositivo trademus; quod olim ab Avicenna, & Averroe in suo Colliget factitatum video: &, quia corpus humanum Medicinæ subjectum, sua principia, & causas internas habet; elementa nimirum; ab iis initium ducemus.
units.tr: Although the physicians, with Galen, establish a threefold order, namely the definitive, the compositive and the resolutive, we shall nevertheless pursue the other two, since the definitive can conveniently be referred to the others. Every order is the relation of many things to one. The analytic or resolutive order teaches that everything in an art is arranged toward one end; beginning from the ultimate end, it investigates the means by which such an end can be attained, as can be seen in Aristotle's Ethics and in his book on demonstration. In this order all the disciplines, both practical and theoretical, are also taught. The compositive or synthetic order, however, beginning from the first and simplest causes or principles, proceeds to those things which are constituted from them. This was done by the Philosopher in the Acroamatic books and the others that follow. Therefore, since every order serves easier understanding, we shall present physiology in the compositive order, which I see was formerly practised by Avicenna and by Averroes in his Colliget. And since the human body, the subject of medicine, has its principles and internal causes, namely the elements, we shall begin with these.

units.la: Pars hæc Physiologia dicitur; quia solius humanæ naturæ, & eorum quę illi secundum naturam insunt, considerationem proponit. Hæc autem sunt septem illæ res, naturales dictę; Elementa, Temperamenta, Humores, Spiritus, Partes, Facultates, Functiones seu Visus.
units.tr: This part is called Physiology, because it sets out the consideration of human nature alone and of those things which belong to it according to nature. These are the seven things called natural: elements, temperaments, humours, spirits, parts, faculties, and functions or operations.

units.la: Quanquam vero elementorum cognitio à Medicis hominis cognitioni sit destinata: tamen referri potest & ad aliorum corporum, quorum in Medicina usus est, cognitionē, quod tum magis constabit, cum medicamentorum vires, & facultates privatim indagabuntur. Nec tamen altius ascendemus, ad curiosam primorum principiorum (de quibus Physici) contemplationem; sed hic pedem figentes, Elementa cum relatione ad mixtionem, consideràbimus.
units.tr: Although the knowledge of the elements is destined by physicians for the knowledge of the human being, it can nevertheless also be referred to the knowledge of other bodies which are used in medicine. This will become clearer when the powers and faculties of medicines are investigated individually. Nor shall we ascend any higher to the curious contemplation of the first principles (which is the business of the natural philosophers); rather, remaining here, we shall consider the elements in relation to mixture.

units.la: Est autem Elementum, (nam suppono esse in natura) corpus simplex, ex quo mixtum sicut primo constat, ita in quod ultimo resolvitar.
units.tr: An element (for I assume that it exists in nature) is a simple body, from which a mixed body is first composed and into which it is finally resolved.

units.la: Dico corpus, ad excludenda prima principia; materiam scilicet & formam. Simplex, non quod careat compositione ex aliis, nimirum materiâ & formâ: sed hoc dicitur per comparationem ad mixtum. quasi dicas, elementum purum, ut aër, non componitur ex aliis elementis, quemadmodum os, aut Rhabarbarum. Et licet corpus cœleste simplex quidem sit, quia tamen non refertur ad aliorum compositionem, (nam res mistæ non componuntur ex cœlo) reliqua definitionis verba porro adduntur.
units.tr: I say body, to exclude the first principles, namely matter and form. Simple, not as lacking composition from other things, namely matter and form, but this is said by comparison with a mixed body; as if you were to say that a pure element, such as air, is not composed of other elements, as bone or rhubarb is. And although the heavenly body is indeed simple, since it is not referred to the composition of other things (for mixed things are not composed of heaven), the remaining words of the definition are added.

units.la: Elementa numero esse quatuor, demonstrant Physici, partim ex qua-litatibus motricibus, partim ex alte-ratricibus, calore, frigore, humidi-tate, & siccitate. Et quanquam elementorum actiones in mixtione fiant à qualitatibus hisce primis; cave putes tamen eas esse formas substantiales: (quod quisquiam putaverit) sunt enim revera ipsarum formarum quasi instrumenta. Et quia mixta omnia hisce qualitatibus, quanquam remis-sis; participant; necessario sequitur, eas in ipsis elementis esse intensissi-mas & perfectissimas. Propter quod enim unumquodque tale est, illud magis est tale. Mista moventur lo-caliter, propter elementum domi-nans; sic etiam calefaciunt aut refri-gerant, ob eandem causam. Et quan-quam Philosophi considerent ele-menta non tantum ut sunt mistorum principia; sed etiam ut partes mun-dum integrantes, quatenus nata sunt certum in mundo locum occupare: Medici tamen, hoc posteriori modo non considerant, sed priori tantum. Qua de causa, omissis eorum qualitatibus motricibus, alteratrices consfiderabimus: Supponendum ex Physica; ignem esse calidissimum & siccissimum: terram siccissimam & frigidissimam; (qualitates passivæ in omnibus sunt intensissimæ, non vero activæ) aquam humidissimam & frigidam; aërem, calidum & humidissimum. Calor est summæ activitatis, sed minimæ resistentiæ. intelligo resistentiam, quam Physici vocant privativam non positivam, quæ semper est activitati æqualis. Siccitas contra, minimæ est activitatis, sed maximæ resistentiæ. Ad caloris activitatem proximè accedit frigus, verum resistentia est major. Humiditas in agendo potentior est siccitate, non item resistendo: Hoc modo elementorum quasi proportiones conservantur. Nam si tam resisteret ignis, quam ageret; dudum reliqua elementa consumsisset. Cum itaq; à natura sit comparatum, ut unumquodque contrarium. rium agat in suum contrarium; fit,ut calidum agendo in frigidum,incalef- cat. Idem de sicco,& humido cenfen- dum. Ex hac mutuâ actione oritur temperies mistorum ; non tantum in rebus naturalibus , sed & artificiali- bus ; ut in officinis videre est.
units.tr: Physicists demonstrate that the elements are four in number, partly from the motive qualities and partly from the altering qualities: heat, cold, moisture and dryness. And although the actions of the elements in mixture are brought about by these primary qualities, take care not to think that they are substantial forms (as someone might suppose); for they are truly, as it were, the instruments of the forms themselves. And since all mixed things participate in these qualities, though remitted, it necessarily follows that in the elements themselves they are most intense and most perfect. For that which makes each thing such is itself more such. Mixed things move locally on account of the dominant element; likewise they warm or cool for the same reason. And although the philosophers consider the elements not only as the principles of mixed things but also as parts integrating the world, inasmuch as they are born to occupy a certain place in the world, physicians nevertheless do not consider them in this latter way, but only in the former. For this reason, omitting their motive qualities, we shall consider the altering ones. It is to be assumed from physics that fire is hottest and driest; earth is driest and coldest (the passive qualities are most intense in all of them, but not the active ones); water is most moist and cold; air is warm and most moist. Heat is of the highest activity but the least resistance; I mean by resistance what the physicists call privative, not positive, which is always equal to activity. Dryness, on the contrary, has the least activity but the greatest resistance. Cold comes closest to the activity of heat, but its resistance is greater. Moisture is more powerful than dryness in acting, but not in resisting. In this way the proportions of the elements are, as it were, preserved. For if fire resisted as much as it acted, it would long since have consumed the other elements. Since, therefore, it has been arranged by nature that each contrary acts upon its contrary, it comes about that the hot, acting upon the cold, warms it. The same is to be judged of the dry and the moist. From this mutual action arises the tempering of mixed things, not only in natural things but also in artificial ones, as can be seen in workshops.

units.la: Et quia elementa ordinata sunt ad miftionē; qualitates primæ dividun- tur in actívas & passivas. Calor enim & frigus habent rationem agentis, quia subjectam materiam determi- nant: sicut humiditas & siccitas, pa- tientis,quia earum interventu,mate- ria subjecta disponitur ad formam misti recipiendam. alioqui hæ etiam agunt, ut diximus,verum remisse. In misto ita est comparatum , ut illius moles & corporatura, à terrrâ, & a- quâ pendeat.; vis tamen & agendi efficacia,à reliquis elementis.Si ergo unum elementum , alterum in agen- do nimium superat ; non erit miftio, sed simplicis elementi generatio. Sin vero paribus quasi viribus , aut non ita imparibus concurrant; gene- rabirabitur mistum. Mistum enim, nec est aqua, aut ignis ; sed quidpiam ter-tium, elementorum vires, remissas tamen, in se cohibens. Mixtio omnis est generatio rei mistæ. Quæ ut fiat, requiritur concursus elementorum in unum locum, (hic plurimum terra est) eorundem in minimas partes divisio, postremò reactio, quâ in se mutuò agunt, donec omnia corrumpantur, & nova forma misti de novo generetur: Ratio ergo mistionis est posita in introductione novæ formæ substantialis ; supposita tamen elementorum alteratione & corruptione. Ergò unio formæ cum materia, non est mistio ; quia utraque manet, at in ferro, lapide, osse, non manent elementa actu, sed tantum potentia; quatenus eorū qualitates in iis continentur. Quæ ita accipi volo, ut singulis rei mistæ partibus omnia insint elementa ; quælibet enim rei mistæ pars, etiam minima ex elementis, eo quo diximus modo, est mista.
units.tr: And since the elements are ordered toward mixture, the primary qualities are divided into active and passive. For heat and cold have the character of agent, because they determine the matter underlying them; as moisture and dryness have that of patient, because by their intervention the subject matter is disposed to receive the form of the mixed body. Otherwise these also act, as we have said, but in a remitted manner. In a mixed body it is so arranged that its bulk and body depend on earth and water, but its power and efficacy of acting on the other elements. If therefore one element, in acting, greatly surpasses another, there will be no mixture but a generation of a simple element. But if they meet with powers that are, as it were, equal, or not so unequal, a mixed body will be generated. For a mixed body is neither water nor fire, but something third, containing within itself the powers of the elements, though remitted. Every mixture is the generation of a mixed thing. For this to happen there is required a concurrence of the elements into one place (here earth is most of it), their division into the smallest parts, and finally a reaction by which they act mutually upon each other, until all are corrupted and a new form of the mixed thing is generated anew. The essence of mixture therefore consists in the introduction of a new substantial form, provided however that alteration and corruption of the elements has taken place. Therefore the union of form with matter is not mixture, because both remain; but in iron, stone, or bone the elements do not remain actually, but only potentially, inasmuch as their qualities are contained in them. I wish this to be understood so that all the elements are present in each single part of a mixed thing; for every part of a mixed thing, even the smallest, is mixed from the elements in the way we have described.

units.la: CAP. III. De Temperamentis.
units.tr: CHAP. III. Of Temperaments.

units.la: EX elementis, hoc modo & alteratis, & corruptis, oritur modus quidam substantiæ, quem quidam emperamentum substantiale dixere, hoc est, substantia cum tali densitate, raritate, crassitie, aut tenuitate. Sed quia hoc sensibus non ita innotescit; eo relicto, Medici provocant ad temperamentum accidentale, quod ex qualitatibus elementorum contemperatis gignitur. Hoc illud est quod κρᾶσις nominatur, sive complexio, unio nimirum, seu conjunctio quatuor primarum qualitatum elementarium, refractarum tamen, & ad quandam mediocritatem redactarum. Hæc est conveniens dispositio ad misti formam tum introducendam, tum conservandam. Formæ enim substantiales, ut canis, lapidis, non possunt agere, aut superesse, nisi habeant subjectum hoc modo temperatum. actiones siquidem animalis proximè à facultatibus fluunt, unt : facultates manant à formis substantialibus ; quæ sine temperamento, tanquam conveniente dispositione, nec esse, nec agere possunt. Facessant igitur Scotus, Conciliator, alijq; existimantes qualitatibus primis pereuntibus, succedere novam quandam qualitatē virtute illas continentem, quam temperamentum dicunt. Qualitas enim huiusmodi nec sensu, nec experientia, nec ratione deprehendi potest. Erroris autem occasio inde est, quod inter temperamentum & facultatem non satis acutè distinguunt. Ridiculum est, quod Fernelius putat temperamentum esse qualitates integras, nec refractas, sed eodem prorsus modo affectas, quo in elementis erant. Quis enim animo concipiat, quomodo calor & frigus in summo gradu sine mutuâ actione cohærere possint. Revera enim est illa qualitatum harmonia instituta à natura ad perfectas mixti actiones edendas. quæ in impartibili seu indivisibili posita non est, ita ut si vel minimum ab ea recef-ferit qualitas, mistum dissolvatur; ha-bet enim quandam latitudinem in singulis mistis, intra quam vagari quasi licet : totius tamen latitudinis quidam sunt termini & fines, quos ultra, citraque nequit consistere mi-stum.
units.tr: From the elements, altered and corrupted in this way, there arises a certain mode of substance, which some have called a substantial temperament, that is, a substance with such-and-such density, rarity, thickness or thinness. But since this is not so readily known to the senses, the physicians, leaving it aside, appeal to an accidental temperament, which is produced from the contempered qualities of the elements. This is what is called krasis [κρᾶσις], or complexion, namely the union, or conjunction, of the four primary elemental qualities, yet broken down and reduced to a certain mean. This is the fitting disposition both for introducing and for preserving the form of the mixed body. For substantial forms, such as those of a dog or of a stone, cannot act or continue to exist unless they have a subject tempered in this way. For the actions of an animal flow directly from its faculties, and the faculties flow from its substantial forms; and these forms, without temperament as the fitting disposition, can neither exist nor act. Away, then, with Scotus, the Conciliator, and others who think that when the primary qualities perish a new quality takes their place, containing them virtually, and that this is what they call temperament. For a quality of this kind can be detected neither by sense, nor by experience, nor by reason. The occasion of this error is that they do not distinguish sharply enough between temperament and faculty. Fernelius is absurd in thinking that temperament consists of qualities that are entire and unbroken, affected in exactly the same way as they were in the elements. For who can conceive how heat and cold, in their highest degree, could cohere without mutual action? In truth, temperament is that harmony of qualities, established by nature for the producing of the perfect actions of the mixed body, which is not placed in something impartible or indivisible, so that if the quality withdraws even slightly from it, the mixed body is dissolved. For in each mixed body there is a certain latitude, within which it may, as it were, wander; yet the whole latitude has certain boundaries and limits, beyond or short of which the mixed body cannot stand.

units.la: Quod si primæ qualitates ex æquo concurrant, inque se agant & refrin-gant in puncto medio, ita ut quot sint gradus caloris, totidem sint frigoris, humiditatis &c; oritur temperamentum ad pondus secundum proportionem Arithmeticam. In hac enim est æqualis excessus, ut 2.4.6.8. 10. nam sicut 10. superant 8 duobus ita 4. superant 2. duobus. Sin vero quatuor qualitates non ex æquo concurrant; sed calor vincat frigus, aut contra; aut siccitas humiditatem, vel humiditas siccitatem; oritur temperamentū ad justitiam secundum proportionē Geometricam; quæ est posita in comparatione diversorū mistorū ad suas operationes. Nam quemadmo-dum dum in repub. distribuuntur dignitates pro civiū conditione, ita in hoc temperamento qualitates distribuuntur pro cuiusq; misti exigentia, aliud enim temperamentum requirit lapis, aliud homo, canis, &c.
units.tr: If the primary qualities concur equally, acting and checking one another at the midpoint, so that there are as many degrees of heat as of cold, of moisture, and so on, there arises temperament according to weight, in accordance with arithmetical proportion. For in this there is an equal excess, as in 2, 4, 6, 8, 10: just as 10 exceeds 8 by two, so 4 exceeds 2 by two. But if the four qualities do not concur equally, and heat overcomes cold or the reverse, or dryness moisture or moisture dryness, there arises temperament according to justice, in accordance with geometrical proportion, which consists in the comparison of different mixed bodies with respect to their operations. For just as in a commonwealth dignities are distributed according to the condition of citizens, so in this temperament qualities are distributed according to the requirement of each mixed body: a stone requires one temperament, a man another, a dog another, and so on.

units.la: Temperamentum ad pondus proponitur tanquam aliorum regula, & norma : proinde à Galeno comparatur statuæ Polycleti. Alioqui nec datur, nec dari posse, multi contendunt. Quanquam quidam distinguant inter qualitates alteratrices, & motrices: & harum quidem ad pondus unionem fieri posse negant, quia rerum mistarum moles supponit dominium terræ, & aquæ: illarum vero temperationem in re animata fieri posse, negant: in inanimato posse dari, non adeò improbabiliter contendunt. Temperamentum hoc est simplex & unicum; sicut illud, quod ad justitiam dicitur, est multiplex, pro varietate qualitatum primarum, quarum una potest aliarum mensuram excedere; ut calor siccitatem, aut frigus calorem. Quod si una tantùm qualitas excedit, temperamentum simplex nominatur, eltque quadruplex, quemadmodum sunt quatuor qualitates primæ.sin autem duç qualitates cæteras vincant, oritur temperamentũ compositum;Calidum siccum,calidum humidũ,frigidum siccũ frigidũ humidum. quæ sola agnoscit Averroes,sicut simplicia rejicit.Corpora homogenea, & inanimata eadẽ ubique temperatione constant ; ut in lapide, metallo, videre est. At animatorum est ratio, in quibus unica temperatio esse nequit, quandoquidem variæ & diversæ functiones sunt obeundæ. Hinc quædam partes sunt duræ & frigidæ, ut offa ; aliæ molles & humidæ, ut cerebrum.
units.tr: Temperament according to weight is set forth as the rule and standard of the others; accordingly Galen compares it to the statue of Polyclitus. Otherwise, many maintain, it is neither found nor can be found. Some, however, distinguish between altering qualities and moving qualities: they deny that the union according to weight can take place among the former, because the mass of mixed bodies presupposes the dominion of earth and water; but they deny that the tempering of the latter can take place in a living thing, while they contend, not improbably, that it can exist in what is inanimate. This temperament is simple and single, whereas the one called according to justice is manifold, according to the variety of the primary qualities, one of which can exceed the measure of the others, as heat exceeds dryness, or cold exceeds heat. If only one quality exceeds, the temperament is called simple, and there are four of these, corresponding to the four primary qualities. But if two qualities overcome the others, a compound temperament arises: hot and dry, hot and moist, cold and dry, cold and moist. Averroes alone recognises these compound ones, just as he rejects the simple ones. Homogeneous and inanimate bodies have the same temperament throughout, as can be seen in stone and metal. But with living things it is otherwise, since in them a single temperament cannot exist, inasmuch as various and diverse functions must be performed. Hence some parts are hard and cold, like bones, and others soft and moist, like the brain.

units.la: Sed quia de viventium temperie nobis potissimum agendum est; age, paululum hîc subsistamus. Distinguendum etiam inter rem vivam & mortuam.Ac primò quidem est temperies quædam innata singulis partibus, ex elementorum qualitatibus priprimis constans ; dispositio nimirum corporis antecedens ad animam recipiendam idonea; diffusa illa quidem per totum corpus, non tamen eodem modo, alia enim est in carne, alia in osse, alia in nervo, &c. Hæc sicut animam antecedit; ita eadem abeunte non perit; verum diu postea superest, nec corrumpitur, nisi per putredinem. In eâ tamen ubique abundat frigus, (de Animalibus loquor; nam plantarum alia est ratio, ut in aromatibus videre est) & cum frigore quibusdam in partibus conjungitur siccitas, ut in osse; in quibusdam humiditas ut in carne & cerebro videre est. Vt enim corpus esset solidum & densum, abundare debebat terra, elementum frigidum. Quando vero pars aliqua dicitur calida, aut frigida, intelligitur semper de hac innatâ temperie; quæ est quasi gradus quidam ad sequentem temperiem, animam comitantem: talis autem, quasi influens & adventitia quæque, anima posita, ponitur: eâdemque sublata, lata, tollitur. Est calida, & humida, instituta tota ad viventis tum conservationem, tum operationem ; &, ut verbo absolvam, est calor vitalis ab humido primigenio receptus, à quo vita pendet. Et licet per totum diffundatur, maxime tamen in corde residet: quia hæc pars est fons caloris & officina spiritus vitalis, à quo ad reliqua membra derivatur. Hoc temperamentum in homine aut cane si consideres, omnes partes prorsus erunt calidæ, nec ulla apparebit frigida ; & quanquam cerebrum temperamento innato sit frigidum, quod in mortuo apparet: tamen eadem pars in homine vivo calida sentitur, ob temperiem istam adventitiam & influentem.
units.tr: But since it is chiefly the temperament of living things that we must treat, let us pause here a little. We must distinguish also between a living and a dead thing. First, there is a certain innate temperament in each part, consisting of the primary qualities of the elements: namely, a disposition of the body, preceding the soul, suited to receiving it. This is diffused through the whole body, yet not in the same way; for it is one in flesh, another in bone, another in nerve, and so on. This temperament, just as it precedes the soul, so when the soul departs it does not perish; rather it remains for a long time afterwards and is not corrupted, except by putrefaction. In it, however, cold abounds everywhere (I am speaking of animals; the case of plants is different, as can be seen in aromatics), and in some parts cold is joined with dryness, as in bone, while in others moisture is found, as in flesh and brain. For the body to be solid and dense, earth, the cold element, had to abound. When any part is called hot or cold, it is always to be understood of this innate temperament, which is, as it were, a certain step towards the following temperament that accompanies the soul. Such a temperament, flowing in and adventitious, is placed once the soul is placed, and when the soul is removed, it is carried away and taken away with it. The following is hot and moist, constituted entirely for the preservation and operation of the living thing; and, to sum up in a word, it is vital heat, received from the primigenial moisture, on which life depends. And although it is diffused throughout the whole body, it resides chiefly in the heart, because this part is the source of heat and the workshop of vital spirit, from which it is derived to the other members. If you consider this temperament in man or dog, all the parts will be altogether hot, and none will appear cold; and although the brain is cold by its innate temperament, as appears in the dead, yet in a living man that same part is felt to be hot, on account of that adventitious and influent temperament.

units.la: Si ista duo temperamenta coniungantur, oritur temperies illa quæ à Medicis vocatur actuata. Quemadmodum ex corpore & anima fit unum quidpiam ; ita ex hisce duabus, una fit absoluta hominis temperatio, in quo calor abundat. Subjectum itaq; huius actuatæ temperiei est pars animata (non humor, spiritus, aut excrementum) homogenea, aut heterogenea: quanquam proprie heterogenea nil aliud sit, quam homogeneorum copulatio. Et quia temperatio ad operationem referetur, anima vero sine calore nihil agit: (nam frigus adversatur animæ) fit, ut talis temperies simpliciter sit calida. Actionum enim multitudo, varietas & perfectio cum sine calore fieri nequeat; declarat satis, temperiem actuatam esse calidam; &, si quibusdam creditur, calidissimam. Sin vero innatam consideres, quæ ex elementorum permistione nascitur, quæque sicut animam precedit, ita & abeunte permanet; aliter sentiendum erit. Homo enim hac temperatione perfectissima præditus est; nec dominator calor, sicut in priore. Cum enim habeat animam longè nobilissimam, æquum porro est & habere corporis temperiem illi respondentem. Quod vel ex tactu manifestum apparebit, qui in homine exquisitior est quam in cæteris animalibus ; quod sanè non fieret, nisi homo haberet perse-ctissimum temperamentum. Si enim comparetur cum reliquis animali-bus, nec crassus est, nec gracilis; ne-que calidus, neq; frigidus; neq; hu-midus, neq; siccus;neque alio modo excedens; sed inter omnia hæc tem-peratus. Nam quanquam ossa dura sint, tamen caro mollis est ; & sicut cor calidum existat,contra cerebrum frigidum. Proinde si partes inter se conferantur ; quantum una declinat ad frigus,tantum altera ad calorem. Idem in aliis qualitatibus judicato. Non ergo omnium membrorum ea-dem temperies, (quod fieri nequit:) sed tamen omnium membrorum, di-verse temperatorum, est debita pro-portio,&,ut ita dicam,competentia.
units.tr: If these two temperaments are joined, there arises that temperature which the physicians call actuated. Just as one thing comes into being from body and soul, so from these two there comes one complete temperature of the man, in which heat abounds. The subject, then, of this actuated temperature is the animate part (not humour, spirit, or excrement), either homogeneous or heterogeneous, although strictly speaking a heterogeneous part is nothing other than a coupling of homogeneous ones. And because temperature is referred to operation, and the soul does nothing without heat (for cold is opposed to the soul), it follows that such a temperature is simply hot. For since the multitude, variety and perfection of actions cannot take place without heat, this sufficiently shows that the actuated temperature is hot, and, if we believe some, very hot. But if you consider the innate temperature, which arises from the mixture of the elements, and which, just as it precedes the soul, so also remains when the soul departs, it must be judged otherwise. For man is endowed with this most perfect temperament, and heat does not dominate as it does in the former. Since he has a soul far more noble, it is fitting that he also have a temperature of body corresponding to it. This will become plain even from touch, which in man is more exquisite than in the other animals; and this certainly would not be so unless man had the most perfect temperament. For if he is compared with the other animals, he is neither gross nor slender, neither hot nor cold, neither moist nor dry, nor excessive in any other way, but is tempered among all these things. For although the bones are hard, the flesh is nevertheless soft; and just as the heart is warm, the brain is cold. Therefore, if the parts are compared with one another, as much as one inclines towards cold, so much does another incline towards heat. Judge the same of the other qualities. Thus there is not the same temperament in all the members (which cannot be), but there is due proportion, and, as I may say, fitness, among all the members, which are diversely tempered.

units.la: Sed ad temperamentum actuatum seu influens redeamus;quod in Cho-lericum, ( ita vulgo dicuntur,quam-vis minus commodè ) Sanguineum, Pituitosum, & Melancholicum di-stinstinguitur; quæ dicuntur respondere quatuor clementis, & quatuor humoribus. Quod cuivis patet: cholera enim est calida & sicca, respondens elemento ignis; ac proinde biliosi calidi & sicci sunt, idem de cæteris judicandum est.
units.tr: But let us return to the active or influencing temperament, which is divided into the choleric (as they commonly call it, though less aptly), the sanguine, the phlegmatic, and the melancholic. These are said to correspond to the four elements and the four humours. This is plain to anyone: choler is hot and dry and corresponds to the element of fire; therefore the bilious are hot and dry. The same is to be judged of the rest.

units.la: Temperies vero cuiusq; ex varijs signis deprehendi potest; tactu nimirum, sanguine, pilis, colore &c. sed omnium optime, meo judicio, ex moribus: biliosi enim sint celeres, inquieti, ingenio acuto; pituitosi contra. Ex temperatione sequitur sexus, sanitas, ægritudo, ætas: spatium scilicet seu duratio vitæ; qua, caloris in humidum actione, corporis constitutio manifeste mutatur. Mutatio ista à primâ hominis generatione incipit. Ætates variè numerantur. Hippocrates Libro de Carne septem numerat: alij quatuor; Adolescentiam nimirum (hæc infantiam, pueritiam, pubertatem & Adolescentiam proprie dictam comprehendit) ad annum 25. aut 30. Juventutem, seu florentem ætcætatem, ad 36. aut 40. annum. tertiò, Consistentem ætatem, ad 45. aut 50. annum. Postremò senectutem quæ & decrepitam comprehendit, extenditurque ad vitæ finem. Singulis ætatibus suum est temperamentum. infantes calidissimi & humidissimi sunt: sicut decrepiti frigidissimi & siccissimi. Senectutis siccitas non est æstimanda ab excrementis quibus abundat; sed secundum partium solidarum substantiam, quæ est siccissima. Controversia tamen non levis exístit, de Iuvenum temperamento; an sit calidus puerorum. Nam Galenus arbitratur parē esse in utrâq; ætate calorē: cum tamen ratio suadeat puerorum intensiorem quidem esse, blandum tamen & vaporosum; juvenū minus intensum, acriorem tamen & mordaciorem; qua de causa sæpius corripiuntur ardentibus febribus. Ætatum vel conservatio, vel corruptio multum pendet à victu, exercitio, rebusque aliis non naturalibus: adeò quidem ut, si annos con-side. lideres, juvenes quidam sint temperamento senili, senes juvenili. Et quamquam humidum nativum possit interdum perfectius, & melius renovari, quam à principio fuit: tamen absolute loquendo, in ordine ad vitæ durationem, nullo unquam tempore potest melius instaurari, sed semper deterius. Nam cum perpetuò debilitetur calor, & ab alimento minuatur, humidum autem consumatur; inevitabilis tandem sequitur mors, rerum linea ultima. Porro dixi senectutem esse frigidam; quod intelligendum est in comparatione præcedentium ætatum; nam interdum contingit duos senes ita esse affectos, ut alter altero longè sit calidior. nam temperamentum ab origine insitum, modum quasi præscribit sequentibus ætatibus: adeò quidem ut qui in infantiâ calidissimus sit, in senectute verò frigidus; tamen comparatione ejus qui ab initio temperamento sit frigidiusculo calidus videri possit: quod intelligi volo, modo nullum fit, aut non adeo magnum in victu erratum.
units.tr: A person's temperament may be recognised from various signs: by touch, by blood, by hair, by complexion and so on, but best of all, in my judgement, from manners. For the bilious are quick, restless and of sharp wit, whereas the phlegmatic are the opposite. From temperament follow sex, health, sickness and age, that is, the span or duration of life, in which the constitution of the body is plainly altered by the action of heat upon moisture. This change begins from the first generation of a human being. Ages are counted variously. Hippocrates in his book On Flesh counts seven; others count four: youth (which comprises infancy, boyhood, puberty and youth properly so called) up to the twenty-fifth or thirtieth year; thirdly, the flourishing age, up to the thirty-sixth or fortieth year; thirdly, the settled age, up to the forty-fifth or fiftieth year; lastly, old age, which also comprises decrepitude, and extends to the end of life. Each age has its own temperament: infants are hottest and moistest, just as the decrepit are coldest and driest. The dryness of old age is not to be judged from the excrements with which it abounds, but according to the substance of the solid parts, which is driest. Yet there is no slight controversy about the temperament of the young: whether the young are hotter than children. For Galen holds that there is equal heat in each age; whereas reason suggests that children's heat is indeed more intense, but mild and vaporous, while that of the young is less intense but sharper and more biting; for this reason they are more often seized by burning fevers. The preservation or corruption of the ages depends greatly on diet, exercise and other non-natural things, so much so that, if you consider the years, some young people have the temperament of the old, and some old people that of the young. And although the native moisture may sometimes be renewed more perfectly and better than it was at the beginning, nevertheless, speaking absolutely with regard to the duration of life, it can never at any time be restored for the better, but always for the worse. For since heat is continually weakened and diminished by lack of nourishment, while the moisture is consumed, inevitable death at last follows, the final limit of all things. Moreover, I have said that old age is cold; this must be understood in comparison with the preceding ages. For it sometimes happens that two old men are so disposed that one is far hotter than the other; for the temperament implanted from birth prescribes, as it were, the manner of the following ages, so that one who was hottest in infancy but cold in old age may nevertheless seem warm in comparison with one who from the beginning was of a somewhat cool temperament. This I wish to be understood, provided there is no error, or no very great error, in diet.

units.la: CAP. IV. De Calido innato, & Spiritu.
units.tr: CAP. IV. Of the Innate Heat and the Spirit.

units.la: Disputationem de Elementis excipit caloris consideratio, quem duplicem faciunt, Elementarem, & Vitalem: cœlestis enim ad hos duos revocatur, non ideo dictus, quod cœlo insit, (nec enim cœlum est capax qualitatis elementaris) sed quod lucis & radiorum cœlestium vi hic apud nos gignitur. In rebus inanimatis mistis est tantum elementaris; viventibus & hic, & vitalis porrò inest. Elementaris est singularum partium, ex innata earum temperatione, elementorumque permistione proprius: qui sicut animam antecedit, ita ea abeunte superest: cujus extinctio non est mors, sed putredo. Vitalis animam comitatur; cujus participatione vita, ejusdemq; extinctione mors definitur. Hic duplex censetur, alter cujusque membri proprius, illique à primo ortu insitus. Partes enim, cum sint animatæ, calorem quoque ministrantem habere debent. Huius subjectum est humidum primigenium, per universum corpus diffusum. Galenus in com. 14. Aph. 1. ait usurpari posse & pro nuda qualitate & pro substantiâ calidâ. est autē calor dispositio in corpore animā conservans, ejusq; immediatum instrumentum. Humidum primigenium, hoc calore perfusum, ingreditur singulorum membrorum substantiam. Præter insitum membris calorem, alius est adventitius, & à corde, viscere calidissimo, influens in cætera membra, eorumque insitum calorem augens. Non est æqualis gradus caloris in singulis membris, plus enim est in uno membro quam alio, plurimum verò in corde. unde calidius membrum agit in minus calidum, impertitque aliquid sui caloris. Proinde si cor consideres, calor hic est illi insitus, non influens: at reliquorum membrorum respectu in quæ agit cor, influens est; pro varietate tate autem operationis aliter, & aliter temperatur. Qui inservit functioni naturali crassior est; qui autem animali subtilior. Influens calor non est diversæ naturæ ab infito; siquidem pars quædam est insiti, ad reliqua membra derivata. Proinde in singulis partibus calor influens & insitus uniuntur; estque calor actuatus, qui non distinguitur ab infito & influente simul junctis. Non est putandum hunc calorem distingui effentiâ & specie, ab elementari, verum modo quodam: nam alimentis calidis confervatur, frigidis vero extinguitur; quod non fieret, fi diversæ effet naturæ. Et quia humidus, magis aëreus, quam igneus judicatur. Quod tamen non impedit, quo minus primigenium humorem consumat, per accidens tamen: nam quamvis illum per fe confervat & reficit, nihil tamen impedit, quo minus per accidens contrarium faciat: quod ex ætatis mutatione conspicuum evadit. Quod fi intendatur, sicut in febre, (in qua augetur getur & intenditur ex febrilis caloris accessu) totum humidum brevi consumet: & quia natura calidior est ambientis calore, nunquam putredine extinguitur: nec unquam visum est animal vivum secundum omnes partes putrescere. Porro, quod quidam dicant huic calori non adversari frigus, mirum est; cum videamus in corde, frigidi aëris appulsu, temperari. remissio ista caloris est à contrario frigore. Accedit quod multi frigore pereant: quod fieri non posset, nisi illi contrarietur.
units.tr: The discussion of the elements is followed by the consideration of heat, which they make twofold: elementary and vital. For the heavenly heat is reduced to these two; it is not so called because it inheres in the heavens (for the heavens are not capable of an elementary quality), but because it is generated here among us by the force of the heavenly light and rays. In mixed inanimate things it is only elementary; in living things both this and, further, the vital heat is present. The elementary heat is proper to each part, arising from the innate temperament of each part and the mixture of the elements; it precedes the soul, as it were, and survives when the soul departs; its extinction is not death but putrefaction. The vital heat accompanies the soul; by its participation life is defined, and by its extinction death. This is held to be twofold: one proper to each member and implanted in it from its first origin. For the parts, since they are animate, must also have heat that supplies them. Its subject is the primigenial moisture, diffused through the whole body. Galen, in his commentary on Aphorism 14 of the first book, says that it may be used both for bare quality and for the hot substance. Heat is a disposition in the body preserving the soul, and its immediate instrument. The primigenial moisture, suffused with this heat, enters into the substance of each individual member. Besides the heat implanted in the members, there is another, adventitious, which flows from the heart, the most hot of organs, into the other members and increases their implanted heat. The degree of heat is not equal in each member: there is more in one member than in another, but most of all in the heart. Hence the hotter member acts upon the less hot and imparts something of its heat. Accordingly, if you consider the heart, this heat is implanted in it, not flowing in; but with respect to the remaining members, upon which the heart acts, it is flowing in; and it is tempered differently according to the variety of its operation. That which serves the natural function is thicker; that which serves the animal function is finer. The flowing heat is not of a different nature from the implanted, since it is a certain part of the implanted, derived to the other members. Therefore in each part the flowing and the implanted heat are united, and it is the actuated heat, which is not distinguished from the implanted and flowing heat joined together. It is not to be thought that this heat is distinguished from the elementary in essence and species, but only in a certain mode: for it is preserved by warm foods and extinguished by cold ones, which would not happen if it were of a different nature. And since it is judged to be more airy than fiery, moist rather than hot. Yet this does not prevent it from consuming the primigenial moisture, though only accidentally: for although it of itself preserves and restores that moisture, nothing prevents it from accidentally doing the contrary, which becomes plain from the change of age. If it is intensified, as in fever (in which it is increased and intensified by the onset of febrile heat), it will consume all the moisture in a short time; and because nature is hotter than the heat of the surrounding air, it is never extinguished by putrefaction; nor has a living animal ever been seen to putrefy in all its parts. Moreover, that some say cold is not opposed to this heat is strange, since we see the heart tempered by the impact of cold air. This remission of heat is from the contrary cold. Add that many perish from cold, which could not happen unless it were opposed to heat.

units.la: Caloris innati & actuati subjectû, (quod in genere humidum primigenium dicitur) est quodvis membrum, tam homogeneum, quam heterogeneum: quodvis enim vivit, ac vita in calore & humore consistit; quidvis nutritur, at nutritio omnis à calore est. At influentis subjectum esse sanguinem & spiritum, docet ejus diffusio per universum corpus. Beneficio enim arteriarum, Cor toti corpori calorem impertit: arteria autem recereceptaculum sanguinis tum calidio-ris, tum acrioris. Sicut ergo innatus calor nascitur cum singulorum membrorum substantia; consequiturque animam, ut est in singulis membris: ita influens à corde tanquam subjecto, & fonte derivatur in reliquas partes: quae possunt dici habere calorem ut ita dicam passivè, sicut cor activè.
units.tr: The subject of the innate and actuated heat (which in general is called the primigenial moisture) is every member, whether homogeneous or heterogeneous: for everything lives, and life consists in heat and moisture; everything is nourished, and all nutrition comes from heat. But that the subject of the flowing heat is blood and spirit is taught by its diffusion through the whole body. For by the benefit of the arteries the heart imparts heat to the whole body, and the artery is the receptacle of blood that is both hotter and more penetrating. Therefore, just as the innate heat arises together with the substance of each member, and the soul is in each member accordingly, so the flowing heat is derived from the heart as from its subject and source into the remaining parts, which may be said to have heat, so to speak, passively, as the heart has it actively.

units.la: Caloris Domicilium maximè proprium, creditur esse spiritus vitalis, non animalis, aut naturalis. Spiritus autem hic corpus est aëreum, tenue, vapori persimile, minime conspicuum, arteriae inclusum, ne dissipetur. Hunc esse in nobis, evincunt cordis structura in sinistro sinu, ceteraque indicia ab anatomicis tradita. Et quanquam sanguis arteriosus vehiculum sit caloris influentis: tamen maxime creditur vigere in tenuissima illius portione, quam Spiritum vocant. Spiritus hic quanquam mobilis sit, animatus tamen non est. Cum enim corporis pars non sit inte-
units.tr: The most proper home of heat is believed to be the vital spirit, not the animal or natural. This spirit is an airy body, thin, very like vapour, scarcely visible, enclosed in the artery lest it be dissipated. That it is in us is proved by the structure of the heart in the left sinus, and by other indications handed down by the anatomists. And although arterial blood is the vehicle of the flowing heat, nevertheless it is most believed to be active in the most subtle portion of it, which they call the spirit. This spirit, although mobile, is nevertheless not animate. For since it is not an integral part of the body, how can it be informed by a soul?

units.la: Note: the printed text reads "consequiturque" and "ceteraque" as shown; "inte-" is the catchword continuing on the next page. tegralis, qui potest anima informari? Est tamen animæ instrumentum, quo cor calorem suum, alijs membris communicat, gigniturque ex sanguine in cordis sinu lævo. Cum ergo aliæ partes ad functiones peragendas sufficientem calorem non habeant; fit, ut eum emendicent à corde; medio tamen spiritu & sanguine arteriofo. Ergo cor permanentem calorem habet, cæteræ partes nonnullum quidem permanentem, sed debilem, at influentem à corde alium multò intensiorem. Atque hæc de spiritu vitali.
units.tr: tegralis, what soul can be formed in it? Yet it is the instrument of the soul, by which the heart communicates its heat to the other members; and it is generated from the blood in the left sinus of the heart. Since, therefore, the other parts do not have sufficient heat to carry out their functions, it comes about that they beg it from the heart, though through the intermediary of the spirit and arterial blood. Thus the heart has a permanent heat, and the other parts a certain permanent heat, but weak, and they receive from the heart another heat, much more intense. And so much for the vital spirit.

units.la: Naturalis nullum usum video; nullum locum in quo generari possit; præsertim cum in hepate nullus sinus appareat, nisi forsan spiritum voces quemvis vaporē, ex sanguine actione caloris, suscitatum. Nec enim insitus partium calor, fovetur hoc spiritu, sed vitali, nec defert facultatem, quod Medici dicunt de animali: facultas enim naturalis singulis partibus est insita, ut non sit necesse hepar alialiquid præter sanguinem eo transmittere. Spiritus animalis, instrumentum sensus & motus functionum animalium, in cerebro gignitur, ex vitali in contextum retiformem delato: in cerebro autem est instrumentum sensuum internorum. Extra vero in membra effusus inservit earum & motioni, &, ut ita dicam, sensationi. communicatur membris per nervos, quorum substantiam tenuitate suâ penetrat, & quasi irradiat. Sicut ergo cor per arterias diffundit calorem; ita cerebrum irradiando nervos diffundit spiritum animalem: vehiculum sensus & motus, si Medicorum filiis creditur.
units.tr: I see no use for the natural spirit; there is no place in which it could be generated, especially since no sinus appears in the liver, unless perhaps you would call any vapour the spirit which is raised from the blood by the action of heat. For the innate heat of the parts is not cherished by this spirit but by the vital one, nor does it bring the faculty which the physicians speak of as belonging to the animal spirit: for the natural faculty is implanted in each part, so that there is no need for the liver to transmit anything else to them besides the blood. The animal spirit, the instrument of sense and of the functions of animal motion, is generated in the brain, from the vital spirit conveyed into the net-like tissue; but in the brain is the instrument of the internal senses. Poured out outside into the limbs, it serves for their motion and, as I may say, for their sensation. It is communicated to the limbs through the nerves, whose substance it penetrates by its fineness and, as it were, irradiates. Therefore, just as the heart diffuses heat through the arteries, so the brain, by irradiating the nerves, diffuses the animal spirit: the vehicle of sensation and motion, if one believes the sons of the physicians.

units.la: CAP. V. De Partibus.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. On the Parts.

units.la: QUamvis Hippocr. 6. Epidem. contex. 7. corpus humanum dividat in contenta, continentia, & impetum facientia; alij tamen partis nomen magis in angustum cogunt: cum sola continentia membra; partes hahabeantur. Contenta id est humores & impetum facientia, hoc est spiritus animalis & vitalis, cum sint inanima- ta & certâ figurâ destituta, in sensu partium numerari non debent. Nam quanquam nec vita, nec sanitas sine humore consistere possit; non tamen sequitur aut sanguinem, aut alium quemvis humorem necessarium, partem proprie dici posse. Est autem corpus toti cohærens, communi vita præditum, certaque figura ad functiones obeundas ornatum. Quæ definitio non tantum spiritus & humores excludit, verum etiam calculos, verrucas, callos, ungues, pilos, & id genus alia. Nec enim ista animata sunt, nec nutriuntur, nisi improprie; ut pilus & unguis per appositionem alimenti.
units.tr: Although Hippocrates, in Epidemics 6, section 7, divides the human body into contained things, containing things, and things that make an impulse, others confine the name "part" more narrowly, holding that only the containing members are parts. The contained things, that is the humours, and the things that make an impulse, that is the animal and vital spirits, since they are inanimate and lack a fixed shape, ought not to be counted among the parts in the proper sense. For although neither life nor health can exist without humour, it does not follow that blood or any other humour, however necessary, can properly be called a part. A part is a body that coheres with the whole, is endowed with common life, and is furnished with a fixed shape for carrying out its functions. This definition excludes not only spirits and humours but also stones, warts, calluses, nails, hairs, and things of that kind. For these are neither animate nor nourished, except improperly, as hair and nail are nourished by the addition of food.

units.la: Tria ista distinguenda veniunt, pars, instrumentum, membrum. Pars in ordine ad totum consideratur, complectiturque partes tam homogeneas, quam heterogeneneas: hæ enim totum componunt, & communi ni vita sunt præditæ. Instrumentum ad functionem refertur seu actioné ; non tamen omnem, sed perfectam, eamque maximè animalem. Nam naturalis actio singulis partibus inest, nisi primam & secundam concoctionem excipias. quę à determinatis instrumentis, ventriculo inquam & hepate fiunt. Operationem istam perfectam edunt omnes partes heterogeneæ ; ut oculus visionem, manus præhensionem, aut aliam actionem toti communem. Et ex homogeneis quædam ; ut arteria pulsum, vena sanguinis distributionem. Atque hoc modo oculi tunicæ & humores, quod hujusmodi actionem non habeant, partes dicuntur, non instrumenta. Quod non est ita accipiendum, quasi nullam actionem habeant ; nam nutriuntur, augentur : sed quia talem non habent. Nec errant qui putant partem similarem, seu homogeneam esse posse instrumentalem, sicut in arteria videre est. Similari parti, proprie opponitur dissimilaris, sicut ininstrumentali non instrumentalis Quanquam κατ' ἐξοχὴν heterogeneas instrumentariæ vocentur, ob figuram, magnitudinem, situm, numerum; quæ hîc magis elucent, quam in homogeneis. Membrum quoque maximè operationem respicit, diciturq; proprie de parte heterogeneâ hæc enim pars est operandi instrumentum maximè notum.
units.tr: Three things must be distinguished: part, instrument, and member. A part is considered in relation to the whole, and embraces parts both homogeneous and heterogeneous, for these make up the whole and share in its common life. An instrument is referred to a function or action; not to any action, but to a perfect one, and especially an animal one. For natural action is present in every part, except the first and second concoction, which are done by determinate instruments, namely the stomach and the liver. All heterogeneous parts carry out this perfect operation, as the eye does vision, the hand grasping, or another action common to the whole. Some homogeneous parts do so too: the artery the pulse, the vein the distribution of blood. Thus the coats and humours of the eye are called parts, not instruments, because they do not have such an action. This is not to be taken as meaning that they have no action at all, for they are nourished and grow; it is because they do not have such an action. Nor are those wrong who think a similar, or homogeneous, part can be instrumental, as may be seen in the artery. The dissimilar part is properly opposed to the similar part, as the non-instrumental is to the instrumental. Although the heterogeneous parts are called instrumental par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχὴν] because of their shape, size, position, and number, which stand out more clearly here than in the homogeneous parts. The member also relates chiefly to operation, and is properly said of a heterogeneous part, for this part is the best-known instrument of operation.

units.la: Similaris pars est cuius partes inter se totique similes sint; id est, in quâ idem est temperamentum partis & totius. Hallucinantur qui putant partis similaris, & totius, idem esse nomen. Verum quidem hoc in parte similari inanimata, lapide, aut aqua: at in animata secus. Pars enim vena secundum longitudinem sectæ non dicitur vena; nec tendinis, tendo: & quanquam pars ossis dicatur os communiter, non dicitur vertebra, aut radius: pars enim omnis certam habet figuram, quæ in divisione amittitur. Est autem mixtum homogeneum à facultate plastica ex semine, vel
units.tr: A similar part is one whose parts are alike among themselves and alike to the whole; that is, one in which the temperament of the part and of the whole is the same. They are mistaken who think that the name of a similar part and that of the whole are the same. This is indeed true of inanimate things, such as a stone or water; but not of animate ones. For a part of a vein cut lengthwise is not called a vein, nor a part of a tendon a tendon; and although a part of bone is commonly called bone, it is not called a vertebra or a radius, for every part has a definite shape, which is lost on division. A homogeneous mixed body is one generated by the plastic faculty from seed or blood, for the sake of a certain action.

units.la: Institut. Med. — (marginal notes partly illegible, ~40 letters) el sanguine genitum, certæ actionis gratia. Dicitur homogeneum ad excludendas partes dissimilares, seu heterogeneas; in quibus non eadem temperies, quæ primarió convenit huic partium generi, secundariò vero dissimilaribus. Hoc illud est, quod dicitur actiones primò à partibus similaribus fieri propter earum temperamenta. Actiones fiunt à facultatibus consistentibus in temperamentis; hæc autem primò insunt partibus simplicibus, seu similaribus; quod ex earum læsionibus apparet. Sola enim refrigeratio reddit pedē immobilem, inviolata magnitudine, situ &c.
units.tr: Institutiones Medicae: [marginal note illegible] or from blood, for the sake of a certain action. It is called homogeneous to exclude dissimilar, or heterogeneous, parts, in which the same temperament is not found that belongs first to this kind of part, but rather secondarily to dissimilar parts. This is what is meant when it is said that actions are performed first by similar parts because of their temperaments. Actions arise from faculties residing in temperaments, and these are present primarily in simple, or similar, parts, as appears from their injuries. For cooling alone renders a foot immobile, while its size, position, and so on remain uninjured.

units.la: Dissimilaris ex diversis similaribus est composita, estque in partes diversæ rationis, divisibilis. Et quia actionem perfectam edere potest, Organica dicitur. Est autem, pars ex similaribus composita debito numero, in convenientem figuram & magnitudinem coëuntibus, cum idoneo situ, à vi plastica ad perfectam actionem genigenita. In hoc partis genere, maximē attenditur compositio, sicut in similari temperamentum.
units.tr: A dissimilar part is composed of different similar parts and is divisible into parts of different kinds. And because it can perform a perfect action, it is called organic. A part of this kind is composed of similar parts, joined in the due number, in a suitable shape and size, and in a fitting position, generated by the plastic power for a perfect action. In this kind of part, composition is chiefly attended to, just as temperament is in a similar part.

units.la: Compositio quatuor exigit, 1. debitum numerum, 2. iustam magnitudinem. 3. conformationem aptam in cavitate, meatu, forma, superficie, figura, interdū etiā & colore: Ut enim oculus videat, debet carere omni alieno colore; quo si imbuatur, ut in itero, ejus conformatio est vitiata, proinde ad videndum ineptus: Postremo situ vel cū aliis partibus consensu.
units.tr: Composition requires four things: (1) the due number; (2) the right size; (3) a fitting conformation in cavity, passage, form, surface, figure, and sometimes even colour, for the eye to see it must lack every foreign colour, and if it is tinged with one, as in jaundice, its conformation is spoiled and it is unfit for seeing; (4) lastly, position, or agreement with the other parts.

units.la: Et quanquam actio à dissimilari parte perficiatur, à similari tamen oritur. Particulae enim organi conspirant in actionem eius partis, quae est facultatis radix, ut in humore crystallino videre est. Illic est visio, reliquę oculi partes concurrunt in subsidium.
units.tr: And although the action is performed by a dissimilar part, it nonetheless arises from a similar one. For the particles of an organ converge into the action of that part which is the root of the faculty, as may be seen in the crystalline humour. There lies the sight, and the other parts of the eye concur to assist it.

units.la: Partes similares creduntur esse decem; nimirum, os cartilago, ligamentum, membrana, nervus, arteria, vena, tendo, caro, cutis. Arteria & vena interdum dicuntur similares partes, interdum non; prout nimirum liter & aliter accipitur pars similaris. Nam si sensum spectes; videtur verum prorsus homogenea, cum tamen fibras habeat. Ita membrana quamquam sensui appareat simplex, habet tamen nervos. Si partium officia, aut functiones consideretur; dividi possunt in principales, & minus principales. Illæ sunt facultatum sedes, individui conservationi dicatæ. Cerebrum est sedes facultatis animalis, Cor vitalis, Hepar naturalis: nam quia sanguis generatur hîc, fit ut hæc facultas hîc potissimum vigeat, aliquì per totum corpus est diffusa. Principalibus quidam addunt testes; nec immerito, si officium & functionem consideres; destinati enim sunt speciei conservationi, & æternitati. Reliquæ humani corporis partes superioribus ministrantes, partes minus principales dicuntur. Observandum tamen, venas, nervos, arterias proprie admodum ministrantes vocari; tum quia à principalibus oriuntur, tum quia ab iis ad reliquas aliquid deferunt, ut vena ab hepate sanguinem, nervus à cerebro motum, & sensum; arteria à corde, calorem. Sunt aliæ partes minus principales toti communes, nec ministrantes principi parti. Sicut caro simplex, cutis, membrana, ligamentū, os, cartilago. Ventriculus, intestina, lien, vesica, renes, quia principis partis actionem quoquo modo juvant, præparando nimirum materiam, aut secernendo excrementa; optimo jure inter partes ministrantes numerari merentur. Anatomici quoq; totum corpus in tres ventres dividunt, pro varietate facultatum, corpus humanum gubernantium; nimirum; Caput, Thoracem, ventrem specialiter sic dictum.
units.tr: Similar parts are believed to be ten: namely bone, cartilage, ligament, membrane, nerve, artery, vein, tendon, flesh, and skin. Artery and vein are sometimes called similar parts and sometimes not, according as "similar part" is taken in one sense or another. For if you look at sense, they seem truly homogeneous, although they have fibres. Thus membrane, though it appears simple to sense, has nerves.
