If you consider the offices or functions of the parts, they can be divided into principal and less principal. The principal parts are the seats of the faculties, dedicated to the preservation of the individual: the brain is the seat of the animal faculty, the heart of the vital, the liver of the natural; for since blood is generated here, this faculty flourishes here especially, although it is diffused through the whole body. Some add the testes to the principal parts, and not without reason, if you consider their office and function, for they are destined for the preservation of the species and for eternity. The remaining parts of the human body, ministering to the higher ones, are called less principal parts. It should be observed, however, that veins, nerves, and arteries are properly called ministering parts, both because they arise from the principal parts and because they convey something from them to the rest: the vein blood from the liver, the nerve motion and sensation from the brain, and the artery heat from the heart. There are other less principal parts common to the whole, which do not minister to a principal part, such as simple flesh, skin, membrane, ligament, bone, and cartilage. The stomach, intestines, spleen, bladder, and kidneys, since they help the action of the principal part in some way, namely by preparing its matter or secreting its excrements, deservedly count among the ministering parts. Anatomists also divide the whole body into three cavities, according to the variety of the faculties governing the human body: namely the head, the thorax, and the belly, so called specifically.

units.la: CAP. VI. De Humoribus.
units.tr: CAP. VI. On Humours

units.la: HUmorem appello, non qualitatem primam, siccitati adversantem, quæ ὑγρότης dicitur; sed corpus mistum. Non tamen omne, sed certum & definitum, ut postea constabit: bit: nam Chylus, fæces, lac, semen, su-dor, urina, inter humores non numerantur. Propriè humor competit succis alimentariis, eorumq; excrementis, bili, succo melancholico &c. Succus alimentarius est sanguinis massa. De quâ vehementer dubitatur, sitne simplex humor, an contineat in se quatuor illa vulgata corpora; sanguinem specialiter sic dictum, bilem, pituitam, & succum melancholicum, ut plerique Medicorum statuunt: nam de sero non laboro, quia nutritioni ineptum est, omnium confessione. Ac primum quidem si in sanguine est bilis, succus flavus, & amarus; cur non amandatur ad suam vesiculam? (loquor hic de homine sano, in cuius venis nunquam conspicitur) Excrementum enim omne debet separari ab eo, cuius est excrementum; quemadmodū videmus fæces & alia separari ab iis, quæ utilia sunt corpori alendo. Aut quare hepar bilem flavam, primò à sanguine separet, si eandem voluit cum sanguine per totum corpus di-stristribui? Frustra enim separatur, quod mox est confundendū. Sanguis præterea est dulcissimi saporis; quod non fieret, si permistam haberet bilem. Ea enim est rerum amararum conditio, ut in parva quantitate magis se explicent, quam alia sapida in majore. Cantharus siquidem vini Hispanici (quod dulce est) dimidiatâ unciâ fel. lis cuiuscunque amaréscit. Quod de bile dico, idem de succo melancholico sentiendum. De pituitâ non laboro: omnium enim confessione ea est sanguis inchoatus, ac crudus. Dicamus ergo in sanguinis massâ non contineri huiusmodi humores tam discrepantes; quanquam non sit negandum in eâ contineri partium diversitatem; ita ut aliæ aliis sint calidiores, frigidiores, &c. quas quidem per me licet voces bilem, pituitam &c. At verò si quis ægrescat, tum in venis mutabitur sanguis, pro naturâ intemperiei; ut in hydropicis, icteri-cis, febricitantibus videre est. Serum pars sanguinis non est, sed vehiculū, quo sanguis subit per corpus venas. Proinde, officio peracto, expellitur per poros, vesicã, aut alia ratione; sudoris enim, lacrymarũ, & urinæ eadẽ est natura, eadẽ materia. Sanguis est alimentum ultimũ partium solidarũ (nam bilis & hujusmodi excrementa non nutriunt) Quod non est ita accipiendum, quasi in partis substantiam semper immediatè faceret; (quanquam interdũ hoc fiat, ut cũ sanguis mutatur in carnem) videmus enim ex sanguine fieri medullam, ex sanguine priusquam transeat in naturam membranæ fieri aliquid membranæ simile; sed quod sanguis non fiat bilis, aut aliquid tale, priusquam assumat naturam partis, lisdem siquidem nutrimur, quibus constamus. Constamus verò sanguine puro, & seminē; semen autem ex sanguine est. Ac quanquam sit magna partium varietas, omnes tamen aluntur sanguine; habente tamen aliquam partium varietatem, quemadmodum diximus.
units.tr: By humour I mean not the first quality opposed to dryness, which is called moisture (hygrotes), but a mixed body. Not every mixed body, however, but a certain and defined one, as will be established later: for chyle, faeces, milk, semen, sweat and urine are not counted among the humours. Properly speaking, the name humour belongs to the nutritive juices and their excrements: bile, melancholic juice and so on. The nutritive juice is the mass of the blood. There is strong doubt about this: whether it is a simple humour, or whether it contains within itself those four commonly cited bodies, namely blood (so called specifically), bile, phlegm and melancholic juice, as most physicians hold. For I am not concerned here with serum, since by universal admission it is unfit for nutrition. First, if there is yellow, bitter bile in the blood, why is it not sent off to its own vesicle? (I speak here of a healthy man, in whose veins it is never seen.) For every excrement ought to be separated from that of which it is an excrement, just as we see faeces and other things separated from those that are useful for nourishing the body. Or why would the liver first separate yellow bile from the blood, if it wanted it to be distributed through the whole body with the blood? For that is separated in vain which must immediately be mixed again. Moreover, blood has the sweetest taste, which would not be so if bile were mixed into it. For it is the nature of bitter things that in small quantity they make themselves more evident than other flavours do in larger quantity. Indeed, half an ounce of any gall makes a cup of Spanish wine (which is sweet) turn bitter. What I say of bile should be understood of melancholic juice too. I am not concerned with phlegm, for by universal admission it is blood that is incipient and raw. Let us say, then, that such discrepant humours are not contained in the mass of the blood; although it must not be denied that a diversity of parts is contained in it, so that some parts are hotter, others colder, and so on, which I am content to call bile, phlegm and the like. But if someone falls ill, the blood changes in the veins according to the nature of the disordered temperament, as can be seen in dropsical, jaundiced and feverish patients. Serum is not a part of the blood, but the vehicle by which the blood passes through the veins of the body. Therefore, once its office is done, it is expelled through the pores, the bladder or some other way; for sweat, tears and urine are of the same nature and the same matter. Blood is the ultimate nourishment of the solid parts (for bile and such excrements do not nourish). This is not to be taken as if blood always changed directly into the substance of the part (although this sometimes happens, as when blood is turned into flesh). For we see marrow made from blood, and before blood passes into the nature of membrane, something resembling membrane is made from it; but blood does not become bile, or anything of that kind, before it takes on the nature of the part, since we are nourished by the same things of which we consist. We consist of pure blood and seed, and seed comes from blood. And although there is great variety among the parts, all are nourished by blood, which nonetheless has some diversity of parts, as we have said.

units.la: De humoribus secundariis, (qucrum author creditur Avicenna, cum tamen Galen. 7. Meth.6. eas innuat) aliquid agendum. Ii perperam quatuor statuuntur,cum duo posteriores sint de substantia partium. Primus est in extremitatibus exilium venarum, estque ipsissimus sanguis; humor tamen est innominatus. Secundus est ros; humor mediæ cujusdam naturæ inter sanguinem & partem. Tertius est carnosa & adiposa humiditas, fibris circumfusa, communi vitâ praedita. Quartus membranosa, partes spermaticas continens,itidem ut prior,animata; ac proinde perperam inter humores collocata. Tertium illum humorem Arabis Medici interpretes, vocarunt cambiū, sicut quartum & postremum gluten.
units.tr: Something must be said about the secondary humours, whose author is believed to be Avicenna, though Galen (Meth. 7.6) hints at them. These are wrongly stated to be four, since the last two belong to the substance of the parts. The first is the fine vessels at the extremities of the veins, and this is the very blood itself; yet it is an unnamed humour. The second is dew, a humour of a certain intermediate nature between blood and part. The third is the fleshy and fatty moisture, surrounding the fibres and endowed with common life. The fourth is the membranous humour, containing the spermatic parts, animate in the same way as the former; and so it is wrongly placed among the humours. The interpreters of the Arab physicians called that third humour "cambium", and the fourth and last "gluten".

units.la: Atq; hæc de humore alimentario, sequitur excrementitius, cujus est aliqua varietas. Nam bilis naturalis, aluum irritat, & intestina sua acrimonia terget; melancholia vero, si multis credimus, appetitum excitat. Generantur humores excrementitij [illegible, ~4 letters] iisdem locis in quibus sanguis, nimi-rum in hepate, ab eâdem facultate, eodemque calore quo sanguis purus; (loquor de naturali bile, & Melan-cholia; ) nisi quod in chylo suppona-tur partium diversitas. Nam ex par-te maximè igneâ, generatur bilis; & ex terreâ, melancholia; ex temperatâ sanguis; nec unquam chylus tam est sincerus, quin habeat diversam dispositionem partium unde generantur ista excrementa. Quæ cum nutritioni inepta sint; à massa sanguinea separata, ad convenientia loca admandantur. bilis flava ad vesicam suam, sicut melancholia ad lienem. Si contingat viscerum temperiem esse vitiatam, hoc est justo calidiorem aut frigidiorem; aut contingat chylum esse corruptum ex cibis vitiatis, porris, allijs, cæpis: tum generabuntur humores excrementitij quidem illi, præternaturales tamen.
units.tr: So much for the nutritive humour; next comes the excrementitious, which has some variety. For natural bile irritates the bowel and cleanses the intestines with its sharpness, while melancholy, if we believe many, stimulates appetite. Excrementitious humours are generated in the same places as blood, namely in the liver, by the same faculty and the same heat by which pure blood is made (I speak of natural bile and melancholy), except that a diversity of parts is supposed in the chyle. For bile is generated from the most fiery part, melancholy from the earthy part, and blood from the temperate part. Nor is chyle ever so pure that it does not have a diverse arrangement of parts from which these excrements are generated. Since they are unfit for nutrition, they are separated from the mass of blood and sent to their proper places: yellow bile to its own vesicle, and melancholy to the spleen. If the temperament of the viscera is vitiated, that is, too hot or too cold, or if the chyle is corrupted by bad foods such as leeks, garlic and onions, then those excrementitious humours will indeed be generated, but they will be preternatural.

units.la: Bilis non naturalis est quadruplex. Prima est vitellina; quàm falsò putat Avicenna generari ex mistione bilis & pituitæ, vocatque bilem majoris famæ;oritur à vehemente calore deurente bilem naturalem, & dissipante partes tenues, donec facessat in consistentiam & colorem vitellorum crudorum. Secunda est bilis porracea. Tertia, æruginea. Postrema, glastea,isatidis calorem referens.Hę tres species ex parte virescunt, nec generantur in venis, sed in ventriculo, vitio alimenti parum temperati. De bile Zinaria Avicennæ nihil dico. adeo enim quæ de eâ traduntur sunt improbabilia, ut assertorem aliquem vix sint inventura.
units.tr: Unnatural bile is of four kinds. The first is vitelline, which Avicenna wrongly thinks is generated from a mixture of bile and phlegm; he calls it "bile of greater fame". It arises from a vehement heat that burns the natural bile and dissipates its fine parts, until it settles into the consistency and colour of raw egg yolks. The second is leek-green bile (porraceous). The third is verdigris-coloured. The last is woad-coloured, resembling the colour of woad. These three kinds turn greenish, and they are generated not in the veins but in the stomach, from food that is faulty and poorly tempered. I say nothing of Avicenna's Zinarian bile, for what is handed down about it is so improbable that they will scarcely find anyone to defend it.

units.la: Melancholia naturalis est succus ater (non verò atra bilis) in hepate cum sanguine genitus, ex terrestri chyli portione. Nam terrestris chyli portio,quatenus ab hepate magis coqui nequit, eatenus excrementum vocari potest,quemadmodum & pituita. Verum quia à splene magis elaborari potest, & in sanguinem bonum permutari;non est eo modo excrementum dicendum quo bilis;quę à vesica non tam trahitur, quam ab hepate isthuc expellitur. Nam Lien hunc succũ ad se trahit, ut magis coquat & alteret, eoque fruatur; non autem ut expellat, quemadmodum vesica bilem, aut renes serum. Nec prorsus aberravit Aristoteles, qui Lienem sinistrum hepar vocavit. Et sane venæ à Liene ortæ demonstrant sanguinem istum esse alimentarium. Quod verò superflua ejus portio, ad famem excitandam, & alimentum complectendum in ventriculum regurgitet, credere non possum: præsertim cum os ventriculi acutissimi sensus, non egeat hujusmodi stimulo. Sane mirum est, hepatis, & lienis excrementa remitti in ventriculum, ut inde alio transmittantur. nec sanus quispiam sentit perpetuo acidos ructus, quod fieret, si hunc usum praestaret melancholia. Illa quæ est præter naturam est noxia & inutilis, generaturque ex adustione, aut putrefactione aliorum excrementorũ. Bilis enim vitellina adusta, in porraceam; ceam ; postea æruginosam, & glasteam ; postremo in atram vertitur. Hæc acerrima est & maligna; tantoque malignior, quanto humor ex quo genita est deterior existit : saporem habet similem aceto acerrimo, & in terram effusa, eam fermentat: Levior est illa species, quæ ex melancholiâ naturali adustâ, generatur. A sanguinis adustione eam generari quoque volunt: verum cum sanguinis tenuior pars faceßat in bilem, crassior verò in melancholiam, non videtur hæc species à superioribus differre. An ex pituitâ fieri possit, dubitatur: nam ejus temperamentum adeò distat, ut nullo modo possit eousq; aduri: quanquam quidam excipiant pituitam salsam, ex quâ generari contendunt.
units.tr: Natural melancholy is a black juice (not black bile), generated in the liver together with the blood from the earthy portion of the chyle. For the earthy portion of the chyle, insofar as it cannot be further cooked by the liver, can be called an excrement, just as phlegm can. But because it can be further worked on by the spleen and changed into good blood, it is not to be called an excrement in the same way as bile, which is not so much drawn from the vesicle as expelled from the liver into it. For the spleen draws this juice to itself, so that it may cook and alter it further and make use of it; it does not draw it in order to expel it, as the bladder expels bile or the kidneys serum. Nor did Aristotle entirely err when he called the left spleen the liver. And indeed the veins arising from the spleen show that this blood is nutritive. But that its superfluous portion should regurgitate into the stomach to excite hunger and take up food, I cannot believe, especially since the mouth of the stomach, which has the most acute sensation, does not need such a stimulus. Indeed it is strange that the excrements of the liver and spleen should be sent back into the stomach to be passed on from there elsewhere; nor does any healthy person feel constant sour belching, which would happen if melancholy performed this function. That which is contrary to nature is harmful and useless, and it is generated from the scorching or putrefaction of other excrements. For yellow bile, when scorched, turns into leek-green, then into verdigris-coloured and woad-coloured, and finally into black. This is the sharpest and most malignant, and it is the more malignant the worse the humour from which it was generated. It has a taste like very sharp vinegar, and when poured on the ground it ferments it. The species generated from scorched natural melancholy is milder. Some want it to be generated from scorching of the blood too; but since the thinner part of the blood turns into bile and the thicker into melancholy, this species does not seem to differ from the earlier ones. Whether it can arise from phlegm is doubted, for the temperament of phlegm is so far removed that it cannot in any way be scorched to that point; although some make an exception for salty phlegm, from which they contend it is generated.

units.la: Restat pituita excrementitia, (nam alimentaria est crudior sanguinis portio, nutritioni partium frigidarũ, cerebri, &c. à naturâ destinata) quæ multiplex est. Quod screatu rejicitur, & quod in os ex cerebro decidit, pituita vocatur. Sed hisce omissis, triplex plex genus pituitae excrementitiae vulgò creditur. Quarum prima est acida; succus admodum crudus, nul-lamque alterationem passus, præter eam quam in ventriculo tulit. Secunda est pituita vitrea Praxagoreæ; quam ita vocavit ob similitudinem quam habet cum fuso vitro. Humor crassus, viscidus, frigidus, adhærensque intestinis; cruciatus immanes excitat. Postrema est pituita salsa, non frigida, ut superiores, sed calida ob admistionem seri salsi; non autem bilis amaræ, ut credidit Avicenna.
units.tr: There remains excrementitious phlegm (for the nourishing portion of the blood, which is cruder, is destined by nature for the nutrition of the cold parts, the brain and so on; this is the alimentary phlegm), and this is of several kinds. That which is spat out by coughing, and that which drops from the brain into the mouth, is called phlegm. But setting these aside, it is commonly believed that there are three kinds of excrementitious phlegm. The first is sour: a very crude juice, undergoing no change except that which it has undergone in the stomach. The second is Praxagoras's glassy phlegm, so called because of its resemblance to melted glass: a thick, viscous, cold humour that adheres to the intestines and causes immense torments. The last is salt phlegm, which is not cold like the others but warm, owing to the admixture of salty serum; it is not, however, bitter bile, as Avicenna believed.

units.la: CAP. VII. De facultatibus in genere, & in specie de naturali.
units.tr: CHAP. VII. Of the faculties in general, and in particular of the natural faculty.

units.la: DE animæ essentia disputare, Medico nihil conducit: quæ enim qualisque sit à Philosopho accipiendum. Quia verò Aristoteles omnium Philosophorum industriam in eâ explicandâ superavit, curiosus lector ejus libros de hac re consulat: nec enim quæstiones Logicas ( ita GaGalenus vocat eas, quæ nihil ad artem faciunt) persequi patitur instituti brevitas. Constat animam omnem esse formam corporis, ejusque actum informantem, & cum eo constituentem animatum; constat etiam animam, omnium operationum esse causam efficientem. Actiones fiunt à facultatibus, inhærentibus membris debito modo dispositis. Facultas est medium inter actionem & animam. Hæc enim hac, aut illâ facultate utitur, pro usus necessitate. Constat & hoc etiam, animam esse triplicem, vegetativam, sensitivam & rationalem: cui respondet triplex facultas, Naturalis & vitalis sequuntur vegetativam in animalibus; sicut Animalis, sensitivam & Rationalem. Quanquam propriè loquendo Rationalis facultas non est considerationis Medicæ, quia nullam corporis partem informat: quia tamen ab organo antecedenter dependet, cujus debitam conformationem & temperiem supponit; fit, ut ejus actio læsa à Medico consideretur. An verò tres sint in homine animæ reapse distinctæ; an sola rationalis virtualiter quasi, duas superiores continens; nihil attinet inquirere.
units.tr: To discuss the essence of the soul is of no use to the physician; what it is and of what kind must be taken from the philosopher. But since Aristotle surpassed all philosophers in explaining it, the curious reader should consult his books on this subject; for the brevity of my purpose does not allow me to pursue the logical questions (as Galen calls those which contribute nothing to the art). It is agreed that every soul is the form of a body, and its informing act, and together with it constitutes the living thing; it is also agreed that the soul is the efficient cause of all operations. Actions are performed by faculties, which inhere in members suitably disposed. A faculty is the intermediary between action and soul. For the soul uses this or that faculty as the need of its use requires. It is also agreed that the soul is threefold: vegetative, sensitive and rational. To these corresponds a threefold faculty: the natural and vital faculties follow the vegetative soul in animals, as the animal faculty follows the sensitive and the rational. Although, properly speaking, the rational faculty does not belong to medical consideration, since it informs no part of the body, yet because it depends beforehand on the organ, whose due conformation and temperament it presupposes, it comes about that its activity, when impaired, is considered by the physician. Whether there are really three distinct souls in man, or whether the rational soul alone, virtually as it were, contains the two higher ones, is not necessary to inquire.

units.la: Ad facultates transeamus; quas Philosophi aiunt esse qualitates, seu potentias naturales, ad operationem per se primò ordinatas. Naturalis cæterarum est basis quasi, & fulcrum; latissimeque patet; siquidem stirpibus & animalibus brutis inest. Aristoteli Δυναμις φυτικὴ vocatur, à Galeno φυτικὴ. Tota inservit individui conservationi, & speciei propagationi: eius enim functio est, accretio, nutritio, generatio. Hæc diffusa est per corpus universum; & quanquam dicatur residere in hepate; id tamen non est ita accipiendum, quasi in aliis membris non sit. Sed id dicitur, quia in hepate generat sanguinem, totius corporis, commune alimentū, quemadmodum antea definivimus. Eius ergo subjectum & instrumentum, non est hæc aut illa pars, sicut oculus vivisus, aut Lingua gustatus; sed quodlibet membrum corporis, quælibet enim pars, & nutritur, & augescit. Inest autem membro, seu instrumento calor, cujus vi & efficacia functiones suas peragit facultas. Observandum hîc, facultati huic, in quolibet membro, subservire quatuor alias; nimirum attracticem, retentricem, concoctricem, expultricem; ad quas revocantur distribuens, secernens & appetens. Si enim facultas quod convenit trahit; non opus est distincta aliqua facultate appetente. Sin alimentum conveniens retinet, ejusque excrementum expellit; non est opus secretrice aliqua aut distributrice. Quodlibet ergò membrum conveniens alimentum attrahit: attractum retinet; retentumque coquit. Quod autem coqui non potest, tanquam excrementum expellitur. Quæ dixi, intelligenda veniunt de privatis facultatum harum actionibus in singulis membris. Alioqui partes quas vocant communes, ventriculus nimirum, rum, hepar, iisq; ministrantes renes, vesica &c. functiones huiusmodi duplices habent. Ventriculus enim non tantum respectu privatae nutritionis, trahit, retinet, coquit & expellit: sed etiam, quatenus communis corporis officina, alimenta, toti corpori convenientia, eodem modo versat. Idem de hepate judicandum. Diximus non semel, facultatem omnem habere organum functioni suae accommodatum. Idem & hic apparet in partium villis, seu fibris, quarum aliae sunt rectae, aliae transversae, quaedam obliquae, impares nimirum facientes angulos: harum enim primae tractioni, secundae excretioni, tertiae retentioni dicatae sunt. Quod ad concoctionem attinet; ea perficitur a facultate membro inhaerente, mediante calore.
units.tr: Let us pass to the faculties, which the philosophers say are qualities or natural powers, primarily ordered by themselves to an operation. The natural faculty is as it were the base and support of the others, and it extends most widely, since it is present in plants and in brute animals. Aristotle calls it the vegetative power [Δυναμις φυτικὴ], and Galen the vegetative [φυτικὴ]. Its whole service is the preservation of the individual and the propagation of the species; for its function is growth, nutrition and generation. This is diffused through the whole body; and although it is said to reside in the liver, this is not to be understood as if it were absent from the other members. Rather it is so called because in the liver it generates the blood, the common nourishment of the whole body, as we defined earlier. Its subject and instrument, therefore, is not this or that part, as the eye is for seeing or the tongue for tasting; but any member of the body, for every part both is nourished and grows. Now in the member, or instrument, there is heat, by whose power and efficacy the faculty performs its functions. It should be observed here that four other faculties serve this faculty in every member: namely the attractive, the retentive, the concoctive and the expulsive, to which are referred the distributive, the secretive and the appetitive. For if the faculty attracts what is suitable, there is no need for a distinct appetitive faculty; but if it retains suitable nourishment and expels its excrement, there is no need for a secretive or distributive faculty. Thus every member attracts suitable nourishment, retains what is attracted, and concocts what is retained; what cannot be concocted is expelled as excrement. What I have said is to be understood of the individual actions of these faculties in the single members. Otherwise, the parts which are called common, namely the stomach, the intestines, the liver, and the kidneys and bladder which serve them, have functions of this kind in a double sense. For the stomach does not only attract, retain, concoct and expel with respect to private nutrition, but also, as the common workshop of the body, it deals in the same way with the nourishments suitable to the whole body. The same is to be judged of the liver. We have said more than once that every faculty has an organ adapted to its function. This appears also here in the villi or fibres of the parts, some of which are straight, others transverse, and some oblique, making unequal angles; for the first are devoted to attraction, the second to excretion, and the third to retention. As for concoction, it is accomplished by the faculty inhering in the member, by means of heat.

units.la: CAP. VIII. De Nutritione, & Accretione.
units.tr: CAP. VIII. On Nutrition and Accretion.

units.la: FAcultatum cognitio haberi non potest, ignoratis objecto & actioætione: definiuntur siquidem cum relatione ad talia. Proinde ut facultas naturalis melius intelligatur, de ejusdem actionibus quædam dicemus. Has diximus esse nutritionem, accretionem, generationem; de quibus ordine agemus. Et primum quidem de nutritione, cujus est magna necessitas. Corpus humanum perpetuo dissolvitur à causis tum internis, tum externis: cujus reparatio, fit nutritione. Est autem nutritio conversio alimenti in substantiam animatam, facta à facultate nutriente in unoquoque membro. Quæ definitio omnes causas requisitas complectitur. Causa conversionis, seu nutritionis efficiens, est facultas membro insita, mediante calore (frigus ad animati actiones per se non concurrit, sed per accidens, temperando nimirum calorem) partim membro insito, partim à corde derivato. Objectum, est alimentum convertendum. In hoc facultas agit, variè coquendo, & temperando. Finis est ut conservetur individuum: quod fieri non potest, est, nisi alimentum in membri sub-stantiam convertatur. Alimentum, quanquam sit varium, & multiplex; semper tamen debet aut animatum fuisse, sicut carnes: aut ab animato processisse, sicut ova, lac, vinum. Res enim aliter affectæ, propter contrarietatem temperamenti, & repugnantiam, in substantiam humanam converti nequeunt; sicut in metallis & lapidibus videre est. Unde alimentum, nec prorsus simile, nec prorsus dissimile esse debet. In principio enim dissimile, in fine simile. Similitudo non modo consideranda est, in qualitatibus primis, calore, frigore, &c. sed etiam in secundis, duritie, mollitie, tenuitate, crassitie: & maxime in modo substantiæ quo sensu dixit Galenus, panem nutrire.
units.tr: The knowledge of the faculties cannot be had if their object and action are unknown, since they are defined in relation to such things. Therefore, so that the natural faculty may be better understood, we shall say something about its actions. We have said these are nutrition, accretion, and generation; of these we shall treat in order. And first of nutrition, of which there is great need. The human body is continually dissolved by causes both internal and external; its repair is effected by nutrition. Nutrition is the conversion of food into animate substance, effected by the nutritive faculty in each member. This definition embraces all the requisite causes. The efficient cause of conversion, or nutrition, is the faculty inherent in the member, by means of heat (cold does not contribute to the actions of the animate in itself, but only accidentally, namely by tempering the heat), partly the heat inherent in the member and partly heat derived from the heart. The object is the food to be converted. In this the faculty acts, cooking and tempering it in various ways. The end is that the individual may be preserved; this cannot happen unless the food is converted into the substance of the member. Food, although it is varied and manifold, must always have been either animate, like flesh, or have come from something animate, like eggs, milk, and wine. For things of a different nature cannot be converted into human substance, because of the contrariety of temperament and repugnance, as may be seen in metals and stones. Hence food must be neither wholly like nor wholly unlike. For at the beginning it is unlike, at the end like. Likeness is to be considered not only in the primary qualities, heat, cold, and so on, but also in the secondary ones, hardness, softness, fineness, coarseness; and above all in the mode of substance, in which sense Galen said that bread nourishes.

units.la: Quæ ut fiant, triplex concoctio est instituta à natura, seu potius, naturæ authore, Deo. Quarum prima est propter secundam, sicut secunda propter tertiam: prima, & secunda, sicut toti corpori communes, tertia sinsingularum partium propria.
units.tr: So that these things may be done, a threefold concoction has been established by nature, or rather by God, the author of nature. Of these the first exists for the sake of the second, as the second for the sake of the third: the first and second are common to the whole body, the third is proper to each individual part.

units.la: Prima fit in ventriculo, χύλωσις dicta; quâ ventriculus insitis viribus, & vicinarum partium calore, cibum, & potum convertit in chylum, succum ptisanæ cremori similem. Omnis pars conatur alimentum sibi assimilare, non tantum in modo substantiæ, sed etiam colore: atque ob eam causam vina rubra, & heluola assumpta, statim, ventriculi alteratione, albescunt. Orificium superius, est acutissimi sensus, (quod ejus dolores indicant) eaque causa elt sedes famis. Est autem fames, dolor ejus partis, institutus ad cibi appetitionem. Animalia enim quanquam edant ad dolorem sedandum, ramen eâdem operâ & naturæ deficienti succurrunt. Nam præparatur alimentum in hac communi officinâ. Dolor autem cessat, assumpto liberaliter cibo. Errant, meo quidem judicio, qui putant famem ex partiū continentium, inanimarum tamen, suctione & tractione fieri. Quis enim credat tam brevi spatio atq; esuriunt hohomines, bene alioqui valentes, consumi posse alimentum in partes jam conversum? Aut quis credat, tam citò exhauriri substantiam in pueris, quam cibum appetunt? Et sanè videmus, assumpto cibo famem cessare; quod non fieret, si tractionis initium procederet à partibus, quæ nihilominus exhaustæ manent, quamdiu in ventriculo cibus coquitur. Nec tamen chylus nutrit ventriculum: eodem enim alimento nutritur, quo reliquæ membranæ; quod ex ejus venis constare potest. Iam cum excrementum sit alimenti pars inutilis; ibidem generabitur, ubi alimentum præparatur. Verum quamdiu est confusum cum alimento, excrementum non vocatur; sed tum demum, cum facta fuerit secretio. Necessariò sequitur, fæces esse huius concoctionis excrementa; quanquam non tingantur prius, quam in intestinis bile perfundantur. Quid? quod quidam volunt, etiam urinam esse hujus partis excrementum; Quia sin-gugulæ concoctiones duplex excrementum habent, tenue, scilicet & crassum.
units.tr: The first takes place in the stomach, and is called chylosis (χύλωσις); by it the stomach, by its inherent powers and the heat of neighbouring parts, converts food and drink into chyle, a juice like barley-water. Every part strives to make the food like itself, not only in the mode of substance but also in colour; and for this reason red and sweet wines, once taken in, immediately turn pale through the alteration of the stomach. The upper orifice is the seat of the most acute sense (as its pains show), and for this reason it is the seat of hunger. Hunger is the pain of that part, established to prompt the appetite for food. For animals eat to relieve the pain, and yet by the same act they come to the aid of the failing nature; for food is prepared in this common workshop. The pain ceases once food has been taken freely. In my judgment those are mistaken who think that hunger arises from the suction and traction of the containing parts, which are inanimate. For who would believe that men who are otherwise healthy can be consumed in so short a time, so that the food is already converted into the parts? Or who would believe that the substance of children is drained so quickly that they crave food? And indeed we see that hunger ceases when food is taken; this would not happen if the beginning of the traction proceeded from the parts, which nevertheless remain drained as long as the food is being cooked in the stomach. Nor does the chyle nourish the stomach: for the stomach is nourished by the same food as the other membranes, which can consist of its veins. Now since excrement is the useless part of the food, it will be generated in the very place where the food is prepared. Indeed, as long as it is mixed with the food, it is not called excrement, but only when secretion has been made. It necessarily follows that the faeces are the excrements of this concoction, although they are not tinged until they are bathed in bile in the intestines. What of the fact that some hold that urine too is the excrement of this part, because each concoction has a double excrement, thin and thick?

units.la: Peractâ coctione primâ, ventriculus per pylorum chylum ad intestina trudit. Quo in discenfu fit separatio & fegregatio alimenti ab excremento. Venæ enim mefaraicæ quicquid utile est & aptum sanguini gignendo, in transitu rapiunt: inutile autem omne ad anum amandatur; ad quem est continuus ductus ab œsophago; hic enim, ventriculus, & intestina inter se continuantur.
units.tr: When the first concoction is complete, the stomach pushes the chyle through the pylorus into the intestines. In this descent the nutritive part is separated and segregated from the excrement. For the mesaraic veins seize in passing whatever is useful and fit for generating blood, and all that is useless is sent on to the anus; to which there is a continuous passage from the oesophagus, for the stomach and intestines are continuous with one another.

units.la: Secunda concoctio in hepate fit. Venæ mefaraicæ alimentum utile in discensu intercipiunt, feruntq; ad hepar, quod insitâ facultate, mediante calore, chylum in sanguinem convertit. hæc actio, seu conversio, est secunda concoctio. Diximus jam antea, partem omnem imprimere alimento patienti sui similitudinem, quemadmodum ergo ventriculus chylum fecit album, ita hepar rubrum: sanguis autem primo venæ cavæ radidices subit, deinde truncum, tandemq; per ramos ejusdem & venas, distribuitur in universum corpus.
units.tr: The second concoction takes place in the liver. The mesaraic veins intercept the useful food in its descent and carry it to the liver, which by its inherent faculty, by means of heat, converts the chyle into blood. This action, or conversion, is the second concoction. We have said before that every part impresses its own likeness on the food it acts upon; therefore, just as the stomach made the chyle white, so the liver makes it red; and the blood first enters the roots of the vena cava, then the trunk, and finally is distributed through its branches and veins to the whole body.

units.la: Porrò ubi generatur alimentum, necessariò ibidem & excrementum debebit: nullum enim est tam purum, quin partes habet superfluas. Ergo partes magis igneæ, ab eodem calore & facultate quibus generatur laudabilis sanguis, facessunt in bilem. Quæ in propriam vesicam transmissa, inde ad duodenum intestinum amandatur; ubi fæces tingit, & vim expultricem intestinorum, alioqui segnem, irritat ad earum excretionem. Sanguinis partes graviores & magis terrestres, Lien ex jecore per ramum venæ portæ ad se trahit, ut eo nutriatur. Iam vero serum seu urina, quanquam in ventriculo generatur, non prius vocatur excrementum, quam facta secretio fuerit à sanguine, partim in renibus, partim in corporis habitu. Colligitur paulatim in vesica, quam copia, aut acrimonia vellicans irritat ad sui expulsionem.
units.tr: Moreover, where the food is generated, excrement must necessarily be generated too, for there is nothing so pure that it does not have superfluous parts. Therefore the more fiery parts, by the same heat and faculty by which the healthy blood is generated, pass off into bile. This, sent into its own vesicle, is then sent on to the duodenum, where it tinges the faeces and irritates the expulsive force of the intestines, otherwise sluggish, to their excretion. The heavier and more earthy parts of the blood the spleen draws to itself from the liver through a branch of the portal vein, so that it may be nourished by them. Now serum, or urine, although it is generated in the stomach, is not called excrement until secretion has been made from the blood, partly in the kidneys, partly in the habit of the body. It gradually collects in the bladder, and by its quantity or sharpness it irritates the bladder to expel it.

units.la: Atq; hæc de prima, & secunda coctione, quæ sunt veluti gradus ad tertiam, quam & nutritionem, & assimilationem vocant. Fit autem, cum partes singulæ sanguinem, in rorem prius conversum, in suam naturam transmutant. Tum sanguis, non est amplius sanguis, sed caro, tendo, membrana, &c. corpus videlicet animatum. Concoctio hæc, sua habet excrementa. Nam & sordes cuti adhærentes, & quod insensibiliter evacuatur, huc pertinent; quanquam cerebrum, viscus frigidum, præter hæc & mucum habet. Ex quibus constat, sanguinem esse alimentum ultimum; quod tamen non sufficeret, nisi actuaretur à sanguine arteriofo; qui, comparatione sanguinis venenosi, est quasi forma & actus.
units.tr: So much for the first and second concoction, which are as steps to the third, which is called both nutrition and assimilation. This takes place when the individual parts transform the blood, first converted into a dew, into their own nature. Then the blood is no longer blood, but flesh, tendon, membrane, and so on, that is, the animate body. This concoction has its own excrements. For both the filth adhering to the skin and what is evacuated imperceptibly belong here; although the brain, a cold viscus, has besides these also mucus. From these things it is clear that blood is the ultimate food; yet this would not suffice unless it were actuated by arterial blood, which, in comparison with venous blood, is as it were form and act.

units.la: Hic obiter nota, vitia prioris concoctionis à posteriore, aut non corrigi, aut difficulter.
units.tr: Here note in passing that faults of the first concoction are either not corrected by the later one, or only with difficulty.

units.la: Nutritio, de quâ egimus, tamdiu durat, quamdiu vita, supponiturque accretioni, de quâ paucis agemus.
units.tr: The nutrition of which we have treated lasts as long as life, and it presupposes accretion, of which we shall speak briefly.

units.la: Constat, animal omne habere certam magnitudinem, functionibus idoneam & aptam. Hanc in principio ortus habere nequit; restat ergo ut sequentibus annis consequatur. Eâ causâ, ossa primo & subsequentibus annis, sunt admodum mollia: hac enim ratione facillime extenduntur: durum enim frangi potest, flecti nequit. Accretio primario est partium similarium, secundario vero dissimilarium. Proinde in eâ omnes partes fiunt majores, secundum omnem dimensionem, quod non fit in incremento acervi lapidum: nam quanquam acervus fiat major, singuli lapides non fiunt majores. Neq; hoc tantum, verum alimentum debet etiam intus sumi. Nam quando convertitur aqua in aërem, non dicitur crescere, sicut neque quando res aliqua rarescit: acquisita quidem est nova quantitas, sed sine assumptione corporis, quod in accretione exigitur. Postremò, in accretione, debet manere idem numero animatum. Ergo go in infantiâ, facultas naturalis admodum valida, plus reponit quam consumpsit. Ex eo autem quod est plus, fit accretio. Nam alimentum in minutis osculis partium receptum, & conversum, extenditur, eo prorsus modo, quo spongia, à manu constricta, postea autem liberata, sese extendit. At quia ossa sicca facta extendi nequeunt, (quod ætatis anno 25. aut 30. fit) incrementum cessat; tumque homines pinguescere incipiunt. Calor autem postea & humor perpetuò debilitantur, donec morte naturali intereat animatum. Nam quamdiu anima corpori communicatur, tamdiu vita superest: communicatur autem, si idoneum sit corpus & ritè præparatum; quod si desit, morietur animatum. Qua de causa Philosophus dixit, mortem esse caloris extinctionem: quæ fit à contrario & hostili frigore; aut calore externo, & febrili internum populante & vastante: internum solutione continui, quâ sanguis omnis effluit; nam tum quoque evaevaporat calor. Quanquam non hoc solum modo pereunt homines ; sed interdum marcore, quo humor omnis est consumptus : quo consumpto, necesse est & calorem una extingui. Contingit interdum, alimentum revera consumi , sicut deficiente oleo, perit ignis & flamma. Interdum tamen calor adeo est debilis , ut appositum alimentum , amplius mutare nequeat. Mors duplex statuitur; quarum altera est naturalis ex defectu caloris , ob humidi exsiccationem jam marcidi ; ad quam senectus est gradus. Altera violenta & praeter naturam ; cum calori adhuc vegeto, subtrahitur alimentum ; aut cum respiratione prohibita , quasi suffocatur; aut alia ratione dissipatur.
units.tr: It is established that every animal has a definite magnitude, suited and fit for its functions. It cannot have this at the beginning of its existence; it remains, therefore, that it attains it in the following years. For this reason the bones in the first and following years are very soft, for in this way they are most easily extended; for what is hard can be broken but cannot be bent. Accretion is primarily of the similar parts, and secondarily of the dissimilar. Therefore in it all parts become larger in every dimension, which does not happen in the growth of a heap of stones; for although the heap becomes larger, the individual stones do not become larger. Nor is this all: the food must also be taken in internally. For when water is converted into air, it is not said to grow, nor is anything said to grow when it becomes rarer; new quantity is indeed acquired, but without the assumption of body, which is required in accretion. Lastly, in accretion the animate must remain the same in number. Therefore in infancy, the natural faculty, being very vigorous, restores more than it has consumed. And it is from this excess that accretion arises. For food received into the minute pores of the parts and converted is extended, just as a sponge, squeezed by the hand and afterwards released, expands. But because the bones, once dried, cannot be extended (which happens about the age of 25 or 30), growth ceases; and then men begin to grow fat. Thereafter the heat and moisture are continually weakened, until the animate perishes by natural death. For as long as the soul is communicated to the body, life remains; it is communicated, however, if the body is fit and duly prepared; but if this is lacking, the animate will die. For this reason the Philosopher said that death is the extinction of heat; this is brought about by a contrary and hostile cold, or by external heat which, being feverish, ravages and lays waste the internal heat; or internally by the dissolution of continuity, by which all the blood flows out, for then the heat also evaporates. Yet men do not perish only in this way, but sometimes by wasting away, in which all the moisture is consumed; and when this is consumed, the heat must be extinguished with it. Sometimes it happens that the food is truly consumed, just as when oil is lacking fire and flame perish. Sometimes, however, the heat is so weak that it cannot change the food applied to it any further. Death is held to be twofold: one kind is natural, from a lack of heat, owing to the drying up of the moisture now wasted away, to which old age is the step; the other is violent and contrary to nature, when the food is withdrawn while the heat is still vigorous; or when respiration is prevented, so that one is as it were suffocated; or it is dissipated by some other means.

units.la: CAP. IX. De Hominis generatione.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. On the generation of man.

units.la: HÆc etiam functio est naturalis facultatis , & quidem nobilissima; dicata propagationi individui , & speciei æternitati. Elementis constanstantia corpora, æterna esse nequeunt; & tamen æternitatem appetunt, quod ergo in individuo (ita loquuntur) consequi nequeunt, in specie tamen obtinent: & quanquam Socrates, Plinius, Annibal, sunt mortales; humana tamen species, æterna est; & quidem hujus facultatis beneficio. Facultas nutrix, & auctrix; (quæ ab eâ non distinguitur) diffusæ per totum corpus sunt; non item generatrix, quæ determinatam in corpore partem, & sedem vendicat, nimirum testes. In his itaque est facultas procreatrix, quâ animal ex semine, aliud sibi simile procreat. Non ago hoc loco de generatione animalium imperfectorum ex putredine; aut quæ generantur ex congressu diversæ speciei animalium, ut equi & asinæ: sed de perfectâ tantum, quam univocam vocant; nec tamen omni, sed hominis tantum.
units.tr: This function also belongs to the natural faculty, and indeed it is the noblest of them. It is devoted to the propagation of the individual and to the eternity of the species. Bodies made of elements cannot be eternal, yet they desire eternity. What they cannot attain in the individual (as people say), they attain in the species. Although Socrates, Pliny and Hannibal were mortal, the human species is eternal, and this is owed to the benefit of this faculty. The nutritive and augmentative faculty, which is not distinct from it, is diffused through the whole body. The generative faculty is not, since it claims for itself a determined part and seat in the body, namely the testicles. In these, then, is the procreative faculty, by which an animal produces from seed another animal like itself. I am not discussing here the generation of imperfect animals from putrefaction, or of those produced by the mating of different species, such as horse and donkey, but only of perfect generation, which they call univocal, and not of every kind of it, but only of man.

units.la: Procreatio specialiter dicta, est unio animæ cum corpore: alioqui solet accipi pro omnibus conjunctis actio[illegible, ~1 letter]ationibus, congressu, conceptu, formatione, partu. Elementa generant semper ex materiâ & objecto externis: quod enim hic generatur, nunquã fuit pars generantis, aut illi unitum. Verum perfectorum animalium, & inprimis hominis generatio est magis operosa, semperque fit ex parte generanti quondam intima; nimirum semine & menstruo sanguine. Quorum illud est maris, sicut hic fœmina. Sanguis solus, aut semen non sufficiunt; sed utrunque conjungendum. Mas habet rationem efficientis, sicut fœmina subjecti, & materiæ. Utriq; insunt vasa muneri huic sufficientissima; (sicut ex anatomia constat) sed tamen figura, situ, & temperie distinctissima. Uterus semen & sanguinem recipit; testes viriles illud auxilio colis effundunt in eum.
units.tr: Procreation, in the narrow sense, is the union of the soul with the body. Otherwise it is commonly taken for all the actions joined together: intercourse, conception, formation and birth. Elements always generate from external matter and object, for what is generated here was never a part of the generator, nor joined to it. But the generation of perfect animals, and above all of man, is more laborious, and it always takes place from a part of the generating parent that is at some point inward, namely seed and menstrual blood. Of these, the one belongs to the male, the other to the female. Blood alone, or seed alone, is not sufficient; both must be joined. The male has the role of efficient cause, as the female has the role of subject and matter. Both have vessels most suited to this office (as is clear from anatomy), yet they are most distinct in shape, position and temperament. The uterus receives the seed and the blood; the male testicles pour the seed into it with the help of the vessels.

units.la: Quanquam mulieres habeant semen; non est tamen efficax, nec concurrit ad generationem activè, sed merè passivè: nec ex omnibus partibus fluit, sed tantùm testibus, quibus inest vis producendi animal perse-&tum. Quod enim dicitur,à partibus principalibus fluere, parum est: nam ultimum capitis alimentum aut hepatis, non repræsentat has partes, nec vim habet ea producendi ; cum fit tantum materia patiens, & jam convertenda in earum partium naturam. Ergo sicut mammæ habent vim generandi lac, seu convertendi sanguinem in lac : ita testes sanguinem ex venâ cavâ prolectum , convertunt in corpus album,spumosum,calidum & humidum , facultate plasticâ prædi-tum;quo primùm ipsi nutriuntur,cujusque reliquiæ generationi destinatæ sunt. Menstruus sanguis est ille qui singulis mensibus ( nisi ætas aut morbus impediant) redundans , tanquam naturam gravans expellitur. Non est venenatus,ut quidam tradere ; nisi forsan putrescat, ut in hystericis. Hic inquam sanguis est generationis materia , ex eâ enim siunt partes sanguineæ,tum est alimentum fœtus.
units.tr: Although women have seed, it is not effective, and it does not contribute to generation actively, but purely passively. Nor does it flow from all parts, but only from the testicles, in which is the power of producing a complete animal. For to say that it flows from the principal parts is of little weight; for the last nourishment of the head or of the liver does not represent these parts, nor does it have the power of producing them, since it is only passive matter, and is yet to be converted into the nature of those parts. Therefore, just as the breasts have the power of generating milk, that is, of converting blood into milk, so the testicles convert blood drawn from the vena cava into a white, frothy, warm and moist body, endowed with a plastic faculty; by it they themselves are first nourished, and its remains are destined for generation. Menstrual blood is that which, every month (unless age or illness prevents it), overflows and is expelled as if it burdened nature. It is not poisonous, as some teach, unless perhaps it putrefies, as in hysterical women. This blood, I say, is the matter of generation, for from it are made the blood-related parts, and it is also the nourishment of the foetus.

units.la: Vis generatrix est plastica illa & divina facultas semini virili tantum insita, cujus vi, partes primum delineantur, tum anima corpori præparato unitur. Servit illi calor blandus, non igneus corrumpens, sed potius cœlestis respondens virtuti cœlesti, ut tradidit Philosophus. Consistit vero in tenuiore seminis portione, & maximè spirituosa, quam si semen muliebre haberet, posset sola generare; quod tamen est inauditum: cum ne sola molam generare possit, ut constans est omnium Medicorum sententia. Nec possint esse duo activa generationis principia, quorum singula efficiant aliquid seorsum; cum unum vitæ principium sufficiat: nec ex utriusq; conjunctione tertia quædam vis emergere potest. Probabile itaque maximè est, semen virile, in generatione & fœtus formatione, causæ efficientis rationem habere: materiam autem & subjectum esse muliebre, unà cũ sanguine menstruo: quæ tria semper concurrere debent.
units.tr: The generative power is that plastic and divine faculty implanted in the male seed alone, by whose power the parts are first outlined, and then the soul is joined to the prepared body. A gentle heat serves it, not a fiery one that corrupts, but rather a heavenly one corresponding to the heavenly virtue, as the Philosopher taught. It resides in the thinner portion of the seed, and especially in its spirituous part, which the female seed would be able to generate alone if it had it; yet this is unheard of, since it could not even generate a mole alone, as is the settled opinion of all physicians. Nor can there be two active principles of generation, each of which effects something separately, since one principle of life suffices; nor can some third power emerge from the union of both. It is therefore most probable that the male seed has the role of efficient cause in generation and in the formation of the foetus, while the matter and subject is the female, together with the menstrual blood. These three must always concur.

units.la: Quando itaque utrunq; semen ab utero receptum est, tum inter se confunduntur & permiscentur; quæ uteri actio est germana conceptio. tum vis plastica incipit vires exserere, partes delineando: quod tamen non prius fit, quam crassiores feminis partes, ad circumferentiam sint expulsæ, ut ex iis fiant membranæ, fœtum involventes. Membranæ sunt tres; (quibusdam duæ tantum) ἀμνιος fœtum immediatè involvit; ἀλλαντοειδὴς zonæ instar, à mucronatâ cartilagine, ad ilia usque cingit; tertia vasa umbilicalia fulcit, eorumque interventu tota utero adhæresçit χόριον dicta.
units.tr: When therefore both seeds have been received by the uterus, they are then mixed and blended together; this action of the uterus is the true conception. Then the plastic power begins to put forth its strength, outlining the parts. This does not happen before the thicker parts of the seeds have been driven out to the circumference, so that from them membranes are made, enclosing the foetus. There are three membranes (some say only two). The amnion [ἀμνιος] immediately encloses the foetus. The allantois [ἀλλαντοειδὴς], like a girdle, encircles it from the pointed cartilage to the flanks. The third supports the umbilical vessels, and through them the whole thing adheres to the uterus; it is called the chorion [χόριον].

units.la: Duplex est partium conformatio, quorum prima est partium spermaticarum, secunda vero sanguinearum; cum vis insita, crassiores feminis partes ad circumferentiam, ut dixi, egerit; paulatim incipit partes spermaticas adumbrare, ossa nimirum, nervos, venas, &c. tum ampullas tres, bullis in aqua excitatis simillimas, rurudimenta nimirum partium principalium, cum suis filamentis, nervis &c. cernere licet. Quo facto, succedit partium sanguinearum adumbratio. Sanguis enim non prius fluit per venam umbilicalem huc, quam spermaticæ partes sint factæ. Tum vero spatia fibrarum vacua explentur; viscerumque παρέγχυμα delineatur; cæteraeq; partes aliæ musculorum succedunt. Quod dum fit, nulla est vita, nullus motus; quia nulla est anima. Nec enim est anima antequam domicilium fit paratum; quod ante tertium mensem fieri nequit: quo tempore omnes partes absolutæ sunt: tum demum nutriri incipit fœtus sanguine materno. Frustra, meo judicio, disputatur, quæ pars in homine primò generetur. Nam etiamsi hepar id sit membrū, nihil faciet sine reliquorum adminiculo: itidem nec cor, nec cerebrum. Sed horum omnium requiritur consensus, & unio.
units.tr: The shaping of the parts is twofold: the first is of the seminal parts, the second of the blood-related parts. When the implanted power has driven the thicker parts of the female seed to the circumference, as I said, it gradually begins to sketch the seminal parts, namely the bones, nerves, veins and so on. Then one can see three bladder-like swellings, very like bubbles raised in water: these are the rudiments of the principal parts, with their own filaments, nerves and so on. When this is done, the outline of the blood-related parts follows. For blood does not flow here through the umbilical vein before the seminal parts have been made. Then the empty spaces of the fibres are filled, the parenchyma [παρέγχυμα] of the viscera is outlined, and the other parts, the muscles, follow. While this is happening, there is no life and no motion, because there is no soul yet. For the soul does not come before the dwelling is prepared, and this cannot be done before the third month, by which time all the parts are complete. Only then does the foetus begin to be nourished by the mother's blood. In my judgement it is pointless to dispute which part in man is generated first. For even if the liver is that member, it does nothing without the help of the others; likewise neither the heart nor the brain. What is needed is the agreement and unity of all of them.

units.la: Porrò quod dicant nonnulli, fœtum primum informari anima vegetantante, tum sequentibus diebus sen-tiente, & ita deinceps; probabilita-te caret. Membra enim humana non inserviunt animæ quæ tantum est ve-getans, aut sentiens; sed rationali, quæ virtualiter superiores duas in se continet. Fœtus ergo animatus in utero nutritur, & crescit quousque robur acquirat, & ore nutriri possit, indigeatque non tantum majore loco, sed & liberaliore cordis refrigerio. Tum, duce naturâ, calcitrando membranas & involucra rumpit. Conspirat tamen uterus, sefeq; pandit: nec hic solum, sed & vicinæ partes.
units.tr: Moreover, what some say, that the foetus is first informed by a vegetative soul, then on the following days by a sentient soul, and so on in turn, lacks probability. For human limbs do not serve a soul that is merely vegetative or merely sentient, but a rational soul, which contains the two lower powers within itself virtually. The animated foetus is therefore nourished and grows in the womb until it acquires strength and can be nourished by the mouth, and it needs not only a larger space but also a more generous cooling of the heart. Then, led by nature, it kicks and breaks through the membranes and coverings. Yet the uterus cooperates and opens itself, and not only it but the neighbouring parts as well.

units.la: In partu naturali & legitimo infans caput & humeros primò exerit; quo facto, reliquæ partes non difficulter sequuntur: si enim brachium, pes aut alia pars in lucem primò prodeat, partus non carebit periculo.
units.tr: In a natural and proper birth, the infant first puts out its head and shoulders; once this is done, the remaining parts follow without difficulty. If an arm, a foot or another part should come out into the light first, the birth will not be free of danger.

units.la: Tempora partus humani incerta sunt. Constat tamen ante sextum mensem, non esse fœtum vitalem. Septimo quidem mense est vitalis, & quod fi robustus simul fit, in lu- cem exibit: fi non, natura ut plurimum differt in nonum, decimum, aut initiū undecimi mensis. Oƈtavo natus infans ( extra Ægyptum ) non est vitalis ; nam cum frustra septimo mense conatus fuerit, debilitatur vehementer ; ac proinde justo mense eget ad virium reparationem. Si ergo oƈtavo prodeat, non potest non debilis esse ; non modò ex irrito superioris mensis conatu, sed etiam ex partu oƈtavi mensis.
units.tr: The times of human birth are uncertain. It is agreed, however, that before the sixth month the foetus is not viable. In the seventh month it is viable, and if at the same time it is robust, it will come out into the light; if not, nature for the most part delays until the ninth, tenth, or beginning of the eleventh month. An infant born in the eighth month (outside Egypt) is not viable; for since it has tried in vain in the seventh month, it is greatly weakened, and therefore needs the full month for the restoration of its strength. If, then, it comes forth in the eighth month, it cannot but be feeble, not only from the fruitless effort of the previous month, but also from the birth in the eighth month itself.

units.la: Naturalis partus est tantum maris, aut fæminæ, & quidem ejusdem speciei, nimirum humanæ. Interdum tamen contingit casu aliquo, aut vitio feminis, uteri &c. nasci monstrum, aut molam, de quibus alias.
units.tr: Natural birth is only of a male or a female, and indeed of the same species, namely the human. Yet sometimes by some accident, or by a fault of the woman or of the uterus, a monster or a mole is born, of which I shall speak elsewhere.

units.la: Sed ad natorum similitudinem veniamus ; quæ triplex à Philosophis & Medicis statuitur. Speciei nimirum, sexus, & effigiēi. Voco speciei similitudinem, convenientiam duorum in naturâ fpecificâ, ut Socratis & Platonis in natura humana. Hæc est à vi plastica non interpellatâ, aut impedita. Nam agens univocum reddit effectum in specie sibi similem. Secunda est in sexu; mas nimirum & fœmina. Causam maris vulgo tradunt robur facultatis plasticæ, unà cum potente calore foras propellente eas partes, quas fœmina intus reconditas habet. Quod probabile non videtur; cum nulla sit similitudo partium genitalium in mare & fœmina: nam etiamsi uterus propendeat, non tamen repræsentabit penem humanum. Quid? quod multæ mulieres reperiantur viris calidiores. Probabilius judico, facultatem plasticam, indifferenter producere marem aut fœminam; verum determinari potius ad maris generationem, quam fœminæ, aut contra, à materiâ subjectâ: nisi mavis, primam causam (quod in multis fieri consuevit) indifferenter, nunc huius, nunc illius sexus, fœtum producere, pro feminis variâ dispositione. Similitudo effigiei liberorum ad parentes (con(consistit hæc similitudo in colore, & lineamentis membrorum seu figurâ) pendet ex temperamento feminis à parentibus profecti. Intelligo hic colorem nam figura pendet à vi formatrice seu plastica; quæ nunc patri, nunc matri fœtum similem fingit; Interdum alió deflectit, si phantasia concurrat; sed quomodo hoc fiat, hîc non disputo.
units.tr: But let us come to the likeness of offspring, which Philosophers and Physicians set down as threefold: namely of species, of sex, and of appearance. I call the likeness of species the agreement of two beings in the specific nature, as of Socrates and Plato in human nature. This arises from the plastic power being undisturbed and unhindered, for a univocal agent produces an effect like itself in species. The second is in sex, that is, male and female. The common account gives as the cause of the male the strength of the plastic faculty together with a powerful heat driving outward those parts which the female has hidden within. This does not seem probable, since there is no likeness of the genital parts in male and female: for even if the womb hangs down, it will not represent the human penis. And what of the fact that many women are found hotter than men? I judge it more probable that the plastic faculty produces indifferently either a male or a female, but that it is determined toward the generation of a male rather than a female, or the reverse, by the underlying matter; unless you prefer to say that the first cause (as often happens) produces the foetus indifferently, now of this sex, now of that, according to the varying disposition of the females. The likeness of the offspring's appearance to the parents (this likeness consists in colour and in the features of the limbs, or their shape) depends on the temperament of the female derived from the parents. I mean here colour; for shape depends on the formative or plastic power, which now fashions the foetus like the father, now like the mother; sometimes it turns it aside to another likeness, if the imagination concurs. But how this comes about I do not discuss here.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: De Facultate vitali, ejusque actionibus.
units.tr: On the Vital Faculty and Its Actions.

units.la: FAcultas vitalis est media quasi inter naturalem, & animalem: nec tamen peculiare animati genus constituit. Conjungitur in animale cum naturali vi, cuius est perfectio: nam sanguis non nutriret, nisi perficeretur, & quasi actuaretur à calore vitali. Hæc est aliarum facultatum basis & fundamentum, ex cuius incolumitate vita hominis pendet. Huius sedes est cor, viscus omnium in homine calidissimum, in quo perturbationes, ira, amor, metus, &c. resident. Ejus situm, & structuram accuratè describere, hoc loco supervacaneum duxi. Eius flabellum est pulmo ; quo illius calor auxilio frigidi aëris temperatur. In eo duo sunt sinus dexter & sinister ; in illo est purus sanguis beneficio venæ cavæ illis implantatæ, cuius ostiolo tres valvulæ intus ductæ prætenduntur. In eodem sinu est vena arterialis, deferens è corde ad pulmones sanguinem; cuius membranæ vel valvulæ eosdem spectant extrorsum. In sinistro sinu est sanguis arteriosus, unà cum orificio arteriæ magnæ ; cuius valvulæ extrorsum spectant. Est etiam ibidem arteria venosa, duabus tantum valvulis introrsum vergentibus instructa. Sinus discluduntur medio septo, magnos habente poros, per quos transit sanguis frigidior ex dextro sinu in sinistrum, elaborandus in vitalem spiritum. Ex quibus facile constabit de controversiâ medicâ, agitatâ non minus inter Galenum & Era-sistrafistratum, quam inter illum & Avi- cennam.; an arteriæ deprimantur, & attollantur cum corde: de quâ Le- ctor, alios consule.
units.tr: The vital faculty is, as it were, midway between the natural and the animal faculty, yet it does not constitute a peculiar kind of living thing. In an animal it is joined with the natural power, of which it is the perfection: for blood would not nourish unless it were perfected and, as it were, actuated by vital heat. This is the basis and foundation of the other faculties, and human life depends on its soundness. Its seat is the heart, the hottest of all the viscera in man, in which the passions (anger, love, fear, and so on) reside. I have thought it superfluous here to describe its position and structure accurately. Its fan is the lung, by whose help its heat is tempered by cool air. The heart has two sinuses, right and left. Into the right comes pure blood, by means of the vena cava implanted in it; at the opening of this three valves, drawn inward, are set out. In the same sinus is the arterial vein, carrying blood from the heart to the lungs; its membranes or valves face outward. In the left sinus is arterial blood, together with the orifice of the great artery, whose valves face outward. There is also there the venous artery, furnished with only two valves turned inward. The sinuses are divided by a middle septum with large pores, through which the cooler blood passes from the right sinus into the left, to be worked into vital spirit. From these points it will easily be clear what the medical controversy is, debated no less between Galen and Erasistratus than between Galen and Avicenna: whether the arteries are depressed and raised together with the heart. On this the reader may consult others.

units.la: Facultas ista resident in cordis sub- stantia ad generationem spiritus vi- talis instituta. Hic constat sanguine vaporoso in dextro sinu contento, qui calidior factus & spirituosior, in totum corpus motu contractionis & dilatationis per arterias distribuitur. Distributionis finis, est incrementum caloris vitalis in singulis membris fi- xi. Nam, ut dixi, ante nativus & fi- xus calor non sufficit partium actio- nibus. Cor ergo, viscus calidissimum de innato calore suo iis nonnihil im- pertit: ergo spirituum generationi, & distributioni subservit pulsus esse- ctio. Nam, quod attinet ad pertur- bationum concitationem; quanquam ea sit in corde, pendet tamen ab ap- petitu, & imaginatione, functionibus animalibus; sicut ex parte respiratio est: nam pulsus motus est penitus na- turalis. Ad quem tria concurrunt, Facultas, Instrumentum, & Vsus, seu finis & necessitas facultatem impellens. Est autem cordis & arteriarum actio composita ex contractione, & dilatatione, intercedente quiete media, ad generationem vitalis spiritus, à facultate insita orta. Componitur ergo ex dilatatione & contractione; quæ cum sint contrariæ, continuari nequeunt. Necesse est ergo quietem mediam intercedere. Quies inter diastolen & systolen, supera vocatur; quæ autem est inter hanc & subsequentem diastolē, infera. Dum aërem ex pulmonibus per venalem arteriam, in sinistrum sinum, deducitur ad temperandum calorem, impletur cor; impletur quoque, dum sanguinem ex vena cava, in sinum dextrum attrahit: at in contractione, fuligines expelluntur; simul etiam ex sinistro sinu, spiritus per universum corpus diffunditur; qui prout augescit, & deficit, vis pulcifica movetur. idem facit in recessu nativi caloris à suâ temperie. Huc pertinet respiratioratio; quæ aut animalis est functio (perficitur enim ope musculorum, motus arbitrarii instrumentorum) aut media inter eam & naturalem. Huius usus est temperies caloris, cordi insiti; ne, scilicet, nimium inflammetur, sed temperetur appulsu frigidi aëris. Sicut pulsus duos contrarios habet motus, ita respiratio, inspirationem & exspirationem; illa frigidus aër ad temperandum calorem attrahitur: ista expelluntur à corde fuligines.
units.tr: This faculty resides in the substance of the heart, established for the generation of vital spirit. Here the vaporous blood contained in the right sinus is made hotter and more spirituous, and by the motion of contraction and dilation it is distributed through the arteries to the whole body. The purpose of this distribution is the increase of the vital heat fixed in the individual members. For, as I said before, the native and fixed heat is not sufficient for the actions of the parts. The heart, the hottest of viscera, therefore imparts something of its innate heat to them; the pulse-motion serves the generation and distribution of the spirits. As for the stirring up of the passions: although it occurs in the heart, it nevertheless depends on appetite and imagination, which are animal functions, just as respiration is partly so; for the motion of the pulse is wholly natural. Three things concur in it: the faculty, the instrument, and the use, or the purpose and necessity that impels the faculty. The action of the heart and arteries is composed of contraction and dilation, with a middle rest intervening, arising from the inborn faculty for the generation of vital spirit. It is therefore made up of dilation and contraction; since these are contrary, they cannot be continuous, so a middle rest must necessarily intervene. The rest between diastole and systole is called the upper, and that between this and the following diastole the lower. While air is drawn from the lungs through the venous artery into the left sinus to temper the heat, the heart is filled; it is filled also while it draws blood from the vena cava into the right sinus. In contraction, the fumes are expelled; at the same time the spirit is diffused from the left sinus through the whole body, and as the pulse-power increases and decreases it is moved. It does the same when the native heat recedes from its temperament. To this belongs respiration, which is either an animal function (for it is performed by the help of the muscles, the voluntary motion of the instruments) or intermediate between that and the natural. Its use is the tempering of the heat implanted in the heart, lest it be inflamed too much, but be tempered by the influx of cool air. Just as the pulse has two contrary motions, so respiration has inspiration and expiration: by the one, cool air is drawn in to temper the heat; by the other, the fumes are expelled from the heart.

units.la: CAP. XI. De facultate Animali.
units.tr: CAP. XI. On the Animal Faculty

units.la: SEquitur tertia, & postrema facultas, animalis; principium motus, sensus, & ex parte intellectionis; quatenus ea phantasiā, sensum nimirū internum, supponit. Alioqui facultas intelligendi, & intellectio, eiusdē functio, nō insident organo, aut determinatæ corporis parti: quia tamen imaginationi, quæ in cerebro est, conjungūtur, fit ut in cerebro subsistat. Cerebrum brum autem principium est & officina spiritus animalis, quo sensus & motus universo corpori, mediantibus nervis, communicantur. Huc spectat uterque appetitus superior, qui voluntas; & inferior, sensitivus dictus, cordi inhærens; à quo proximè excitantur perturbationes. Sentire, sicut & intelligere, est cognoscere: cognitio est repræsentatio rerum in potentiâ cognoscente. Nam potentiâ, cognoscens, ut visus aut intellectus, fit res ipsa cognita; modò tamen spirituali: quemadmodum in speculo videre est, in quo repræsentatio fit rei externæ; modò tamen intentionali. Appetitus versatur circa profequutionem, aut fugam; cuius objectum est tantum bonum: nam malum fugit, non vero appetit. Ut verbo absolvam, facultas ista comprehendit, sensitivam, intellectivam, appetitivam, & locomotivam: quarum functiones obeuntur ministerio spirituum animalium in cerebro genitorum. Instrumentum est nervus, isque duplex; qui à cerebro procedit, sensationis causa, mollior est: qui à spinali medulla, (est autem eiusdem cum cerebro substantiae) durior quidem, sed motui aptior. A cerebro, aut eius basi, septem paria procedunt. à spinali medulla triginta, quae per musculos distributa, motum efficiunt arbitrarium. Ergo spiritus communicantur partibus, non verò facultates, si proprie loquendum est: nam facultas est organo insita, ut visus oculo; sed non potest videre sine spiritu per nervos opticos communicato. Idem judicium esto de aliis facultatibus; quarum objecta, & media melius intelligentur in particulari singulorum sensuum explicatione.
units.tr: Follows the third and last faculty, the animal faculty: the principle of motion and of sensation, and in part of understanding, inasmuch as it presupposes the phantasy, that is, the internal sense. Otherwise the faculty of understanding and understanding itself, its function, do not inhere in an organ or in a determinate part of the body. Yet because they are joined to the imagination, which is in the brain, it comes about that they subsist in the brain. The brain is the principle and workshop of the animal spirit, by which sensation and motion are communicated to the whole body through the nerves. To this belong both appetites: the higher, which is the will, and the lower, called sensitive, which adheres to the heart, and from which the perturbations are most immediately excited. To sense, like to understand, is to know; knowledge is the representation of things in a knowing power. For the knowing power, such as sight or the intellect, becomes the thing known itself, yet in a spiritual mode, just as in a mirror one sees, where a representation of an external thing is made, yet in an intentional mode. Appetite is concerned with pursuit or flight; its object is only good, for it flees evil but does not desire it. To sum up: this faculty comprises the sensitive, the intellective, the appetitive and the locomotive, whose functions are carried out by the ministry of the animal spirits generated in the brain. The instrument is the nerve, and this is twofold. That which proceeds from the brain, for the sake of sensation, is softer; that which comes from the spinal marrow (which is of the same substance as the brain) is harder, but better suited to motion. From the brain, or its base, seven pairs proceed; from the spinal marrow, thirty, which, distributed through the muscles, produce voluntary motion. Therefore the spirits are communicated to the parts, but the faculties are not, if one speaks properly. For a faculty is inherent in an organ, as sight is in the eye, but it cannot see without the spirit communicated through the optic nerves. The same judgment holds for the other faculties, whose objects and means will be better understood in the particular explanation of the individual senses.

units.la: Dividuntur in internos, & externos. hi quinque numero creduntur. Visus, Auditus, Olfactus, Gustus, Tactus: de quibus tanto brevius dicemus, quantò accuratius à Physicis illi considerantur. Et primò visus, omnium mnium nobilissimus, occurrit. cognoscitur (sicut & reliqui sensus) ex relatione ad objectum. Est autem objectum omne visile, color, nimirum, lux, & tertium innominatum, in tenebris lucens, piscis squamma &c; quod tamen ad superiora non incommode reduci potest. Colores generantur ex elementis, non qua calidis, aut frigidis &c. sed quâ perspicuis & opacis. Color visum non movet nisi illuminetur: unde eius actus & forma lumen appellatur; aliqui color in tenebris existit: verum tum non est aptus visum movere. Ipsum lumen in Diaphano non cernitur; est tamen Diaphani seu perspicui quâ tale, forma: nam perspicuum indifferenter se habet ad lumen, & tenebras; at quatenus est medium conveniens, eius actus est lumen. Lumen est lucis quasi intentio. Lux est in corpore lucido; at propagatio eius per medium est lumen. Diximus jam, generari colores ex miftione lucidi, cum opaco: ex quorum varia proporportione resultant colores varii, tam extremi, quam medii. Color immediate non movet visum, verum mediante specie; similitudine nimirum, seu repraesentatione, & signo formali. Iam vero an lumen sit necessarium propter solum obiectum coloratum, an medium, an solum oculum; disputatur: quidam propter omnia, quidam propter solum obiectum necessarium arbitrantur.
units.tr: They are divided into internal and external. The external are believed to be five in number: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. Of these we shall speak the more briefly, the more carefully the physicists have treated them. And first sight, the most noble of all, presents itself. It is known, as the other senses are, from its relation to its object. The object is anything visible: colour, namely, and light, and a third unnamed thing that shines in the dark, such as the scale of a fish, etc.; yet this can conveniently be reduced to the above. Colours are generated from the elements not as hot or cold, etc., but as transparent and opaque. Colour does not move sight unless it is illuminated; hence its act and form is called light. Although colour exists in darkness, then it is not apt to move sight. Light itself is not seen in the diaphanous, yet it is the form of the diaphanous or transparent as such. For the transparent is indifferently related to light and to darkness, but insofar as it is a suitable medium, its act is light.
