Light (lux) is, as it were, the intention of light (lumen): lux is in the luminous body, but its propagation through the medium is lumen. We have already said that colours are generated from a mixture of the luminous with the opaque, and from their varied proportion there result various colours, both the extremes and the intermediate ones. Colour does not move sight immediately, but through the species, that is, the likeness or representation, which is a formal sign. Now whether light is necessary on account of the coloured object alone, or the medium, or the eye alone, is disputed. Some think it necessary for all of these, others for the object alone.

units.la: Sed transeamus ad visionem, quomodo nimirum ea fiat: quam quidam putant solâ radiorum ad obiectum emissione fieri: quidam contra sola specierum receptione: quidam utroque modo. Aristotelis sententia meo judicio maximè est probabilis; nihil scilicet ex oculo ad obiectum procedere, sed contra obiectum per mediam speciem oculum immutare. Nuda tamen speciei receptio non est visio, sed oculus, receptâ specie, (quae concurrit per modum formae actuantis, & determinantis) promit videndi actum, quo obiectum sufficienter repraesenrepræsentatur, oculusque fit res visa; modo tamen spirituali. Instrumentum est oculus, non tamen quęcunq; eius pars, (nam jam diximus, actiones fieri à parte dissimilari, ratione alicuius similaris) sed humor crystallinus, ubi residet facultas: reliquę subserviunt tantum.
units.tr: But let us pass to vision, and how it comes about. Some think it is effected by the emission of rays to the object alone; others by the reception of species alone; others by both. In my judgment the opinion of Aristotle is most probable: nothing proceeds from the eye to the object, but on the contrary the object alters the eye through the intervening species. Yet the bare reception of the species is not vision. Rather, the eye, having received the species (which concurs by way of an actuating and determining form), puts forth the act of seeing, by which the object is sufficiently represented, and the eye becomes the thing seen, yet in a spiritual mode. The instrument is the eye, yet not any part of it whatever (for we have said that actions are performed by a dissimilar part on account of some similar part), but the crystalline humour, where the faculty resides. The rest merely serve.

units.la: Sequitur Auditus, in quo enarrando eundem ordinem servabimus; hoc est, objectum, medium, & organum examinabimus. Sonus est objectum in quod facultas ista fertur; qualitas genita ex aëre colliso inter duo solida corpora. Nam ad perfectissimum sonum, concurrunt duo corpora sese collidentia, & quidem celeriter: tum intermedius aër fractus; cuius, ut dixi, fractionem sequitur sonus. Soni ad aures propagatio, non fit per lineam rectam, quemadmodum in visu, sed per circulare; diffunditurq; eo modo, quo circuli in aquâ ex lapilli injectione. Differentiæ soni maxime pendent ex corporum variâ collisione; nam alij sunt graves, alij acuti.
units.tr: Next is hearing, and in describing it we shall keep the same order: that is, we shall examine the object, the medium and the organ. The object at which this faculty is directed is sound, a quality generated from air struck between two solid bodies. For the most perfect sound, two bodies colliding with each other, and indeed swiftly, must come together; then the intervening air is broken, and, as I said, sound follows its breaking. The propagation of sound to the ears does not occur along a straight line, as in sight, but in a circular way. It spreads in the manner of circles in water when a pebble is thrown into it. The differences of sound depend chiefly on the varied collision of bodies, for some sounds are grave and others acute.

units.la: Differunt sonus, vox, sermo, tanquam superius, & inferius; quod enim à rebus inanimatis fit, sonus tantum est, quod in animalibus brutis ab instrumentis respirationi dicatis, vox est, & ea quidem inarticulata. Verum si eadem sit articulata, sermo erit homini proprius. Fit autem, cum aër ex pulmone in caput asperæ arteriæ impulsus varie colliditur: epiglottis siquidem aërem impulsum repellit & temperat; si enim subito exiret, nuda esset exsufflatio, non vox. Instrumentum est lingua, cui subservient, palatum, dentes, labia, nares &c. Eadem lingua est gustus instrumentum: nam didicimus ex Philosopho, eandem partem variis usibus inservire posse. Atque hæc de objecto, medium, est aqua vel aër, quibus communicatur sonus auditui. Instrumentum est internum, tenuis membrana, aëre plena: non quidem aër, ut voluit Philosophus, sed ut dixi, membrana cui insidet facultas audiendi. Cum ergo receperit seu sonum, num, seu illius speciem, facultas ea imbuta, promit audiendi functio-nem, hoc est audit.
units.tr: Sound, voice and speech differ as higher and lower. What comes from inanimate things is only sound; what in brute animals comes from the instruments dedicated to breathing is voice, and that unarticulated. But if the same is articulated, it will be speech, which is proper to man. This happens when the air, driven from the lung into the head of the windpipe, is variously struck. For the epiglottis repels and tempers the impelled air; if it came out suddenly, it would be a bare blowing out, not a voice. The instrument is the tongue, to which the palate, teeth, lips, nostrils, etc., subserve. The same tongue is the instrument of taste, for we have learned from the Philosopher that the same part can serve various uses. So much concerning the object. The medium is water or air, by which sound is communicated to hearing. The instrument is internal: a thin membrane full of air. It is not the air itself, as the Philosopher held, but, as I said, the membrane in which the faculty of hearing inheres. When therefore it has received the sound, or its species, the faculty, imbued with it, puts forth the function of hearing, that is, it hears.

units.la: Sequitur Olfactus;sensus in homi-ne admodum hebes. Objectum est odor,qui cognoscitur ex analogia ad saporem propter sensus & instru-menti imperfectionem. Quidam putant esse aut exhalationem,aut illi ta-men conjunctam. generatur ex sicco in humido à calore concocto: sicut enim sapor pendet ab humore, ita odor contra à siccitate. Dixi jam hunc sensum in nobis esse hebetem propter organum. Quae causa est imponendi nomina odoribus ex saporibus, qui nobis multo notiores sunt: gustus enim humanus est exquisitissimus. Medium non tantum est aër, sed & aqua, ut in piscibus videre est. Instrumentum, cui inhaeret facultas, est processus mammillaris, in anteriore cerebri parte, prominens.
units.tr: Next is smell, a sense very dull in man. The object is odour, which is known by analogy to taste, on account of the imperfection of the sense and of the instrument. Some think it is either an exhalation or something joined to one. It is generated from the dry in the moist, by heat concocting it: for just as taste depends on moisture, so odour depends on dryness. I have already said that this sense is dull in us on account of the organ. This is the reason why names are given to odours from tastes, which are much better known to us, for the human taste is most exquisite. The medium is not only air but also water, as may be seen in fish. The instrument in which the faculty inheres is the mammillary process, projecting in the anterior part of the brain.

units.la: Sequuntur Gustus, & Tactus, qui nec medium habent, nec speciem repraesentantem objectum, sicut superiores sensus, quemadmodum experientia, philosophiæ magistra, convincit. Officio ergo defungemur, si objectum & organum explicuerimus breviter. Gustus objectum est Sapor; qualitas secunda, genita à calore in humido sicco ; ita tamen, ut superet humidum. Et sapor, & odor, in alimentis sunt illecebrę quibus eorum convenientia exploratur: quanquam odor locum habeat in rebus non nutrientibus. Saporum alii extremi, alii intermedii. Illi ex sententiâ philosophi sunt amarus, & dulcis: Galenus tamen, considerans saporum causas, alios substituit, ponticum nimirum & acutum. Intermedii sapores sunt salsus, acris, austerus, acidus, acerbus. Instrumentum est lingua, & quidem pars interior seu cuspis. Frustra sunt qui aut medium internum, aut speciem hic requirunt.
units.tr: Next come taste and touch, which have neither a medium nor a species representing the object, as the higher senses do, as experience, the teacher of philosophy, proves. We shall therefore discharge our task if we explain the object and the organ briefly. The object of taste is savour, a second quality generated by heat in what is moist and dry, yet so that it exceeds the moist. Both savour and odour in foods are allurements by which their suitability is tested, although odour has its place in things that do not nourish. Of savours, some are extreme and others intermediate. The extremes, according to the opinion of the Philosopher, are bitter and sweet; Galen, however, considering the causes of savours, substituted others, namely pontic and sharp. The intermediate savours are salt, acrid, austere, sour and astringent. The instrument is the tongue, and indeed its inner part or tip. Those are labouring in vain who seek here either an internal medium or a species.

units.la: Tactus sequitur; qui quanquam dignitate sit postremus, necessitate tamen est primus. Hic, ut reliqui, non deposcit peculiare organum, aut parpartem, sed fusus est per universum corpus, si ossa excipias, & cerebrum: quanquam hoc sentire, licet obscurè, contendant quidam. Hic non est multiplex, quemadmodum nonnulli tradidere, sed simplex. quia in omnibus partibus est eadem ratio, idem modus tangendi. Sicut enim vis videndi non est multiplex, licet plures sint colores, quia omnes eodem modo afficiunt visum eumque alterant; ita de tactu judicandum. In omnibus enim partibus eodem modo fit alteratio; nimirum sine medio, aut externo, aut interno, ab iisdem qualitatibus primis, quarum excessus tantum percipiuntur. Reliqui sensus carent qualitatibus iis, quas percipiunt: humor enim crystallinus non est coloratus; nec auris habet in se sonum; aut lingua peculiarem saporem: at tactus, cum sit vitæ fundamentum, consistatque in elementis convenienter temperatis, debet habere in se qualitates primas. quas tamen non percipit eo gradu quo in se habet; id est, manus calida, ut duo, (exempli causa) non percipit objectum eodem modo calidum; verum calidius aut frigidius. & hinc est, quod excessus tantum qualitatum primarum percipere credatur. Objectum est qualitas prima, ad quam exiguntur omnes secundæ tactiles: medium nullum; sicut nec species; quemadmodum in oculo. Porro, hunc sensum, sicut & gustum, homo habet perfectissimum. & quanquam visu, aut olfactu, ab aliis superetur animalibus, tamen eadem superat in hisce duobus, propter exquisitissimam membri temperiem: quesi corrumpatur interitum animali adfert; secus ac in aliis sensibus contingit. Instrumentum est, caro, cutis, membrana; omnis denique pars cui insidet nervus; hic licet facultatem non ferat à cerebro, defert tamen spiritum animalem, sine quo sensatio obiri nequit.
units.tr: Touch comes next. Although it is the last of the senses in rank, it is the first in necessity. Like the others, it does not require a special organ or part of its own, but is spread through the whole body, excepting the bones and the brain, although some contend that these also feel, though obscurely. It is not manifold, as some have taught, but simple, because the same principle and the same mode of touching hold in all parts. For just as the power of sight is not manifold, though there are many colours, since all affect the sight in the same way and alter it, so we must judge of touch. In every part alteration occurs in the same way, namely without any medium, whether external or internal, by the same primary qualities, of which only the excesses are perceived. The other senses lack the qualities they perceive: the crystalline humour is not coloured, the ear does not contain sound, and the tongue does not have a particular taste. But touch, since it is the foundation of life and consists in elements suitably tempered, must have the primary qualities in itself. Yet it does not perceive them to the degree that they are in itself. That is, a hand which is warm, for example, does not perceive the object as equally warm, but as warmer or colder. Hence it is believed that touch perceives only the excesses of the primary qualities. The object is the primary quality, to which all the secondary tactile qualities are reduced. There is no medium, nor any species, as in the eye. Moreover, humans possess this sense, like taste, in the most perfect degree. Although other animals surpass us in sight or smell, we surpass them in these two senses, on account of the most exquisite temperament of the organ. If it is corrupted, it brings death to the animal, unlike what happens with the other senses. The instruments are the flesh, the skin, the membrane, and, in short, every part in which a nerve lies. Although the nerve does not bring its faculty from the brain, it conveys the animal spirit, without which sensation cannot be performed.

units.la: Commune est omni sensui à vehementi sensibili lædi; ut in oculo, à nimio splendore, videre est; auditu etiam iam à sono nimium vehementi.
units.tr: It is common to every sense to be injured by a very strong sensible object; in the eye, one sees this from excessive brightness, and in hearing, from a sound that is too loud.

units.la: Atque hæc de sensibus externis, sequuntur interni: quorum numerus cognoscitur ex operationum varie-tate. Vnde alii plures, alii pauciores fecere; nos duos ponimus; sensu com-munem, & phantasiam; ad quam revocatur memoria. Sensus communis, ita est comparatus ad sensus externos, quemadmodum centrum, ad cir-cumferentiam; estque judex quasi sensuum externorum. Nam oculus judicat quidem de colore, & auditus de sono; verum non potest distin-guere inter colorem & sonum quem ignorat; & tamen nos distinguimus inter illa duo objecta; ergo sensu di-stincto à sensibus externis, quem vo-camus communem. cuius instrumen-tum est cerebrum, inprimis ea pars, unde oriuntur nervi, & communi-cantur spiritus cæteris partibus, sen-sibusque externis. Iudicat autem non de absentibus rebus, sed tantum præ-sentibus, quarum species à sensibus externis ad eum tanquam judicem dedeferuntur. Verũ cum animalia bruta, absentia etiam cognoscant, & de præsentibus, modo aliquo, licet imperfecto discurrant,& ratiocinentur, ut in cane, elephanto videre est;imo quædam fingant, quæ in externum sensum nunquam incurrerunt; functiones hæ à dicta facultate fieri nequeunt. Nec tamen referendæ sunt in intellectum, cum pariter brutis animantibus insint. Reliquum, est ut à phantasia oriantur. Hæc facultas est media inter intellectum, & sensum communem: nam,ut dixi, discurrit, & ratiocinatur, speciesque à sensu communi ad se transmissas componit inter se, & versat. In bruto est suprema facultas,in homine non item; sed mens, cui tamen proximè & immediate ancillatur. Sedes, est cerebrum. Huc pertinet memoria:(nec enim est nova facultas) eadem enim vis, & species retinet,& retentis utitur. Verum quidem est memorandi actum esse rei præteritæ & antea cognitæ repetitionem; sed quid quæso necesse est
units.tr: So much for the external senses. The internal senses follow, whose number is known from the variety of their operations. Hence some have posited more, others fewer. We posit two: the common sense and the phantasy, to which memory is referred. The common sense is related to the external senses as the centre is to the circumference, and it is, as it were, the judge of the external senses. For the eye judges indeed of colour, and the ear of sound, but it cannot distinguish between colour and sound, which it does not know; and yet we do distinguish between those two objects. Therefore there is a sense distinct from the external senses, which we call common. Its instrument is the brain, especially that part from which the nerves arise and through which spirits are communicated to the other parts and to the external senses. It judges not of absent things but only of present ones, whose species are conveyed by the external senses to it as judge. But since brute animals also know absent things, and reason in some manner, though imperfectly, about present ones, as can be seen in the dog and the elephant, indeed even imagine certain things which never fell under an external sense, these functions cannot be performed by that faculty. Nor, however, are they to be referred to the intellect, since they likewise belong to brute animals. It remains that they arise from the phantasy. This faculty is intermediate between the intellect and the common sense: for, as I said, it runs to and fro and reasons, and it combines and handles the species transmitted to it from the common sense. In brutes it is the highest faculty; in man it is not so, but the mind is, to which it nevertheless serves as handmaid, immediately and nearby. Its seat is the brain. To this belongs memory (for it is not a new faculty), since the same power both retains the species and uses what has been retained. It is true that the act of remembering is the repetition of a past and previously known thing; but why, I ask, is it necessary

units.la: E est statuere novam facultatem distinctam à phantasia? Atque hæc de sensibus internis, sensu communi & phantasiâ, quam Medici inter principes facultates numerant.
units.tr: to posit a new faculty distinct from the phantasy? So much for the internal senses, the common sense and the phantasy, which physicians rank among the principal faculties.

units.la: Porro ad sensum communem, tum Medici tum Philosophi referunt somnum, & vigilias; has tanquam habitum, illum ut tanquam privationem. Vigilare dicitur animal, cū sensuum externorum functiones obit. sicut contra cessatio ab huiusmodi operatione, somnus est. Cessatio hic non est quælibet, sicut in veterno, & commate, dispositionibus scilicet morbosis: sed naturalis affectus & consequens vigilias: earum siquidem tempore spiritus animalis consumitur, qui ut reparetur, quiescendum est animali. Cerebrum ergo, perfusum benigno vapore, non potest sensibus externis communicare spiritus; (via enim obstruitur) quod impedimentum est somnus. Quod tamen non est ita accipiendum, quasi nulli prorsus spiritus à cerebro diffundantur: (nam vide-
units.tr: Moreover, both physicians and philosophers refer sleep and waking to the common sense; they treat waking as a habit and sleep as a privation. An animal is said to be awake when it performs the functions of the external senses, and sleep is the cessation of such operation. This cessation is not any kind whatever, as in lethargy and coma, which are morbid dispositions, but a natural affection following upon waking. For during waking the animal spirit is consumed, and in order that it may be restored the animal must rest. Therefore the brain, bathed in a gentle vapour, cannot communicate spirits to the external senses, since the way is obstructed; this obstruction is sleep. Yet this should not be understood as meaning that no spirits at all flow out from the brain

units.la: videmus dormientes respirare; loqui, interdum ambulare, ) sed quia non tam sufficientes, quam requiruntur in externorum sensuum actionibus rite obeundis. Quod si phantasia species & imagines in cerebro secundum quietem versec, & considerret; generabitur somnium, idque animale. Credibile admodum est homines in somnio ea maximè cogitare, quæ interdiu tractare solent.
units.tr: (for we see sleepers breathe, speak, and sometimes walk), but that they are not as sufficient as are required for the proper performance of the actions of the external senses. If the phantasy turns over and considers the species and images in the brain during rest, a dream is generated, and an animal one. It is quite credible that men in dreams chiefly think of those things which they are accustomed to handle by day.

units.la: Quanquam intelligendi vis, non insideat corpori, quemadmodum superiores de quibus egimus; quia tamen eius functio pendet à phantasię, aliorumque sensuum ministerio; ordo poscit, ut eam perstringamus leviter. Est autem potentia intelligendi, eadem cum mente, & ratione; nam varia habet nomina ex modo operandi. Intellectus hic patiens, (non agens, qui non intelligit) est sedes omnium habituum intellectualium, scientiæ, artis &c. suprema in homine facultas: nec habet determinatum: aliquod objectum, ut oculus colorem, rem, sed indifferenter omnia cognoscit; materialia, immaterialia, substantias, accidentia; quanquam objectum maximè proportionatum sit res sensibilis. Potentiæ sensitivæ à vehementi sensibili lædalthough... color illuminatus in oculum. Comparatur à Philosopho lumini eâdem de causa. Nam sicut lumen colores actuat, efficitque ut videantur ; ita intellectus agens junctus phantasmatis, facit illa intelligibilia. Intellectui huic patienti respondet proprius appetitus, qui voluntas seu liberum arbitrium, dicitur. Appetitus, ut dixi, non cognoscit, sed cognitionem sequitur; proinde objectum est bonum, à ratione monstratum & propositum. Duæ hæ potentiæ sunt universales respectu objecti ; nec enim more aliarum facultatum determinatum sibi poscunt. Suntque etiam immateriales, nec organum aliquod poscunt quia tamen voluntas pendet ab intellectu, hic verò à phantasia; (quæ si lædatur, vitiatur & intellectio ut in furioso videre est) fit ut per accidens domicilium poscant cerebrum.
units.tr: Although the power of understanding does not inhere in the body, as the higher faculties of which we have spoken do, nevertheless, since its function depends on the phantasy and the service of the other senses, order requires that we touch on it lightly. The power of understanding is the same as the mind and reason; it has various names according to its mode of operating. The passive intellect (not the agent, which does not understand) is the seat of all intellectual habits, of science, of art, and so on, and is the highest faculty in man. It has no determinate object, as the eye has colour, but knows all things indifferently: material and immaterial things, substances and accidents, although the most proportionate object of it is the sensible thing. The sensitive powers are injured by a vehement sensible object, although the coloured object, illuminated, strikes the eye. The Philosopher compares it to light for the same reason: for as light actuates colours and makes them visible, so the agent intellect, joined to the phantasm, makes those things intelligible. To this passive intellect corresponds its own appetite, which is called the will or free choice. Appetite, as I said, does not know but follows knowledge; therefore its object is the good, shown and proposed by reason. These two powers are universal with respect to their object; for they do not, as the other faculties do, demand a determinate object for themselves. They are also immaterial, and they require no organ. Yet since the will depends on the intellect, and the intellect on the phantasy (which, if it is injured, is also vitiated, as is seen in the madman), it comes about that by accident they require the brain as their dwelling.

units.la: Porrò virtutes morales, fortitudo, temperantia, aliæque huic insunt, non appetitui sensitivo: cui tamen perturbationes, amor, ira, odium, insunt. sunt. appetitus sensitivus eodem modo se habet ad phantasiam, quo voluntas ad intellectum; sedes tamen est cor, cui perturbationes inhærent. videmus enim eas cum motu cordis intendi & remitti. Quod enim vis concupiscibilis dicatur residere in hepate, nihil est: nullus enim motus, aut actio animalis inde oritur, sed à corde tantum. Porrò facultas locomotiva est musculis insita; quæ tamen non potest se expedire sine spiritu animali per nervos à cerebro communicato. Quâ de causa cerebrum dicitur, sedes facultatis animalis. Quod non est ita intelligendum, quasi vis illa animæ, seu facultas à cerebro per nervos communicetur: nam, ut dixi, hæc suo organo est insita; sed quia non exit in actum sine spiritu animali, cuius vehiculum est nervus, cuius ut loquuntur, irradiatione, influit cerebrum in subjecta membra. Ad motum localem plura concurrunt: primo quidem appetitus, tanquam movens proximè facultatem tatem motricem; verum cum facul- tas hæc cœca sit, dirigitur à phantasiâ & intellectu. Bruta enim animantia tantum habent appetitum sensitivum, & phantasiam; homo præter ista, intellectum & voluntatem. Ergo directio est à potentiâ cognoscente, appetitus vero movet membra, ad quæ à cerebro confluunt spiritus animales, quibus instructa moventur in hunc, aut illum locum. Atque hæc quidem breviter de primâ Medicinæ parte; quam tanto leviore brachio absolvi, quanto magis ad Philosophiam spectat.
units.tr: Moreover, the moral virtues, fortitude, temperance, and the rest, inhere not in the sensitive appetite but in the will; yet the perturbations, love, anger, hatred, inhere in the sensitive appetite. The sensitive appetite stands to the phantasy in the same way as the will stands to the intellect; its seat, however, is the heart, in which the perturbations inhere. For we see that these are increased and relaxed together with the motion of the heart. That the concupiscible power is said to reside in the liver is nonsense: no motion or action of the animal arises from there, but only from the heart. Moreover, the locomotive faculty is implanted in the muscles, yet it cannot put itself into action without the animal spirit communicated from the brain through the nerves. For this reason the brain is said to be the seat of the animal faculty. This should not be understood as meaning that that power of the soul, or faculty, is communicated from the brain through the nerves; for, as I said, it is implanted in its own organ. Rather, it does not pass into act without the animal spirit, whose vehicle is the nerve, and by whose so-called irradiation the brain flows into the limbs placed under it. Several things concur in local motion: first, the appetite, as the proximate mover of the motive faculty; but since this faculty is blind, it is directed by the phantasy and the intellect. For brute animals have only the sensitive appetite and the phantasy; man has, besides these, the intellect and the will. Therefore the direction comes from the cognitive power, while the appetite moves the limbs, to which the animal spirits flow from the brain, and by which they are equipped to move to this or that place. So much, briefly, on the first part of medicine, which I have completed with a lighter arm the more it belongs to philosophy.

units.la: Finis Libri primi,
units.tr: End of the First Book,

units.la: LIBER II. De morbis, eorumq; Differentiis.
units.tr: BOOK II. On diseases and their differences.

units.la: CAP. I. De Morbi definitione.
units.tr: CHAPTER I. On the definition of disease.

units.la: INgredimur primùm Medicinam, quæ enim diximus libro superiore, physica magis sunt, quam medica; qua de causa negligentius ea tractavimus: sequitur Pathologia; in quâ de morbis eorumq; differentiis, agetur; de rebus nimirum contra naturam; morbo scilicet, causa, & symptomate. sicut in superiore ea, quibus corpus humanum constat, complexi sumus; quæ propterea vocantur res naturales. Contraria nata sunt idem subjectum respicere; ita virtutes & vitia voluntatem, tanquam subjectum informant, è quo se expellunt. Sanitas, & morbus, cum sint dispositiones contrariæ; idem necessarium cessariò habebunt subjectum: jam vero sanitatis subjectum est corpus animatum; non humor, non spiritus, res inanimes: eidem ergo & morbus inerit. Sanitas est ea corporis constitutio; quâ functiones omnes, naturales, vitales, animales inculpatè obeuntur; cui cum repugnet morbus; erit necessariò actionis alicuius impedimentum, seu dispositio contra naturam actionem impediens. Quod non est ita accipiendum, quasi sanitas sit ipsa corporis inculpata functio: sed est ea corporis constitutio à quâ actiones inculpatè procedunt: quando nimirum partes tam similares, quam dissimilares habent dispositionem naturæ convenientem. Unde organum sanum convenienter agit: ægrum autem, aut morbidū inconvenienter. Sicut sanitas non est ipsa actio; (nā dormientes etiamsi nihil agāt, sani tamen sunt,) ita morbus non est lesa actio, sed eius causa & principium.
units.tr: We now come first to pathology, since the things we discussed in the previous book are more physical than medical, and for that reason we treated them rather carelessly. Next follows pathology, in which we shall treat of diseases and their differences, that is, of things contrary to nature: namely disease, its cause, and its symptom. Just as in the previous book we dealt with the things of which the human body consists, which for that reason are called natural things, so here we take up what is against nature. Contraries are by nature apt to inhere in the same subject: thus virtues and vices shape the will as their subject, and from it they drive each other out. Health and disease, since they are contrary dispositions, must of necessity have the same subject. Now the subject of health is the animate body, not the humours or the spirits, which are inanimate things; therefore disease also must inhere in the same. Health is that constitution of the body by which all its functions, natural, vital and animal, are performed without fault; since disease opposes this, it must necessarily be an impediment to some action, or a disposition contrary to nature that hinders action. This is not to be understood as if health were the faultless function of the body itself; rather it is that constitution of the body from which actions proceed without fault, namely when both the similar and the dissimilar parts have a disposition agreeing with nature. Hence a sound organ acts suitably, while a diseased or sick organ acts unsuitably. Just as health is not the action itself (for those who are asleep, though they do nothing, are nonetheless healthy), so disease is not the impaired action but its cause and origin.

units.la: Est autem morbus dispositio animati corporis, præter naturam, per se primò actionem manifeste lædens. Dico præter naturam ; ut removeatur impotentia naturalis;nemo enim dixerit oculum malè videre, si in tenebris non videat : aut ventriculum male concoquere, si lapidem in chylum non commutet : sunt enim impotentiæ naturales ab ortu homini sano insitæ : idem hic est præter naturam, & contra naturam. Dico animati; ut innuam morbi subjectum: cum enim sanitas sit in membro bene habente, ita contra morbus in eodem membro erit, malè tamen habente. constat verò membra esse animata, sicut & aliæ partes solidæ: & quanquam humores efficiant morbos, nunquam ipsi dicuntur in se eos recipere, aut eorum esse subjecta. Dico manifestè lædens &c.ut leves in corpore dispositiones removeantur: nec enim dicitur febricitare, si præter modum quispiam ludendo incaleat; si modo calor sit in fieri, non autem in facto esse. alioqui si leves huiusmodi dispositiones haberi debent pro morbis, introducetur ἀνάπνοια, tantopere à Galeno explosa; omnibus siquidem constat magnam esse sanitatis latitudinem, nec in indivisibili positam esse. Dico tandem per se primò; ut excludamus causam, quæ lædit actionem, sed mediante morbo. Quanquam quidam putant differentiam poni inter læsionem eam quæ fit ex consensu, & quæ per essentiam parti inest. Duobus modis contingit actionem quampiam lædi; aut quia pars ledens actionem, est in se ipsa læsa, ut in febre hectica, cor: aut quia consentit parti alicui læsæ; sicut dolet caput ex intemperie ventriculi. Quod tribus modis contingit; aut quia communicatur illud, quod non debebat communicari, ut in dicto exemplo: aut quia non communicatur, quod debebat communicari; ut spina male affecta facit digiti resolutionem, quia impeditur spiritus animalis, & intercipitur: ita vulnera thoracis impediunt vocem, quia eius materia, aër, per vulnus efflaefflatur, nec communicatur quod debebat communicari. Itaque quando pars ipsa in se est affecta, sine alterius consensu, tum propriè morbidam esse & ægrotare veteres dicebant: verum si pars ex consensu prius laborans, recipiat dispositionem constanter, tum non laborat ex consensu; quia curata alia parte, à quâ processit, adhuc perseverat. Morbus interdum est morbi causa; sicut peripneumonia, phrenitis, efficiunt febrim ex propriâ naturâ recipientiũ & agentium partium. Interdum ex partium connexione, & societate; quomodo ventriculus per nervos vapores ad cerebrum transmittit. Nonnunquam situs partium in causa est: quomodo asthma generatur ex cerebri excrementis. & membra superiora supermittunt ad inferiores humores demittunt ad inferiora. Quid? quod membra valida exonerant se in debiliora, eaque præter naturam male disponunt. Porro frustra Argenterius carpit Galeni definitionem morbi: putat enim eum non primò læderc actionem, sed facultatem: Quasi vero ista pugnent? nam lædit facultatem, tanquam forma male disponens; sicut intemperantia lædit voluntatem, tanquam vitiosa forma; lædit actionem quoque; sed in genere causæ efficientis; efficit enim malam actionem.
units.tr: Now disease is a disposition of an animate body, contrary to nature, which of itself and primarily manifestly impairs action. I say "contrary to nature" in order to remove natural inability; for no one would say that the eye sees badly if it does not see in the dark, or that the stomach digests badly if it does not turn a stone into chyle; these natural inabilities are implanted in a healthy man from birth, so this is not contrary to nature. I say "animate" to indicate the subject of disease: since health is in a well-disposed member, disease in the same member will be in one that is ill-disposed. It is certain that the members are animate, as are the other solid parts; and although humours produce diseases, they are never said to receive them in themselves, or to be their subjects. I say "manifestly impairing", so that slight dispositions in the body are removed; for a man is not said to have fever if he grows warm at play beyond the usual measure, provided the heat is in becoming and not in being. Otherwise, if such slight dispositions were to be counted as diseases, there would be introduced an anapnoia [ἀνάπνοια], so greatly scorned by Galen; for everyone agrees that there is a wide latitude of health, and that it is not placed in an indivisible point. I say finally "primarily and of itself", so that we exclude a cause which impairs action but through the mediation of a disease. Although some think a difference is to be drawn between an injury that arises from sympathy and one that inheres in the part by its essence. An action can be impaired in two ways: either because the part that impairs the action is itself injured, as the heart in hectic fever; or because it sympathises with some injured part, as the head aches from a disorder of the stomach. This happens in three ways: either because what ought not to be communicated is communicated, as in the example given; or because what ought to be communicated is not communicated, as when a diseased spine causes the loss of movement in a finger, since the animal spirit is impeded and cut off; so wounds of the chest impair the voice, because its matter, air, escapes through the wound and what ought to be communicated is not. Therefore, when a part is affected in itself, without the sympathy of another, the ancients said that it is properly diseased and sick; but if a part that was previously suffering from sympathy takes on a disposition that persists, then it is no longer suffering from sympathy, because even when the other part from which it arose has been cured, it still persists. Sometimes a disease is the cause of another disease, as peripneumonia and phrenitis produce fever from the proper nature of the parts that receive and act. Sometimes it is through the connection and fellowship of the parts; thus the stomach sends vapours to the brain through the nerves. Sometimes the position of the parts is the cause: thus asthma is generated from excrements of the brain, and the upper members send down humours to the lower, and the lower ones send them up. What more? Strong members discharge themselves into weaker ones and dispose them badly, contrary to nature. Moreover, Argenterius carps at Galen's definition of disease in vain: he thinks that it impairs not primarily the action but the faculty. As if these things were at odds! For it impairs the faculty as a badly disposing form, just as intemperance impairs the will as a vicious form; it impairs the action too, but in the genus of efficient cause, for it produces a bad action.

units.la: CAP. II. De Morborum divisione.
units.tr: CAP. II. On the division of diseases.

units.la: COgnitâ morbi essentiâ, reliquum est ut eius differentias persequamur. Quod tamen priusquam fiat, difficultas quædam est removenda. Sanitas & morbus sibi mutuò contrariantur. Ergo quot modis dicitur morbus, tot sanitas dicetur: quod tamen falsum videtur; cum sanitas non dividatur in alias species distinctas, sicut morbus. Respondeo sanitatem eodem prorsus modò dividi quo morbum; verum quia laboramus verborum penuriâ, species usurpant generis sui nomen. Consistit enim sanitas in conveniente dispositione,
units.tr: Having grasped the essence of disease, it remains to pursue its differences. Yet before this is done, a certain difficulty must be removed. Health and disease are mutually contrary. Therefore as many ways as disease is spoken of, so many ways will health be spoken of; which however seems false, since health is not divided into other distinct species as disease is. I reply that health is divided in exactly the same way as disease, but because we labour under a lack of words, the species borrow the name of their genus. For health consists in a suitable disposition,

units.la: quæ multiplex existit : alia enim est dispositio cerebri secundùm naturam, alia hepatis, alia cordis, non tantum in qualitatibus activis, sed & passivis. Idem de partium conformatione judicium esto. Nam sicut singulis inest sua temperies ; ita & partium figura, magnitudo, situs &c. Morborum differentiæ aliæ sunt essentiales, desumptæ nimirum à rei essentia; aliæ accidentales; quas tamen Medici suis usibus accommodarunt. Cum itaque sanitas corporis consistat in bonâ partium similarium temperie, organorum convenienti dispositione, in numero, situ, figura &c. & partium utrarumque unitate naturalique conjunctione ; oriuntur necessariò primæ morborum species, habentes differentias essentiales.Partium similarium est intemperies;quę totuplex est, quotuplex est qualitas prima, alia calida, frigida, humida, sicca;atque hæc prima est morbi species. Secunda est partium dissimilarium mala conformatio vel compositio tio; Tertia unitatis solutio.
units.tr: which exists in many forms. For the disposition of the brain is one thing according to nature, another of the liver, another of the heart, and this holds not only for active but also for passive qualities. Let the same judgment be made concerning the conformation of the parts. For just as each part has its own temperament, so also has its shape, size, position and so on. The differences of diseases are some essential, namely those taken from the essence of the thing, and others accidental, which nonetheless physicians have adapted to their own uses. Since therefore the health of the body consists in a good temperament of the similar parts, in a suitable arrangement of the organs in number, position, shape and so on, and in the unity and natural conjunction of both kinds of parts, the first species of disease necessarily arise, having essential differences. Intemperance of the similar parts is one; it is as many-fold as the first quality is: hot, cold, moist, dry. This is the first species of disease. The second is the bad conformation or composition of the dissimilar parts. The third is the dissolution of unity.

units.la: Divisionis ratio inde constat. Morbus omnis est dispositio praeter naturam; jam intemperies calida est praeter naturam, est enim caloris excessus: ita prava compositio est praeter naturam, ut si membrum insigniter fit magnum, aut parvum. idem statuendum de unitatis solutione; quanquam species subjectae non ita distinguantur, sicut in solutione unitatis, musculi, & nervi videre est. Caeterum divisio febris in biliosam, pituitosam &c. est commoda usibus medicis, non tamen procedit per differentias essentiales, sed accidentales: nec enim variatur calor sive sit in pituita, sive in sanguine, sive aqua. idem judicium esto de morbo longo, & brevi. Sed ad rem.
units.tr: The reason for this division follows from what has been said. Every disease is a disposition contrary to nature. Now hot intemperance is contrary to nature, for it is an excess of heat; so too a faulty composition is contrary to nature, as when a limb becomes remarkably large or small. The same should be held concerning the dissolution of unity, although the subordinate species are not so clearly distinguished there, though in the dissolution of unity one can see muscles and nerves. Moreover, the division of fever into bilious, pituitous and so on is convenient for medical uses, but it does not proceed by essential differences, only accidental ones: for the heat does not vary whether it is in phlegm, in blood, or in water. The same judgment should be made of long and short disease. But let us return to the matter.

units.la: Temperies, sicut & intemperies, debentur parti similari; cuius & est conditio ut totum, & pars quaevis idem habeant temperamentum. quando ergo elementorum proportio est violata, ita ut pars depravatè agat, oritur morbus similaris. Exempli causa ; in corde si calor superet reliquas qualitates, aut calor & siccitas, oritur febris : & quia sunt quatuor temperamenta simplicia, & totidem composita,tot erunt morbi similares.
units.tr: Temperament, as well as intemperance, belongs to the similar part, and it is its condition that the whole and any part of it have the same temperament. When therefore the proportion of the elements is violated, so that the part acts in a depraved way, a similar disease arises. For example, in the heart, if heat exceeds the other qualities, or heat and dryness do, fever arises. And since there are four simple temperaments and as many composite ones, there will be as many similar diseases.

units.la: Secundum genus morbi est mala compositio,estque quadruplex; conformationis nimirum , numeri , magnitudinis, situs.
units.tr: The second genus of disease is bad composition, and it is fourfold: namely of conformation, number, magnitude and position.

units.la: Quod ad primam speciem attinet, conformationem scilicet;ea comprehendit tres species, quarum prima est vitiata figura ; ut si pars quæ secundum naturam recta ille debet,incurvetur, aut contra, ut in claudis videre est. Secunda est vitiata superficies ; quando scilicet pars quæ debebat esse levis , est aspera, aut contra. illius exemplum est in faucibus ab acri catarrho obsessis ; huius in lienteria. Tertia species est in cavitatibus ; quando scilicet partes nimium aut contrahuntur,aut dilatantur.Non incommodè referri potest huc vitiatus color humoris aquei in oculis icte-
units.tr: As for the first species, namely conformation, this comprises three species. The first is a vitiated shape, as when a part which by nature ought to be straight is bent, or the reverse, as is seen in the lame. The second is a vitiated surface, when a part which ought to be smooth is rough, or the reverse. An example of the former is in the throat beset by sharp catarrh; of the latter, in lientery. The third species is in the cavities, when the parts are either contracted or dilated too much. Not inappropriately the vitiated colour of the aqueous humour in the eyes of the jaundiced may be referred here,

units.la: bi[?]&tericorum. nam laedit actionem. debebat enim oculus naturaliter tali colore destitui: nec audiendus est Valesius aliter distinguens.
units.tr: for it harms the action. For the eye ought naturally to be devoid of such a colour. Nor is Valesius to be heeded, who distinguishes otherwise.

units.la: Secundum genus morbi organici est ex nuneri vitio; quando scilicet pars aliqua deficit, aut redundat. Re-dundantia ista non tantum est intel-ligenda in parte aliquâ integrâ, ut sexto digito, tertio teste: sed etiam in parte adnascente organo naturali; ut polypus, lumbrici, calculi: respe-ctu enim partis cui insident, eius structuram laedunt, suâq; praesentiâ actiones laedunt. deficit membrum in mu-tilato.
units.tr: The second genus of organic disease arises from a fault of number, when some part is either lacking or redundant. This redundancy is to be understood not only of an entire part, such as a sixth finger or a third testicle, but also of a part growing upon a natural organ, such as polyps, worms or stones. For with respect to the part on which they sit, they damage its structure, and by their presence they harm its actions. A part is lacking in the mutilated.

units.la: Tertium genus morbi organici nascitur magnitudiuis vitio; quando pars non habet justam magnitudi-nem, sed est aut justo maior, aut mi-nor: huc pertinent tumores partium, oedema, scirrus.
units.tr: The third genus of organic disease arises from a fault of magnitude, when a part does not have its proper size but is either larger or smaller than it should be. To this belong swellings of parts, oedema and scirrhus.

units.la: Postremum genus est in vitiato si-tu, cum scilicet membra non habent naturalem locum; ut procidentia ute-ri, pedis luxatio. huc pertinet membrobrorum consensus, & debita connexio, quæ si violetur morbus erit. ut si labia coalescant &c.
units.tr: The last genus lies in a faulty position, when the members do not have their natural place, as in prolapse of the uterus or dislocation of the foot. To this belongs also the loss of the consensus of the members and of their due connection; if this is violated, there will be disease, as when the lips grow together and so on.

units.la: Tertium morbi genus est solutio continui, communis parti tum similari, tum dissimilari: utraque enim, ut inculpatè functiones obeat, requirit partium unionem. Hoc genus continet varias species & differentias, pro partis affectæ diversitate, & causarum natura. si enim subjectum consideres, carnem; vulnus, ulcus ei tribuitur: ossibus, fissura, fractura; nervis convulsio. Sin causam spectes; est vulnus à re incidente, secante.
units.tr: The third genus of disease is solution of continuity, common to both similar and dissimilar parts, for each, in order to perform its functions without fault, requires the union of its parts. This genus contains various species and differences, according to the diversity of the affected part and the nature of the causes. If you consider the subject, namely flesh, a wound or ulcer is attributed to it; to bones, a fissure or fracture; to nerves, convulsion. If you look at the cause, it is a wound from a cutting, incising thing.

units.la: Non ignoro magnum authorem addere præterea morbos formæ & materiæ: sed frustra; nam materiæ morbi referuntur ad pravam compositionem idque facillime. Morbi formæ nulli sunt distincti à morbis similaribus. nisi mavis formam substantialem immediatè lædi, non læso temperamento; quod inauditum est. ergo temperamento partis integro, & figura quoque, lædituraction ex solo formæ vitio; quod falsum est. nam si de homine loquimur, illius forma lędi non potest; est enim immortalis. Sed plura dicere hoc loco, ob propositam brevitatem non licet.
units.tr: I am not unaware that a great author adds, besides these, diseases of form and of matter, but in vain. For the diseases of matter are referred to bad composition, and very easily so. Diseases of form are not distinct from similar diseases, unless you prefer to say that the substantial form is harmed immediately while the temperament is not harmed; which is unheard of. Therefore, with the temperament of the part intact, and its figure too, the action would be harmed by a fault of form alone; which is false. For if we speak of man, his form cannot be harmed, for it is immortal. But to say more on this point is not permitted, because of the brevity I have proposed.

units.la: Nec sunt simplicissima morborum genera, ex quibus conjunctis oriuntur morbi compositi. Variis autem modis componuntur: interdum similares, cum similaribus; interdum similares cum morbis organicis, aut solutione continui. exempla sunt obvia.
units.tr: Nor are the simplest genera of diseases such that compound diseases arise from their conjunction. They are compounded in various ways: sometimes similar with similar, sometimes similar with organic diseases or with solution of continuity. Examples are obvious.

units.la: Dixi præter differentias morborum essentiales, de quibus jam egi, esse alias accidentarias, convenientes tamen medicis usibus; quales sunt quæ petuntur à morborum consequentibus, causis, subjectis, quæ omnia sunt extra essentiam morbi. ac primo ratione magnitudinis (est autem magnitudo recessus magnus à naturali constitutione, ut in ardente febre caloris immodica intentio & incrementum) magnus alius, alius parvus morbus erit; qui æstimantur
units.tr: I have said that, besides the essential differences of diseases, of which I have already treated, there are other accidental differences, nevertheless suited to medical uses. Such are those taken from the consequences, causes and subjects of diseases, all of which lie outside the essence of disease. First, by reason of magnitude (magnitude is a large departure from the natural constitution, as in an ardent fever with the immoderate intensity and increase of heat), one disease will be great and another small, as they are estimated

units.la: & cognoscuntur ex adjunctis sym-ptomatis. ergo magnus morbus magna habet symptomata ; parvus contra; quanquam in definiendâ magnitudine, non omnes consentiant. Interdum magnus morbus dicitur qui suâ essentiâ & naturâ est talis, ut apoplexia: magnum enim vitæ minatur periculum. Interdum morbi magnitudo æstimatur ex præstantia & necessitate affectæ partis, ut vulnus cordis, aut jecoris. Si enim vulnus sit in parte ignobili, est parvus morbus; at idem in membris prædictis magnus erit. Quid? quod morbi maligni interdum magni dicuntur, ut pestis. Aduratione (est autem permanentia seu continuatio morbi in esse ut loquuntur præhabito) nova oritur morborum accidentaria divisio in longos & breves. hi cito finiuntur, ut diaria febris, pestis: illi diutius durant, ut elephantiasis. Si morbus sit & brevis & magnus, dicitur acutus: cuius magna est varietas. Dividitur enim in peracutum, acutum um simpliciter, & ex decidentiâ acutum, sive ἐξ μεταπτώσεως. Tum peracutus in exquisitè talem, & minus exquisitè: ille velocissime moretur ac tertio nimirum aut quarto die subeunte; ut pestis, apoplexia: hic ad septimum cunctatur. Acutus simpliciter perdurat 14. dies: si non sit exquisitè acutus, ad 20. protrahitur. at acutus ex decidentiâ, vel degeneratione, ad 40. diem extenditur. Qui vero diutius durant, longi dicuntur & chronici.
units.tr: and recognised from the accompanying symptoms. Therefore a great disease has great symptoms, a small one the contrary; although in defining magnitude not all agree. Sometimes a disease is called great which by its essence and nature is such, as apoplexy, for it threatens great danger to life. Sometimes the magnitude of a disease is judged from the excellence and necessity of the affected part, as a wound of the heart or of the liver. For if the wound is in an ignoble part, it is a small disease, but the same wound in the aforesaid members will be great. Moreover, malignant diseases are sometimes called great, as the plague. By duration (duration being the continuance of the disease in being, as they say, previously held) a new accidental division arises into long and short diseases. The short ones are quickly ended, as quotidian fever and the plague; the long ones last longer, as elephantiasis. If a disease is both short and great, it is called acute, and of acute diseases there is great variety. For it is divided into peracute, acute simply, and acute from decline, or by transition [ἐκ μεταπτώσεως]. Then the peracute is divided into the exquisitely such and the less exquisitely such: the former runs its course very swiftly, namely on the third or fourth day as it approaches, as plague and apoplexy do; the latter lingers to the seventh day. The acute simply lasts fourteen days; if it is not exquisitely acute, it is protracted to twenty. But the acute from decline, or degeneration, extends to the fortieth day. Those which last longer are called long, or chronic.

units.la: Sciendum hîc; quemadmodum in ætatibus, ita in morbis variæ sunt mutationes, dependentes à causis morbificis; unde emergunt morborum tempora, principium, augmentum, status & declinatio. Quatuor hæc tempora vel sunt universalia respectu totius morbi; vel particularia respectu partis alicuius in morbo; quemadmodum videre est in febribus intermittentibus. Principium morbi variè definiri solet; nos tempus vocabimus quo morbi causa manifestè nifestè & sensibiliter lædere incipit Augmentum ; quando causæ vehe-mentius agunt , morbusque crescere incipit, tumque natura manifestè re-sistit. Status morbi ( aliter in ætati-bus à quibusdam usurpatur) quando est lucta vehementissima inter facul-tatem, & morbum; quo tempore vi-gent symptomata. Postremo est de-clinatio,in quâ morbo profligato na-tura victrix evadit. Postremum hoc tempus locum habet in solis morbis salutaribus : nam si lethalis sit , nulla erit declinatio , in quâ non moriun-tur ægri, sed in augmento , aut alio tempore. Non omnes morbi habent eiusmodi tempora ; sed illi soli qui non remittunt, sed à principio ad fi-nem continenter moventur. Quibus vero in morbis est aut intermissio aut remissio , habent præter illa qua-tuor , totidem in singulis paroxismis tempora particularia ; ut in tertiana intermittente videre est.
units.tr: It should be noted here that, just as there are changes in the ages of life, so too in diseases there are various changes, depending on the morbific causes; from these arise the times of diseases: beginning, increase, state, and decline. These four times are either universal, with respect to the whole disease, or particular, with respect to some part of the disease, as can be seen in intermittent fevers. The beginning of a disease is defined in various ways; we will call it the time when the cause of the disease begins to injure clearly and perceptibly. The increase is when the causes act more violently, the disease begins to grow, and then nature clearly resists. The state of the disease (which some use differently in the case of ages) is when there is the most violent struggle between the faculty and the disease; at this time the symptoms are strong. Lastly comes the decline, in which, the disease having been overcome, nature emerges victorious. This last time occurs only in salutary diseases; for if the disease is lethal, there will be no decline in which the sick do not die, but they die in the increase or at another time. Not all diseases have such times, but only those which do not remit, but proceed continuously from beginning to end. In those diseases, however, which have intermission or remission, there are, besides those four, as many particular times in each paroxysm; as can be seen in tertian intermittent fever.

units.la: Dividitur quoque morbus in con-tinuum & intermittentem. Ille con-tinuc continuò affligit, nec intermittit. Quod si non modò continuo affligat, sed etiam sine omni remissione, est morbus continens, ut synochus: at si per intervalla & certas periodos remittat, morbus est simpliciter continuus; ut tertiana continua. Intermittens ad perfectam integritatem solet devenire, & intermissionem, ut tertiana intermittens. Itaque huiusmodi morbi quinque habent tempora. nimirum ipsam intermissionem, & quatuor tempora particularia paroxismi, principium, augmentum &c. intermissio ipsa cum paroxismo, constituit periodum.
units.tr: A disease is also divided into continuous and intermittent. The former afflicts continually and does not intermit. If it not only afflicts continuously but also without any remission at all, it is a continent disease, as synochus; but if it remits at intervals and fixed periods, the disease is simply continuous, as continuous tertian. The intermittent usually comes to perfect integrity and intermission, as intermittent tertian. Thus diseases of this kind have five times: namely the intermission itself, and the four particular times of the paroxysm, beginning, increase, etc. The intermission itself together with the paroxysm constitutes the period.

units.la: Respectu symptomatum, morbi quidam dicuntur mites, quidam maligni, quidam inter hos medii. Dividi solet morbus in salutarem, qui curari potest; & lethalem, qui est incurabilis; & in eum qui medio modo se habet: nam elephantiasis, & lues venerea, saepè non possunt curari, nec tamen sunt lethales; unde medio modo se habent,
units.tr: With respect to symptoms, some diseases are called mild, some malignant, and some between these. A disease is usually divided into the salutary, which can be cured; the lethal, which is incurable; and that which stands in a middle way: for elephantiasis and venereal lues often cannot be cured, yet they are not lethal; hence they stand in a middle way.

units.la: Dividitur quoque morbus ratione subjecti multis modis: nam alii dicuntur temperamento similes, alii dissimiles. alii morbi sunt virorum, alii fœminarum proprii ut suffocatio uteri, alii puerorum, alii juvenum, alii denique senum. Sic morbi dicuntur universales, ut febris, quia totum corpus occupant; alii particulares, qui unam partem affligunt, ut polypus nasum: &c.
units.tr: A disease is also divided in many ways with respect to the subject: for some are said to be like the temperament, others unlike. Some diseases belong to men, others specifically to women, such as suffocation of the womb; some to children, some to young people, and finally some to the aged. Thus diseases are called universal, such as fever, because they occupy the whole body; others particular, which afflict one part, such as polypus of the nose, etc.

units.la: Respectu regionum & locorum differunt morbi. alii enim sunt sporadici, quando specie diversi eodem in loco & tempore grassantur. alii pandemii eiusdem nimirum generis morbi, eodem tempore & loco grassantes. qui diiiduntur in Endemios & Epidemios. Illi sunt vernaculi, locique vitio semper fiunt, ut struma in Valesiis. Hi loci vitio non fiunt, sed alia causa generantur; proinde diversas regiones simul infestant, ut pestis. Quibus omnibus adjici potest divisio morborum in veteres & novos. illos voco Græcis & imprimis HippoHipocrati & Galeno notos, ut Apoplexiam : hos nuper natos, ut luem venereám, sudorem Anglicum, pliam Polonicam; quibus addunt nonnulli variolas, morbillos, scorbutum.
units.tr: Diseases differ with respect to regions and places. For some are sporadic, when diseases differing in kind rage in the same place and time. Others are pandemic, diseases of the same kind, raging at the same time and place. These are further divided into endemic and epidemic. The former are native and always arise from a fault of the place, as goitre among the Valesians. The latter do not arise from a fault of the place but are generated by another cause; therefore they infest different regions at once, as plague. To all these can be added the division of diseases into ancient and new. The former I call those known to the Greeks and especially to Hippocrates and Galen, such as apoplexy; the latter recently born, such as venereal lues, the English sweat, the Polish plica; to which some add smallpox, measles and scurvy.

units.la: CAP. III. De Morborum Causis.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. On the Causes of Diseases.

units.la: Morbi cognitio & curatio haberi nequeunt, ignoratis eius causis quibus constat. qua parte Rationales Medici praestant Empiricis: hi enim causâ neglectâ, solum morbum intuentes, non possunt rectè curare. Causa est principium cuius vi effectus producitur: estque quadruplex; efficiens, finalis, materialis & formalis: exemplarem Peripatetici reduxerunt ad efficientem. Quae porro dividi possunt in causas per se & per accidens. Illae sunt à quibus effectus secundum essentiam quam habent pendent; ut insolatio & liberalior generosi vini potus, sunt causae per se febris: hae secundum esse quod habent non pendent à talibus causis, sed aliaaliarum interventu faciunt, quod faciunt; quemadmodum frigus producit febrem, condensando cutem, & impediendo fuliginum transpirationem. qua de causa ventres hyeme creduntur calidiores. Efficiens & finis sunt externæ causæ; reliquæ internæ. Quod intelligendum venit de substantiis physicis. Nam in morbis non est materia ex qua, sed in quâ, sicut in omnibus accidentibus videre est. Ergo morbi materia est subjectum quod malè disponit: hoc autem corpus animatum est. Diximus antea humorem, & spiritum non esse subjectum morbi, verum causam efficientem: idem enim est contrariorum subjectum; res autem inanimes non sunt sanæ: ergò nec ægræ dici possunt. Forma morbi est dispositio illa præter naturam de quâ egimus. Accidens omne sibi ipsi est forma, nec aliam habere potest: albedo enim non habet formam à seipsâ distinctam; ergo nec morbus, qui est accidens. Finis morbi nullus est. Nam à natunatura non intenditur: est enim quidam malū & imperfectum, proinde nā natura nō appetibile. Quod si hirurgus secet, & urat sanitatis causā, ut maius incommodum declinetur; sciendum ustionem esse tum auxilium & remedium, non mortum. Omissis ergo hisce tribus causarum generibus, ad efficientem veniamus. quæ semper intelligitur à Medicis, quando absolutè sit causæ mentio.
units.tr: Knowledge and cure of a disease cannot be had unless its causes, on which it depends, are known. In this respect the Rational physicians surpass the Empirics, for the Empirics, neglecting the cause and looking only at the disease, cannot cure it properly. A cause is the principle by whose power an effect is produced. There are four kinds: efficient, final, material and formal. The Peripatetics reduced the exemplary cause to the efficient. Causes may further be divided into causes per se and per accidens. The former are those on which an effect depends according to the essence it has: for example, exposure to the sun and a rather generous drinking of strong wine are per se causes of fever. The latter do not depend on such causes according to the being they have, but produce what they produce through the intervention of others: as cold produces fever by condensing the skin and hindering the transpiration of vapours, for which reason stomachs are thought warmer in winter. The efficient and final causes are external; the rest are internal. This must be understood of physical substances, for in diseases there is no material from which, but only material in which, as can be seen in all accidents. Therefore the matter of a disease is the subject that is badly disposed, and this subject is an animate body. I said before that humour and spirit are not the subject of disease but its efficient cause, for the same thing cannot be the subject of contraries, and inanimate things are neither healthy nor sick, so they cannot rightly be called diseased. The form of a disease is that unnatural disposition of which we have spoken. Every accident is its own form and can have no other: whiteness has no form distinct from itself, and so neither has disease, which is an accident. A disease has no final cause, for nature does not aim at it; it is a certain evil and imperfection, and so is not something nature desires. If a surgeon cuts or burns for the sake of health, so that a greater harm may be avoided, it must be understood that the burning is then an aid and remedy, not a disease. Setting aside these three kinds of cause, then, let us come to the efficient cause, which is always what physicians understand when cause is mentioned without qualification.

units.la: Est autem efficiens causa, principium a quo morbus fit. Sciendum hic efficientem causam semper supponere subjectum habile; alioqui non efficeret. Unde sæpè videas tempore pestis, etiamsi in loco infecto plures morentur, non omnes tamen eâ corripi, ob nullam causam aliam, nisi quod hic habeat subjectum, & corpus dispositum; ille autem non.
units.tr: An efficient cause is the principle from which a disease arises. It must be noted here that an efficient cause always presupposes a suitable subject, otherwise it would not be efficient. Hence you will often see that during a plague, even if many people stay in an infected place, not all are seized by it, for no other reason than that this man has a subject and a body disposed to it, and that man does not.

units.la: Causæ efficientis multiplex est divisio, est enim alia interna, alia externa; quæ divisio est in ordine ad nostrum corpus. illa siquidem est extra tra ut aër, balneum; hæc in ipso corpore subsistit, ut cacochymia. Secun-do dividitur in manifestam & occultam. hæc ut investigetur, eget artificiali conjectura; illa sensibus est obvia & manifesta. Celeberrima est divisio causarum in προκαταρκτικὰς[?], προηγουμένας[?], & συνεκτικὰς[?]. Προκαταρκτικὰς[?] quidam vocant primitivas, præinci-pientes, prægressas; dictæ sunt à veteribus non tam morborum causæ, quam occasiones: quia nunquam morbum faciunt, nisi corpus habeat dispositionem pravam & morbosam: ac proinde corpora valida non assi-cit. Quemadmodum exercitium non ita vehemens, in corpore valido fe-brem non producit, at in corpore pravè affecto latentem dispositio-nem excitat. Ergo hæc causa semper est evidens; sed non reciprocantur, ita ut omnis evidens causa sit procata-rctica. Gladius vulneris est causa evidens, sed non procatarctica; quia nullam supponit in corpore dispositionem. Causa προηγουμένη[?] causa est anteantecedens ; dispositio scilicet in corpore abdita & latens, quæ morbum præcedit. Hæc causa consideratur in potentia, non autem in actu. Nec enim ea posità ponitur morbus; nam tolli potest, ita ut non sequatur morbus, habetque locum in morbis ut loquuntur humoralibus, seu ab humore pendentibus. Materia illa est προληπτικὴ & κακοχυμία; quæ dispositiones si præcîdantur venæ sectione, aut purgatione; morbus non generabitur. Dicitur ergo hæc causa antecedens; quod morbum antecedat, eumque, si excitetur, generare possit. At excitata, actuque morbum efficiens, non amplius vocatur antecedens, sed conjuncta seu continens: nam, ut dixi, consistit in efficiendi potentiâ. Conjuncta seu continens (de quâ tam morosè disputatur) est, quâ posità, ponitur morbus; qua sublata tollitur. Ut pleuritide posita, ponitur quoque febris; eadem ablata, auferitur. Est ergo hæc causa semper immediata, nec in omnibus morbis habet locum.
units.tr: The division of efficient causes is manifold. There is one internal and another external, a division made with respect to our body: the external lies outside the body, as air and bathing; the internal subsists in the body itself, as cacochymy. Second, causes are divided into manifest and hidden. The hidden needs artificial conjecture to be discovered; the manifest is obvious and plain to the senses. The most celebrated division of causes is into procatarctic [προκαταρκτικάς], proegumenal [προηγουμένας] and synectic [συνεκτικάς]. Some call the procatarctic causes primitive, preliminary or preceding. The ancients called them occasions rather than causes of disease, because they never produce disease unless the body has a bad and morbid disposition; accordingly they do not attack strong bodies. A moderate exercise, for example, does not produce fever in a strong body, but in a body badly affected it stirs up the latent disposition. Therefore this cause is always evident, but the converse does not hold, so that not every evident cause is procatarctic. The blade is an evident cause of a wound, but not a procatarctic one, because it presupposes no disposition in the body. The proegumenal cause is the antecedent cause, namely the hidden and latent disposition in the body that precedes the disease. This cause is considered in potency, not in act, for the disease is not posited merely by its being posited; it can be removed so that the disease does not follow. It applies to diseases which they call humoral, or dependent on humour. That matter is the preparatory and the cacochymy; if these dispositions are cut off by venesection or purgation, no disease will be generated. This cause is therefore called antecedent, because it precedes the disease and can generate it if it is stirred up. But once it is excited and actually producing the disease, it is no longer called antecedent but conjunct or continent, for, as I said, it consists in the power of producing. The conjunct or continent cause (about which there is such tedious disputation) is that which, being posited, posits the disease, and which, being removed, removes it. When pleurisy is posited, fever is posited too; when pleurisy is removed, fever goes away. This cause is therefore always immediate, and it does not apply to all diseases.

units.la: Greek words in the printed text are rendered approximately; see notes. locum, Quis enim febris hectica vidit causam continentem? Quando audis causam continentem politam, morbum ponere, & ablatam, eundem tollere; non est quod putes eo modo rem esse comparatam quo inter solem, & lucem: hæc enim dictum factum evanescit sublato sole: quod tamen hic non semper obtiner, quanquam interdum contingit;ut in ablatione digiti sexti, aut calculi:sed intelligendum est eâ ablatâ, brevi post & morbum periturum. Fallun-tur qui causam continentem morbi, cum eiusdem formâ & essentiâ confundunt. nec enim dubium est, quin morbus habeat suam qualemcunque formam,& essentiam,quam diximus esse dispositionem non naturalem: at de continente hac disputatur, & ambigitur. Nam quidam putant morbos similares eâ destitui: at dissimilares habere: quidam putant esse planè commentitiam: nonnulli verò esse in omni morbo. Si ergo, præjudicio amoto, rem eximinaris; videbis pis causam continentem esse & conjunctam. Hæc eadem semper est interna & immediata, quanquam immediata, latius patet: nam gladius est immediata causa vulneris; nec tamen eo ablato tollitur vulnus; quod in causa continente fieri amat. Ergo, ut paucis rem complectamur, ita habeto: cacochymia in corpore latens & non excitata, est causa tantum antecedens, excitata vero, est conjuncta & continens. Quæ Argenterius hic dicit de causarum multitudine, putida nimis sunt, & indigna Galeni censore; qualis, si diis placet, videri vult.
units.tr: For who has ever seen a continent cause of hectic fever? When you hear that a continent cause, once posited, posits the disease, and once removed, removes it, do not think the matter is arranged in the way the light stands to the sun, for light vanishes at once when the sun is taken away. Yet this does not always hold here, though it sometimes happens, as when a sixth finger or a stone is removed; but it must be understood that once the cause is removed, the disease will perish shortly after. Those who confuse the continent cause of a disease with its form and essence are mistaken. There is no doubt that every disease has its own form and essence, which we said is the unnatural disposition; but about the continent cause there is dispute and doubt. For some think that similar diseases lack it but dissimilar diseases have it; some think it is entirely fictitious; others hold that it is present in every disease. If, then, you examine the matter with prejudice set aside, you will see that the cause is both continent and conjunct. This same cause is always internal and immediate, though the immediate extends more widely: the blade is the immediate cause of a wound, yet the wound is not removed when the blade is taken away, which is what happens with a continent cause. So, to sum up briefly, hold this: cacochymy lying hidden in the body and not yet excited is only an antecedent cause; once excited, it is conjunct and continent. As for what Argenterius says here about the multitude of causes, it is far too silly and unworthy of Galen as a critic, whom, God willing, he wishes to appear to be.

units.la: Quæ diximus de causis morborum, in abstracto diximus, non, ut loquuntur, in concreto: proinde methodi ratio exigit, ut videamus in genere res eas in quibus huiusmodi causarum genera inveniuntur. Ac primo quidem evidentes causæ, aliæ sunt necessariæ, quibus carere non possumus: aliæ fortuitæ & contingentes, ut gladius, lapis. Illæ sunt res non natunaturales,quæ suâ natura nec lędunt, nec juvant : verum earum mediocritas vitam conservat, immoderatus usus eandem corrumpit. Suntq; numero sex. 1. aër. 2. cibus, potus. 3. retenta, excreta. 4. somnus, vigilia. 5. motus, quies. 6. Animi perturbationes. Harum quædam materiam morborum suggerunt ; ut alimenta nimis copiosa ; & excrementa : cæteræ res non naturales, qualitatem, nostris corporibus inimicam, imprimunt.
units.tr: What we have said about the causes of diseases we have said in the abstract, not, as they say, in the concrete. Therefore the order of method requires that we look at the kinds of things in which these kinds of causes are found. And first, of evident causes, some are necessary, without which we cannot be: others are chance and contingent, such as a blade or a stone. The necessary causes are the non-natural things, which by their nature neither harm nor help; yet their moderate use preserves life, and immoderate use corrupts it. There are six of them: (1) air; (2) food and drink; (3) retained and excreted matter; (4) sleep and waking; (5) motion and rest; (6) disturbances of the mind. Some of these supply the matter of diseases, such as excessively abundant food and excrements; the rest impress on our bodies a quality hostile to them.

units.la: Primò aër magnam vim habet in alterando corpore, propter respirationem continuam. qui temperatus, purus, serenus, vitam conservat : sin vero sit intemperatus, crassus pestilens, eandem corrumpit. Calidus enim nimis,febrim excitat,bilem auget, spiritus evocat. Contrariam dispositionem inducit frigidus. nimium siccus,sicut putredinem impedit ; ita meatus obstruit, corpusque exsiccat. Contrarium facit aër humidus:sin idem corrumpatur & putrescat, pestem, inducit, aliosque Epi-demidemicos morbos.
units.tr: First, air has great power to alter the body, because of continual breathing. Air that is temperate, pure and serene preserves life; but if it is intemperate, thick and pestilential, it corrupts life. Air that is too hot excites fever, increases bile and draws out the spirits. A cold air induces the opposite disposition. Air that is too dry, while it prevents putrefaction, obstructs the passages and dries out the body. Humid air does the opposite; but if the air is corrupted and putrefies, it brings on plague and other epidemic diseases.

units.la: Secundò alimentum consideran-dum venit. læditur sanitas, non modo ex cibo, sed etiam ex modo eum sumendi. Si enim victus sit nimis crassus aut tenuis; oriuntur morbi. Ille calorem extinguit, vires obruit: hic paulatim solvit vitam, facultatemque debilem reddit. Ille generat plethoram, & cacochymiam, plurimorum morborum parentes: hic partium substantiam & spiritus consumit. Nec tantum ciborum consi-deranda est substantia, sed & qualitas; nimirum sintne calidi, an frigidi; humidi, an sicci. Exuperans enim qualitas corpus nostrum afficit. Cibus alieno tempore sumptus nocet etiam; nam si priore non cocto, novus sumatur, generantur cruditates. Idem de assumendi ordine judicandum.
units.tr: Secondly, food must be considered. Health is impaired not only by food but also by the manner of taking it. If the diet is too coarse or too thin, illnesses arise. The former extinguishes the heat and overwhelms the powers; the latter gradually dissolves life and renders the faculty feeble. The former generates plethora and cacochymia, the parents of very many diseases; the latter consumes the substance of the parts and the spirits. Nor is only the substance of foods to be considered, but also their quality, namely whether they are hot or cold, moist or dry. For an excessive quality affects our body. Food taken at the wrong time also harms; for if fresh food is taken before the previous meal has been digested, crudities are generated. The same judgement is to be made about the order in which things are taken.

units.la: Tertiò consideranda sunt excreta, & retenta, conservatur optimè sanitas, si retineantur quæ retineri debent; & contra expellantur, suo modo, & tempore, excrementa quæ re-tinetineri non debent. Si secus fiat, generatur morbus. Ergo si expellatur sanguis, qui retineri debet; vires dissolvuntur. sin urina, sudor, fæces & eiusmodi retineantur, idem usu venit. Idem erit judicium de femine, & sanguine menstruo: nam si copia aut malignitate peccent; retineri non debent.
units.tr: Thirdly, the excreted and the retained matters must be considered. Health is best preserved if those things that ought to be retained are retained, and, conversely, those excrements that ought not to be retained are expelled in the proper manner and at the proper time. If it happens otherwise, disease is generated. Thus if blood, which ought to be retained, is expelled, the powers are dissolved; if urine, sweat, faeces and such like are retained, the same thing comes about. The same judgement holds concerning semen and menstrual blood: for if they err in quantity or in malignancy, they ought not to be retained.

units.la: Quartò somni & vigiliarum habenda est ratio. Somnus facit plurimum ad concoctionem alimenti, vigilia ad ejusdem distributionem: sanitas conservatur utriusq; usu temperato. Ergo somnus nimius, crudos humores accumulat, calorem obruit: vigiliæ vires dissipant & exhauriunt, corpus exsiccant, bilemque procreant.
units.tr: Fourthly, account must be taken of sleep and waking. Sleep contributes very much to the concoction of food, waking to its distribution; health is preserved by the temperate use of both. Therefore excessive sleep accumulates crude humours and overwhelms the heat; wakefulness dissipates and drains the powers, dries up the body and produces bile.

units.la: Quintò motus & quies parum abeunt à naturâ somni, & vigiliarum. Motus temperatus ante cibum, calorem excitat, corpus roborat, spiritusque alacriores reddit: intemperatus vero, vires exhaurit, humores dissipat, bilem acuit. contrarium judicium esto de quiete & otio.
units.tr: Fifthly, motion and rest depart little from the nature of sleep and waking. Moderate motion before food excites heat, strengthens the body and makes the spirits more lively; but immoderate motion drains the powers, dissipates the humours and sharpens the bile. Let the opposite judgement be made concerning rest and idleness.

units.la: Sextò pathemata animi magni sunt momenti in omnem partem, sive ad vitam, sive ad mortem. Eorum enim ivi spiritus & concitantur per corpus, & contrahuntur ad cor. Horum est diversa ratio. Nam motus, tristitia, dolor, cor obruunt: eo enim trahunt spiritus & sanguinem, unde extremorum frigus, partiumq; debilitas; quod docet pulsus languidus & debilis, conjunctus interdum cum syncope. At gaudium & laetitia diffundunt in extrema membra calorem & spiritum: proinde, si modum excedant, syncopen & interdum mortem inducunt. Ira est conjuncta cum motu spirituum misto, quo sanguis in corde effervescit. Ergo sanitatis studiosus debet modum in hisce movendis & sedandis ponere; alioqui fiunt morborum causæ.
units.tr: Sixthly, the passions of the mind are of great moment in every respect, whether for life or for death. For the spirits both go out through the body and are drawn back to the heart.
