The effects of these are various. For sorrow, grief and pain overwhelm the heart: they draw the spirits and blood thither, whence comes coldness of the extremities and weakness of the parts, which a languid and feeble pulse shows, sometimes joined with a faint. But joy and gladness diffuse heat and spirit into the outer limbs; accordingly, if they exceed due measure, they induce a swoon and sometimes death. Anger is joined with a mixed motion of the spirits, by which the blood boils in the heart. Therefore one who is zealous for health must set a measure in stirring up and calming these; otherwise they become causes of disease.

units.la: Huc etiam revocantur contagium & venenum. Illud est seminarium vel in aëre sparsum, vel vestibus aliisve rebus affixum, à corpore morbido profectum, vim habens sano corpori morbum imprimendi. mendi; quemadmodum in peste, & scabie videre est. Venenum est cordi humano inimica substantia, destruens primò facultatem vitalem; ut in morsibus serpentum, aliisque venenis cernere licet.
units.tr: Contagion and poison are also brought under this head. The former is a seed either scattered in the air or fixed to clothes and other things, proceeding from a diseased body and having the power of imprinting disease upon a healthy body; as may be seen in plague and in scabies. Poison is a substance hostile to the human heart, destroying first the vital faculty; as may be perceived in the bites of serpents and other poisons.

units.la: CAP. IV. De Plethora, & Cacochymia.
units.tr: CHAP. IV. Of Plethora and Cacochymia.

units.la: Transeamus ad causas morbo-rum internas. Constat humanum corpus continentibus, contentis, & impetum facientibus. Contenta sunt duûm generum, naturalia, & præter naturam. Illa intelligo quæ homine sano & optimè se habente insunt; qualia sunt humores alimentarii, (quo pertinent semen, lac,) & excrementitii illi qui ex materiê necessitate consequuntur: Nullum siquidem alimentum tam est purum, quin habeat sua excrementa, ut in concoctionibus videre est. talia sunt bilis utraque, pituita, seces, urina. Præter naturam sunt pus, calculus, lumbrici &c. Hæc semper noxia sunt, malæmalæque causæ: at illa sua natura non sunt noxia, nisi recesserint à naturæ legibus, tum demum sunt morborum causæ. Peccant vero modis duobus; qualitate scilicet & quantitate. Illam voco, quando in humoribus non est ea dispositio, quæ secundum naturam adesse debet; ut si humores sunt justo calidiores, frigidiores, crassiores: quo pertinet eorum putredo. Hanc, quando augentur supra mediocritatem, aut contra infra eam subsistunt. Quibus præmissis Plethora & Cacochymia examen ingradiamur.
units.tr: Let us pass on to the internal causes of diseases. The human body consists of containing parts, contained matters, and things making an assault. The contained matters are of two kinds, natural and contrary to nature. By the former I mean those which are present in a healthy person who is in the best condition: such as the alimentary humours (to which belong semen and milk) and those excrementitious humours which follow necessarily from the matter; for no food is so pure that it does not have its own excrements, as may be seen in the concoctions. Such are both biles, phlegm, the lees, and urine. Contrary to nature are pus, calculus, worms, etc. These are always harmful and bad causes; but the former are not harmful in their own nature, unless they have departed from the laws of nature; only then are they causes of disease. They err, however, in two ways: namely in quality and in quantity. I call the former when in the humours there is not that disposition which ought to be present according to nature; as when the humours are hotter, colder or thicker than is right; to this belongs their putrefaction. The latter is when they increase beyond the mean, or on the contrary remain below it. With these things premised, let us enter upon the examination of Plethora and Cacochymia.

units.la: Est autem Plethora redundantia æqualis & secundum proportionem omnium humorum, aut alioqui sanguinis solius. Iam quomodo in massa sanguinis dicantur humores contineri, ante dictum est. Est vero duplex, ad vasa, & vires. Plethora ad vasa est, quando sanguis suâ copiâ & multitudine vasa distendit & in tumorem attollit; habetque semper conjunctam pulsus magnitudinem. Ad vires autem est, quanquando vasa sanguine non ita turgent, tanta tamen est copia, ut, vires alioqui debiles, graventur & fatiscant, percipiturque sensus oneris incumbentis.
units.tr: Now plethora is an equal redundancy, in due proportion, of all the humours, or otherwise of the blood alone. It has already been said how the humours are contained in the mass of blood. It is indeed twofold: plethora as to the vessels, and plethora as to the powers. Plethora as to the vessels is when the blood, by its quantity and abundance, distends the vessels and raises them into swelling; and it always has joined with it a largeness of pulse. Plethora as to the powers is when the vessels are not so swollen with blood, yet the quantity is so great that the powers, otherwise feeble, are burdened and faint, and a sense of a weight pressing upon them is perceived.

units.la: Cacochymia est vitiosi humoris, pituitosi, biliosi, &c. ut in hydrope, ictero videre est, in corpore redundantia.
units.tr: Cacochymia is a redundancy in the body of a vicious humour, phlegmatic, bilious, etc., as may be seen in dropsy and jaundice.

units.la: Redundat sanguis, firque plethora vitio (ut ita dicam) facultatis, & alimenti. Nam facultas valida, bonum alimentum, idque copiose sumptum optime coquit & digerit, sanguinisque proventum magnum facit. Huc pertinent reliquarum rerum non naturalium usus; otium enim & vita hilaris, retentioq; consuetæ evacuationis, multum etiam faciunt ad sanguinis generationem. Eodem modo cacochymia fit, vitio vel facultatis & partium sanguinem generantium, vel alioqui alimenti, & aliarum rerum non naturalium depravato usu. Si ergo hepar, ventriculus, cor, justo magis frigent; generabitur pituita: sin optimè se habent, offeratur autem cibus justo frigidior, crudior; hior; pituita itidem generabitur. Iam antea dixi, in Physicis alterationibus non solam esse causam efficientem considerandam, sed & materialem: nemo ergo mirabitur si homo, alioqui bene valens, ex copioso usu ciborum frigidorum, incidat in cacochymiam pituitosam. Idem judicium esto cacochymiae biliosae, & melancholiae. At vero corrumpuntur humores & depravantur ex maligna viscerum intemperie: sicut in elephantiacis videre est: vel ex putredine & corruptela; quando scilicet humores ob calorem ambientis corrumpuntur; causa siquidem putredinis est calor externus & corporis ambientis, evocans internum rei calorem. Vel alioqui corrumpuntur humores ex vitiato alimento & putrido, ut surgis &c. Interdum ex aëris contagio. Redundat flatus quando calor debilis vapores frigidos discutere nequit, verum attollit, sed non consumit; generaturque ex materia frigida, viscida &c. Inanitio est defectus utilis & alimen-tarii humoris ; unde corpus extenuatur, spiritus dissolvuntur. fitque calida & sicca temperie, rarâ textura, facultatis retentricis debilitate immodicis evacuationibus, curis, vigiliis &c. Diximus in corpore contineri excrementa toto genere praeter naturam, ut calculos, vermes &c. quæ omnia solent morbum excitare, quod omnibus est notum.
units.tr: The blood overflows, and plethora arises from a fault (so to speak) of the faculty and of the food. For a strong faculty, with good food taken in abundance, concocts and digests it very well and produces a large supply of blood. To this belongs the use of the remaining non-natural things; for leisure and a cheerful life, and the retention of customary evacuation, also contribute much to the generation of blood. In the same way cacochymia arises, from a fault either of the faculty and of the parts that generate blood, or otherwise from a depraved use of food and of the other non-natural things. If therefore the liver, stomach and heart are too cold, phlegm will be generated; but if they are in good condition, yet food that is too cold and crude is offered, phlegm will likewise be generated. I have said before that in physical alterations one must consider not only the efficient cause but also the material cause: no one therefore will wonder if a man otherwise in good health, from a copious use of cold foods, falls into phlegmatic cacochymia. The same judgement holds for bilious cacochymia and melancholy. Moreover, humours are corrupted and depraved from a malignant intemperature of the viscera, as may be seen in elephantiasis; or from putrefaction and corruption, namely when the humours are corrupted by the heat of the surrounding air; for the cause of putrefaction is an external heat and the heat of the surrounding body, calling forth the internal heat of the thing. Or otherwise the humours are corrupted from vitiated and putrid food, as in the case of ulcers, etc.; sometimes from contagion of the air. Flatulence overflows when a weak heat cannot dispel cold vapours, but raises them without consuming them; and it is generated from cold, viscid matter, etc. Inanition is a defect of the useful and alimentary humour; whence the body is wasted and the spirits dissolved. It comes about with a hot and dry temperament, a rare texture, a weakness of the retentive faculty, from immoderate evacuations, cares, watchings, etc. We have said that excrements of every kind contrary to nature are contained in the body, such as stones, worms, etc., all of which are wont to excite disease, as is known to all.

units.la: CAP. V. De Morborum causis in specie.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. On the causes of diseases in particular.

units.la: QUæ de morborum causis dixi-mus, communia nimis sunt, & confusa ; quæ magis intelligentur, si ad magis particulares morborum causas descendamus, doceamusque morborum similarium, & communium causas. Diximus esse quatuor temperamenta simplicia, & totidem composita; nam temperamentum ad pondus nunc in examen non venit ; ergo totidem erunt intemperies; quæ interdum solitariæ existunt, interdum lum cum materiâ conjunctæ, quæ quomodo gignantur, jam videamus.
units.tr: What I have said about the causes of diseases is too general and confused. It will be better understood if we descend to the more particular causes of diseases, and teach the causes of diseases that are alike and common. We said there are four simple temperaments and as many compound ones, for the temperament by weight does not come into examination here. Therefore there will be as many intemperies, which sometimes exist alone and sometimes are joined with matter. Let us now see how they arise.

units.la: Calida intemperies, vel totius corporis, vel partis alicuius, quinque potissimum habet causas. non quasi hæ omnes semper concurrant, sed quia una harū causa est sufficiens ad temperamentum evertendum. Sunt autem hæ, 1. contractus rei calidæ, 2. motus nimius. 3. putredo, 4. obstructio. 5. assumpta.
units.tr: Hot intemperies, whether of the whole body or of some part, has chiefly five causes. Not that all of these always concur, but because any one of them is enough to overturn the temperament. They are: (1) contact with a hot thing; (2) excessive motion; (3) putrefaction; (4) obstruction; (5) things taken in.

units.la: Ac primò quidem res calida vicina assidue afficiens corpus, calorem inducit; ut aër sole calefactus, mora in balneo. Neque tantum causæ externæ inducunt intemperiem, sed una pars calida sæpe agit in aliam; ut in febribus natis ex inflammatione liquet; nisi forsan huiusmodi revocare velis ad partium putredinem. Utut sit, constat unam partem calidam agere in aliam sibi vicinam.
units.tr: First, a hot thing that constantly acts on the nearby body induces heat, as air warmed by the sun, or a stay in a bath. Nor do external causes alone induce intemperies; one hot part often acts on another. This is clear in fevers arising from inflammation, unless perhaps you prefer to refer such cases to putrefaction of the parts. However that may be, it is established that one hot part acts on another adjacent to it.

units.la: Secundò motus calorem auget. Nomine motus non tantum intelliguntur exercitia, & labores corporum; sed & animi curæ & solicitudines, ira.
units.tr: Second, motion increases heat. By motion are understood not only exercises and bodily labours, but also cares and anxieties of the mind, and anger.

units.la: Motus localis per se non terminatur ad calorem; proinde non producit calorem per se, sed per accidens, quatenus excitat spiritus sopitos, eosq; per corpus fundit; ex quorum appulsu vicinae partes inflammantur.
units.tr: Local motion in itself does not terminate in heat, so it does not produce heat directly, but accidentally, insofar as it stirs up dormant spirits and pours them through the body. From their impact the neighbouring parts are inflamed.

units.la: Tertiò Putredo inducit intemperiem calidam, quatenus calor externus internum rei intendit & auget. Hoc modo excitantur febres putridae. Quid? quod septica medicamenta putredinem parti accersant.
units.tr: Third, putrefaction induces hot intemperies, insofar as external heat intensifies and increases the internal heat of a thing. In this way putrid fevers are excited. And what of the fact that septic medicines bring putrefaction to a part?

units.la: Quartò Obstructio partium parit calorem non naturalem; sed per accidens. Pori enim obstructi intus cohibent calidas exspirationes, & fuligines, unde partium & humorum calor intenditur.
units.tr: Fourth, obstruction of the parts produces unnatural heat, but accidentally. For obstructed pores hold hot exhalations and soot within, and so the heat of the parts and humours is intensified.

units.la: Postremò assumpta, hoc est alimenta & medicamenta calida, idem efficiunt; ut in vino, & aromatibus videre est. Idem etiam fit à multis cibis.
units.tr: Last, things taken in, that is, hot foods and medicines, do the same, as can be seen with wine and spices. The same also happens with many foods.

units.la: Frigida intemperies per se inducitur à re frigida; per accidens autem, à calida. Ac primò quidem contactus rei [illegible, ~3 letters]ei frigidæ, ut nivis, glaciei, per se refrigerant. Idem de alimentis frigidis judicium esto. Idem efficiunt inedia, evacuationes immodicæ: illa siquidem caloris pabulum subtrahit, quæ spiritus dissipant. Quomodo & rara corporis textura frigus inducit. Motus item immodicus, idem eodem modo efficit. Otium nimium & somnus calorem torpidum & debilem efficiunt, cui succedit frigus.
units.tr: Cold intemperies is induced in itself by a cold thing, but accidentally by a hot one. First, the contact of a cold thing, such as snow or ice, cools in itself. The same judgement holds for cold foods. Fasting and immoderate evacuations do the same, for the former withdraws the fuel of heat, and the latter dissipates the spirits. A loose texture of the body also induces cold in the same way. Likewise, immoderate motion does the same. Excessive idleness and sleep make the heat sluggish and weak, and cold follows.

units.la: Intemperies sicca inducitur ab admotis rebus siccis; aëre sicco, balneis aluminosis; ab assumptis tum medicamentis, tum alimentis siccis. Per accidens exsiccant corpus, quæcunque humores evacuant utiles; ut nimia venus, sanguinis profusio, & cetera huiusmodi; ut curæ, solicitudines &c.
units.tr: Dry intemperies is induced by dry things applied to the body: dry air, aluminous baths, and dry medicines and foods taken in. Accidentally, whatever evacuates useful humours dries the body, such as excessive sexual activity, profuse bleeding and other things of that kind, and likewise cares, anxieties and the like.

units.la: Intemperies humida fit ex aëre humido, balneo dulci, & aliis corpori admotis. assumpta item alimenta & medicamenta humida idem præstant: retentio item humorum, ocium, somnus, &c.
units.tr: Moist intemperies arises from moist air, a sweet bath, and other things applied to the body. Moist foods and medicines taken in likewise produce it, as do retention of humours, idleness, sleep and so on.

units.la: ConCompositæ discrasiæ compositas habent causas; quas, cum ex superioribus facilè intelligere possit lector, tradere supervacuum est.
units.tr: Compound discrasias have compound causes. Since the reader can easily work these out from what has gone before, it is superfluous to set them out.

units.la: Intemperies compositæ à materie pendentes ( nam simplices tantum tradidimus ) causam habent humorem in corpore redundantem. Hic si parti impactus eam distendat, generatur tumor. Huius causa est tum humorum congestio, tum fluxio eorundem. Cum pars quæpiam alimentum non ritè digerit, aut excrementa foras pellit, congeritur in parte humor, tumoris causa. Fluxio humoris, tumorem facientis, est semper ab unâ parte in aliam; quando scilicet pars, irritata copia vel malignitate humorum, eos in aliam propellit; quemadmodū hepar ad inguina, cor ad alas, cerebrum ad aures.
units.tr: Compound intemperies, depending on matter (for we have treated only the simple ones), have as their cause a humour superabounding in the body. If this humour lodges in a part and distends it, a swelling is produced. Its causes are both the gathering of humours and their flux. When some part does not digest food properly, or drives excrements outward, humour collects in that part, and this is the cause of the swelling. The flux of a humour making a swelling is always from one part to another, namely when a part, irritated by the quantity or malignancy of the humours, drives them into another, as the liver sends them to the groin, the heart to the armpits, and the brain to the ears.

units.la: Ad fluxionem intelligendam quatuor examinanda veniunt. 1. pars mandans sive fons fluxionis. 2. pars recipiens. 3. humor qui mittitur & movetur. 4. via per quam fit motio. ergo 1. pars (ut à primo incipiamus) humorum copia aut malignitate irritatur eos alió amādat. hoc modo partes nobiliores & validiores, ad ignobiles & debiles excrementa mittunt.
units.tr: To understand the flux, four things must be examined: (1) the sending part, or source of the flux; (2) the receiving part; (3) the humour that is sent and moved; (4) the way by which the movement occurs. Taking the first, the sending part is irritated by the quantity or malignancy of its humours and sends them elsewhere. In this way the nobler and stronger parts send their excrements to the ignoble and weak.

units.la: 2. Pars recipiens est debilis, non potens resistere influxui humorum. ad quod facit eius laxitas, & situs declivis. Huc revocant quidam dolorem; nam dolor & calor vulgò trahere solent; quod tamen non facit per se, sed irritando tantum aliorum membrorum facultatē expultricem.
units.tr: (2) The receiving part is weak and unable to resist the influx of humours. Its laxity and downward position contribute to this. Some attribute pain to this cause, for pain and heat are commonly thought to draw. This, however, does not happen in itself, but only by irritating the expulsive faculty of other members.

units.la: 3. Materia quae mittitur, non debet esse crassa, sed tenuis; crassa enim non facile movetur.
units.tr: (3) The matter sent should not be thick but thin, for thick matter is not easily moved.

units.la: 4. Via est consideranda; hoc est, vasa, per quae movetur tumor, debent esse laxa, non angusta. Ex quibus patet humorē parti impacta (nisi insensibiliter transpiret) necessariò corrūpi & putrescere; impedita enim transpiratione, degenerat à suâ naturâ, ejusq; calor intenditur.
units.tr: (4) The way must be considered, that is, the vessels through which the swelling is moved must be lax, not narrow. From this it is evident that a humour lodged in a part, unless it transpires imperceptibly, must necessarily be corrupted and putrefy. For when transpiration is impeded, it degenerates from its nature and its heat is intensified.

units.la: Tumor pro humoris varietate, multiplex est; nimirum sanguineus, pituitosus, melancholicus, biliosus.
units.tr: A swelling is manifold according to the variety of humour: sanguineous, phlegmatic, melancholic, and bilious.

units.la: Phlegmone enim est tumor ex sanguine sincero, rubens renitens cum dolore. Oedema est tumor ex pituitâ frigidus, mollis, doloris expers, laxus. Quod est in parte, est œdema in toto vero corpore, anasarca. Erysipelas fit ex bile flavâ sincerâ, adjunctum habens ardorem, doloremqupurgentem. Scyrrhus est tumor esucco melancholico sincero,durus tamen & doloris expers. mixti humores mixtos etiam faciunt tumores.
units.tr: For phlegmon is a swelling of pure blood, red, tense and painful. Oedema is a cold, soft, painless, lax swelling of phlegm. What occurs in a part is oedema; in the whole body it is anasarca. Erysipelas arises from pure yellow bile and has an accompanying burning and stinging pain. Scirrhus is a swelling of pure black bile, hard yet painless. Mixed humours also make mixed swellings.

units.la: Et hæc quidem tumorum nomingeneralia & communia sunt; cæterum in hac aut illa parte aliter nominantur. Tumor sanguineus, seu phlegmone pleuræ, pleuritis dicitur meningum cerebri, phrenitis; eiusdem œdema lethargus, & ita deinceps. Atque hæc hactenus; transfeamus ad causas morborum organicorum.
units.tr: These are the general and common names of swellings, but in this or that part they are named differently. A sanguineous swelling, or phlegmon, of the pleura is called pleurisy; of the membranes of the brain, phrenitis; the oedema of the same part is lethargy; and so on. So much for these. Let us pass on to the causes of organic diseases.

units.la: Occurrit primùm mala conformatio, quæ est multiplex, ut constabit. Vitiata figura multas habet causas. Nam & fit à facultate plasticâ debili, aut interpellatâ à phantasiâ. Fit ex vitio feminis & sanguinis menstrui. Nonnunquam obstetricis vitio, cum parit mater. Idem faciunt fuse externe in infantibus, & nuper tis. Ad conformationem pertinet quoque commoda partium superficies ut habeat nimirum asperitatem & lævitatem actionibus convenientem. Omnis ergò materia acris exasperat partem, ut in catharrho videre licet. Lævitas est, cum superficies nitidium æquatur, quod à lentis, & pinguibus humoribus fieri solet. Meatus duo sunt, dilatatio & angustia. Illa fiunt ab emollientibus alimentis, aut medicamentis: interdum etiam ab abstersoribus & detergentibus. Sanguis e venis effluit duobus modis. Primò per ἀναστόμωσιν, quando materia acris, aut alia quæpiam venam aperit. Secundò per διαπήδησιν, cùm humor tenuior ipsius transcolatur, per poros laxiores vicinos additos. Quod ad vasorum angustiam; ea plures habet causas. Medicamenta & alimenta adstringentia ea contrahunt. Idem fit si evacuetur humor contentus ; tum enim coincidunt latera quasi venarum. Quid quod tumor præter naturam, lapis humor viscidus idem faciant.
units.tr: First comes bad conformation, which is manifold, as will be clear. A vitiated figure has many causes. It arises from a weak plastic faculty, or one disturbed by the imagination. It comes from a fault in the seed and in the menstrual blood, and sometimes from the midwife's fault when the mother gives birth. External pressures likewise do the same to infants and newborns. Conformation also involves the proper surface of the parts, namely that they have roughness and smoothness suited to their actions. Every sharp matter roughens a part, as can be seen in catarrh. Smoothness is when the surface is made shiny and even, which usually comes from viscous and fatty humours. There are two states of the passages, dilatation and narrowing. The former are caused by emollient foods or medicines, and sometimes also by abstergent and detergent ones. Blood flows out of the veins in two ways. First by anastomosis, when a sharp matter or some other thing opens a vein. Second by diapedesis, when the thinner part of the humour is strained through the neighbouring looser pores that have been opened up. As for narrowing of the vessels, it has several causes. Astringent medicines and foods contract them. The same happens if the humour contained in them is evacuated, for then the sides of the veins, as it were, come together. What of the fact that an unnatural swelling or a viscous humour does the same?

units.la: Morborum organicorum secundum genus est in magnitudine, quæ præter naturam augetur, vel minuitur. Si augeatur magnitudo ex rebus naturalibus, ita ut figura convenienterservetur; signum est vires esse robustas, esseque copiam humoris alimentarii. At si aucta sit ex rebus præter naturam, sicut in tumoribus, de quibus dixi; eadem causa erit, quæ ipsorum tumorum. Interdum ruptis vinculis, pars in partem prolabitur; ut in enterocele; ubi concurrunt, morbus in magnitudine, & situ. Si enim consideres partem tumidam, morbus est magnitudinis; si partem delapsam a suo loco, morbus est in situ. Minuitur justa magnitudo, vel defectu alimenti, vel ob debilitatem facultatum, vel deniq; à causâ externâ, ferro, igne &c.
units.tr: The second kind of organic disease concerns magnitude, which is increased or diminished beyond nature. If the magnitude is increased by natural things, so that the figure is kept in proper form, it is a sign that the powers are robust and that there is an abundance of nourishing humour. But if it is increased by unnatural things, as in the swellings I have described, the cause will be the same as that of the swellings themselves. Sometimes, when the bonds are broken, one part slips into another, as in enterocele, where disease of magnitude and of position come together. If you consider the part as swollen, the disease is one of magnitude; if you consider the part as displaced from its place, the disease is one of position. The proper magnitude is diminished either by lack of nourishment, by weakness of the faculties, or finally by an external cause such as iron, fire and so on.

units.la: Morbi in numero sunt duplices; vel enim redundat pars, vel deficit. Redundantia interdum est rei præternaturam, ut polypus in naso, calculus in renibus. Illius causa est copia materiæ utilis, cum facultatis robore. Huius causa, est excrementorum abundantia. Quod si quis ab ortu habeat partem naturalem redundantem, ut sextum digitum; causa est facultatis robur; magis autem materiæ utilis copia. Sin ab ortu desit membrum, aut eius particula; contrariæ causæ talem morbum inducent; nimirum debilitas facultatis, defectus materiæ utilis unde partes generantur. Sed si post ortum hoc accidat; causæ erunt variæ; sectio, ustio, rosio &c. Postremo si partes eæ uniantur, quæ coniungi debent, aut contra, si ut in vitiato situ contingit; oritur morbus organicus. Iam pars deserit locum naturalem, ob vinculorum relaxationem, laxationem &c. ut in procidentia uteri, aut sphincteris vitiere est. Idem in articulorum luxa-tione
units.tr: Diseases are of two kinds in number: for either a part is in excess or it is lacking. Excess is sometimes of something contrary to nature, as a polyp in the nose or a stone in the kidneys. The cause of the former is an abundance of useful matter together with strength of the faculty; the cause of the latter is an abundance of excrements. But if someone has from birth a natural part in excess, such as a sixth finger, the cause is the strength of the faculty, but rather the abundance of useful matter. If on the other hand a limb or a fragment of it is lacking from birth, opposite causes will produce such a disease, namely weakness of the faculty and a lack of the useful matter from which parts are generated. But if this happens after birth, the causes will be various: cutting, burning, gnawing and the like. Lastly, if those parts that ought to be joined are joined, or conversely, as happens in a faulty position, an organic disease arises. Again, a part leaves its natural place through relaxation or loosening of its ligaments, as in prolapse of the uterus or in a faulty sphincter. The same happens in dislocation of the joints.

units.la: G tione contingit. Sæpè vulnera,ulce-ra, & huiusmodi faciunt coalescere, quæ coalescere non debent.
units.tr: Often wounds, ulcers and the like cause to unite what ought not to unite.

units.la: Ultimum morborum genus est solutio continui; quæ fit interdum à materia erodente, aut alioqui distendente: interdum ab aliqua re incidente, & frangente.
units.tr: The last kind of disease is a solution of continuity, which comes about sometimes from an eroding matter or one that otherwise distends, and sometimes from some cutting and breaking thing.

units.la: Quod ad causas facientes differentias morborum accidentales; eæ faciles sunt. Nam morbus magnus vel parvus talem supponunt causam. Item brevis, longus, supponunt robur virium, copiam materiæ, eiusque acrimoniam, aut contra &c. Idem judicium esto de morbis malignis. tantum observa particulares & sporadicos morbos habere particulares causas: communes autem & Epidemicos, habere etiam communem causam, ut aërem, cibum corruptos. Qui cum sint necessarii; fit ut tales morbi indifferenter pueros, senes, viros & fœminas invadant.
units.tr: As for the causes that make the differences among accidental diseases, these are easy to grasp. For a disease that is great or small presupposes such a cause; likewise brief or long diseases presuppose a strength of the powers, an abundance of matter and its sharpness, or the contrary, and so on. The same judgment holds for malignant diseases. Only observe that particular and sporadic diseases have particular causes, but common and epidemic diseases have a common cause as well, such as corrupted air or food. Since these are unavoidable, it follows that such diseases attack boys, old men, men and women alike, without distinction.

units.la: CAP. VI. De Symptomatis.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI. On Symptoms.

units.la: TRia in corpore esse præter naturam, morbum, causam, & symptoma, dudum diximus. Causa, morbum antecedit; eundē sequitur symptoma, eo modo quo umbra corpus. Alio nomine ἐπιγίνομαι nominatur; quasi dicas, quidpiam morbo superveniens. Est autem, affectus (propter vocabulorum inopiam dicitur) morbum consequens, eo modo quo umbra corpus. Quod non est ita accipiendum, quasi sublato morbo statim evanescat symptoma, (quanquam interdum hoc fiat,) sed quod non diu perseveret, sublato morbo. Distinguendum est inter symptomata, & naturæ opera; inter se admodum similia. Si quis enim, alioqui benevalens, sponte liberaliter purgetur, aut alioqui purgetur à medicamento, actiones hæ sunt naturæ, non symptomata: quia morbum non consequuntur. Hic propterea distinguendum inter symptomata, ta, & naturalem facultatis impoten-tiam. Si quis enim ex liberaliori usu porrorum & cæparum, magnam copiam bilis non naturalis generet, non est symptoma, sed naturalis impotentia: nec enim facultas, alioqui valida, bonum succum ex huiusmodi herbis generabit. Ita si lapillos non coquat; non est symptoma, sed impotentia naturalis; nec enim coctionis ullo modo sunt capaces. Ita si infans nuper natus, non incedat, aut oculus, bene alioqui valens, non videat parietem; hæc & huiusmodi sunt impotentiæ naturales. Quod cum non satis observasset Vega; valde meo quidem judicio erravit.
units.tr: We said long ago that three things are present in the body contrary to nature: the disease, the cause, and the symptom. The cause precedes the disease; the symptom follows it, as a shadow follows a body. It is called by another name, epiginomai [ἐπιγίνομαι], as if to say something supervening on the disease. It is, however, an affectus (the word is used for lack of a better term), following the disease, as a shadow follows a body. This should not be taken to mean that the symptom vanishes at once when the disease is removed (although sometimes this does happen), but that it does not last long once the disease is gone. We must distinguish between symptoms and the works of nature, which are very similar to one another. If someone who is otherwise in good health is purged freely by nature, or is purged by a medicine, these actions belong to nature and are not symptoms, because they do not follow a disease. Here, therefore, we must distinguish between symptoms and the natural impotence of a faculty. If someone, from a rather generous use of leeks and onions, generates a large quantity of unnatural bile, this is not a symptom but a natural impotence: a faculty otherwise strong will not produce good juice from such herbs. Likewise, if someone does not digest pebbles, this is not a symptom but a natural impotence, since they are in no way capable of digestion. Likewise, if a newborn infant does not walk, or an eye, otherwise healthy, does not see a wall, these and similar things are natural impotences. Since Vega did not observe this sufficiently, in my judgement he certainly erred.

units.la: Symptoma omne sequitur morbum; sive is primario partem afficiat, sive per consensum, sive immediatè, sive mediante alio symptomate morbum sequatur. Nihil tamen impedit, quin symptoma sit alterius morbi causa; ut pituita consequens, refrigeratum cerebrum, est causa obstructionis in pulmone. Fortasse concurrunt mornorbus & symptoma; ut flavus ocu-li color symptoma est oculi: idem ta-men respectu visionis est morbus. Idem judicium de febribus sympto-maticis.
units.tr: Every symptom follows a disease, whether the disease first affects a part, or does so by sympathy, or follows the disease directly or through another symptom. Nevertheless, nothing prevents a symptom from being the cause of another disease: for instance, a rheum that follows a chilled brain is the cause of an obstruction in the lung. Sometimes disease and symptom coincide: the yellow colour of the eye is a symptom of the eye, yet with respect to vision it is at the same time a disease. The same judgement applies to symptomatic fevers.

units.la: Symptomata omnia revocantur ad tria capita; quorum primum est actio laesa; secundum est excremento-rum, aut alioqui contentorum vitium: tertium est qualitas aliqua in corpore mutata; ut color: de quibus ordine agendum.
units.tr: All symptoms are referred to three heads. The first is a damaged action; the second is a fault in the excrements or in other contents; the third is some quality in the body that has been altered, such as colour. These must be treated in order.

units.la: Ac primum genus est actionis laesae. Diximus jam, actionem omnem esse aut vitalem, aut naturalem, aut animalem; ex qua differentia symptomata distinguuntur. Alia enim sunt facultatis naturalis, ut cruditas: alia vitalis, ut syncope: alia animalis, ut surditas. Sin modum laedendi, aut actionem vitandi spectes; singulae actiones tripliciter laeduntur. Vitiatur actio, vel quia non fit, ut in surditate; vel quia diminutè, ut in tremore; vel denique depravatè, ut in convulsione: actio enim est vehementior, tior, quam naturæ convenit. Huc revocatur actio quæ debitum tempus anticipat; ut in stranguria videre est. Unde nullo negotio actionis læsæ symptomata colliguntur. Ac primùm abolita functio omnium actionum animalium, est apoplexia; abolita cogitatio, est extrema fatuitas; diminuta, stultitia: depravata, delirium. Idem de sensu communi, quò pertinent somnus & vigilia, judicandum est: nam carus, lethargus auferunt omnem vigiliam; diminuitur in comate; in pervigilio depravatur. Idem judicium esto de actionibus sensuum externorum. Ita membri alicuius motus voluntarius abolitus, est paralysis: diminutus, est stupor. depravatus, convulsio. Idem judicium esto functionis vitalis. Facultatis naturalis symptomata sunt multiplicia: singulæ enim partes attrahunt, retinent, concoquunt, expellunt. Vnaquæque harum actionum tribus modis lædi-tur: aut enim est abolita, aut diminuta, aut depravata. Ac proinde huius
units.tr: The first kind is a damaged action. We have already said that every action is either vital, natural or animal, and symptoms are distinguished by this difference. Some belong to the natural faculty, such as indigestion; some to the vital, such as fainting; some to the animal, such as deafness. If you look at the manner of harm or the avoidance of action, each single action can be damaged in three ways. An action is impaired either because it does not occur, as in deafness; or because it occurs diminished, as in tremor; or finally because it is depraved, as in convulsion, for the action is more violent or weaker than nature allows. Here belongs also the action that anticipates its due time, as can be seen in strangury. Hence the symptoms of a damaged action are easily collected. First, the abolished function of all the animal actions is apoplexy; abolished thought is extreme idiocy; diminished, stupidity; depraved, delirium. The same must be judged of the common sense, to which sleep and waking belong: for coma and lethargy remove all waking; it is diminished in coma and depraved in pervigilium. The same judgement holds for the actions of the external senses. Thus the abolished voluntary motion of a limb is paralysis; diminished, stupor; depraved, convulsion. The same judgement holds for a vital function. The symptoms of the natural faculty are many: for each part attracts, retains, concocts and expels. Each of these actions is harmed in three ways: for it is either abolished, diminished or depraved. And accordingly, of this

units.la: Vnaquaque ius facultatis duodecim sunt sympto-mata : quælibet enim pars similaris, quatenus nutritur, habet quatuor facultates;quarum actiones tribus modis lædi possunt. Verum partes illæ quæ ministrant aliis, & funguntur publico quasi munere, ut ventriculus & hepar;habent ista symptomata duplicata ; ut in ventriculo & hepate videre est. Nam ventriculus non tantum respectu alimenti,quod sibi privatim attrahit, sed etiam chyli,male attrahit; retinet, concoquit,expellit. Nec hoc tantum,sed idem sentit; respectu cuius tria oriuntur alia symptomata; adeò ut habeat viginti septem. Reliquæ partes quæ sibi serviunt respectu alimenti duodecim habebunt symptomata. Sin etiam sentiant, ut membrana; tria alia. Sin eædem moveantur, ut musculus; respectu motus tria nova habebunt symptomata. unde huiusmodi partes octodecim habent. At oculus,exempli causa, videt; quæ actio cum lædi possit, & quidem tribus modis;emergunt gunt tria alia symptomata: habebit ergò unum & viginti duodecim quà nutritur: quà sensum tactus habet tria:quà movetur, totidem; quà videt, totidem etiam. Porrò quæ de affixione alimenti,eiusdemque appetione adduntur à Valesio symptomata, huc scitè revocantur: nam appetitio ad attractionem pertinet, affixio ad nutritionem. Nec enim verum est affixionem nullius facultatis functionem esse. Huc porrò vitia facultatis generatricis,& auctricis sunt revocanda. Nempe & hæ facultates sua habent symptomata.
units.tr: Each single faculty thus has twelve symptoms. For every similar part, insofar as it is nourished, has four faculties, whose actions can be harmed in three ways. But those parts which serve others and perform a kind of public office, such as the stomach and the liver, have these symptoms doubled, as can be seen in the stomach and the liver. For the stomach not only attracts badly with respect to the food it draws to itself privately, but also with respect to the chyle; it retains, concocts and expels badly. And not only this, but it also feels; with respect to which three further symptoms arise, so that it has twenty-seven. The remaining parts which serve themselves, with respect to nourishment, will have twelve symptoms. But if they also feel, as a membrane does, three others are added. If they also move, as a muscle does, three new symptoms arise with respect to motion; so such parts have eighteen. But the eye, for example, sees; since this action can be harmed in three ways, three other symptoms emerge. It will therefore have twenty-one. Insofar as it is nourished it has twelve; insofar as it has the sense of touch, three; insofar as it moves, as many; insofar as it sees, as many too. Moreover, the symptoms that Valesius adds concerning the affixion of food and its appetite are fittingly referred here: for appetite pertains to attraction, affixion to nutrition. For it is not true that affixion is the function of no faculty. Furthermore, the faults of the generative and augmentative faculties must be referred here too. Indeed these faculties have their own symptoms.

units.la: Secundum genus symptomatum est qualitas sensibilis, habitui corporis inhærens;quæ interdum actionem lædit, ut tinnitus aurium; interdum non lædit, ut simplex rubedo cutis. Idem de reliquis sensibus judicandum;nisi quod odores & sapores excrementorum ad tertium genus sint reducendi.
units.tr: The second kind of symptom is a sensible quality inhering in the habit of the body; sometimes it damages an action, as ringing in the ears does; sometimes it does not, as a simple redness of the skin. The same judgement applies to the other senses, except that odours and tastes of excrements are to be referred to the third kind.

units.la: Tertium genus est in retentis,aut excretis. Observa obiter, si excremenmentum præter naturam in corpore sano generetur vitio alimenti, ut calculus, lumbricus, non est symptoma; at si hæc sequantur morbum, tum de-mum fiunt. Quæ excernuntur, aut retinentur, tribus modis dicuntur: primò substantia; secundò qualitate: tertiò quantitate. Ad substantiam pertinet expulsio sanguinis laudabi-lis; aut retentio inutilis excrementi, ut in obstructione renum & vesicæ videre est. Ad qualitatem pertinent retentorum putredo, calor, acrimonia &c. Ad quantitatem pertinet ex-cretio, aut expulsio immodica excre-mentorum. exempla sunt obvia. Huc pertinent mensium retentio, & ex-cretio: item excretionis modus, & tempus, si indebito modo fiat. Hæc vulgatissima est apud Medicos sym-ptomatum distinctio. Non nego quin excretorum retentio alio possit re-ferri: nos tamen nihil innovabimus; vel eo maximè, quod hæc divisio maximè inserviat usibus medicis. Symptoma omne, aut mediatè aut imme-diatè diatè à morbo procedit. Vitiatus corporis calor, causam agnoscit humorem exuberantē: hic autem morbum seu facultatem læsam. Nam causæ sive internæ, sive externæ, actionem non lædent, nisi imprimendo parti pravam dispositionem. Ergo si objectum non sit facultati proportionatum, frustrabitur facultas; ut si manu domum non evertero, aut tremuero sub ingenti onere, quæ tamen actiones non sunt morbidæ: nec enim membro aliquid est præter naturam, sed sola naturalis impotentia; ut ante dictum est.
units.tr: The third kind concerns things retained or excreted. Observe in passing: if a matter contrary to nature is generated in a sound body by a fault of food, such as a stone or a worm, it is not a symptom; but if these follow a disease, then they become symptoms. Things excreted or retained are spoken of in three ways: first with respect to substance; second with respect to quality; third with respect to quantity. The expulsion of healthy blood, or the retention of a useless excrement, as can be seen in obstruction of the kidneys and bladder, pertains to substance. Putrefaction, heat, acrimony and so on of retained matter pertain to quality. Excretion, or immoderate expulsion of excrements, pertains to quantity; examples are obvious. Here belong retention and excretion of the menses, likewise the manner and time of excretion, if it occurs in an improper way. This is the most common division of symptoms among physicians. I do not deny that the retention of excreta may be referred to another head; yet we shall innovate nothing, chiefly because this division serves medical uses most of all. Every symptom proceeds either mediately or immediately from the disease. A heat of the body that has been altered acknowledges as its cause an exuberant humour; this in turn points to the disease, or to the damaged faculty. For causes, whether internal or external, do not damage an action unless by impressing a depraved disposition on the part. Therefore if the object is not proportionate to the faculty, the faculty will be frustrated; as when I do not overturn a house with my hand, or tremble under a huge burden, which actions are nevertheless not morbid: for nothing in the limb is contrary to nature, but only a natural impotence, as was said before.

units.la: Finis Libri secundi.
units.tr: End of the Second Book.

units.la: LIBER III. De Symptomatum causis in specie. CAPVT I. De causis symptomatum cerebri &c.
units.tr: Book III. On the causes of the symptoms in particular. Chapter I. On the causes of the symptoms of the brain, etc.

units.la: Facultatis animalis sedem, & domicilium cerebrum esse, jam ante evicimus: ab eo siquidem sensus & motus universo corpori communicantur: tres quoque functiones principes, imaginatio, cogitatio, memoria in eodem perficiuntur. Supervacaneum quoque est repetere, tria illa ad idoneam functionem necessaria; scilicet temperiem, conformationem, unionemque partium: quibus vitiatis necesse est & actionem quoq; lędi. His itaq; intellectis, ad nobilissimæ huius partis morbos (quorum plerique à symptomatibus denominantur) transeamus; initio facto à Phrenitide (desipientiam simplicem, febrium quarundam comitem, hic omitto) verâ.
units.tr: We have already shown earlier that the seat and dwelling-place of the animal faculty is the brain: for from it sensation and motion are communicated to the whole body, and the three principal functions, imagination, thought and memory, are carried out in it. It is also superfluous to repeat that those three things are necessary for a fitting function: namely, a proper temperament, structure and union of the parts; and when these are impaired, the action must necessarily be harmed too. With these things understood, let us pass on to the diseases of this most noble part (many of which are named from their symptoms), beginning with true phrenitis, leaving aside here the simple delirium that accompanies certain fevers.

units.la: Quæ est, delirium continuum, cum febre acutâ, ortâ ex inflammatione meningum calidâ. Locus affectus est substantia cerebri, quam meninges afficiunt. Causa est intemperies calida, adjunctam habens inflammationem. Causa inflammationis est humor tenuis, biliosus, in parte affectâ putrescens. Quid? quod pro varietate materiæ, varietur Phrenitis. alia est à sanguine bilioso, alia à bile flavâ vel atrâ.
units.tr: It is continuous delirium, with an acute fever, arising from a hot inflammation of the membranes. The seat of the disease is the substance of the brain, which the membranes affect. The cause is a hot intemperament with an attached inflammation. The cause of the inflammation is a thin, bilious humour, putrefying in the affected part. Why, phrenitis also varies with the variety of the matter: one arises from bilious blood, another from yellow or black bile.

units.la: Melancholia est desipientia sine febre, cum metu & tristitiâ absque evidente causâ, ab intemperie frigidâ, siccâ, ex vapore melancholico cerebrum occupante.
units.tr: Melancholy is madness without fever, with fear and sadness without any evident cause, arising from a cold, dry intemperament, from melancholic vapour occupying the brain.

units.la: Causam tradunt, intemperiem cerebri frigidam & siccam. Signa ex definitione constant. Nec enim est symptoma, si quis metuat imminentem sibi calamitatem: sicut nec si quis tristetur objacturam rerum pretiosarum. Porro metus & tristitia in corde sunt affectus appetitus: quia tamen est sympathia appetitui cū facultate cogitante, & imaginante; fit simul imaginatione cerebri sequatur affectus cordis. Est vero triplex, quæ vitio solius capitis fit, melancholia per essentiam dicitur: at quæ fit ob melancholiam in toto corpore redundantem; aut flatus hypochondriorum, est per consensum. De hypochōdriacâ hac disputant artis progeneres; quod tamen persequi, instituti operis brevitas non permittit.
units.tr: They give as its cause a cold and dry intemperament of the brain. The signs follow from the definition. For it is not a symptom if someone fears a calamity hanging over him, nor if someone grieves at the loss of precious goods. Moreover, fear and sadness are affections of the appetite in the heart; yet because there is a sympathy between the appetite and the thinking and imagining faculty, it happens that, when the imagination of the brain follows, the affection of the heart arises at the same time. There are three kinds. That which arises from the fault of the head alone is called melancholy in essence; but that which arises from melancholy abounding in the whole body, or from wind of the hypochondria, is by sympathy. The masters of the art dispute about this hypochondriac melancholy, but the brevity of the present work does not allow me to pursue it.

units.la: Hūc pertinent Lycanthropia, Cynanthropia, &c.
units.tr: To this belong lycanthropy, cynanthropy, etc.

units.la: Mania est desipientia cum exandescentiâ sine febre, à calida cerebri intemperie sine tumore. Maniaci aliter sunt affecti quam melancholici, nec metuunt, nec tristantur; sed audaces, temerarii, obvia quæque raptantes.
units.tr: Mania is madness with fury without fever, from a hot intemperament of the brain without swelling. Maniacs are affected otherwise than melancholics: they do not fear, nor are they sad, but are bold and reckless, seizing whatever lies before them.

units.la: Vertigo est falsa conversionis imaginatio, una cum lasione voluntarii motus; oriunda in cerebro ex vitiato motu spiritus animianimalis. Vitiatur motus spirituum à flatulento spiritu comprimente cerebri ventriculos. In vertigine imaginatio non est corrupta; nam motum illum falsum esse, sciunt ægri: quia tamen falsa motus species exhibetur imaginationi, eius functio depravari quoque creditur. Vapores spiritus irritantes & commoventes interdum sunt in ipso cerebro, interdum ei aliunde communicantur. Levis vertigo est in quâ omnia circumagi tantum videntur. Alia est gravior (quæ & σκοτόδινος) in quâ præter circumactionem, oculi tenebris quasi offunduntur.
units.tr: Vertigo is a false imagination of turning, together with an impairment of voluntary motion, arising in the brain from a disordered motion of the animal spirit. The motion of the spirits is disordered by a windy spirit compressing the ventricles of the brain. In vertigo the imagination is not corrupted, for the patients know that the motion is false; yet because a false appearance of motion is presented to the imagination, its function is also believed to be depraved. Vapours that irritate and stir the spirit are sometimes in the brain itself, and sometimes are communicated to it from elsewhere. Slight vertigo is that in which everything seems only to be spinning around. Another is more severe (called skotodinos [σκοτόδινος]), in which, besides the spinning, the eyes are as it were overspread with darkness.

units.la: De incubo nihil dico; videtur enim somnium potius esse, quam morbus. Hæ sunt depravatæ principis facultatis actiones.
units.tr: I say nothing of incubus; for it seems to be a dream rather than a disease. These are the depraved actions of the principal faculty.

units.la: Amentia sive fatuitas est diminuta ratiocinatio, seu rationis defectus, sine lesione tamen sensus & motus ab intemperie frigidâ cerebri. Fatui itaque integrum habent sensum & motum, quod in Apoplexia non fit.
units.tr: Amentia, or foolishness, is a diminished reasoning, or defect of reason, without any injury, however, to sensation and motion, from a cold intemperament of the brain. Fools, therefore, have whole sensation and motion, which is not the case in apoplexy.

units.la: Oblivio est abolita memoria functio à frigidâ cerebri intemperie orta.
units.tr: Forgetfulness is the abolition of the function of memory, arising from a cold intemperament of the brain.

units.la: Apoplexia est subita privatio omnium functionum animalium, tam ad sensum, quam motum (excepta respiratione) pertinentium, ab angustiâ cerebri profecta. Morbi huius gravitas æstimatur ex respiratione. Angustia istam facit obstructio; interdum compressio cerebri ab inflammatione.
units.tr: Apoplexy is a sudden privation of all the animal functions, both those pertaining to sensation and to motion (except respiration), proceeding from a narrowing of the brain. The seriousness of this disease is judged from the breathing. The narrowing is caused by obstruction, sometimes by compression of the brain from inflammation.

units.la: Epilepsia proprie est motus depravatus; quia tamen adjunctam habet alimentis oblæsionem, huc revocari solet. Est enim convulsio totius corporis, cum lesione mentis conjuncta, orta a maligna qualitate cerebrum infestante. Reperidet quidem malignitas interdum in humore, sæpissimè in vapore; unde frequentia paroxysmorum; nam humor non tam facile discutitur. Ergo differt longè ab Apoplexia, in qua motus abolitus & facultas oppressa; quia Epilepsia est motus depravatus: cerebrum enim expellit maleficam causam. Est autem alia primaria; in quâ causa non est extra cerebrum. Secundaria alia, sive per consensum in quâ vapor à parte corporis attolli-tur ad cerebrum. Pars mittens inter-dum est uterus, interdum ventriculi orificium est.
units.tr: Epilepsy, properly speaking, is a depraved motion; yet because it has an attached impairment of the nourishment, it is customarily referred to here. For it is a convulsion of the whole body, joined with an injury to the mind, arising from a malignant quality infesting the brain. The malignancy is indeed sometimes found in a humour, but most often in a vapour; hence the frequency of the paroxysms, for a humour is not so easily dispersed. Therefore it differs greatly from apoplexy, in which motion is abolished and the faculty oppressed; for epilepsy is a depraved motion, since the brain expels the harmful cause. There is one kind that is primary, in which the cause is not outside the brain. Another is secondary, or by sympathy, in which a vapour is sent up to the brain from a part of the body. The sending part is sometimes the uterus, sometimes the orifice of the stomach.

units.la: Ἀπάρθος, Latinis veternus, est insomnium explebile dormiendi desiderium, conjunctum cum mentis læsione, & febre symptomatica, ortâ à pituitâ in cerebro putrescente. Interdum est adjuncta cerebri inflammatio interdum non,
units.tr: Aparthos [ἀπάρθος], called veternus by the Latins, is a sleepiness with a desire to sleep that can be satisfied, joined with an injury to the mind and a symptomatic fever, arising from putrefying phlegm in the brain. Sometimes an inflammation of the brain is attached, sometimes not.

units.la: Carus, est abolita functio animalis facultatis (integra tamen manente respiratione) ob angustiam cerebri, prohibentem exitum spiritui animali. Ideoq; hic affectus est similis Apoplexiæ: verum respiratio est illæsa, & puncti, sentiunt qui eo laborant, nec in paralysin definit.
units.tr: Carus is an abolition of the animal faculty's function (respiration, however, remaining intact) on account of a narrowness of the brain, preventing the exit of the animal spirit. Hence this affection is similar to apoplexy; but respiration is unharmed, and those who suffer from it feel pricking, and it does not end in paralysis.

units.la: Catalepsis, est principis functionis abolitio, cum tactus & arbitrarii motus destructione (servata tamen respiratione) in quâ ægri eodem corporis habitu manent, quo erant correpti, orta à materiâ frigidâ, siccâ, spiritus animalis congelan-te, , cerebrumque tendente. Membra in hoc affectu manent rigida & immobilia. Phantasia quoque adeo est viciata, ut punctionem non percipiant aegri.
units.tr: Catalepsy is an abolition of the principal function, with destruction of touch and voluntary motion (respiration, however, being preserved), in which the patients remain in the same bodily posture in which they were seized, arising from cold, dry matter congealing the animal spirit and stretching the brain. The limbs in this affection remain rigid and immobile. The perception is also so impaired that the patients do not feel a prick.

units.la: Cataphora, seu coma somnolentum est somnus profundus, quem in cerebro excitat humor frigidus; qui si nimium aucta fuerit, conjungitur mentis stupor; sin minus, mens non laeditur, sed sensus tantum communis. In comate vigilante aegri oculos clausos tenent, nec tamen dormiunt, sed variis quasi insomniis infestantur. Humori frigido (nam nunquam abest hic) in hoc affectu conjungitur alius calidus vigilias inducens. Hic affectus interdum habet delirium phreneticum adjunctum, & febrim, sed symptomaticam. Immodico somno pervigilium opponitur; in quo tamen sensus ratio & sensus sibi constent; tamen quia longiore tempore, quam vires ferunt; in eo perseveramus, laeditur corpus humanum. Causa est humor calidus & acer, impediens est collectionem vaporum benignorum cerebrum irrigantium; sicut in f[?]bre ardente videre est.
units.tr: Catophora, or drowsy coma, is a deep sleep, which a cold humour excites in the brain; if this is increased too much, a stupor of the mind is joined to it; if not, the mind is not injured, but only the common sense. In waking coma the patients keep their eyes closed and yet do not sleep, but are troubled by various kinds of sleeplessness. To the cold humour (for this is never absent) in this affection is joined another, hot, which induces wakefulness. This affection sometimes has frenetic delirium attached, and fever, but a symptomatic one. Excessive sleep is opposed by sleeplessness; in the latter, however, sensation and reason are still consistent with themselves; yet because it lasts longer than strength can bear, the human body is harmed by it. The cause is a hot and sharp humour, which hinders the gathering of the beneficial vapours that water the brain, as may be seen in a burning fever.

units.la: Huc pertinet Catharrus, fluxus humoris excrementitii præter naturam è capite in subjectas partes, ex intemperie frigidâ cerebri ortus. Sicut in omni fluxione, ita hic quatuor considerantur: terminus à quo, ad quem, via & materia. Terminus à quo interdum est cerebrum, secundum ventriculos maxime: interdum est extra cranium sub vertice, unde morbi articulares, si credimus Fernelio. Terminus ad quem est multiplex; interdum est pectus, & tum specialiter vocatur Catharrus: interdum nasus, estque tum coryza: interdum fauces, diciturque raucedo: interdum nervorum initium, estque tum paralysis, & ita deinceps. Catharrus pro membro quod afficit nomen commutat.
units.tr: To this belongs catarrh, a flow of excrementitious humour out of its natural course from the head into the parts below, arising from a cold intemperament of the brain. As in every flux, four things are considered here: the starting point, the destination, the route and the matter. The starting point is sometimes the brain, especially the ventricles; sometimes it is outside the skull under the crown, whence come the joint diseases, if we believe Fernel. The destination is manifold: sometimes it is the chest, and then it is specially called catarrh; sometimes the nose, and it is then coryza; sometimes the throat, and it is called hoarseness; sometimes the beginning of the nerves, and it is then paralysis, and so on. Catarrh changes its name according to the member it affects.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: De causis symptomatum exter-norum sensuum.
units.tr: On the causes of the affections of the external senses.

units.la: EXterni sensus, cum facultatem membro insitam, ut volunt Melici, non habeant, sed à cerebro in-fluentem; laedi possunt, non tantum vitio proprii instrumenti, sed & cerebri; seu partis vim & facultatem communicantis, & nervorum, instrumentorum illi subservientium. Ad nervos revocantur spiritus animales, qui ad motum & sensum juxta sunt necessarii. Quando itaque cerebrum graviter affectum est, spiritus convenienter generare non potest, sine quibus sensus esse nequit. Quando ipsum cerebrum malè se habet, omnes sensus actiones habebunt laesas: at si cerebrum ejusque facultates & instrumenta rectè se habeant laedi potest, hic vel ille sensus in specie; at causa erit in proprio sensus laesi organo.
units.tr: The external senses do not possess the faculty inherent in their organs, as the Medici hold, but receive it flowing in from the brain. They can be harmed not only by a defect of their own instrument but also by a defect of the brain, or of the part that communicates power and faculty to them, and of the nerves, the instruments that serve them. Animal spirits are conveyed to the nerves, and these are necessary for motion and sensation. So when the brain is seriously affected, it cannot generate spirits properly, and without them sensation cannot exist. When the brain itself is unwell, all the actions of the senses will be impaired. But if the brain, with its faculties and instruments, is sound, one particular sense may still be harmed, and then the cause lies in the organ of the sense that is injured.

units.la: His præmissis initium faciemus nobilissimo sensu; visu nimirum. Huius membrum & subjectum est oculus, imprimis humor crystallinus; reliqua enim, ut antea diximus, usu præstant; sicut in aliis sensibus patest. Cœcitas multas habet causas. Nam, nihil dicam de ipso cerebro; si nervi optici ob angustiam quampiam spiritum non recipiant, aut humor crystallinus nimis sit crassus, aut tunica cornea ex supervacuo humore addensetur, aut hæ partes vulnerentur, inducetur cœcitas. Visus debilis αμαυρώσις αυλώσις... est, ex angustia nervorum opticorum: sicut gutta serena perfectam eorundem angustiam, non admittens spiritum, comitatur. in hoc affectu oculi nullum apparet vitium. Lusciosi proxima vident, remota vero non, ob inopiam spirituum. Nam quanquam qui fluit spiritus clarus & bonus est; paucus tamen cum sit, huiusmodi affectum inducit. Quod spiritus crassus concurrat cum tunica cornea crassitie, inducit φυκταλώσις
units.tr: With these points premised, we will begin with the noblest sense, namely sight. Its member and subject is the eye, above all the crystalline humour; for the other parts, as we said before, serve its use, as is also the case with the other senses. Blindness has many causes. To say nothing of the brain itself: if the optic nerves do not receive spirits because of some narrowing, or the crystalline humour is too thick, or the cornea thickens from superfluous humour, or these parts are wounded, blindness follows. Weak sight [amaurosis, auplosis] comes from a narrowing of the optic nerves; a clear drop (gutta serena) accompanies a complete narrowing of them, not admitting spirit. In this affection no defect of the eye itself appears. Blear-eyed people see nearby things but not distant ones, because of a lack of spirits. For although the spirit that flows is clear and good, when it is scanty it produces this condition. When thick spirit coincides with a thickened cornea, it produces phyctalosis [φυκταλώσις].

units.la: [?]Glaucoma (in quo ægri per nebulam [?]quasi vident) est humoris crystallini [?]strassities. Humor crystallinus si sur-[?]sum deorsumque moveatur, genera-tur strabismus ille, quo omnia appa-rent duplicia. Habet hic humor & [?]ali-os affectus, communes tamen sibi [?]cum aliis partibus; quales sunt, in-flammationis omne genus, solutio con-tinui quæcunque. Excidit enim de suâ dissectâ aranea tunica, & foramine uveæ, cum aqueo coin-cidit. Suffusio est humor aqueus con-tractus, in humore albugineo visio-nem impediens, sive inter corneam & crystallinum humorem. Interdum poros aliunde sublati, instante cri-si, vomitu, aut simili evacuatione, sentiuntur suffusionem. Pupillæ ni-tida laxatio, aut constrictio, lædit [?]etiam similiter visum. Cornea justo crassior, aut alioqui alieno colore tincta, vi-sum lædit. Tingitur autem & cras-scit ab affluxu supervacui humoris, [?]cujus sæpè pustulas illic generat. Cras-ties inducitur in senectute corneæ, eodem
units.tr: Glaucoma (in which patients seem to see as if through a mist) is a hardening of the crystalline humour. If the crystalline humour is moved upwards or downwards, that squint arises by which everything appears double. This humour has other affections too, though they are common to it along with other parts, such as every kind of inflammation and any solution of continuity. For the spider-like tunic is torn from its dissected place and, through the opening of the uvea, coincides with the aqueous humour. Suffusion is the aqueous humour contracted, impeding vision in the albuginous humour, or between the cornea and the crystalline humour. Sometimes pores blocked from elsewhere, when a crisis is imminent, are felt as suffusion through vomiting or some similar evacuation. A pupil that is excessively dilated or constricted likewise harms sight. A cornea thicker than it should be, or otherwise tinged with an alien colour, harms sight. It is tinged and thickened by an influx of superfluous humour, which often generates pustules there. Thickening of the cornea comes in old age, in the same way as in the nails, and is called caligo.

units.la: Glaucoma: the first letters of several lines are hidden by the gutter; the bracketed starts are conjectural.
units.tr: Glaucoma: the first letters of several lines are hidden by the gutter; the bracketed starts are conjectural.

units.la: eodem modo quo unguibus, qui a sectus Caligo dicitur. Eiusdem ruptio, & continui solutio, facit pupillam de loco suo excidere. & corneae conjungitur tunica adnata, cui familiare est pterygium. Est vero excrescentia membranosa eiusdem ex affluxu sanguinis crassioris. jam si inflammetur adnata, generabitur Ophthalmia; cuius eadem est, & aliarum inflammationum, causa. Strabismus convulsio oculorum, quâ in oblíquum, sive ad latus ita contorquentur, ut non sit idem aspectus utrius-que. Huius causa eadem est, quæ & aliorum spasmorum: quanquam interdum & consuetudo in pueris idem faciat. Paralysis oculi est eiusdem generis cum aliis resolutionibus, de quibus alibi. Idem de Atrophiâ judicandum. Επίφορα est defluxus præter naturam humoris (calidi, acris, salsi interdum frigidi) è capite in oculos. Caruncula in maiore angulo si minuatur, oritur ῥύας: si augetur, est ὑγρότης. Ἀγγίλωσ est inflammatio in-ter maiorem oculi angulum & nares: ideoque eadem sunt causæ, quæ & aliarum inflammationum.
units.tr: In the same way as in the nails, and this is called caligo. Its rupture and solution of continuity cause the pupil to fall from its place, and the adnate tunic joins the cornea, to which pterygium is characteristic. It is a membranous excrescence of that tunic, arising from an influx of thicker blood. Now if the adnate tunic becomes inflamed, ophthalmia will be generated; its cause is the same as that of other inflammations. Strabismus is a convulsion of the eyes by which they are twisted obliquely or to the side, so that the two eyes do not look in the same direction. Its cause is the same as that of other spasms, although sometimes habit in children produces the same effect. Paralysis of the eye belongs to the same kind as other resolutions, which are discussed elsewhere. The same judgment applies to atrophy. Epiphora [Επίφορα] is an abnormal flow of humour (warm, sharp, salty, and sometimes cold) from the head into the eyes. If the caruncle at the greater angle is diminished, rhyas [ῥύας] arises; if it is enlarged, it is hygrotes [ὑγρότης]. Angillosis [Ἀγγίλωσ] is an inflammation between the greater angle of the eye and the nostrils, and therefore its causes are the same as those of other inflammations.

units.la: Ad oculum palpebra quoque percutiet; cuius tumores præter naturam maximè considerantur hordeolum, & chalazion. Illud est tuberculum in abscessum degenerans. Hæc est tuberculum, durum mobile. ἐντρόπιον palpebrae inversio est, facta interdum à cicatrice, interdum à carneâ excrescentia.
units.tr: The eyelid too is struck by affections. Its tumours that depart from nature are chiefly considered to be the hordeolum and the chalazion. The former is a small tubercle that degenerates into an abscess; the latter is a hard, mobile tubercle. Entropion [ἐντρόπιον] is an inversion of the eyelid, caused sometimes by a scar, sometimes by a fleshy excrescence.

units.la: Atque hæc de præcipuis oculorum affectibus. progrediamur ad auditum, qui eodem modo lædituur quo sensus.
units.tr: So much for the principal affections of the eyes. Let us proceed to hearing, which is harmed in the same way as the other senses.

units.la: Surditas oritur vitio cerebri ; vel nervi quinti paris, interdum ob spirituum impuritatem, & organi dispositionem malam. Ac proinde humor omnis meatum auditorium dilatendens aut obturans, surditatem facit. Idem faciet & ictus nimium comprimens ossa. Hic idem affectus contingit ex pravo situ trium auditus officiculorum. Huc pertinet & inflammatio matio. Quæ de surditate diximus intelligenda etiam sunt de diminuta auditione; quæ ad illam est gradus Obauditio, ὑπήκοος dicta, est actio depravata, qua flatulentus spiritus, praeter naturam commovens internum aërem, facit auditionem sine externa causa. Spiritus iste aut vapor, interdum descendit è capite, interdum contra ascendit, & fertur impulsu ab inferioribus membris; unde per intervalla abit, & redit, variaturque pro materiæ generantis varietate; unde sibilus, tinnitus, strepitus.
units.tr: Deafness arises from a defect of the brain or of the fifth pair of nerves, sometimes from impurity of the spirits and a bad disposition of the organ. Accordingly, any humour that dilates or blocks the auditory passage causes deafness. A blow that compresses the bones does the same. The same affection arises from a faulty position of the three small bones of hearing. Inflammation also belongs here. What we have said about deafness must also be understood of diminished hearing. The degree next to deafness is called obauditio, hypekoos [ὑπήκοος]: a depraved action in which a flatulent spirit, moving the internal air against nature, produces hearing without any external cause. This spirit or vapour sometimes descends from the head, sometimes rises up, and is carried by impulse from the lower limbs; hence it comes and goes at intervals and varies with the variety of the matter that generates it. Hence hissing, ringing, and roaring.

units.la: Quod ad tertium sensum olfactum attinet; variis modis & hic quoque laedi potest. Si enim spiritus animalis intercludatur; aut processus mammillares intemperie, imprimis frigida laborant; abolebitur functio. Idem accidet in ulcere genito in anteriori cerebri parte. Os quoque colatorium obstructum, eundem affectum inducet. Quid? quod nares exulcerat idem efficient. Vlcus narium graveolens, ozæna dicitur; quæ latè se diffundens ere solet. Ulceribus neglectis caro dcrescit; quæ si longa sit, polypus à bloris varietate dicitur, ingens ma-um, & quod in cancrum desinere solet. Putrida ulcera narium, & fœdi icinarum partium odores, olfactum epravare solent.
units.tr: As for the third sense, smell, it too can be harmed in various ways. If the animal spirit is intercepted, or the mammillary processes suffer from an intemperance, especially a cold one, the function will be abolished. The same will happen with an ulcer arising in the anterior part of the brain. An obstructed cribriform bone will induce the same affection. Why should I say more? Ulceration of the nostrils produces the same effect. A foul-smelling ulcer of the nostrils is called ozaena, and it tends to spread widely. If ulcers are neglected, flesh grows up in them; if this growth is long, it is called a polypus from the variety of its shape, a huge mass, and it tends to end in cancer. Putrid ulcers of the nostrils, and foul odours from neighbouring parts, tend to deprave the sense of smell.

units.la: Perit & minuitur gustus, non tantum vitio cerebri, & nervorum; sed etiam ipsius linguæ; quod eiusdem aralysis docet. Verum si lingua imuatur vitioso aliquo humore, ut bile, quod in febribus fieri amat; depravatur gustus: omnia, etiam dulcia, judicabit esse amara.
units.tr: Taste is lost and diminished not only by a defect of the brain and nerves but also by a defect of the tongue itself, as the paralysis of the tongue shows. But if the tongue is infected by some vicious humour, such as bile, which tends to occur in fevers, taste is depraved, and the patient will judge everything, even sweet things, to be bitter.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: De Tactus symptomatibus.
units.tr: On the symptoms of touch.

units.la: Veniamus ad tactum, cuius symptomata, dolor & voluptas, per omnem medicinam magni sunt momenti. Omnis in capite dispositio, descensum spirituum impediens, tantum aufert, non tantum sensum, sed motum; ut in Apoplexia videre est. Abolitus in membro tactus, aut etiam diminutus, caret nomine ; excepto si in dente fiat ; tumque vocatur hæmodia; quam succi acidi, interdum etiam acres, efficere solent. Aboletur quoque aut minuitur, vitio not solùm cerebri, eiusque instrumentorum inservientium, sed & ipsius partis & instrumenti; ut in gangræna vi dere est. Interdum idem nervus sensus, motusque est instrumentum ; in quo tamen aboleri potest motus, servato sensu; sed nunquam contra: qui maior spirituum copia requiritur ad motum, quam sensum. Verum si alius nervus inserviat sensui, alius motui tum potest manere motus, sublato sensu, & contra.
units.tr: Let us come to touch, whose symptoms, pain and pleasure, are of great importance in all medicine. Any disposition in the head that impedes the descent of the spirits takes away not only sensation but also motion, as can be seen in apoplexy. When touch is abolished in a limb, or even diminished, the condition has no name, except when it happens in a tooth; then it is called hæmodia, which sour juices, and sometimes sharp ones, are wont to produce. Touch is also abolished or diminished through a fault not only of the brain and the instruments serving it, but also of the part and instrument itself, as can be seen in gangrene. Sometimes the same nerve is the instrument of both sensation and motion. Motion can be abolished in it while sensation remains, but never the reverse, since more of the spirits is needed for motion than for sensation. If, however, one nerve serves sensation and another serves motion, then motion can remain when sensation is removed, and the reverse.

units.la: Huc pertinet dolor, & voluptas, quæ ut intelligantur, distingui debent dolor animi à corporis dolore, quo agimus. Illum voco motum solius cordis tristem, ex mali perceptione, sine corporis lesione. Quemadmodum si quis doleat mortem patris, aut alioqui tristetur propter jacturam bonorum. ubi tamen corpori nihil hil accedit, nec decedit; & hic do-r non est cognitio. idem de volup-te judicandum. Verum quidem est corporis dolorem trahere secum & animi, ut in vulneratis videre est; non contra; nisi forsan quis ex animi ægritudine incidat in morbum, quem comitatur dolor.
units.tr: Pain and pleasure belong here. To understand them, we must distinguish the pain of the mind from the pain of the body with which we are concerned. I call the former a sad movement of the heart alone, arising from the perception of an evil, without injury to the body. For example, if someone grieves over the death of a father, or is otherwise saddened by the loss of goods, while nothing is added to or taken from the body; and this is not a symptom. The same judgment applies to pleasure. It is true that bodily pain brings the pain of the mind along with it, as can be seen in the wounded; but not the reverse, unless perhaps someone, from distress of mind, falls into a disease that is accompanied by pain.

units.la: Dolor huius loci proprius, est actus depravatus, seu tristis sensatio (cognitio nimirum) partium nervosarum, (ossa enim & huiusmodi partes terrestres omni sensu carent) orta ex repentina alteratione, aut continui solutione. Objectum tactus debet esse illi proportionatum. Si ergo nimium sit calens, subito & vehementer alterabit sensum istum; ut in perfusione manus ab aqua calidissima videre est. Quia vero frigus & calor effi-ciences sunt qualitates, soli possunt dolorem inferre, siccitas & humiditas quaquam; quia harum actio est ignava: nisi humiditas adjunctam habeat materiam distentem, calidam, frigidam; ubi dolor non excitatur tatur per se ab humiditate. Scio quod- dam arbitrari & siccitatem induce-re dolorem; verum intelligunt sicci-tatem illam, quæ calorem sequitur; ut in ustione, cui inesse volunt sen-sum & caloris, & siccitatis. Ergo al-teratio sola, vitiando temperiem, ef-ficit dolorem. si enim hoc faceret sol-vendo continuum, quî fit solutionem istam à nobis non percipi? Dicunt solutionem continui non esse hic manifestam, credo admodum, sed cum sit doloris causa, hoc est efficiat tri-stem sensationem; debebat tanquam objectum à nobis cognosci. Iam vero si dolor fieret à tali solutione partium, debebat medicamentis unien-tibus & glutinantibus curari; quod tamen neutiquam fit, sed curatur contrariâ alteratione. Dolorem quoque facit continui solutio manifesta, quemadmodum in vulneribus vi-dere est.
units.tr: The proper pain of this place is a depraved act, or sad sensation (that is, a perception) of the nervous parts (for bones and such earthy parts lack all sensation), arising from a sudden alteration or dissolution of continuity. The object of touch must be proportionate to it. If, then, something is too hot, it will suddenly and violently alter that sense, as can be seen when the hand is plunged into very hot water. Since cold and heat are active qualities, they alone can bring on pain; dryness and moisture cannot, since their action is sluggish, unless the moisture has an attached matter that is distending, hot or cold, and then pain is not aroused by moisture alone. I know that some think dryness also induces pain, but they mean that dryness which follows heat, as in a burn, in which they wish both the sensation of heat and of dryness to be present. Therefore alteration alone, by vitiating the temperament, produces pain. For if it did so by dissolving continuity, how is it that this dissolution is not perceived by us? They say the dissolution of continuity is not here manifest, I quite believe, but since it is the cause of pain, that is, produces a sad sensation, it ought to be known to us as an object. Moreover, if pain arose from such a dissolution of parts, it ought to be cured by uniting and gluing medicines; which in fact is by no means the case, but it is cured by the contrary alteration. A manifest dissolution of continuity also causes pain, as can be seen in wounds.

units.la: Voluptas est convenientis objecti per-ceptio, quæ pro natura partium sen-tientium, & spirituum copia, maio- & m[?] & minor esse solet; ut cernere licet in partibus genitalibus, vola manus, ventriculi ore; cuius dolores naturales(nec enim omnes praeter naturam) sunt fames, & sitis.
units.tr: Pleasure is the perception of a suitable object, which is wont to be greater or less according to the nature of the sentient parts and the abundance of the spirits, as may be seen in the genitals, the palm of the hand, and the mouth of the stomach. Its natural pains (for not all are against nature) are hunger and thirst.

units.la: Tactus fundamentum est, sicut vitae, ita aliorum sensuum, proinde dolent[?] hi propter laesum tactum. Verum an insit[?] illis dolor, & voluptas in propriis functionibus, auditione, visione, dubitari potest. Sane in gustu & olfactu videre est huiusmodi dolorem: gravis enim odoris perceptio est tristis, sicut visio rei parum convenientis: huiusmodi tamen actiones non sunt symptomata; quia non oriuntur à dispositione praeter naturam partem laedente. Intemperies calida & frigida solę dolorem faciunt; sed sine ullâ tensione, aut gravitate. Aliter se res habet ubi materia est conjuncta.
