Huc pertinent omnium partium dolores, qui eodem semper modo fiunt; à solutione nimirum continui[?], vel intemperie, quae raro sola persistit sine materiae affluxu; ut in aurium dolore, ὠπαλγία[?] dicto, patet, quem sanguis tenuis biliosus plerunque concitat. Eadem dentium ratio, nam quanquam dentibus nullus insit sensus; (quicquid reclamet Trallianus) eorum tamen radicibus inserti sunt nervuli, quos calidus humor, aut alioqui aër, irritare solet. Non nego, quin frigida intemperies sola, eundem dolorem paritura sit; verum sepissimè adjunctum habet similem humorem.
units.tr: Touch is the foundation of life, and so of the other senses; hence these also feel pain on account of an injured touch. But whether pain and pleasure are inherent in their own functions, hearing and sight, may be doubted. Certainly in taste and smell such pain can be seen, for the perception of a strong odour is painful, as is the sight of a thing little suited to us. Such actions, however, are not symptoms, since they do not arise from a disposition contrary to nature injuring the part. Hot and cold intemperies alone produce pain, but without any tension or heaviness. It is otherwise where matter is joined to them. Here belong the pains of all parts, which always arise in the same way, namely from a dissolution of continuity or from intemperies, which rarely persists alone without an influx of matter; as is clear in earache, called ὠπαλγία [ōpalgia], which thin bilious blood usually provokes. The same is true of the teeth: although teeth have no sensation of their own (whatever Trallianus may say), nerve fibres are inserted into their roots, which hot humour, or indeed air, is wont to irritate. I do not deny that a cold intemperies alone might produce the same pain, but it very often has a similar humour attached to it.

units.la: Huc pertinet Arthritis, articulorum dolor, per intervalla affligens ex humoris defluxu. Articuli secundum omnes partes non dolent, sed partes sensiles nervosas; tendines nimirum musculorum, membranas, cutem: ligamenta enim, cartilagines, & ossa sensu destituuntur. Humor itaque descendens, prædictas partes divellit & distendit. Jam vero antea monui, in omni fluxione humorum quatuor esse consideranda, terminus quo, & ad quem, viam & materiam. Terminus ad quem est articulus af sectus; qui si sit manus, vocatur χει- ρāγρα (Arthritis enim est communis) sin pedis, ποδάγρα; sin genu, γονάγρα; sin coxendicis, ἰσχιάς vocatur; reli-quorum carent proprio nomine. Istæ partes debiles & raræ promptissimè materiam delatam recipiunt. Debi-litantur sæpe vitio parentum, (nam morbus est hæreditarius) sepè pra-vus victus eundem affectum inducit.
units.tr: To this belongs arthritis, pain of the joints, afflicting by intervals from a flux of humour. The joints do not hurt in all their parts, but the sensitive nervous parts: namely the tendons of the muscles, the membranes, and the skin; for ligaments, cartilages and bones are destitute of sensation. The descending humour therefore tears and distends the aforesaid parts. Now I have already noted that in every flux of humours four things must be considered: the terminus from which, the terminus to which, the way, and the matter. The terminus to which is the affected joint; if this is the hand it is called χειράγρα [cheiragra] (for arthritis is common), if the foot ποδάγρα [podagra], if the knee γονάγρα [gonagra], if the hip it is called ἰσχιάς [ischias]; the rest lack a proper name. These parts, being weak and loose, most readily receive the matter that is brought to them. They are often weakened by the fault of parents (for the disease is hereditary), and a bad diet often induces the same affection.

units.la: De termino à quo, seu parte man-dante, lis non contemnenda existit inter Medicos. Quidam existimant esse pericranium; alii vero non hanc solam partem esse originem; sed & alias præterea; ut uterum, hepar, ca-put. Materia dolorem efficiens ab iis qui volunt originem esse pericra-nium, est pituitosus & serosus humor. alii aliter philosophantur. Nam ca-lor, rubor, dolor, febris, aliaq; symp-tomata potius indicant bilem, aut sanguinem. Ergo aiunt omne genus humoris, hunc affectum generare posse; quanquam rarò simplex aliquis fluat, via per quam, est spatium inter carnem & cutem; vel alioqui ipsæ membranæ, vasæ. Quando ergò partes mandantes irritantur, deponunt sua excrementa in subjectos articulos, ex quibus generatur atrocissimus iste dolor. Atque hæc de dolore, quan-tum licuit, breviter perstrinximus; nam alios dolores alibi commodius pertractabimus.
units.tr: Concerning the terminus from which, or the commanding part, there is no slight dispute among physicians. Some think the pericranium is the origin; others hold that this is not the only source, but also others, such as the uterus, the liver, and the head. The matter producing pain, according to those who make the pericranium the origin, is a phlegmatic and serous humour. Others reason differently: for heat, redness, pain, fever and other symptoms rather indicate bile or blood. Therefore they say that every kind of humour can produce this affection, although rarely does a single kind flow alone; the way by which it travels is the space between flesh and skin, or else the membranes and vessels themselves. When therefore the commanding parts are irritated, they deposit their excrements into the joints concerned, from which that most dreadful pain is generated. And these things about pain we have touched on briefly, as far as was permitted; for we will treat other pains more conveniently elsewhere.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAP. IV.

units.la: De Motus symptomatibus, eorumque causis.
units.tr: On the symptoms of motion and their causes.

units.la: NOn agimus hic de omni motu, sed arbitrario, qui perficitur ministerio musculorum: nam motus insitus partibus, quo convenientia attrahuntur, & superflua expelluntur, non est huius loci. Definivimus jam ante, nullum motum aut sensum fieri posse sine subsidio spirituum animalium, & nervorum. Symptomata ergo motus, non tantum partis affectę sequuntur dispositionem, sed & ipsius capitis, & nervorum. Motus, sicut & aliæ functiones, tribus modis lædilæditur. vel enim aboletur, vel depravatur, vel minuitur; de quibus breviter. Est autem Paralysis, abolita functio voluntarii motus in membris, manente facultate principe integrâ (propter apoplexiam) producta ab humore nervos obstruente, vel ob ipsum membrum pravè dispositum. Postrema verba addo, ut innuam paralysin non semper habere causam caput, aut spinalem medullam. Resolutio ani fit à solâ loci illius intemperie sine damno spinæ, aut capitis: quia tamen plerunque mali causa est in partibus jam dictis, hinc est quod illæ solæ considerentur. Ergo si origo nervorum obstruatur, impediaturque influxus animalis spiritus in musculos & nervos, orietur affectus hic. Neque hoc tantum, sed si spiritus in magnis cerebri vulneribus dissipentur; idem eveniet. Verum quia omnes sub facie partes, exceptis visceribus, & vocis organis, nervos à spina accipiunt; fit, ut illic princeps causa existat. Cerebro itaque affecto secundum dextram aut sinistram partem, non tantum eiusdem lateris sequitur resolutio, sed & eiusdem in facie partis, cum vocis impedimento. Sin obstructio principium spinæ occupet; omnes sub facie partes resolventur. Sin eius dimidia pars ita sit affecta, dextra nimirum aut sinistra; dimidia corporis pars resolvetur. Verum solius manus paralysis aut pedis exempli causa, supponit eam spinæ partem malè esse affectam, à quâ nervos accipit.
units.tr: Here we are not concerned with all motion, but with voluntary motion, which is carried out by the service of the muscles. The motion inherent in the parts, by which what is fitting is drawn in and what is superfluous is expelled, does not belong to this place. We have already defined that no motion or sensation can occur without the help of the animal spirits and the nerves. The symptoms of motion therefore follow not only the disposition of the affected part but also that of the head and the nerves. Motion, like the other functions, is harmed in three ways: it is either abolished, depraved, or diminished, and of these we shall speak briefly. Paralysis is the abolition of the function of voluntary motion in the limbs, while the principal faculty remains intact (on account of apoplexy), brought about by a humour obstructing the nerves, or by the member itself being badly disposed. I add the last words to indicate that paralysis does not always have its cause in the head or the spinal marrow. Loss of movement of the limb arises from an intemperature of that place alone, without damage to the spine or the head; but because the cause of the evil usually lies in the parts just mentioned, these alone are considered. Therefore, if the origin of the nerves is obstructed and the flow of animal spirit into the muscles and nerves is impeded, this affection will arise. Nor is this the only way: if the spirits are dissipated by large wounds of the brain, the same will happen. But since all the parts below the face, except the viscera and the organs of voice, receive their nerves from the spine, it follows that the principal cause lies there. Thus, when the brain is affected on the right or left side, there follows not only loss of movement on the same side but also in the part of the face on that side, together with an impairment of speech. But if the obstruction occupies the origin of the spine, all the parts below the face will be paralysed. If only half of the spine is so affected, namely the right or the left, then half of the body will be paralysed. But paralysis of the hand alone, or of the foot for example, presupposes that the part of the spine from which the nerve comes is badly affected.

units.la: Stupor gradus est ad paralysin; proinde eædem causæ, differentes tantum secundum magis, & minus.
units.tr: Stupor is a step towards paralysis, so the same causes apply, differing only in degree.

units.la: Convulsio, Græcis σπασμὸς, est depravatus membrorum motus: cuius causa, & modus, in obscuro latent. Distingui scio inter motum convulsivum, & ipsam convulsionem, illum volunt à facultate, à materiâ, vel causâ morbificâ irritatâ fieri; quemadmodum in morbo Herculeo videre licet: hanc esse solius morbi opus, non concurrente facultate. Quæ dif-ficulficulter intelligi possunt salvis fundamentis antea jactis: Si enim est depravatus motus animalis, necesse est facultatem animæ concurrere. Diximus præterea antea, idem esse subjectum contrariorum, nisi alterum naturaliter insit, sanitas verò & morbus sunt contraria, idem ergo habebunt subjectum, eandemque facultatem pravè, aut benè afficient. Jam vero, si dixeris convulsionem esse opus solius morbi, non autem facultatis irritatæ; quomodo idem erit subjectum; præsertim cum facultas sine organo non agat? Quid? si proprie loquendum est, actiones sunt organorum, facultatibus informatorũ; nam morbus non tam est causa actionis, quam vitii in actione: dicere ergo spasmum fieri à solo morbo, non natura, perinde est ac si dicas, depravatam febricitantium coctionem fieri ab illo gradu caloris qui naturali supervenit; non verò naturali qui præfuit. Quod ridiculum est, unicus enim est calor; constans tamen gradibus dibus quibusdam naturalibus, quibusdam præter naturam. Est autem Spasmus, depravatus motus (contractio scilicet) & invitus musculorum versus originem, ortus ex eorum brevitate, inducta à repletione & inanitione. Et locus affectus & causa huius morbi, adeò controvertuntur à Medicis, ut non immeritò exclamet Averroës lib. 3. Coll. cap. 33. Nam quia convulsio adjunctum habet plerumque delirium, putant nonnulli locum affectum esse ipsum cerebrum. Alii contra nituntur, aiuntque solos musculos esse affectam partem; quia eorum actio læditur. Verum de causâ dubitatur; nam musculorum brevitas, supponit aliquam in iis causâ à quâ generatur; quam Hippocrates dicit esse repletionem & inanitionem. Quæ cum sint dispositiones contrariæ; non possunt eundem affectum producere per se; nisi forsan conveniant in uno tertio. sicut in venenis videre est; quorum licet quædam sint calida, quædam frigida, da, conveniunt in malignitate. Notum est Galeni exemplum chordarum, quæ & à siccitate, & humiditate contrahuntur. Sed causa hæc multis displicet.nam motus non fit à nervo, sed à musculo; nervus autem defert spiritum, quem facultatem vocant. nec dispositio sicca aut humida subitò introducitur : nec siccitas & humiditas, qualitates passivæ, tam validum edunt motum. Constat etiam eas per se dolorem non inferre; qui tamen hic ingens est. Restat ergo, ut dicamus affectum excitari à malignis vaporibus, repletione corporis, & inanitionem sequentibus.
units.tr: Convulsion, called spasmos [σπασμὸς] by the Greeks, is a depraved movement of the limbs. Its cause and mode lie hidden in obscurity. I know that some distinguish between convulsive motion and convulsion itself: they hold that the former arises from the faculty, from the matter, or from a morbific cause that irritates it, as may be seen in the Herculean disease; the latter, they say, is the work of the disease alone, without the faculty concurring. These things can hardly be understood if the foundations laid down earlier are preserved. For if it is a depraved animal motion, the faculty of the soul must necessarily be involved. We have said before that the same subject holds contraries, unless one of them is naturally present; health and disease are contraries, so they will have the same subject and the same faculty, which they affect either well or badly. Now, if you say that convulsion is the work of the disease alone and not of the irritated faculty, how can it have the same subject, especially since a faculty does not act without an organ? Moreover, if we must speak strictly, actions belong to the organs, informed by the faculties; for disease is not so much the cause of the action as the fault in the action. To say therefore that spasm arises from the disease alone, and not from nature, is just like saying that the depraved concoction in feverish people arises from that degree of heat which supervenes beyond nature, and not from the natural heat which was present before. This is absurd, for there is only one heat, though it consists of certain degrees that are natural and certain degrees that are beyond nature. Spasm is a depraved motion (namely contraction) and an involuntary drawing of the muscles towards their origin, arising from their shortening, induced by repletion and emptying. The affected place and the cause of this disease are so disputed among the physicians that Averroes rightly cries out, Coll. book 3, chapter 33. For since convulsion usually has delirium attached to it, some think the affected place is the brain itself. Others, on the contrary, insist that only the muscles are the affected part, because their action is impaired. But the cause is doubtful, for the shortening of the muscles presupposes some cause in them from which it is generated, which Hippocrates says is repletion and emptying. Since these are contrary dispositions, they cannot of themselves produce the same affection, unless perhaps they agree in some third thing, as may be seen in poisons, some of which are hot and some cold, yet they agree in their malignancy. Galen's example of the strings is well known, which contract both from dryness and from moisture. But this cause displeases many, for motion arises not from the nerve but from the muscle; the nerve conveys the spirit, which they call the faculty. Nor is a dry or moist disposition introduced suddenly, nor do dryness and moisture, being passive qualities, produce so strong a motion. It is also agreed that they do not of themselves bring pain, which here is great. It remains, therefore, that we say the affection is excited by malignant vapours, following upon repletion and emptying of the body.

units.la: Respectu partium contractarum dividitur convulsio in universalem, & particularem. Illius exemplum est epilepsia, ἐμπεσθόπνος, in quo curvantur musculi ut mentum pectus contingat, corpusque carinam repræsentet : ὀπισθότονος, cum contrahuntur musculi posteriores : Τέτανος, cum uterque motus concurrit, estq; compositus : utriusque enim partis musculi culi ita contrahuntur, ut corpus ma-neat rigidum. Particularis convulsio, oculorū est strabismus, oris ab utrâ-que parte, dicitur spasmus caninus.
units.tr: Convulsion is divided, with respect to the parts contracted, into universal and particular. An example of the universal kind is epilepsy, emprosthotonos [ἐμπροσθότονος], in which the muscles are bent so that the chin touches the chest and the body resembles a keel; opisthotonos [ὀπισθότονος], when the posterior muscles are contracted; and tetanus [Τέτανος], when both movements concur and it is compound: for the muscles of both sides are so contracted that the body remains rigid. A particular convulsion of the eyes is squinting; of the mouth on either side it is called canine spasm.

units.la: Tremor est motus membrorum depra-vatus, ex contrariis compositus, facultatis scilicet attollentis, & membrum suo pondere deprimentis. Causa est debilitas membrorum, induḉta vel oppressione virium vel exsolutione. Tremor hic non est morbus, si pondus longè sit suprâ vires,sed potius naturalis impotentia.
units.tr: Tremor is a depraved motion of the limbs, composed of contraries, namely a faculty lifting and the limb being pressed down by its own weight. The cause is weakness of the limbs, brought on either by the oppression of the powers or by their loosening. This tremor is not a disease if the weight is far beyond the strength, but rather a natural inability.

units.la: Pandiculatio est dilatatio musculorum irritatorum à vaporibus excrementitiis in carne collectis.
units.tr: Pandiculation is the dilatation of muscles irritated by excrementitious vapours collected in the flesh.

units.la: Oscitatio est depravatus motus musculorum in facie irritatorum ab vaporibus tenuibus intus collectis.
units.tr: Yawning is a depraved motion of the muscles of the face, irritated by thin vapours collected within.

units.la: Frigus, horror, & rigor differunt tantum secundum magis, & minus: (In horrore sola cutis concutitur; in rigore vero musculi totius corporis vibrantur:irritantur enim à re aliquâ noxia:) de quorum causâ ambigitur. Vulgo creditur esse acris materia pungens, per partes sensibiles delata; quod non accipio. Demus quidem huiusmodi materiam excitare posse horrorem momentaneum; quod non nego; sed qui possint horror, & rigor, qui in febribus sunt diuturni, à materiâ calidâ excitari, non video. Materia illa acris & vellicans, inducet ne frigus? quomodo unum contrarium aliud generabit? acris enim humor est biliosus & calidus. Repetendum hic ex Physiologiâ, calorem, insitum partibus, non sufficere functionibus: necesse itaque est à corde mitti uberiorem calorem per arterias. ergo si vapor aliquis malignus (quod fieri amat in paroxismis febrium intermittentium) cor, fontem caloris, impetat, non potest tum calorem per arterias fundere; necesse est ergò extrema corporis, & alias partes calore destitutas, rigere, & horrrescere, quod est evidentissimum in naso, digito, pede, qui primò omnium tentantur. Tam diu autem durat iste motus depravatus, quamdiu impeimpetitur cor; at ubi liberatum fue-rit consumptis vaporibus, redeunt membra ad pristinam naturam. suffi-citur enim illis abunde calor. Non itaque est necesse calorem recurrere à membris ad cor; sed contra verisi-milius est cor male affectum non transmittere.
units.tr: Chill, shivering, and rigor differ only in degree. (In shivering only the skin is shaken; but in rigor the muscles of the whole body quiver, for they are irritated by some harmful thing.) About their cause there is doubt. It is commonly believed to be a sharp, pricking matter conveyed through the sensible parts; this I do not accept. Let us grant that such matter can excite a momentary shivering, which I do not deny; but how the shivering and rigor which last long in fevers can be excited by hot matter, I do not see. Will that sharp and irritating matter produce cold? How will one contrary generate the other? For the sharp humour is bilious and hot. Here we must recall from physiology that the heat inherent in the parts does not suffice for their functions; it is therefore necessary that a richer heat be sent from the heart through the arteries. So if some malignant vapour (which tends to happen in the paroxysms of intermittent fevers) attacks the heart, the fount of heat, it cannot then pour heat through the arteries; it is necessary, therefore, that the extremities and the other parts, deprived of heat, grow rigid and shiver, which is most evident in the nose, finger, and foot, which are the first to be affected. This depraved motion lasts as long as the heart is attacked; but when it has been freed, the vapours having been consumed, the limbs return to their former nature, for enough heat is supplied to them abundantly. It is therefore not necessary that heat return from the limbs to the heart; on the contrary, it is more likely that the heart, being ill affected, does not transmit it.

units.la: Sternutatio, est vehemens efflatio per nares cum sono à facultate cerebri, irrita-tâ à materiâ vel vapore pungente. Ad istum motum concurrunt musculi thoracis.
units.tr: Sneezing is a vehement expulsion of breath through the nostrils, with a sound, from a faculty of the brain irritated by a matter or a pungent vapour. The muscles of the chest join in this motion.

units.la: Oscitatio, pandiculatio, sternuta-tio, non sunt morbi effectus, sed naturæ: in sanis enim eveniunt, eo-dem modo quo naturalis fæcum aut urinæ excretio. Lassitudo non incom-mode & huc revocari potest; quæ tamen non est morbus, sed dispositio morbosa. Lassitudo alia est tensiva, (non loquor de eâ quæ exercitium consequitur) in quâ corpus intendi-tur: quam humores per musculos su-si producunt; estque signum plethorae. Alia est ulcerosa, in quâ ægri pun-ctioctiones sentiunt, & ab humoribus excitatur; estque cacochymiæ sig-num. Ex hisce duabus generatur las-situdo phlegmonides, in qua præte-rea musculi quasi elevantur: in hac ergo sanguis est & pravus, & mul-tus. Huc pertinet ea lassitudo quæ contundens dicitur, ὀσφύϊον vocant; in quâ offa dolere, & quasi frangi vi-dentur. Omnibus hisce lassitudini-bus, est communis movendi impo-tentia, conjuncta cum sensus tristitiâ.
units.tr: Yawning, stretching and sneezing are not effects of disease but of nature: they occur in healthy people, in the same way as the natural excretion of faeces or urine. Lassitude may also reasonably be referred here; yet it is not a disease but a morbid disposition. One kind of lassitude is tensive (I am not speaking of that which follows exercise), in which the body is stretched taut; the humours produce it by distending the muscles, and it is a sign of plethora. Another is ulcerous, in which the sick feel pricking pains, and it is caused by humours; it is a sign of cacochymia. From these two arises the phlegmonous lassitude, in which the muscles moreover seem as it were raised up; in this, therefore, the blood is both bad and abundant. To this belongs the lassitude called bruising, which the Greeks name osphyion [ὀσφύϊον]; in it the bones seem to ache and as if broken. Common to all these lassitudes is an inability to move, joined with a sad feeling.

units.la: CAP. V. De Symptomatibus vocis, loque-læ, respirationis.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. On the Symptoms of the Voice, of Speech and of Breathing.

units.la: AD sermonem & vocem articu-latam formandam, multa concurrunt. Requiritur enim spiritus animalis; quæ si deficiat; (ut in apo-plexia & syncope videre est,) non edetur vox. Idem fit in linguæ para-lysi. Brevitas nimia linguæ idem ef-ficit; sicut & nimia magnitudo. Huc revocatur linguæ convulsio. Ad esse-ctum producendum perfectum, re-quiquiritur concursus omnium causa-rum; ad malum verò unius defectus sufficit; sicut hic contingit. Quælibet enim causarum supra memoratarum, sufficiunt voci impediendæ. Hæ eæ-dem causæ; minores, tamen efficiunt vocem debilem. Idem fit cum malè est parvibus ministrantibus; ut in po-lypo, coryza, erofo palato videre est. Usus columellæ est non tantum vo-cem instar plectri musici, sed & fri-gidum aërem temperare. qui impe-ditur, si aut nimis fit magna ab hu-more distendente, & inflammante; aut alioqui parva; quod in lue vene-reâ contingit.
units.tr: Many things come together to form speech and an articulate voice. For animal spirit is required; if this is lacking (as is seen in apoplexy and syncope), no voice will be produced. The same happens in paralysis of the tongue. An excessive shortness of the tongue has the same effect, as does an excessive size. To this belongs convulsion of the tongue. To produce the effect fully, the concurrence of all the causes is required; but for harm, the defect of one is enough, as happens here. For any one of the causes mentioned above is sufficient to impede the voice. These same causes, when weaker, make the voice feeble. The same happens when the parts serving the voice are in poor condition, as is seen in polyp, coryza and an eroded palate. The use of the uvula is not only to temper the voice like the plectrum of a musical instrument, but also to temper the cold air. This is impeded if it becomes either too large, distended and inflamed by humour, or otherwise too small, which happens in venereal disease.

units.la: Angina est respirandi deglutiendiq; difficultas & impotentia, ex inflamma-tione musculorum gutturi faucibusque ministrantium; comitem habens febrem continuam. Læditur respiratio non tantum vitio proprio membrorum, ut in angina, sed per aliarum partium consensum, ut postea constabit.
units.tr: Quinsy (angina) is difficulty and inability of breathing and swallowing, arising from inflammation of the muscles serving the throat and fauces, with continuous fever as its companion. Breathing is harmed not only by a fault in the parts themselves, as in quinsy, but by the sympathy of other parts, as will be shown later.

units.la: Asthma est respiratio crebra cum anhelatione & tussi sine febre, orta à pituita crassâ crassâ pulmonis bronchios farciente.idem facit tuberculum.
units.tr: Asthma is frequent breathing with panting and cough, without fever, arising from thick phlegm filling the bronchial tubes of the lung. A tubercle does the same.

units.la: Quod si obstructio sit nimia, erit Orthopnæa; in qua nisi erecta cervice, respirare nequeunt. Quod si vires sint admodum debiles, respiratio evadit sublimis; in quâ per nares fit exsufflatio. Aufertur respiratio in ἀπνοίᾳ; quam apoplexia, syncope & hysterica passio inferunt, ob causas tamen diversas. nam in primâ desi-deratur spiritus animalis; in reliquis vitalis, animalis materia.
units.tr: But if the obstruction is excessive, it will be orthopnoea, in which people cannot breathe unless the neck is held erect. If the strength is very weak, the breathing becomes raised, in which air is blown out through the nostrils. Breathing is taken away in apnoea [ἀπνοίᾳ], which apoplexy, syncope and hysterical fits bring on, though for different causes: in the first, animal spirit is lacking; in the others, vital spirit, the matter of animal spirit.

units.la: Tussis est vehemens efflatio cum stre-pitu, per guttur erumpens, à facultate expultrice, à causâ morbificâ irritâ. Lo-cus affectus est pulmo. Causa irri-tans est multiplex; fumus, humores acres, viscidi interdum &c. Humor nimium tenuis non expellitur, quia impulsum thoracis subterfugit; ni-mium crassus idem facit; arctè enim adhæret pulmonibus, quod ergò ex-pellitur, mediæ debet esse consisten-tiæ.
units.tr: Cough is a vehement expulsion of air with noise, bursting out through the throat, from an expelling faculty, irritated by a morbid cause. The seat of the affection is the lung. The irritating cause is manifold: smoke, sharp humours, sometimes viscid ones, and so on. A humour that is too thin is not expelled, because it slips away from the push of the chest; one that is too thick does the same, for it clings tightly to the lungs. What is to be expelled, therefore, ought to be of medium consistency.

units.la: Verum respiratio non læditur tan-tum tum vitio pulmonis, sed & pectoris, quod quomodo fiat videamus. Ergo si pleura inflammetur, impedietur respiratio. Inflammatio ista vocatur pleuritis. Est vero lateris dolor puncto-rius, cum febre acutâ, dyspnæa pulsu duro, inæquali, crebro, tussi vehementi, orta ex inflammatione pleuræ, mediastinum inflammari solet, sed rarò. Generatur inflammatio hîc, quemadmodum & in aliis partibus, ex materiâ transmissâ à parte validâ, ad debilem. Materia ista plerumque est sanguis biliosus, rarò pituitosus aut melancholicus. Idem sanguis si incidat in pulmones, efficiet peripneumoniam, inflammationem pulmonum; cui adjungitur respirandi difficultas, gravitas sine dolore, febris continua, (omnes symptomaticæ, quales sunt quæ inflammationes partium sequuntur, continuæ sunt) tussis vehemens, rubor faciei &c. Pulsus hîc non est durus, sed mollis & undosus.
units.tr: Indeed, breathing is harmed not only by a fault of the lung but also of the chest, and let us see how this happens. If the pleura is inflamed, breathing will be impeded. This inflammation is called pleurisy. It is a stabbing pain in the side, with acute fever, difficult breathing, a hard, uneven, frequent pulse and violent cough, arising from inflammation of the pleura. The mediastinum is also wont to be inflamed, but rarely. Inflammation here is generated, as in other parts, from matter passed from a strong part to a weak one. This matter is mostly bilious blood, rarely phlegmatic or melancholic. If the same blood falls upon the lungs, it will produce peripneumonia, inflammation of the lungs, to which is added difficulty of breathing, heaviness without pain, continuous fever (all symptomatic fevers, such as those that follow inflammations of parts, are continuous), violent cough, redness of the face and so on. The pulse here is not hard but soft and undulating.

units.la: Empyema est collectio puris in thoracis cacis capacitate, respirandi difficultatem inducens, cum tussi, & sputo purulento, orta ex abscessu. Sequitur peripneumoniam & pleuritidem; sanguine nimirum in pus converso, & rupto abscessu.
units.tr: Empyema is a collection of pus in the cavity of the chest, causing difficulty of breathing, with cough and purulent sputum, arising from an abscess. It follows peripneumonia and pleurisy, namely when the blood is turned into pus and the abscess bursts.

units.la: Tabes est consumptio totius corporis, cum febre lentâ, impeditâ respiratione, tussi, sputo, orta ex pulmonis ulcere. Pus enim in thorace collectum, si intra quadraginta dies non expurgetur; erodit pulmonem, & hanc, de quâ agimus, tabem producit.
units.tr: Tabes is wasting of the whole body, with slow fever, impeded breathing, cough and sputum, arising from an ulcer of the lung. For pus collected in the chest, if it is not purged within forty days, erodes the lung and produces this tabes of which we are speaking.

units.la: CAP. VI. De Cordis symptomatibus & causis.
units.tr: CAP. VI. On the symptoms and causes of the heart.

units.la: Dictum est non semel, caloris domicilium esse cor; cui incumbit, generatio, conservatio, distributio caloris sive spiritus vitalis. Quæ functiones, quanquam vivo homine penitus tolli non possint, sensus tamen judicio videntur aboleri; ut in Syncope videre licet. Est autem, repentinus viriū lapsus (nam sensim omnis magnus nus morbus vires carpit) à debilitate facultatis orta, quæ, ob causam malefi-cam, spiritus non communicat cæteris partibus.Debilitatis causa est multiplex; sed nulla tam familiaris, quam malignus vapor ascendens ab utero, ut in passione hysterica; interdum à ventriculo, inprimis superiore orificio, quod est acutissimi sensus. Debilitatur etiam facultas à spirituum dissipatione, ut in immodico gaudio, interdū suffocatione, ut in metu, quod tamen raro contingit. Huc pertinent λειποθυμία, λειποψυχία, ἔκλυσις; quæ aut non differunt, aut secundum magis & minus tantum. Motus cordis depravatus, seu inordinatus, est palpitatio, (nam tremor motus arbitrarius improprie illi tribuitur) quæ est motus cordis depravatus, constans dilatatione & constrictione, ortus à vapore crasso, facultatem vitalem irritante. Motus iste, si multis credimus, arteriis non communicatur; non erit ergo depravata pulsatio vero palpitatio, sed illegitima.
units.tr: It has been said more than once that the heart is the seat of heat, and that generation, preservation and distribution of heat, or vital spirit, depend on it. These functions, although they cannot be wholly abolished while a man is alive, nevertheless seem to be suspended as far as the senses are concerned, as can be seen in syncope. Now a sudden collapse of strength (for every serious illness wears down strength gradually) arises from a weakness of the faculty which, because of a harmful cause, does not communicate spirit to the other parts. The cause of weakness is manifold, but none is so common as a malignant vapour rising from the womb, as in hysterical passion; sometimes it comes from the stomach, especially its upper orifice, which has the most acute sensation. The faculty is also weakened by dissipation of the spirits, as in immoderate joy, and sometimes by suffocation, as in fear, though this rarely happens. To this belong leipothymia [λειποθυμία], leipopsychia [λειποψυχία], and eklysis [ἔκλυσις], which either do not differ or differ only in degree. A depraved or irregular motion of the heart is palpitation (for trembling, which is an involuntary motion, is improperly attributed to it), and this is a depraved motion of the heart, constant in dilation and constriction, arising from a thick vapour irritating the vital faculty. If we believe many authors, this motion is not communicated to the arteries; so it will not be a depraved pulse but, strictly, palpitation, though an irregular one.

units.la: Nullus morbus familiarior est cordi, quam intemperies calida, quam febrem vocant; de qua paucis agendum. Quod fiet initio sumpto à definitione; est enim, intemperies calida cordis, actiones eius manifeste ledens. Dico intemperiem; quia calori cordis naturali adduntur alii gradus praeter naturam; unde Galenus vocavit calorem nativum, in igneum conversum. Ridiculum est, quod quidam dicunt, febrem esse solum illum calorem adventitium, & superadditum. Nam revera hic solus non manifeste laederet actionem, nisi conjungeretur naturali; nec esset calida intemperies, sed potius frigida. jam vero accidentarium est quod calor diffundatur mediante spiritu per reliqua membra; nam etiamsi id non fieret, (ut initiis paroxismorum) homo tamen febricitare propter solam cordis intemperiem. Locus affectus est cor secundum substantiam; spiritus, & humores causa sunt potius, quam subjectum. Jam, quanquam alius
units.tr: No disease is more familiar to the heart than the hot intemperature which they call fever, and this must be discussed briefly. We shall begin with a definition: it is a hot intemperature of the heart, plainly harming its actions. I say intemperature, because other degrees beyond the natural are added to the natural heat of the heart; hence Galen called it the native heat turned fiery. It is ridiculous to say, as some do, that fever is only that adventitious and superadded heat. For in truth this heat alone would not plainly harm the action unless it were joined to the natural heat; and the intemperature would not be hot but rather cold. Moreover, it is incidental that the heat is diffused through the remaining limbs by means of the spirit; for even if this did not happen (as at the beginning of paroxysms), a man would still be feverish from the intemperature of the heart alone. The seat of the affection is the heart itself in its substance; the spirits and humours are causes rather than the subject. Now, although one part of the body becomes hotter than another,

units.la: aliûs alius partis temperies calidior fiat; non erit prius febris, quam cordi communicetur, ut in Phrenitide, Pleuritide videre est. Calor in corde accensus diffunditur per reliquum corpus, si non impediatur; impeditur autem in lypiria, accessionibus intermittentium, & Epialâ ex parte. Quęcunq; causę alia membra calefaciunt, eædem & cor accendent. talia sunt illa quinq; supra commemorata, motus, contactus rei calidæ, suppressio fuliginum &c.
units.tr: there will be no fever until it is communicated to the heart, as can be seen in phrenitis and pleurisy. Heat kindled in the heart is diffused through the rest of the body, unless it is hindered; it is hindered, however, in the chill of lypiria, in the attacks of intermittent fevers, and in part in epiale. Whatever causes warm the other limbs will also kindle the heart. Such are those five causes mentioned above: motion, contact with a hot thing, suppression of soot, and so on.

units.la: Febris symptomata sunt pulsus & respirationis mutatio, sitis, vigiliæ, dolor capitis, cibi fastidium &c.
units.tr: The symptoms of fever are a change in the pulse and in breathing, thirst, sleeplessness, headache, loss of appetite, and so on.

units.la: Dividitur febris in simplicem, & compositam. In illa similis est calorí forma; in hac non. Divisio febris simplicis in Ephemeram, Synochum, & Hecticam, non tam est sumpta à subjecto quàm causa inflammante, si hecticam excipias; nam revera res inanimatæ spiritus & humor, non sunt subjectum. Tres ergo istæ sunt in eâdem cordis substantiâ, differentes tantum fecundum calorem, magis aut minus radicatum.
units.tr: Fever is divided into simple and compound. In the former the form of the heat is uniform; in the latter it is not. The division of simple fever into ephemeral, synochus and hectic is taken not so much from the subject as from the inflaming cause, if you except hectic; for in truth spirit and humour, being inanimate things, are not the subject. These three, then, are in the same substance of the heart, differing only according to the heat, which is more or less deeply rooted.

units.la: Dividitur febris in putridam, & non putridam, qualis est nuda diaria, aut diaria extensiva. Putrida est continua, vel intermittens. In illâ humores putrescunt in vasis, venis scilicet & arteriis; quæ ad infebricitationem non solet pervenire. In hac humor est extra vasa; in habitu nimirum corporis, si antiquis creditur; aut potius continetur in primâ corporis regione, circa hepar, ventriculum &c. quæ ad infebricitationem solet devenire. Continua putrida (nam non putrida ad diariam revocatur) est duplex. Alia enim est, quæ putredinem sine remissione cordi impertit; synochus putrida, & causus. Aliæ non semper putredinem impertiunt, sed remittunt subinde; ut quæ simpliciter dicuntur continuæ, quo pertinet terna continua. Intermittens febris pro conditione humoris peccantis, est vel tertiana, vel quotidiana, vel quartana. In primâ, causa est bilis; in secundâ, pituita; in tertia, melancholiâ. In prima, est accessio tertio quoque die; in secundâ, quotidie fit exacerbatio; in postremâ, quarto die. Huc pertinent febres quintanæ, sextanæ, &c.
units.tr: Fever is divided into putrid and non-putrid; the non-putrid kind is the plain daily fever or the extended daily fever. A putrid fever is either continuous or intermittent. In the former the humours putrefy in the vessels, namely the veins and arteries, which does not usually lead to the onset of fever. In the latter the humour lies outside the vessels, in the habit of the body if one believes the ancients, or rather it is contained in the first region of the body, around the liver, stomach and so on, which usually brings on fever. Continuous putrid fever (for the non-putrid kind is referred to the daily) is of two kinds. One imparts putrefaction to the heart without remission; these are putrid synochus and causus. Others do not always impart putrefaction but remit from time to time, such as those simply called continuous, to which the continued tertian belongs. Intermittent fever, according to the condition of the offending humour, is either tertian, quotidian or quartan. In the first the cause is bile; in the second, phlegm; in the third, melancholy. In the first the attack comes every third day; in the second the exacerbation comes daily; in the last, every fourth day. To this belong the quintan and sextan fevers, and so on.

units.la: Celebris est febrium divisio in essentiales, & symptomaticas. In illis substantia cordis est habitualiter, ut ita dicam, malè disposita; proinde sublatâ causâ conjunctâ perseverant. In his cor habitualiter non calet: proinde sublatâ causâ continente seu conjunctâ, dictum factum evanescunt; ut in Peripneumoniâ, Pleuritide videre est. Proinde si inflammatio alicuius viscēris, ut cerebri, habeat corpus dispositum ad febrim; febris consequens non est symptomatica; consequens nimirum inflammationem: nam etiamsi nulla fuisset inflammatio antecedens, genita fuisset febris. Sed si partibus optimè dispositis superveniat febris ex visceris inflammatione; talis febris ex symptomatica; quæ sublata causa, dictum factum tollitur, quod genus febris absolute. absolutè non dicebatur morbus à maioribus, sed febris accidens.
units.tr: The well-known division of fevers is into essential and symptomatic. In the former the substance of the heart is, so to speak, habitually ill-disposed; therefore they persist when the conjoined cause is removed. In the latter the heart is not habitually hot; therefore when the containing or conjoined cause is removed, the fever vanishes as soon as it is said and done, as can be seen in peripneumony and pleurisy. Accordingly, if the inflammation of some viscus, such as the brain, falls on a body disposed to fever, the fever that follows is not symptomatic; it follows the inflammation, for even if there had been no preceding inflammation, the fever would have been generated. But if fever supervenes from inflammation of a viscus when the parts are very well disposed, such a fever is symptomatic; when the cause is removed, it is removed as soon as it is said and done. This kind of fever was not called a disease in the strict sense by the ancients, but an accident of fever.

units.la: Omnis febris, ex motione causarum morbificarum, dividitur in quatuor tempora; principium, augmentum, statum, declinationem; de quibus supra.
units.tr: Every fever, arising from the motion of the morbific causes, is divided into four periods: beginning, increase, state and decline; of which we have spoken above.

units.la: Putrescunt humores in corpore, quomodo & alibi; à calore nimirum ambientis. ambientis nomine intelligendus venit omnis calor, qui parti non est naturalis. Quando ergo spiracula cutis & pori obstruuntur, fuliginês intus contenti, evocant internum partis, aut humoris calorem; in quâ evocatione essentia putredinis posita est. solvitur enim unio humidi cum sicco. Quod fætor credatur signum omnis putredinis; non est admittendum; multa enim putrescunt sine fœtore; & contra multa fœtent sine putredine; ut in castoreo, assâ fœtidâ cernere licet. Sicca cordis intemperies sine calore, est Marasmus.
units.tr: Humours putrefy in the body, as they also do elsewhere, namely from the heat of the surroundings. By surrounding heat is to be understood every heat which is not natural to the part. When therefore the pores and openings of the skin are obstructed, the soots contained within draw out the internal heat of the part or humour; in this drawing out the essence of putrefaction lies, for the union of moist with dry is dissolved. That a stench is held to be the sign of all putrefaction must not be admitted; for many things putrefy without stench, and on the contrary many stink without putrefaction, as can be seen in castoreum and asafoetida. A dry intemperature of the heart without heat is marasmus.

units.la: CAP. VII. De Morbis ventriculi & intestinorum.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. On Diseases of the Stomach and Intestines.

units.la: VEntriculus, corporis culina, non tantum habet functiones sibi inservientes ; sed & alias publicas toti corpori ministrantes;ut in generatione chyli communis alimenti videre est. Eâ de causâ appetitum habet, quam animalem vocant; cuius tristis sensatio est fames; ut ante dictum. Conflictatur sæpe non tantum cum morbis similaribus, sed & dissimilaribus ; nec non solutione continui, morbo communi. Corpus humanum, dissolutioni obnoxium, eget continuâ instauratione per cibum & potum. Stimulus autem appetitus est fames & sitis, hæc in faucibus; illa in ventriculi orificio superiore residet. Sublatâ fame, tollitur appetitus, ut postea constabit: proinde desymptomatis appetitum consequentibus, agemus primò. Depravatur tribus modis, sicut aliæ functiones; nam aboaboletur, diminuitur, vel depravatur.
units.tr: The stomach, the kitchen of the body, has not only functions serving itself but also other functions serving the whole body, as can be seen in the generation of chyle from common food. For this reason it has the appetite, which they call animal; its sad sensation is hunger, as said before. It is often troubled not only by similar diseases but also by dissimilar ones, and also by solution of continuity, a common disease. The human body, subject to dissolution, needs continual restoration through food and drink. The spur of appetite is hunger and thirst: thirst resides in the throat, hunger in the upper opening of the stomach. When hunger is removed, appetite is removed, as will be established later. Therefore, having dealt with the symptoms that follow appetite, we shall first treat its disorders. It is depraved in three ways, like the other functions: for it is abolished, diminished, or depraved.

units.la: Abolita appetentia (ἀνορεξία Græcis) cibi, id est, calidi, sicci, est ex defectu fuctionis in orificio ventriculi. Non fugit autem; quia vis & facultas est abolita ab intemperie calidâ; ut in febribus; vel quia cerebrum læsum non impertit spiritum animalem; ut in Apoplexiâ, similibusque affectibus evidens est. Ab his causis, debilioribus tamen, oritur diminuta appetentia.
units.tr: Abolished appetite (ἀνορεξία [anorexia] to the Greeks) for food, that is, for what is hot and dry, arises from a defect of function in the opening of the stomach. It does not escape notice, because the power and faculty are abolished by a hot intemperature, as in fevers; or because a damaged brain does not impart animal spirit, as is evident in apoplexy and similar affections. From these causes, though weaker ones, diminished appetite arises.

units.la: Contraria ventriculi dispositio, est fames inexpleta; immodica scilicet ciborum appetentia; quam nimia ventriculi fuctio excitat. Quæcunque os ventriculi nimium constringunt, & corrugant, appetitum stimulant; ut intemperies frigida, quæ raro est in ventriculo sola; sed sæpè comitem habet melancholiam, aut pituitam acidam, os ventriculi infestantem. Huius generis est Caninus appetitus; inexplebilis ciborum appetentia cum vomitu, excitata à materiâ acidâ cardiam oblimente. βούλιμος est inexplebile ciborum desiderium, sine vomitu tamen; genitum ab iisdem causis. Hic in principio appetentia est aucta, verum paulatim minuitur.
units.tr: The opposite disposition of the stomach is insatiable hunger, that is, an immoderate appetite for food, which excessive activity of the stomach excites. Whatever constricts and wrinkles the mouth of the stomach too much stimulates appetite, such as a cold intemperature, which is rarely alone in the stomach but often has as its companion melancholy or sour phlegm, which harasses the mouth of the stomach. Of this kind is canine appetite, an insatiable appetite for food with vomiting, provoked by acid matter clogging the cardia. βούλιμος [boulimos] is an insatiable desire for food, yet without vomiting, produced by the same causes. Here appetite is at first increased, but gradually diminishes.

units.la: Depravatur appetentia in Pica; quæ est alimenti non naturalis (carbonis, calcis) desiderium. Fit à sucцis pravis ventriculi tunicis impactis, quanquam in tali affectu non videtur omnino sana facultas princeps. Morbus familiaris gravidis, tribus potissimum mensibus primis: quanquam viri non omnino ab eo sint liberi, ut in elephantiacis patet.
units.tr: Appetite is depraved in pica, which is a desire for unnatural food (charcoal, lime). It arises from depraved juices clogging the coats of the stomach, although in such an affliction the leading faculty does not seem altogether sound. It is a familiar complaint of pregnant women, chiefly in the first three months; yet men are not entirely free of it, as is clear in elephantiasis.

units.la: Appetentia sitis, eodem modo vitiatur. Nam & aboletur, si fauces sint imbutæ pituitâ; sæpe videas febricitantes non sitire, ob nullam aliam causam, nisi quod amygdalæ copiosâ pituitâ sint perfusæ. Inducetur idem affectus, si cerebrum laboret; sicut ante diximus.
units.tr: Thirst is spoiled in the same way. For it is also abolished if the throat is soaked with phlegm; you often see feverish patients not thirsting for no other reason than that the tonsils are drenched in copious phlegm. The same affliction is induced if the brain is affected, as we said before.

units.la: Si faucium humiditas (errant, qui putant sitim esse in ventriculi orificio) consumatur ab intemperie calidâ & siccâ; inducetur sitis inexplebilis; immoimmodica cupiditas frigidi & humi-di, orta à tristi fuctione faucium, ex defectu propriæ humiditatis.
units.tr: If the moisture of the throat (those are wrong who think thirst lies in the mouth of the stomach) is consumed by a hot and dry intemperature, insatiable thirst is induced: an immoderate craving for what is cold and moist, arising from the sad function of the throat owing to a lack of its own moisture.

units.la: Ventriculus nunquam cibum concoquet, nisi arctè complectatur. Proinde si ventriculus cibum non contineat, generantur fluctuationes cum sonitu, ubi ventriculus cibũ à se propellit in hanc, aut illam partem. Causa est intemperies admodum frigida: nam minus frigida excitat flatum, magnus calor flatuum materiam discutit; debilis excitat quidem, sed non consumit. Hic eadem functio diminuitur à minoribus causis. Depravata retentio hic non adeò est conspicua; in eâ quædam palpitatio & tremor deprehenditur; sed affectus rarus est.
units.tr: The stomach never concocts food unless it grips it tightly. Therefore, if the stomach does not hold its food, fluctuations with a sound are produced, when the stomach drives the food from itself into this or that part. The cause is a very cold intemperature: for a less cold one excites wind, while great heat dispels the matter of wind; a weak one indeed excites it but does not consume it. Here the same function is diminished by lesser causes. A depraved retention is not very conspicuous here; in it some palpitation and trembling are detected, but the affection is rare.

units.la: Amυλία est abolita alimentorum in ventriculo concoctio, ab intemperie frigidâ. Frigidâ dico; nam calida depravat magis, quam abolet. Idem fiet, si retentrix vis debilitetur, aut aboleatur; ita ut cibus justo tempore non contineatur. Quod si plus cibi potusque sumatur, quam natura regere gere potest, idem affectus inducetur. Si causæ memoratæ leviores fuerint, efficient βεχδπποψίαν in qua cibus non sufficienter mutatur. Δυσπεψία est depravata concoctio ; corruptio nimirum ciborū in alienam substantiam ; nidorosam scilicet, interdum acidam. Nidorosam efficit intemperies calida; aridam frigida; nisi vitium sit in alimento.
units.tr: Amylia is the abolished concoction of food in the stomach, from a cold intemperature. I say cold, for a hot one depraves more than it abolishes. The same thing happens if the retentive power is weakened or abolished, so that the food is not held for its proper time. If more food and drink is taken than nature can govern, the same affliction is induced. If the aforesaid causes are milder, they produce βεχδπποψία (dyspepsia), in which the food is not sufficiently changed. δυσπεψία [dyspepsia] is depraved concoction, namely the corruption of food into an alien substance, that is, a fumy substance, sometimes sour. A hot intemperature produces a fumy one, a cold one a dry one, unless the fault lies in the food itself.

units.la: Chylus concoctus expelli debet. quæ etiam functio tripliciter lædi-tur. Abolita & diminuta expulsio rari sunt affectus; qui tamen oriuntur ab intemperie frigidâ &c. Depravata expulsio familiare symptoma, ubi ventriculus expellit, vel quomodo non oportebat, vel quale, vel quantum. Causa est facultas irritata, quod quomodo fiat, videamus.
units.tr: Concocted chyle ought to be expelled. This function too is injured in three ways. Abolished and diminished expulsion are rare affections, which nevertheless arise from a cold intemperature, etc. Depraved expulsion is a familiar symptom, when the stomach expels either in a way it ought not, or of a kind, or in an amount that it ought not. The cause is an irritated faculty; let us see how this happens.

units.la: Vomitus alius naturalis de quo non loquor; nec enim fit à morbo, nec vires deiicit, alius symptomaticus, morbi opus; estque depravatus motus ventriculi irritati, quo cibus in ventriculi capacitate contentus manifestè & sensibiliter biliter expellitur per os. In hoc affectu orificium ventriculi non est tempe-ratum; alioqui non tam facile irrita-retur. multum facit ciborum copia; aut aliena qualitas, excrementorum proventus &c. Gradus ad vomitum est nausea;habet enim easdem causas, sed leviores: in qua nihil expellitur, adest tantum inane vomendi deside-rium & conatus. Huc pertinet mor-bus, cholera dictus; motus deprava-tus ventriculi expellentis per utrum-que os materiam contristantem. hæc est bilis omne genus in ventriculo ex vitiato alimento genitum. Est alia cholera, sicca seu notha, (nam prior est humida) in quâ nihil expellitur: acer enim & flatulentus spiritus, do-lorem ventriculi cum inflammatione excitat.
units.tr: Vomiting, the natural kind, of which I do not speak, since it does not arise from disease nor weakens the strength, is one thing; the symptomatic kind, the work of disease, is another, and it is a depraved motion of the irritated stomach, by which food contained in the capacity of the stomach is clearly and perceptibly expelled through the mouth. In this affection the mouth of the stomach is not tempered; otherwise it would not be so easily irritated. The quantity of food contributes much, or an alien quality, or an outpouring of excrements, etc. The step toward vomiting is nausea; for it has the same causes, but milder ones, and nothing is expelled in it; there is only an empty desire and effort to vomit. To this belongs the disease called cholera: a depraved motion of the stomach expelling through both mouths the matter that distresses it. This is bile of every kind generated in the stomach from spoiled food. There is another cholera, dry or spurious (for the former is moist), in which nothing is expelled: for a sharp and flatulent spirit excites pain of the stomach with inflammation.

units.la: Singultus perperam ad convulsio-nes revocatur; est enim affectio ven-triculi, non musculi. Est vero depra-vatus motus cum sono, à materiâ tunicis ventriculi impacta, & facultatem irri-tante. Fibræ hic contrahuntur & ten-dunduntur ad expellendum impedimen-tum.
units.tr: Hiccup is wrongly referred to the convulsions; for it is an affection of the stomach, not of the muscle. It is indeed a depraved motion with a sound, from matter lodged in the coats of the stomach and irritating the faculty. Here the fibres are contracted and stretched to expel the obstruction.

units.la: Ventriculum excipiunt intestina, quæ omni genere morborum infestantur, intemperie, vitiatâ compositione, & solutione continui. Ad vitium compositionis pertinent lumbrici, tanquam partes quædam adhærentes intestinis, unde constituunt morbum in numero aucto. Sunt vermorbum in numero aucto. Sunt animalia toto genere præter naturâ animalia toto genere præter naturam, genita in intestinis ex putri materiâ, lædentia functiones. Corporis totius sententina sunt intestina, non ergo mirum excrementa illic congesta converti in huiusmodi vermiculos. Idem enim videmus, non tantum in aliis corporis partibus, sed & in sterquiliniis, in quibus ex putrescente materiâ generantur. Nam in ventriculo propter concoctionem & calorem generari nequeunt; si inveniantur ab intestinis isthuc repserunt. Triplex est horum genus, sunt enim quidam rotundi, quidam lati, quidam & rotundi; ἀσκαρίδες dicti, in inteintestino recto geniti, generantur ex pituitâ crassâ putrescente: amara & acida, qualia sunt bilis & melancholia, extinguunt potius, quam generant. De modo generationis, & causa principali, viderint Philosophi. Porro nullum est functionis genus, quod ab lumbricis non lædatur. Vitiantur intestina ex prava eorum situ; si quando nimirum suo loco moveantur, descendantque ad scrotum, inguen &c.
units.tr: The intestines follow the stomach, and they are attacked by every kind of disease: by intemperature, by a spoiled composition, and by solution of continuity. To the fault of composition belong the worms, as certain parts adhering to the intestines, whence they constitute a disease in an increased number. They are creatures, of a whole kind contrary to nature, generated in the intestines from putrid matter, injuring the functions. The intestines are the sewer of the whole body, so it is no wonder that the excrements gathered there turn into such little worms. For we see the same thing not only in other parts of the body but also in dung heaps, where they are generated from rotting matter. For they cannot be generated in the stomach because of its concoction and heat; if they are found there, they have crept up from the intestines. There are three kinds of them: some are round, some broad, some both round, called ascarides [ἀσκαρίδες]; those born in the straight intestine are generated from thick putrid phlegm; bitter and sour humours, such as bile and melancholy, rather destroy them than generate them. The philosophers may consider the mode of generation and the principal cause. Moreover, there is no kind of function that is not injured by worms. The intestines are damaged by their faulty position, when indeed they are moved from their place and descend to the scrotum, groin, etc.

units.la: Colica est tristis tactus seu sensus intestinorum crassorum à causâ violentâ. Causa hæc raro est intemperies nuda; sæpe est materia descendens, ut pituita crassa; interdum spiritus descendens, exitu carena: si fiat ab inflammatione, comitem habet acutissimam febrem & vomitum biliosum.
units.tr: Colic is a sad touch or sensation of the large intestines from a violent cause. This cause is rarely a bare intemperature; often it is a descending matter, such as thick phlegm; sometimes a descending spirit, with a flatulent outlet; if it arises from inflammation, it is accompanied by a most acute fever and bilious vomiting.

units.la: Volvulus, εἱλεὸς & χολδάλος est tenuium intestinorum (imprimis ilci unde nomen Græcum) dolor, cum turpi, vehementique vomitu, ventris tumore incitans ea ad expulsionem per os, ortus ex materiâ acri, interdum inflammatione. tione. Hic inferiora intestina sunt obstructa, interdum ob inflammationem, & fæces.qui etiamsi libera sint, tamen quia acrimoniam humorum ferre nequeunt,motu epistaltico conferre nequeunt, trahuntur versus superiora, tandemque ipsas fæces ore excernunt.
units.tr: Volvulus, εἱλεὸς [heileos] and χολδάλος [choladalos], is pain of the small intestines (especially the ileum, whence the Greek name), with foul and violent vomiting, provoking by swelling of the belly the expulsion of those contents through the mouth, arising from a sharp matter, sometimes from inflammation. Here the lower intestines are obstructed, sometimes by inflammation, and by the faeces; and although they are free, yet because they cannot bear the acrimony of the humours, they cannot assist by peristaltic motion; they are drawn upward, and at last they expel the faeces themselves through the mouth.

units.la: Expulsio intestinorum naturalis est per podicem: quæ tamen labefactatur tribus modis, sicut aliæ functiones. Constat nullam deiectionem fieri, nisi facultas expultrix irritetur. ergo si excrementa sint pauca,nec facultatem irritantia, aut alioqui sint his conditionibus prædita, sensus tamen aut diminutus, aut abolitus sit, ut in apoplexia, non erit dejectio. Fæces itaque ut facultatem irritent, debent perfusæ esse bile flavâ;ob cuius defectum tarda erit dejectio.
units.tr: Expulsion of the bowels is natural through the anus, but it is weakened in three ways, as are the other functions. It is agreed that no evacuation takes place unless the expulsive faculty is stimulated. Therefore if the excrement is scanty and does not stimulate the faculty, or if the faculty is otherwise endowed with these conditions but sensation is either diminished or abolished, as in apoplexy, there will be no evacuation. Thus, for the faculty to be stimulated, the faeces ought to be drenched in yellow bile; with its lack, evacuation will be sluggish.

units.la: Porro fæces copiosæ aut paucæ æstimantur ex assumptis alimentis; nisi forsan alimenta sint planè excrementitia. Diarrhæa est crebra dejectio humorum excrementitiorum, nata à facultate expultrice irritata. Irritationem facit non tantum copia, sed & excrementorum qualitas. Morbosa hæc diarrhæa supponit semper pravam dispositionem & morbum lædentem vires, in quâ non expelluntur quę debebant & qualia, sed cruda, & vitiosa, cum molestiâ. Multiplex est, pro varietate materiæ; unde alia biliosa, alia Melancholica est. Pars mandans, interdum est ventriculus: sæpissimè verò totum corpus. Huc pertinet hecticorum fluxus colliquativus, in quo partium substantia & pinguedo à calore dissolvitur.
units.tr: Moreover, faeces are judged copious or scanty from the food taken in, unless perhaps the food is wholly excrementitious. Diarrhoea is a frequent discharge of excrementitious humours, arising from the expulsive faculty being irritated. It is not only the quantity but also the quality of the excrements that causes the irritation. This morbid diarrhoea always presupposes a faulty disposition and a disease weakening the strength, in which things that ought to be expelled, and in the right kind, are not expelled, but raw and vitiated, with discomfort. It is manifold, according to the variety of the matter; hence one kind is bilious, another melancholic. The part sending it down is sometimes the stomach, but most often the whole body. To this belongs the colliquative flux of hectics, in which the substance of the parts and their fat are dissolved by heat.

units.la: Lienteria, partim huc pertinet, partim ad ventriculum; idem de passione cœliacâ judicandum. Lienteriam vocant celerem ciborum non transmutatorum per alvum dejectionem, quam efficit facultas retentrix ventriculi, plane abolita. aboletur ab intemperie frigidâ, humidâ, pituitâ, &c. Quidam putant expultricem, irritatam ab acri materiâ, idem efficere. In hac dejectione cibus non alteratus expellitur. verum si expellatur, sed aliquo quo modo coctus & alteratus, fiet Cœliaca passio, solâ magnitudine à Lienteriâ differens.
units.tr: Lientery pertains partly here and partly to the stomach; the same judgement is to be made concerning coeliac passion. They call lientery a rapid evacuation through the bowel of food not transformed, which is brought about by the retentive faculty of the stomach being wholly abolished. It is abolished by a cold, moist intemperance, phlegm, etc. Some think that the expulsive faculty, irritated by sharp matter, produces the same effect. In this evacuation the food is expelled unaltered. But if it is expelled somewhat cooked and altered in some way, it becomes coeliac passion, differing from lientery only in degree.

units.la: Dysenteria proprie dicta (nam aliter sumi, non ignoro) est deiectio cruenta, cum torminibus ventris; quam intestinorum ulcus facit. Humor insigniter acer, ut bilis, pituita salsa, rodit sæpe intestina, eaque exulcerat. Pars mandans, non est certum aliquod membrum. Affectus hic quibusdam quasi gradibus incedit. humor enim primò intestinorum mucum, vel pinguedinem abradit; tum superficiem; postremò ipsum intestinorum corpus. Porro communis est hic morbus intestinis omnibus, si recte excipias. eadē enim passio in recto est Tenesmus; nisi quod hîc non sint vētris tormina, sed tensio & pondus intestini recti.
units.tr: Dysentery, properly so called (for I am aware that it is taken otherwise), is a bloody discharge with griping pains of the belly, which an ulcer of the intestines produces. A humour remarkably sharp, such as bile or salt phlegm, often gnaws at the intestines and ulcerates them. The part sending it down is not some certain member. This affection proceeds by certain degrees, as it were: the humour first scrapes away the mucus or fat of the intestines; then the surface; lastly the substance of the intestines itself. Moreover this disease is common to all the intestines, if you rightly take them up; for the same passion in the rectum is tenesmus, except that here there are not griping pains of the belly, but tension and weight of the rectum.

units.la: Præter hanc Dysenteriam veram & germanam, sunt aliæ nothæ & spuriæ: quarum prima est dejectio cruenta; non à morbo, sed à naturâ facta. quando enim tanta sanguinis copia gignitur, ut naturę sit molesta, tum facultas irritata, sicut per nares, hæmorrhoides,uterum,ita etiam per intestina, eū expellit, sed citra morbum.Hęc sanguinis excretio non nocet,imo liberat ab imminentibus malis. Deinde huius generis est fluxus hepaticus ille,in quo sanguis niger & splendens, diutiusque in hepate assatus, expellitur in intestina. Tertia species est dejectio sanguinis aquosi, similis carnis loturæ, orta ab insigni intemperie frigidâ. Constat ex anatome; ani officium esse, fæces continere & ad libitum expellere. si ergò musculus exitum claudens σφιγκτὴρ dictus, resolvatur ab intemperie frigidâ, invitis nobis fæces excidunt: Contrarium facit convulsio.
units.tr: Besides this true and genuine dysentery there are other bastard and spurious kinds. The first of these is a bloody discharge, made not by disease but by nature. For when so great a quantity of blood is generated that it is troublesome to nature, then the faculty, irritated, expels it, as through the nostrils, haemorrhoids, or the uterus, so also through the intestines, and this without disease. This discharge of blood does no harm; indeed it frees from impending evils. Next to this kind is that hepatic flux in which black and shining blood, roasted longer in the liver, is expelled into the intestines. A third species is a discharge of watery blood, like the washing of flesh, arising from a marked cold intemperance. It is clear from anatomy that the office of the anus is to retain the faeces and to expel them at will; if therefore the muscle closing the outlet, called the sphincter, is relaxed by cold intemperance, the faeces fall out against our will. Convulsion has the contrary effect.

units.la: Fissuræ huius partis, dicuntur Rhagades; quas acer humor sæpe gignit. Tubercula ani, condylomata dicuntur; quæ à vitiosis humoribus isthuc confluentibus generantur. Marisçæ verrucis similes sunt; tubercula scilicet oblonga, carnosa, proprè cutem tenuia, supra lata, rubra, aspera; eædem,
units.tr: Fissures of this part are called rhagades, which a sharp humour often produces. Tubercles of the anus are called condylomata, which are generated by vitiated humours flowing together there. They are like fig-warts; namely, oblong, fleshy tubercles, thin close to the skin, broad above, red and rough.

units.la: dem, à similitudine floris thymi, dicuntur thymi: si fuerint maiores, dicuntur ficus: causa frequentissima est, sanguis melancholicus.
units.tr: The same, from their resemblance to the flower of thyme, are called thymi; if they are larger, they are called figs. The most frequent cause is melancholic blood.

units.la: Hæmorrhoides sunt fluxus sanguinis venarum in ano. Venæ hæ sunt duplices, internæ & externæ. Si naturâ per eas expellat id quod noxium est, multum confert huiusmodi apertio: sin minus, lædit.
units.tr: Haemorrhoids are a flux of blood from the veins in the anus. These veins are double, internal and external. If nature expels through them what is harmful, such an opening greatly benefits; but if not, it does harm.

units.la: CAP. VIII. De Morbis Hepatis, Lienis, &c.
units.tr: CAP. VIII. On Diseases of the Liver, Spleen, etc.

units.la: IN Physiologiâ dictum est secundam concoctionem peragi in hepate, membro, ut loquuntur officiali & publico: habet enim facultates dispensantes alimentum, sicut ventriculus quæ non tantum inserviunt ipsi hepati, sed corpori universo: commune siquidem alimentum hic generatur: unde & sedes facultatis nutritivæ, eâ causâ, dicitur. Verum ad perfectam sanguificationem, non modo requiritur bona eius dispositio, sed & partium ministrantium lienis scilicet & vesicæ fellis &c. Omni morborum genere tentatur; nimirum intemperie, pravâ compositione, & solutione continui. Intemperies quæcunque tandem, eodem modo generatur hîc, quo in aliis partibus. Hęc si magna fuerit, debilitatur viscus in functionibus, attractione, concoctione, &c. Tentatur sæpè obstructione à materiâ viscidâ venas obstruente, sanguinisque distributionem impediente. Cuius signum est gravitas & tensio in dextro hypochondrio. Si diu perseveret; facessit tandem in inflammationem. Est vero tumor calidus, ortus ex sanguine putrescente in hepatis substantiâ, comites habens febrem continuam, dolorem, sensumque gravitatis in dextro hypochondrio. Causa inflammationis est eadem quę & aliarum partium, eadem fluxionis causa; pars mandans valida, debile hepar, humor acer, tenuis &c. febris, comes, noctu potissimum affligit. Musculi jecori incumbentes, si inflammentur, viscerıs huius phlegmonem nem mentiuntur: at in hepate tumor rotundus eius figurâ circumscribi-tur, cutisque incumbens naturali modo se habet; musculorum vero tumor oblongus, minor, febris, & maior dolor. Eiusdem lateris pleuritis, nullum habet pondus; verum respiratio in eâ est difficilior, & dolor adest punctorius. Scirrus, hepati familiaris morbus, est tumor durus, renitens; indolens, à sanguine melancholico impa-cto genitus. Hic interdum sponte gignitur, interdum hepatis inflammationem sequitur, cum humore tenui, & acri discusso, manet tantum pars terrea, abest febris.
units.tr: In Physiology it has been said that the second concoction takes place in the liver, which, to use their official and public term, is an organ that dispenses nourishment, as the stomach does. Its faculties serve not only the liver itself but the whole body, since the common nourishment is generated here. For this reason it is also called the seat of the nutritive faculty. But for perfect sanguification, not only its good disposition is required, but also that of the parts that minister to it, namely the spleen, the gall bladder, and so on. It is attacked by every kind of disease: by intemperature, by faulty composition, and by solution of continuity. Whatever intemperature arises here arises in the same way as in other parts. If it is great, the organ is weakened in its functions of attraction, concoction, and so on. It is often troubled by obstruction, when viscid matter blocks the veins and hinders the distribution of the blood. The sign of this is heaviness and tension in the right hypochondrium. If it persists for a long time, it finally turns into inflammation. There is indeed a hot swelling, arising from putrefying blood in the substance of the liver, accompanied by a continuous fever, pain, and a sense of heaviness in the right hypochondrium. The cause of the inflammation is the same as that of other parts, the same cause of flux: a strong mandating part, a weak liver, and a sharp, thin humour, and so on. The fever that accompanies it troubles most at night. The muscles lying on the liver, if they become inflamed, imitate a phlegmon of this viscus. But in the liver the swelling is round and bounded by its shape, and the skin lying over it stays in its natural state. The swelling of the muscles, however, is elongated and smaller, with less fever and greater pain. Pleurisy of the same side has no such weight, but breathing is more difficult in it, and a stabbing pain is present. Scirrhus, a disease familiar to the liver, is a hard, resistant swelling, painless, produced by blocked melancholic blood. This sometimes arises spontaneously, and sometimes follows an inflammation of the liver. When the thin, sharp humour has been dispersed, only the earthy part remains, and there is no fever.

units.la: Visceris huius functiones laeduntur vitio partium ministrantium; ventriculi nimirum, intestinorum & venarum mesaraicarum. Ex malo chylo non potest sanguis fieri bonus; nam licet secunda concoctio corrigat utcunque primam, generatur tamen excrementorum proventus. Hinc Cachexia, habitus corporis mala dispositio; tumida nimirum, & decolor, ex vitioso sanguine proprocedens. Aut non potest perfectè assimilari parti; crudus enim est, & pituitosus, causam habet in ventriculo interdum, sæpè in hepate intemperiem frigidam. Cachexia est gradus ad Hydropem; tumorem aut totius corporis, aut saltem ventris, a sanguine pituitoso, hepatis errore genitum. Est autem triplex, Anasarca, in qua totum corpus tumet a pituita alba. Ascites, in quo non totum corpus, sed venter, interdum scrotum & pedes, humore aqueo replentur, instar utris aquâ pleni. Tympanites, sicca hydrops, in quâ venter percussus, tympani sonum refert. Hîc spatium ventris inter peritoneum & intestina flatibus turget. adest quidem humor, unde flatus suscitantur; paucus tamen. Atque hæc postrema affectio non tantum sequitur hepatis vitium, sed &, eo interdum integro, sequitur alterius partis corruptelam.
units.tr: The functions of this viscus are harmed by faults in the parts that minister to it: namely the stomach, the intestines, and the mesaraic veins. Blood cannot become good from bad chyle. For although the second concoction corrects the first to some extent, still a surplus of excrements is generated. Hence cachexia, a bad disposition of the body's habit, swollen and pale, proceeding from vitiated blood. Either it cannot be perfectly assimilated to the part, since it is raw and phlegmatic. Its cause is sometimes in the stomach, but more often in the liver, a cold intemperature. Cachexia is a step toward dropsy, a swelling either of the whole body or at least of the belly, arising from phlegmatic blood, produced by an error of the liver. It is threefold. Anasarca, in which the whole body swells from white phlegm. Ascites, in which not the whole body but the belly, sometimes the scrotum and feet, are filled with watery humour, like a leather bag full of water. Tympanites, a dry dropsy, in which the belly, when struck, gives the sound of a drum. Here the space of the belly between the peritoneum and the intestines is swollen with wind. There is indeed humour from which the wind is raised, but little. This last condition not only follows a fault of the liver, but sometimes, even when the liver is sound, follows a corruption of another part.

units.la: Athrophia est corporis extenuatio, ex gravi hepatis intemperie frigidâ profecta. Partis alicuius, ut manus, brachii, agnosagnoscit causam non hepar, sed membri affecti frigidam & siccam dispositionem. Eundem affectum inducit impedita sanguinis distributio ex obstructione hepatis &c.
units.tr: Atrophy is a wasting of the body, arising from a severe cold intemperature of the liver. When a certain part, such as the hand or arm, wastes away, the cause is not the liver but the cold and dry disposition of the affected limb. The same affection is brought on by impeded distribution of the blood from an obstruction of the liver, and so on.

units.la: Cacotrophia est conversio alimenti in substantiam, ab humanâ alienam, vitio hepatis corrupti; ut in elephantiasi videre est. Hic idem facit pravum corruptumque alimentum, ex quo bonus sanguis generari nequit; unde Scabies, Impetigo seu lichen, lepra, Elephantiasis. Est autem Impetigo asperitas cutis, cum levi pruritu, orta ab humore acri, salso. Scabies, maior est cutis asperitas, comitem habens pruritum. Causam agnoscit interdum succum acrem, salsum; interdum melancholicum, aut biliosum. Lepra est magna cutis asperitas cum gravi pruritu, ex multo, acri, crasso melancholico humore, cutem erodente genita. Elephantiasis est totius corporis tumor cancrosus, contagiosus, à bile venenatâ in hepate genito ortus. Credibile admodum est, cum totum corpus pravè sit vè sit affectum, sedem facultatis naturalis, hepar scilicet, esse corruptum, quanquam lien hic non omnino bene habeat. Hæc est Græcorum Elephantiasis: nam Arabum est tumor pedū cum varicibus, Græcis ignotus.
units.tr: Cacotrophy is the conversion of food into a substance foreign to the human, from a vitiated and corrupted liver, as may be seen in elephantiasis. Here too corrupt and bad nourishment, from which good blood cannot be generated, produces the same effect. Hence scabies, impetigo or lichen, leprosy, elephantiasis. Impetigo is a roughness of the skin, with slight itching, arising from a sharp, salty humour. Scabies is a greater roughness of the skin, accompanied by itching. It sometimes recognises as its cause a sharp, salty juice, and sometimes a melancholic or bilious one. Leprosy is a great roughness of the skin with severe itching, produced by a large amount of sharp, thick melancholic humour that erodes the skin. Elephantiasis is a cancerous, contagious swelling of the whole body, arising from poisonous bile generated in the liver. It is quite credible that, since the whole body is badly affected, the seat of the natural faculty, namely the liver, is corrupted, although the spleen here is not entirely well. This is the Greeks' elephantiasis. For the Arabs' is a swelling of the feet with varicose veins, unknown to the Greeks.

units.la: Lues venerea est morbus contagiosus, adjunctum habens capillorum defluvium, maculas, ulcera, tubercula in tibiis potissimum, genitus ex putrido humore in concubitu. Morbus veteribus ignotus. Americanis epidemius. Quanquam hic totum corpus sit vitiatum, tamen origo corruptelæ est hepar, quod ex bubonibus adjunctis patet. Solet enim hoc viscus in inguina excrementa sua deponere. Dolor, morbi huius comes, noctu potissimum invalescit. Non sunt audiendi qui-am negantes hunc morbum esse novum; quasi novus morbus generari nequeat. Quid dicemus de sudore Britannico? de plica Polonica? Icterus proprie dictus seu flavus, est fædus corporis color, genitus ex bile flava per corpocorporis superficiem diffusa. Bilis, à sanguine non segregatus, diffundit se per totum corpus, aut quia hepar excrementum hoc in vesiculam expellere non potest ; aut, ut alii volunt, quia vesicula ad se non trahit. contingit sæpe vitio alimentorum magnam bilis copiam generari : nonnunquam etiam vitio ipsius hepatis nimium calidi. At Ꝼlterus niger est livi-dus corporis color, genitus à succo melancholico in summam cutem effuso, eodem modo, quo in flavo ; nisi quod hic lien male habet sicut vesicula fellis illic. Huc pertinet scorbutus ( Plinii Scelerytbe ) vitiosus corporis habitus, cum crurum debilitate, maculis lividis, gingivis tumidis, sanguinolentis ; ortus a melancholicis succis ; lienis, non satis attrahentis vitio, lien sæpe hic obstruitur, vigorque animi, & alacritas pereunt.
units.tr: Venereal syphilis is a contagious disease, having as accompaniments loss of hair, spots, ulcers, and tubercles mainly on the shins, produced by putrid humour in intercourse.
