The disease was unknown to the ancients. It is epidemic among the Americans. Although the whole body is vitiated here, the origin of the corruption is the liver, as is clear from the accompanying buboes. For this viscus is accustomed to deposit its excrements in the groin. The pain that accompanies this disease grows strongest at night. Those are not to be listened to who deny that this disease is new, as if a new disease could not arise. What shall we say of the British sweating sickness? Of the Polish plica? Jaundice, properly so called, or yellow, is a foul colour of the body, produced by yellow bile spread through the surface of the body. The bile, not separated from the blood, spreads itself through the whole body, either because the liver cannot expel this excrement into the gall bladder, or, as others hold, because the gall bladder does not draw it to itself. It often happens that through a fault of the food a great quantity of bile is generated, and sometimes also through a fault of the liver itself, being too hot. But black jaundice is a livid colour of the body, produced by melancholic juice poured into the outermost skin in the same way as in yellow jaundice, except that here the spleen is in bad condition, just as the gall bladder is there. To this belongs scurvy (Pliny's scelerythe), a diseased habit of the body, with weakness of the legs, livid spots, swollen and bleeding gums, arising from melancholic juices, through a fault of the spleen, which does not draw enough. Here the spleen is often obstructed, and the vigour and cheerfulness of the mind perish.

units.la: CAP. IX. De Morbis Renum & Vesicæ, &c.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. On the Diseases of the Kidneys and Bladder, etc.

units.la: REnum munus est serum à sanguine segregare, & ad vesicā mittere. cere. Vesicæ autem est illud contine-re, quousque videatur opportunum pellere. acrimoniâ enim suâ, interdū & copiâ facultatē irritat.hæ duę partes, malè se habentes, mictum lædunt.
units.tr: RThe office of the kidneys is to separate the serum from the blood and send it to the bladder. The office of the bladder is to hold the urine until it seems fit to expel it, since it irritates the expulsive faculty by its own sharpness and sometimes by its quantity. These two parts, when ill-disposed, injure urination.

units.la: Renes omni morborum genere tentantur, quorum plerosq; examinabimus; breviter tamen. Inflammantur renes eodem pacto quo aliæ partes, à sanguine biliosò irruente in substantiam, eamq; in tumorem attollente. Febris hic est continua; dolor in omnes partes vicinas diffusus; hepar ninirum, lienē; vesicam: difficilis hic est minctio: terminatur in abscessum, interdū in schirrum; cuius eadem natura quę & aliorum schirrorum, eadem generationis ratio: abest dolor, abest febris & ardor. Exulcerantur renes interdū ob abscessum ruptum, interdum ob ruptionē vasorum insitorū, interdum à calculo &c. urina hic est cruenta, purulenta, fætida, cum febris. Generantur calculi in diversis corporis partibus; sed nullibi frequentius quā hîc. Materia est humor terrestris, stris, viscidus, crassus, cuius partes tenuiores & magis aqueas absumsit calor. Calor dico; nam frigus nullum est in corpore vivo, quod calculum efficere potest. Fateor quædam à frigore constringi, ut glaciem, metalla; sed hæc à calore solvuntur, sunt etiam extra corpus humanum; quorum neutrum hic obtinet. Calculus renum familiaris senibus magis quam pueris, sicut vesicæ contra. Calculi nondum moti, sed quiescentis signa sunt, sensus gravitatis in lumbis re-nis affecti, abest tumor, sed non dolor, coxa lateris affecti stupet. Si calculus è renum substantiâ in cavitatem eorundem, vel ureteres (acutissimi sensus vasa) penetret, oriuntur dolores nephretici acutissimi & gravissimi. paroxysmi initio, urinæ paucæ, & aquosæ, minguntur & si calculus asperior fuerit, cruentæ; affecti lateris testis contrahitur, vomitusque ex consensu ventriculi oboriturtur, eodem modo, quo in affectu colico. Nam huius dolor, illum mentitur. tur: colicus tamen magis vagus est; est quoque supra renes, facilius miti-gatur, nullum adest urinæ impedi-mentum. Vesica omni morborum ge-nere infestatur. temperamentum sæ-pè labefactatur, interdum à qualitate simplici, sæpè à materiâ conjunctâ: itque hinc fit inflammatio, quæ eo-dem modo hic fit, quo in aliis parti-bus, ut sæpè dictum. Huius comites sunt dolor, gravitas, ardor, rubor circa inguina, febris continua; quæ eo gravior, quo humor calidior: ma-jor enim est à sanguine bilioso, quam pituoso: partes aliæ, in consensum trahuntur: degenerat sæpè in absces-sum; unde exulceratio vesicæ, (quæ tamen alias causas habere potest) cu-jus signa sunt, urina crassa initio, cum sanguine aut pure; succedunt quammulæ, non carnosæ, sed mem-branosæ, furfuris speciem repræsen-tantes, &c.
units.tr: The kidneys are attacked by every kind of disease. I shall examine most of them, though briefly. The kidneys become inflamed in the same way as other parts, when bilious blood rushes into their substance and raises it into a swelling. The fever here is continuous, and the pain spreads to all the neighbouring parts: the liver, the spleen, and the bladder. Urination is difficult. The inflammation ends in an abscess, or sometimes in a scirrhus, which has the same nature and the same mode of generation as other scirrhi. Pain is absent, and so are fever and burning. The kidneys are sometimes ulcerated, from a ruptured abscess, sometimes from the rupture of the vessels embedded in them, and sometimes from a stone, etc. The urine here is bloody, purulent and foul-smelling, with fever. Stones are generated in various parts of the body, but nowhere more often than here. The matter is an earthy humour, viscid and thick, whose finer and more watery parts heat has consumed. I say heat, for there is no cold in a living body that can produce a stone. I grant that some things are hardened by cold, like ice and metals; but these are dissolved by heat, and they also lie outside the human body. Neither of these holds here. Renal stone is more common in the old than in children, and bladder stone is the reverse. Stones not yet moved are signs of one at rest: a sense of heaviness in the loins of the affected kidney; there is no swelling, but there is pain, and the hip of the affected side goes numb. If a stone passes from the substance of the kidney into its cavity or into the ureters (very sensitive vessels), most acute and severe nephritic pains arise. At the onset of the paroxysm the urine is scanty and watery; if the stone is rougher, it is bloody. The testicle of the affected side contracts, and vomiting arises from sympathy with the stomach, in the same way as in colic. For its pain imitates the other. Colic, however, is more wandering; it also lies above the kidneys, is more easily relieved, and there is no obstruction of urine.

units.la: An calculus vesicæ illic etiam sit sementitus, an vero rudimentum alibi acceperit, disputant Medici. causam tamen non video, quo minus possit generari hic atque in renibus. Notæ eius sunt urina cruda, aquosa, sero lactis non dissimilis in pueris, sedimentum habens arenosum: pruritus circa pudenda, virga intenditur, adest dysuria cum dolore: &c. Mictio urinæ varia habet symptomata, analoga illis quæ in dejectionibus alvi contingunt, ut constabit.
units.tr: Physicians dispute whether the bladder stone is in that place spontaneously generated or acquires its beginnings elsewhere. I see no reason, however, why it could not be generated here as in the kidneys. Its signs are raw, watery urine, like whey of milk in children, with a gritty sediment; itching about the genitals; the penis is stretched; there is dysuria with pain, etc. Passing of urine has various symptoms, analogous to those which occur in evacuations of the bowels, as will be clear.

units.la: Ischuria vera (notha est, in quâ urina non effunditur, quia in vesica non est vitio aliarum partium) in quâ vesica est sero plena, respondet alvi suppressioni: est autem abolita mictio, procedens à vi expultrice labefactatâ, vel alioqui ob angustiam oris vesicæ. Ergo gravis intemperies inducens torpore vel paralysin, corpori vesicæ admit omnem sensum; ita quidem, ut non expellat, si eius cervix, aut musculus hoc modo lædatur, erit involuntaria urinæ expulsio. Gravis sopor, aut mala affectio partium principum, ischuriam inducent. Idem fit in cervicis obstructione à calculo, in flam
units.tr: True ischuria (it is spurious when the urine is not discharged because the fault lies in other parts and not in the bladder itself), in which the bladder is full of serum, corresponds to suppression of the bowels. It is an abolished urination, proceeding from a weakened expulsive force, or otherwise on account of narrowness of the neck of the bladder. Therefore a severe intemperance inducing torpor or paralysis takes away all sensation from the body of the bladder; indeed, if its neck or its muscle is injured in this way, there will be involuntary expulsion of urine. Deep sleep, or a bad affection of the principal parts, induces ischuria. The same happens with obstruction of the neck by a stone, in inflam-

units.la: [Marginal notes on the right edge, partly cut off by the binding and illegible at this scan resolution; they begin with "Instit." and "flammatio", "vesica nimis", "Diabetes", "Ischuria" and similar words, and are not transcribed.] flammatione, carunculâ, compressio- ne vicinarum partium &c. Quod si vesica nimium tendatur à nimiâ urinæ copiâ, (quod in longis conviviis fieri amat) contrahere se nequit; tum obturabitur meatus, & generatur Ischuria.
units.tr: [Marginal notes on the right edge, partly cut off by the binding and illegible at this scan resolution; they begin with "Instit." and "flammatio", "vesica nimis", "Diabetes", "Ischuria" and similar words, and are not transcribed.] mation, a caruncle, compression of the neighbouring parts, etc. But if the bladder is stretched too much by an excessive amount of urine (which it is apt to do at long banquets), it cannot contract; then the passage is blocked and ischuria is generated.

units.la: Diabetes, renum affectus lienteriæ similis, est celerrima & copiosa mictio potus non transmutati, cum siti; orta à depravatis facultatibus retentrice, & attractrice.
units.tr: Diabetes, a disease of the kidneys similar to lientery, is a very rapid and copious urination of drink that has not been changed, with thirst; it arises from depraved retentive and attractive faculties.

units.la: Involuntarius mictus fit ex resolutione sphincteris vesicæ, quam facit intemperies frigida, vulnus, contusio, &c. Stranguria simplex similis est tenesmo; assiduus mejendi conatus, sine dolore, quo urina guttatim effluit, pauca quidem, sed frequenter, proveniens à facultatis retentricis debilitate, quæ à nimiâ copia gravatur. Causa debilitatis sæpe est intemperies frigida vesicæ. Sin verò urina guttatim exeat cum conatu & dolore, expultricem irritante, est stranguriosa dysuria. Dysuria dysenteriæ respondet, estque mictio dolorifilorifica ex intervallo accidens sine conatu assiduo, quâ urina interdum affatim, interdum guttatim exit. Mingitur interdum sanguis, pus, &c. quæ ex superioribus facile intelligi possunt.
units.tr: Involuntary urination comes from relaxation of the sphincter of the bladder, which is caused by cold intemperance, wound, contusion, etc. Simple strangury is similar to tenesmus: a constant straining to urinate, without pain, by which urine trickles out, scanty indeed but frequent, arising from weakness of the retentive faculty, which is burdened by excess. The cause of the weakness is often a cold intemperance of the bladder. But if the urine comes out in drops with effort and pain, irritating the expulsive faculty, it is stranguric dysuria. Dysuria corresponds to dysentery, and is painful urination occurring at intervals without constant straining, by which urine sometimes comes out in a stream and sometimes in drops. Blood, pus, etc. are sometimes passed in the urine, which can easily be understood from what has gone before.

units.la: CAP. X. De paritum Genitalium Morbis.
units.tr: CHAPTER X. On the Diseases of the Genital Parts.

units.la: DE Generatione, & instrumentis Dei inservientibus, de utroque item sexu, in Physiologia satis diximus: restat ut de harum partium vitiis ordine agamus.
units.tr: We have said enough about generation and the organs that serve God in it, and about both sexes, in the Physiology. It remains to deal, in order, with the faults of these parts.

units.la: Quod ad testes attinet; ii omni morborum genere infestari solent; intemperie, mala compositione, & solutione continui. Continentur in viris à scroto. Scroti vitium est hernia <bl>ἐγκοιλία</bl>; cuius multiplex est causa. Ileum & cæcum intestina in scrotum decidentia attollunt illud in tumorem, oriturque <bl>ἐντεροκήλη</bl> similiter & omentum, unde <bl>ἐπιπλοκήλη</bl> dicta provenit. Idem faciunt aqua, spiritus, caro adnascens. Descendit intestinum, stinum, vel omentum ex laxato foramine per quod vasa spermatica à testibus feruntur.
units.tr: The testicles are commonly troubled by every kind of disease: by intemperature, by faulty composition, and by solution of continuity. They are contained in the scrotum in men. The scrotum's fault is hernia, the scrotal hernia [ἐγκοιλία], which has many causes. The ileum and the cecum, slipping down into the scrotum, raise it into a swelling; in the same way the omentum does, whence the condition called epiplocele [ἐπιπλοκήλη] arises. Water, wind and proud flesh do the same. The intestine, or the omentum, descends through the loosened opening by which the spermatic vessels run from the testicles.

units.la: Ad generationem requiritur penis erectio, & feminis effusio; quæ si aboleantur, est vera impotentia. Ad erectionem concurrit semen, spiritus in fistuloso penis nervo, postremò attollentium: si quid horum desit non attollitur. Spiritus deficit, aut quia non generatur, aut quia avocatur, aut quia non recipitur ab instrumento languido, aut aliter vitiato. huc pertinet maleficium, & incantatio. Priapismus est pudendi tensio præter naturam, sine veneris desiderio, orta à flatu fistulosum penis nervum implente. Satyriasis à plerisque creditur eadem, cum priapismo: à quibusdam distinguitur. qui enim distinguunt aiunt esse commune viris cum fæminis; palpitationem membri genitalis seu penis, ortam ex inflammatione vasorum spermaticorum. Gonorrhœa, est involuntaria feminis effusio sine tensione pudenpudendi, & veneris desiderio, orta à debilitate facultatis retentricis vasorum spermaticorum. Est & virulenta gonorrhæa à fædo concubitu orta, ex acri & virulento semine, penem & vasa spermatica exulcerante. Huc refertur profluvium feminis in tabe dorsali, novis maritis quibusdam in regionibus familiare. Pollutio noctur-na est feminis secundum quietem emissio, cum veneris insomnio & pudendi tensione.
units.tr: Generation requires erection of the penis and emission of the seed; if either is abolished, there is true impotence. For erection, seed, spirits in the hollow nerve of the penis, and finally the muscles that raise it all work together; if any of these is lacking, it does not rise. The spirit fails either because it is not generated, or because it is drawn away, or because it is not received by the enfeebled instrument, or because that instrument is otherwise damaged. Here belong sorcery and enchantment. Priapism is a tension of the private parts beyond nature, without desire for intercourse, arising from wind filling the hollow nerve of the penis. Satyriasis is held by most to be the same as priapism, while some distinguish it. For those who distinguish say that it is common to men and women, a palpitation of the genital member or penis, arising from inflammation of the spermatic vessels. Gonorrhoea is an involuntary emission of seed in women, without tension of the private parts and without desire for intercourse, arising from weakness of the retaining power of the spermatic vessels. There is also a virulent gonorrhoea, arising from foul intercourse, from sharp and virulent seed that ulcerates the penis and the spermatic vessels. To this is referred the flow of seed in dorsal consumption, which is common among some newly married men in certain regions. Nocturnal pollution is an emission of seed in sleep, with dreams of intercourse and tension of the private parts.

units.la: Omne morbi genus uterum vexat. Angustia est in ipso pudendo, vel alis, vel in orificio uteri, vel etiam in cervice. Interdum ex ipso ortu contrahitur, interdum vitio aliquo adnascitur caruncula, membrana, tumor &c. Si substantiæ uteri impingantur humores, generabitur tumor; qui tam est varius quam humor generans; phlegmone nimirum, œdema, erysipelas, schirrus. dignoscuntur suis notis. Hydrops uteri, est tumor ex aquoso humore, aut seroso genitus, propter debilitatem caloris nativi. Col-ligiligitur humor, non tantum per congestionem, sed & transmissionem ex aliis partibus. Dignoscitur hic affectus ex strepitu, gravitate, mensium suppressione. Nympha est substantia carnosa, in commissura alarum pudendi sita; quæ vestimentorum attritu arrigitur, & ad venerem impellit, nihil tamen excernitur. Nymphæ similis est cauda; alibi tamen generatur; nimirum in uteri orificio, implens muliebre pudendum, coitumque impediens: foris interdum pendet. utriusque causa est sanguinis copia. Procidentia est dimotio eius ex naturali loco, à gravitate insita, ob vinculorum aut laxationem, aut ruptionem. Laxantur à frigidis, humidis, &c. at casus, partus difficilis, & eiusmodi eadem rumpunt. In hoc affectu, uterus in pudendum cadit. Tradunt authores non tantum uterum procidere, sed adscendere, & in lateera ferri, ob vasorum brevitatem: si enim æqualiter trahantur, uterum sursum ferri; sin inæqualiter, in hoc aut illud latus. Brevitas & contra-ctio oriuntur ex repletione ligamen-torum ob menstrua retenta, interdum ob alias causas. Scio horum affectuum alias tradi causas, & inter eas ingenitam uteri vim, quâ salubria prosequitur, & ingrata fugit; de quibus prolixius agere non licet. In quam partẽ inclinet uterus, cognoscitur ex loci tumore, dolore, tensione.
units.tr: Every kind of disease troubles the womb. Narrowness is found in the private parts themselves, or in the wings, or in the mouth of the womb, or even in the neck. Sometimes it is contracted from birth; sometimes some growth, a caruncle, membrane, tumour and so on, grows there. If humours fall upon the substance of the womb, a tumour will be produced, which is as varied as the humour producing it: namely phlegmon, oedema, erysipelas, or scirrhus. They are told apart by their own signs. Dropsy of the womb is a tumour produced by watery or serous humour, because of weakness of the native heat. The humour gathers not only by congestion but also by transmission from other parts. This affection is recognised by a rumbling, heaviness, and suppression of the menses. The nymph is a fleshy substance placed at the junction of the wings of the private parts; it is roused by rubbing of the clothes and drives toward intercourse, yet nothing is discharged from it. Like the nymph is the cauda; it is however generated elsewhere, namely at the mouth of the womb, filling the female private parts and hindering intercourse; sometimes it hangs outside. The cause of both is abundance of blood. Prolapse is the displacement of the womb from its natural place by its inborn heaviness, because of the loosening or rupture of its ligaments. The ligaments are loosened by cold, damp and the like, but a fall, a difficult birth and such things rupture them. In this affection the womb falls into the private parts. Authors report that the womb not only prolapses but also rises upward and is carried to one side, because of the shortness of the vessels: for if they are drawn equally, the womb is carried upward; if unequally, to this side or that. The shortening and contraction arise from the swelling of the ligaments when the menses are retained, and sometimes from other causes. I know that other causes of these affections are taught, among them the innate power of the womb, by which it pursues what is wholesome and shuns what is unpleasant; but it is not permitted to treat these more fully. The side toward which the womb leans is recognised by swelling of the place, pain, and tension.

units.la: Corpus muliebre per uterum superfluum sanguinem expellit; quae functio læditur sæpissimè. Et primò quidem in fœminis justæ ætatis abo-letur: cuius causa interdum est sanguis, interdum debilitas facultatis expultricis, nonnunquam angustia vasorum uteri. Sanguis interdum viscidus est, & crassus, omnique motui ineptus. Signum huius est lassitudo tensiva, dolor lumborum, cibi fastidium, nausea &c. Interdum alió revocatur. Quid? quod sæpè non gignitur, quando debebat. Nam menstruorum suppressio in gravidis, nutricibus, viraginibus, non est symptc-ma. ma. In aliis justæ ætatis vitium est; quod faciunt curæ, vigiliæ, victus parcior, vulnera, hæmorrhoides, dysenteria &c. Jam verò membri huius angustia varias habet causas, obstructionem, compressionem, obturationem à membrana, caruncula, &c. Causæ eædem fi leviores fuerint, diminutam evacuationem menstruorum efficiunt, in quâ guttatim fluit sanguis fine dolore. Profluvium menstruorum est immodica sanguinis per uterum evacuatio, à totius corporis vel præcipuorum viscerum facultate expulstrice stimulata. Stimulus interdum est sanguinis copia, vel acrimonia. idem contingit in vasorum uteri apertione. fluxus antevertit debitum tempus ob easdem causas. Profluvium muliebre est vitiosorum humorum expurgatio per uterû, facta ab irritatione facultatis expultricis viscerû. Sicut in aliis fluxibus; ita hic, quatuor considerantur; pars mandans &c. quæ hic non est unica; interdum enim est totû corpus, interdum præcipua viscera. pars recipiens piens est uterus. at materia que fluit, est corrupta, tenuis, alba ; interdum aliter affecta. cuius causa est aut in viscEribus inprimis hepate, aut pravo alimento & victu. In hoc affectu pedes tument, facies est decolor, difficilis respiratio &c. Fluxus hic, si sit materiæ candidæ, similis est gonorrhææ muliebri. Vteri suffocatio est respirationis debilitas (sæpè quoad sensum abolita videtur) cum vitalium, & animalium functionum lasione, genita à vapore putrido ab utero ascendente. Sanguis enim & semen si in utero putrescant, malignos vapores suscitant, magnarum calamitatum causas. sicut epilepsia à partis alicuius consensu procedens, per intervalla recurrere solet, idem de hoc affectu judicandum. malum viduis familiare est. Differt à syncope, quod aliquis ut plurimum pulsus hic percipiatur, frigidus sudor non erumpat, nec facies liveat, nec odoratis, ut in syncope, juventur, nisi inferiori ventri admoveantur. Correptæ hoc malo, lo, si pungantur, sentiunt; quod in apoplexia non amat fieri; vocatæ etiam audiunt, ac recordantur post paroxysmum; quod non faciunt Epileptica: facies quoque in hoc affectu rubet & tumet. Ad immodicum veneris desiderium pertinet satyriasis. Est autem ardens coëundi appetentia, cum ingenti pruritu, & pudendi dolore, ab inflammatione partium genitalium orta. Furor uterinus, est magnum veneris desiderium, conjunctum cum pudendi pruritu, ortum ab ingenti uteri calore, malignos vapores ad cerebrum mittente; unde nihil aliud, aut loquuntur, aut cogitant, quam venerem. In hoc affectu est desipientia, quæ in satyriasi non contigit. Sterilitas, est mulieris justæ ætatis, & utentis viro, concipiendi impotentia, seminis, uterique vitio proveniens. Impotentia coëundi ob uteri & pudendi angustiam, ad sterilitatem revocatur. Omnis uteri affectus attractionem, retentionem, & seminis vivificationem labefactans, sterilitatem inducit. Viragines nes ob sanguinis defectum, sicut & præpingues, steriles sunt. Semen quoque intemperatum, aut alioqui malè affectum, eandem inducet impotentiam. Fæcunditatis & sterilitatis signa, à Medicorum vulgo jactata, incerta, & fallacia sunt. Si semen nimis copiosum sit, aut paucum, aut alioqui phantasia, & facultas plastica interpellentur, monstra producuntur. Huc pertinet mola; caro nimirum informis, in uteri cavitate ex vitioso femine, & copioso sanguine genita, multis venis prædita. Hanc facultate naturali pręditam esse contendunt, & more plantarum alimentum attrahere. Videas tamen sæpe molas informes, quæ an animatæ sint ambigitur. animæ enim certissima nota est figura certa.Mola genuinum conceptum sæpe mentitur; attollitur enim uterus, deficiunt menses: abest tamen blandus motus, qui tertio mense in vera gravidatione percipitur: mammæ sine lacte tument, legitimèque pariendi tempus, longè excedit. Quod si semen in utero corrumpatur, eique conjungatur humor pituitosus, aut alius malignus, erit falsa gravidatio. Abortus est motus depravatus uteri, fœtum jam animatum (embryonis enim ejectio, non est abortus) ante legitimum tempus expellentis. Symptoma hoc contingit sæpè vitio uteri, interdum fœtus, & sanguinis materni. Uterus malè dispositus, fœtus justo maior, aut aliter affectus, sanguis quantitate aut qualitate peccans, irritant facultatem uteri expultricem, ante debitum tempus.
units.tr: The female body expels superfluous blood through the womb, and this function is very often impaired. And first of all, in women of due age it is abolished. Its cause is sometimes the blood, sometimes weakness of the expelling power, and sometimes narrowness of the vessels of the womb. The blood is sometimes viscid and thick, and unfit for any movement. The sign of this is a tensive weariness, pain in the loins, loss of appetite, nausea and so on. Sometimes it is drawn back elsewhere. Why, indeed, is it often not produced when it ought to be? For suppression of the menses in pregnant women, nursing mothers and viragos is not a symptom. In other women of due age it is a fault, which cares, watchings, a sparer diet, wounds, haemorrhoids, dysentery and so on bring about. Now the narrowness of this part has various causes: obstruction, compression, blocking by a membrane, a caruncle and so on. If these same causes are milder, they bring about a diminished evacuation of the menses, in which the blood flows drop by drop without pain. A flux of the menses is an excessive evacuation of blood through the womb, stimulated by the expelling power of the whole body or of the chief viscera. The stimulus is sometimes abundance or sharpness of the blood. The same happens when the vessels of the womb are opened. The flux comes before the due time for the same causes. The female flux is a purging of vitiated humours through the womb, brought about by the irritation of the expelling power of the viscera. As in other fluxes, four things are considered here: the sending part, and so on, which here is not single, for sometimes it is the whole body, sometimes the chief viscera; the receiving part is the womb; but the matter that flows is corrupt, thin, and white, or sometimes otherwise affected. Its cause is either in the viscera, especially the liver, or in bad food and diet. In this affection the feet swell, the face is discoloured, breathing is difficult and so on. This flux, if the matter is white, is like female gonorrhoea. Suffocation of the womb is a weakness of breathing (which often seems abolished as far as sensation goes), with injury to the vital and animal functions, produced by putrid vapour rising from the womb. For if blood and seed putrefy in the womb, they raise malignant vapours, which are causes of great calamities. As epilepsy, arising from the sympathy of some part, is wont to recur at intervals, so the same must be judged of this affection. It is a disease common to widows. It differs from syncope in that a pulse can usually be perceived in it, no cold sweat breaks out, the face does not turn livid, and it is not relieved by smelling salts, as in syncope, unless these are applied to the lower belly. Women seized by this malady feel it if they are pricked, which does not usually happen in apoplexy; if they are called they also hear, and they remember afterwards what happened during the fit, which epileptics do not. The face in this affection also grows red and swollen. Satyriasis belongs to excessive desire for intercourse. It is an ardent appetite for coupling, with great itching and pain of the private parts, arising from inflammation of the genital parts. Uterine fury is a great desire for intercourse joined with itching of the private parts, arising from great heat of the womb, which sends malignant vapours to the brain; so that such women speak of nothing and think of nothing but intercourse. In this affection there is folly, which does not happen in satyriasis. Sterility is the inability of a woman of due age who lives with a husband to conceive, arising from a fault of the seed or of the womb. Impotence for coupling, because of narrowness of the womb and private parts, is referred to sterility. Every affection of the womb that weakens its attraction, retention and vivification of the seed induces sterility. Viragos, because of lack of blood, are sterile, and so are very fat women. Seed that is intemperate, or otherwise badly affected, will induce the same impotence. The signs of fertility and sterility, which the common run of physicians boast of, are uncertain and deceptive. If the seed is too abundant, or too scanty, or if the imagination and the plastic faculty are otherwise hindered, monsters are produced. To this belongs the mole: formless flesh, namely, generated in the cavity of the womb from faulty seed and abundant blood, endowed with many veins. Some contend that it is endowed with a natural faculty and, after the manner of plants, draws nourishment to itself. Yet you will often see formless moles, and it is doubtful whether they are animate, for shape is the most certain mark of a soul. A mole often counterfeits a true conception: the womb swells and the menses cease; yet the gentle movement, which is perceived in the third month of true pregnancy, is absent; the breasts swell without milk, and the proper time of delivery is far exceeded. But if the seed corrupts in the womb and a phlegmatic or other malignant humour is joined to it, there will be a false pregnancy. Abortion is a depraved movement of the womb, expelling a foetus already animated (for the ejection of an embryo is not an abortion) before the proper time. This symptom often arises from a fault of the womb, sometimes of the foetus, and of the mother's blood. A womb ill-disposed, a foetus larger than it should be or otherwise affected, blood sinning in quantity or quality, irritate the expelling power of the womb before the due time.

units.la: Partus naturalis non tantum debito tempore, & modo, sed sine magno dolore fieri debet, citra tamen fœtus aut uteri læsionem: si in uno horum peccatur, partus non erit naturalis.
units.tr: A natural birth must occur not only at the due time and in the right way, but without great pain, and yet without injury to the foetus or the womb. If a fault is made in any one of these, the birth will not be natural.

units.la: MEDICARVM LIBER IV. De SIGNIS. CAP. I. Signorum Divisio.
units.tr: Book IV of the Medical Works. On Signs. Chapter I. The Division of Signs.

units.la: MOrborum natura & sedes innotescunt nobis signorum auxilio; quibus ignoratis, illa pariter ignorari necesse est. Ordinis ergo ratio huc manuducit ut Σημειωτικὴν persequamur, dignissimã medicinæ partem. Nec enim sufficit morbos, eorumq;causas investigasse, nisi etiam eorū notas, & quasi characteres explicuerimus; quod signorum doctrina abundè præstat. Signum logici vocāt illud, quod ducit in alterius cognitionē, aliumq; usū non habet quā significandi; ut campanæ sonitus ad id institutus est, ut denūciet conconcionem, aliumque usum non habet. Hinc eius divisio in naturale, & ex instituto. Illud vocant, quod vim significandi naturæ debet; hoc, quod humanæ institutioni illius exemplum est ploratus; huius autem sermo. At Medici aliter de signis philosophantur, eaque omnia signa vocant, quæ significant morbum; qualia sunt symptomata consequentia, etiam si nec naturâ, nec arte instituta sint ad significandum: sunt enim naturales effectus consequentes suas causas, ut fumus ignem; aut alioqui causæ futurorum affectuum. Signa petuntur vel ab affectibus signatum consequentibus, vel à causis præcedentibus. Causarum nomine intelliguntur, non tantum externæ, ut aër; sed internæ, ut temperamentum. Signatum respondens signo, est corporis constitutio; quæ triplex est, sana, ægra, neutra. Ergo signa omnia aut sunt salubria, aut insalubria, aut neutra. prima sanitatem, secunda morbum, tertia vero mediam constitutionem significant. cant. Respectu temporis dividuntur signa in Διαγνωστικά, Προγνωστικά, Αναμνηστικά. prima præsentem constitutionem, secunda futurã, at postrema præteritã significant. Postrema hæc signa non sunt magni momenti ; at priora illa magnũ habent in Medicinâ usum. Quia vero propter morbos agimus de signis, de insalubribus agemus primò. Hæc dividuntur in communia, & propria; in separabilia & in inseparabilia, si vero conjungas inter se inseparabilia, & propria, orientur παραδυναμωτικά. Hæc cum morbo incipiunt, & desinunt, augenturque & minuuntur cum eodem, ut in pleuritide, dolor lateris punctorius, tussis, anhelitus difficultas, febris acuta, pulsus ferratilis. Signa communia, & separabilia συνεπόμενα vocantur, seu assidentia. Hæc cum morbis non cohærent necessariò, nec ab eorum essentiis fluunt ; declarant tamen aliquid circa morbum, magnitudinem nimirum, durationem, morem &c. Huc spectant signa critica, lethalia, & non
units.tr: The nature and seat of diseases become known to us with the help of signs; if these are unknown, the diseases must necessarily be unknown too. The order of our treatment therefore leads us to pursue semeiotics [Σημειωτικὴν], the most worthy part of medicine. For it is not enough to have investigated diseases and their causes unless we have also explained their marks and, as it were, their characters, and the doctrine of signs supplies this abundantly. Logicians call a sign that which leads to the knowledge of something else and has no other use than to signify. Thus the sound of a bell is set up to announce a sermon, and has no other use. Hence the division into natural and instituted signs. They call natural that which owes its power of signifying to nature, and instituted that which is an example of human institution, such as a cry is of natural signs, or speech of instituted ones. But physicians philosophize about signs differently, and call all those things signs which signify a disease, such as the symptoms that follow, even if they were established neither by nature nor by art for signifying. For they are natural effects following their causes, as smoke follows fire, or else causes of future affections. Signs are sought either from the affections of the signified that follow, or from the preceding causes. By causes are understood not only external ones, such as air, but internal ones, such as temperament. The signified that corresponds to the sign is the constitution of the body, which is threefold: healthy, diseased, or neutral. Therefore all signs are either salubrious, insalubrious, or neutral. The first indicate health, the second disease, and the third a middle condition. With respect to time, signs are divided into diagnostic [Διαγνωστικά], prognostic [Προγνωστικά], and anamnestic [Αναμνηστικά]. The first indicate the present constitution, the second the future, and the last the past. These last signs are not of great importance, but the former have great use in medicine. Since we treat of signs on account of diseases, we shall first deal with the insalubrious ones. These are divided into common and proper, and into separable and inseparable. If you join inseparable and proper signs together, paradynamotic [παραδυναμωτικά] signs arise. These begin and end with the disease, and increase and decrease along with it, as in pleurisy: a stabbing pain in the side, cough, difficulty of breathing, acute fever, and a hard pulse. Common and separable signs are called accompanying [συνεπόμενα], or attendant. These do not necessarily cohere with the diseases, nor flow from their essences, yet they declare something about the disease, namely its magnitude, duration, manner and so on. To these belong critical signs, lethal and non-lethal,

units.la: [marginal notes at right edge are partly cut off and illegible; not transcribed] & non læthalia, signa cruditatis & coctionis. Hæc signa sunt prognosti-ca; sicut pathognomica, diagnostica. In ægro quatuor considerantur, asse-ctus, pars affecta, causa affectus, & symptoma. Quartum hoc, symptoma nimirum, manifestat tria superiora : hoc quomodo fiat, porrò videamus.
units.tr: and non-lethal signs of crudity and concoction. These signs are prognostic; likewise pathognomonic and diagnostic signs. In the sick person four things are considered: the affection, the affected part, the cause of the affection, and the symptom. This fourth, namely the symptom, manifests the three preceding; how this happens we shall now see.

units.la: CAP. II. De Signis quibus pars affecta investigatur.
units.tr: Chapter II. On the Signs by Which the Affected Part Is Investigated.

units.la: IN signorum examine initiū faciemus à diagnosticis, præsentē ægri statu̅ manifestantibus, & primò quidem sedem affectam videamus; quā quinq; modis cognosci tradunt Medici: nimirū actionis lesione, excretis, situ, doloris proprietate, accidentibus propriis.
units.tr: In examining signs we shall begin with the diagnostic ones, which show the present state of the sick person. And first let us look at the affected seat, which physicians teach may be known in five ways, namely by injury to the action, by the excretions, by position, by the quality of the pain, and by the proper accidents.

units.la: Primum est actio læsa, quæ optimè designat partem affectam; eâ enim læsâ, necessariò lædītur actio. Ad actionem revocatur usus. Læsâ ergo actione similari, lædetur temperies. Organicâ læsâ, lædetur organi structura, vel ea pars similaris unde actio proprocedit, aut partibus connexis. Observandum tamen, quod non semper uni læsæ actioni, respondet unica pars, sed sæpe plures; ut in respiratione videre est, quæ plurium adminiculo partium indiget, quæ interdum omnes laborant. Nec contra pluribus læsis functionibus plures lę-duntur partes; ut in Apoplexiâ, & Syncope videre est. nam in illâ motus & sensus abolentur, cerebrum tamen solum est male affectum. Artificiosâ itaque utendum hic est conjecturâ, animoque lustrandæ actiones naturales, vitales, animales, cum suis fontibus, corde hepate, cerebro: Videndum porrò quomodo actio sit læsa; depravata sit an diminuta, & abolita; an pars primariò laboret, an ex consensu.
units.tr: First is the injured action, which designates the affected part best; for when the action is injured, the part must necessarily be injured. Use is referred back to action. Therefore, when a similar action is injured, the temperament is injured. When an organic action is injured, the structure of the organ is injured, or that similar part from which the action proceeds, or the parts connected with it. It must be observed, however, that one injured action does not always correspond to a single part, but often to several; as is seen in respiration, which needs the help of several parts, and sometimes all of them suffer. Nor, conversely, do several injured functions always mean several injured parts; as is seen in apoplexy and syncope. For in the former, motion and sensation are abolished, yet the brain alone is badly affected. Therefore a skilful conjecture must be used here, and the natural, vital and animal actions must be surveyed in mind, along with their sources: the heart, the liver, the brain. Next we must see how the action is injured: whether it is depraved, or diminished and abolished; and whether the part suffers primarily or through sympathy.

units.la: Secundò partem affectam demonstrant excreta: in quibus considerantur substantia, magnitudo, & excernendi modus. Quod ad primam attinet; ea interdum est pars membri; ut in dysenteriâ, interior membrana intestinorum: norum : in phtisi, pars pulmonis. Interdum excrementum parte contentum; urina scilicet, calculus, lumbrici. Interdum alimentum; ut chylus, sanguis ; & sanguis interdum est venosus, interdum arteriosus; quæ omnia abunde locum denunciant. Nam, exempli causâ, ejectio chyli vulnus esse in ventriculo significat : at fæcum & urinæ, intestinorum & vesicæ vulnera arguunt.
units.tr: Second, the affected part is shown by the excreta, in which the substance, quantity, and manner of excretion are considered. As to the first, sometimes it is a part of the member itself, as in dysentery, the inner membrane of the intestines; in phthisis, a part of the lung. Sometimes it is an excrement contained in the part, namely urine, a stone, or worms. Sometimes it is food, such as chyle or blood; and blood is sometimes venous, sometimes arterial. All these indicate the place abundantly. For example, the ejection of chyle signifies a wound in the stomach, while faeces and urine indicate wounds of the intestines and bladder.

units.la: Tertiò, situs affectam sedem ostendit, quod ex duritie, tumore, aut partis tensione cognoscere licet. Dextri hypochondrii tumor non sublimis, lunari figura, est nota affecti jecoris ; sinistri hypochondrii simili tumor, signum est lienis malè dispositi. verum si hisce in partibus tumor fuerit sublimis, arguit impositos musculos inflammatos.
units.tr: Third, position shows the affected seat, which may be recognized from hardness, swelling, or tension of the part. A swelling of the right hypochondrium that is not raised up and has a lunar shape is a sign of an affected liver; a similar swelling of the left hypochondrium is a sign of a badly disposed spleen. But if in these parts the swelling is raised up, it indicates inflamed muscles lying upon them.

units.la: Quartò, proprietas doloris idem facit. Audivimus dolorem esse tristem sensationem ; subjectum ergo debet esse sensu præditum : quanto ergo pars exquisitius sentit, tanto magis dolet; quanto minus exquisitè sentit, contra. Si ergo causæ doloris sint vehementes, & pars affecta sit acuti sensus; intendetur dolor. Dolores ergo intemperiei calidæ maiores sunt, quam frigidæ. Ita materia acris & mordax dolorem ingentem excitabit. Pars nervis abundans, ut membrana, dolore corripietur acuto, & punctorio; ut in pleuritide videre est.
units.tr: Fourth, the quality of the pain does the same. We have heard that pain is a sad sensation; the subject therefore must be endowed with sense. The more exquisitely a part feels, the more it grieves; the less exquisitely it feels, the less. If therefore the causes of pain are vehement, and the affected part is of acute sensation, the pain will be intensified. Pains from hot intemperance are therefore greater than from cold. So too a sharp and biting matter will excite great pain. A part abounding in nerves, such as a membrane, is seized by a sharp and stabbing pain, as is seen in pleurisy.

units.la: Quinto, propria accidentia manifestant locum affectum; ut citrinus color totius corporis, obstructionem jecoris, aut vesicæ fellis; niger color, lienis obstructionem designant. Eadem est & aliarum partium ratio. Tantū observa uni symptomati non esse nimium fidendum. Hisce omnibus addi poterit, consensus partium, laesis enim meningibus, biliosi vomitus oboruntur; laeso ventriculo, cerebri deliria. Hæc quæ de signis sunt dicta, confirmantur ex sexu, ætate, victu, consuetudine.
units.tr: Fifth, the proper accidents reveal the affected place: for example, a yellow colour of the whole body designates an obstruction of the liver or of the gall-bladder; a black colour designates an obstruction of the spleen. The same is the case with the other parts. Only observe that one symptom is not to be trusted too much. To all these may be added the sympathy of the parts: for when the meninges are injured, bilious vomiting arises; when the stomach is injured, deliria of the brain. What has been said here about signs is confirmed by sex, age, diet and habit.

units.la: CAP. III. De Signis morborum, & causarum internarum.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. On the Signs of Diseases and Internal Causes.

units.la: Quanquam cognitâ affectâ parte, innotescat unà morbus eiusque causa; quia tamen secus interdum accidit, extendenda longius est oratio, inquirendumq; in signa morborum. Videndum ante omnia, utrum pars laboret ex consensu, an proprio affectu tentetur. Si enim morbus sit permanens, ex se laborat: at si alia parte irritata, morbus irritetur, & non irritata, quiescit; pars ex consensu laborat. Quod dico est conspicuum in morbis sensum & motum vitiantibus. Nam cum instrumenta sensus egeant spiritu animali à cerebro delato; fit ut lædantur eorum actiones cerebri vitio, ut in apoplexia videre est; deficit enim visio, non oculi vitio, sed cerebri. Morbi species & idea, cognoscitur ex quatuor capitibus; nimirum excretis, loci natura, dolore, postremò accidentibus tibus propriis. hoc idem faciunt signa pathognomonica. Finge itaque chylum non mutatum expelli, signum est lienteriæ; aut urinam sabulosam; signum est calculi. Quod ad loci naturam; sciendū morbos quosdam, partibus quibusdam familiares esse; nam lumbrici in intestinis solis generantur? quosdam alienissimos; ut cor abscessum non fert, nec cerebrum schirrum; pulmo non dolet. Doloris propietas signum est affectus, & causæ: dolor enim pulsatorius arguit inflammationem partis carnosæ; dolor pungens. Signum est membranæ inflammatæ. Postremò cognoscitur morbus ex propriis accidentibus; ut icterus ex colore flavo, febris ardens ex nigrore linguæ. Ad accidentia propria revocantur morborum tempora, tam universalia, quam particularia, periodi, & typi. Nam typus est periodorum ordo: periodus tempus excandescentiæ, seu intensionis, & remissionis. Morbus enim omnis vel continenter affliaffligit, vel intermittit, & remittit; ut in febribus constat. Huc addi poterunt alia signa secundaria, desumpta ab ægrotandi promptitudine. Quæ pendet ex corporis constitutione, ex temperie, sexu, ætate &c. nec non causis, externis, aëre, regione &c. Homo enim temperamento frigido, non facile hyeme incidet in febrem. nam quanquam omnibus temporibus generari possint morbi; tamen quibusdam magis, quibusdam minus. Sunt morbi quibusdam populis familiares, ut scorbutus littoris Baltici incolis, struma Valesiis, quæ omnia à strenuo Medico sunt consideranda.
units.tr: Although, once the affected part is known, the disease and its cause become known at the same time, this does not always happen, so the discussion must be extended further and inquiry made into the signs of diseases. Before all else one must see whether the part suffers by sympathy or is attacked by its own affection. If the disease is persistent, the part suffers of itself; but if it is irritated when another part is irritated, and is quiet when that part is not, the part suffers by sympathy. This is plain in diseases that impair sensation and movement. For since the organs of sense need animal spirit conveyed from the brain, their actions are damaged by a fault of the brain, as can be seen in apoplexy: the sight fails, not through a fault of the eyes but of the brain. The species and idea of a disease are recognised from four heads: namely, the excretions, the nature of the place, the pain, and lastly the peculiar accidents. Pathognomonic signs do the same. Suppose undigested chyle is expelled: this is a sign of lientery; or gritty urine: this is a sign of stone. As to the nature of the place, it must be noted that some diseases are peculiar to certain parts (for worms are generated only in the intestines), while others are quite foreign to some parts: the heart does not bear an abscess, nor the brain a scirrhus, and the lung does not feel pain. The quality of the pain is a sign of the affection and its cause: a throbbing pain indicates inflammation of a fleshy part; a pricking pain is a sign of an inflamed membrane. Lastly, a disease is recognised by its peculiar accidents: jaundice by yellow colour, burning fever by blackness of the tongue. The times of diseases, both general and particular, periods and types, are also referred to their peculiar accidents. For the type is the order of the periods, and the period is the time of increase, or intensity, and of remission. Every disease either continues without intermission, or intermits and remits, as is established in fevers. To these may be added other secondary signs, drawn from the readiness of the patient to fall ill. This depends on the constitution of the body, on temperament, sex, age and so on, and likewise on external causes: air, region, and so on. For a man of cold temperament will not easily fall into fever in winter; for although diseases can be generated at all seasons, some arise more and some less at certain times. Some diseases are peculiar to certain peoples, as scurvy to the inhabitants of the Baltic coast and goitre to the people of the Valais; all these must be considered by the diligent physician.

units.la: Nec tamen necesse est semper plura signa adhibere, eaque inter se conferre. nam sufficit quandoque unum signum pathognomicum; ut in Apoplexia videre est. Quod si unum non sufficit; plura sunt investiganda, eaque inter se componenda erunt; ut in deliriis videre est.
units.tr: Yet it is not always necessary to apply several signs and compare them with one another; for sometimes one pathognomonic sign suffices, as can be seen in apoplexy. But if one does not suffice, several must be investigated, and these must be weighed against each other, as can be seen in delirium.

units.la: Sed jam tempus est descendere ad morbo-
units.tr: But now it is time to descend to the species of diseases.

units.la: morborum species. Et primò intem-periesnuda subitò nec gingitur, nec actiones subitò tollit ; ut in iis mor-bis fieri amat, qui fiūt ab humoris af-fluxu, quemadmodum Apoplexia : nec partes tenduntur , aut gravitaţis sensu afficiuntur. Calidum morbum demonstrant causæ præcedentes cor-pus calfacientes; ut aër, cibus, potus &c. rubor partis affectæ.frigidæ in-temperiei contraria sunt indicia. I-dem judicium esto cęterarum intem-perierum. Morbi compositionis cog-noscuntur ex causis prægressis , & symptomatis. Nimiæ apertionis va-sorum signum est contentorum præ-ter naturam evacuatio , ab expultri-ce debilitatâ. juvantur obstruenti-bus. Vasorum angustorum contraria sunt signa; contenta enim præter na-turam intus retinentur. Si magnitu-do in parte externâ augeatur , sensi-bus est obvia. sin autem latet in par-te internâ , cognoscitur ex dolore gravante,aut distendente,calore,fri-gore, tumoris situ. Diminutæ mag-nitunitudinis contraria sunt signa. Morbus in numero partis externæ aućto aut minuto, sensibus occurrit. sin sit partis internæ & abditæ vitio conformationis in utero, cognoscitur ex actione læsa, & figura cutis non naturali, quà parte residet morbus. sin pars interna suo moveatur loco; non modo cognoscitur ex tumore & dolore eius partis, in quam decumbit; sed etiã ex causis efficientibus membrum de sede deturbantibus. Ulcus internum cognoscitur ex sanie, pure, sanguine. Et hoc quidem modo cognoscuntur morbi præsentes & loci affecti.
units.tr: And first, an intemperies does not suddenly lay bare nor suddenly remove the actions, as it is wont to do in those diseases that arise from an influx of humour, like apoplexy; nor are the parts stretched or affected with a sense of heaviness. Causes that heat the body, such as air, food, drink and so on, indicate a hot disease, as does redness of the affected part; the contrary signs indicate a cold intemperies. The same judgment holds for the other intemperies. Diseases of composition are known from preceding causes and symptoms. Excessive opening of the vessels is signalled by the evacuation of contents contrary to nature, the expulsive power being weakened; such diseases are helped by astringents. The signs of narrow vessels are the contrary, for the contents contrary to nature are retained within. If the size increases in an external part, it is obvious to the senses; but if it lies hidden in an internal part, it is known from a burdensome or distending pain, from heat or cold, and from the situation of the swelling. The signs of diminished size are the contrary. A disease in the number of parts, whether an external part is increased or decreased, meets the senses. If it lies in an internal and hidden part through a fault in the conformation of the womb, it is known from the impaired action and from skin of unnatural shape, by which part the disease resides. If an internal part is moved from its place, it is known not only from the swelling and pain of the part into which it has sunk, but also from the efficient causes that dislodge the member from its seat. An internal ulcer is known from sanies, pus and blood. And in this way present diseases and the affected places are known.

units.la: Sed dices, quomodo cognoscam causas latentes, quæ morbos sæpe faciunt? contigit enim non raro, ut morbus cum loco affecto cognoscatur, ignorata tamen causa; cuius tamen cognitio est necessaria ad curandum. Causa omnis est vel externa, eoque nota, & evidens: vel occulta, & interna; ut contenta in corpore præter naturam, nec non plethora thora & cocochymia, quæ contentorum sunt dispositiones medicæ quæ suis signis manifestantur. Temperamentum corporis, ætas, consuetudo, sexus, evacuatio naturalis suppressa, regio, aër &c. non tantum signa sunt humorum redundantium, sed etiam causa. Plethora est redundantia æqualis omnium humorum in venis contentorum. Interdum solius sanguinis redundantia, plethora dicitur. Est autem duplex, quoad vasa, & quoad vires. Illius signum & causa, est temperamentum calidum humidum, adolescentia, victus plenior, vita jucunda, sanguinis evacuatio suppressa. Signum tantum est color rubeus, habitus carnosus &c. Redundantia ad vires cognoscitur ex corporis gravitate. Cacochymia est redundantia humoris ; a sanguine diversi; melancholiæ scilicet, pilis, pituitæ. Corpus ergo calidum siccum, juventus, æstas, victus calidus & parcus, immodica exercitatio, sicut bilem generant, ita & designant: tum enim facies
units.tr: But you will say: how shall I recognise the hidden causes that often produce diseases? For it not rarely happens that a disease is recognised together with the affected place while its cause remains unknown, and yet knowledge of that cause is necessary for cure. Every cause is either external, and therefore known and evident, or occult and internal, such as contents in the body contrary to nature, and also plethora and cacochymia, which are medical dispositions of the contents and are made manifest by their signs. The temperament of the body, age, habit, sex, suppressed natural evacuation, region, air and so on are not only signs of redundant humours but also causes. Plethora is an even redundancy of all the humours contained in the veins. Sometimes the redundancy of the blood alone is called plethora. It is twofold, with respect to the vessels and with respect to the strength. The sign and cause of the former is a warm and moist temperament, youth, a fuller diet, a pleasant life, and suppressed evacuation of blood; the sign alone is a ruddy colour, a fleshy habit and so on. Redundancy with respect to strength is recognised from heaviness of the body. Cacochymia is a redundancy of a humour different from blood, namely of melancholy, phlegm or bile. Therefore a hot, dry body, youth, summer, a hot and sparing diet, and immoderate exercise both generate bile and indicate it; for then the face

units.la: [illegible, ~20 letters] marginal notes on the right edge are largely cut off and illegible; not transcribed. facies est citrei coloris, habitus corporis siccus, macilentus, pulsus celer, urina ignea &c. Eadem est ratio cacochymiæ pituitosæ, melancholicæ; quæ ex suis signis, & causis cognosci possunt eo modo quo biliosa, de qua jam actum. Corporis inanitio cognosci potest ex contrariâ repletione, eiusque causis & signis.
units.tr: is of a lemon-yellow colour, the habit of the body dry and emaciated, the pulse quick, the urine fiery and so on. The same reasoning applies to phlegmatic and melancholic cacochymia, which can be known from their signs and causes in the same way as the bilious, of which we have already spoken. Emptiness of the body can be known from the contrary repletion, and from its causes and signs.

units.la: CAP. IV. De Pulsibus.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV. On Pulses

units.la: SUnt duo signa medica maximi momenti, pulsus, & urina: nam non solum præsentem ægri conditionem significant, sed & futurum eventum denunciant. Quanquam pulsus primò facultatem vitalem, eiusque sedem cor nobis ostendat; secundariò tamen robur totius corporis; & vigorem manifestè significat, quatenus reliquæ facultates à vitali pendent. Urina hepar, renes, vesicam, genusque venosum, eorumque constitutionem oculis subjicit, at horum viscerum robur minus arguit.
units.tr: There are two medical signs of the greatest importance, the pulse and the urine, for they reveal not only the patient's present condition but also announce the future outcome. Yet the pulse first shows us the vital faculty and its seat, the heart; secondarily, it clearly indicates the strength of the whole body and its vigour, insofar as the other faculties depend on the vital one. The urine lays open to view the liver, the kidneys, the bladder and the venous vessels, and their condition, but indicates the strength of these viscera less well.

units.la: Unde quæritur jure à Medicis, utri horum signorum magis sit fidendū. Constat pulsum esse signum virium in quocunque affectu; proinde latius patet urina, quæ nec omnia viscera, nec omnes affectus indicat. quoties tamen concurrunt, (concurrunt autem non raro.) fidendum magis urinæ.Pulsus enim differentiæ non sunt tam evidentes, nec futurum morbi eventum tam declarant: urina, eiusque contenta oculis patent; nec tantum vires & morbū, sed etiam morbi longitudinem eiusq; eventum demonstrant. quanquam non puto pessimam urinam conjungi posse cum bono pulsu, aut contra.
units.tr: Hence physicians rightly ask which of these signs deserves more trust. It is agreed that the pulse is a sign of strength in every affection; so the urine, which does not indicate all the viscera or all the affections, has the narrower scope. Whenever they agree, however (and they often do), more trust should be placed in the urine. For the differences of the pulse are not so evident, nor do they reveal the future outcome of the disease so clearly. The urine and its contents lie open to the eyes, and they show not only the strength and the disease but also the length of the disease and its outcome. Yet I do not think that a very bad urine can be combined with a good pulse, or the reverse.

units.la: Veteres Græci definiunt pulsum hoc modo; est actio propria, primum cordis, secundario arteriarum, quâ, distensione, & contractione, moventur à facultate vitali, tum propter conservationem temperiei caloris innati, tum propter generationem spiritus animalis in cerebro. Quæ definitio omnes pulsus causas continet, ut examinanti patet.
units.tr: The ancient Greeks define the pulse thus: it is the proper action, first of the heart and secondarily of the arteries, by which they are moved by expansion and contraction, by the vital faculty, both for the preservation of the temperature of the innate heat and for the generation of the animal spirit in the brain. This definition, as anyone who examines it will see, contains all the causes of the pulse.

units.la: Pulsuum alii sunt simplices alii compositi; quod si pulsum cum pulsu conferas, vel unius partem cum alia, oritur pulsuum relatio.
units.tr: Some pulses are simple, others compound; and if you compare one pulse with another, or one part of a pulse with another part, a relation of pulses arises.

units.la: Quinque sunt genera prima pulsus simplicis. Primum est quantitas discensionis; respectu cuius corpus arteriae in omnem extensionem, longam, latam, profundam movetur; aut contra, unde oriuntur pulsus magnus, mediocris, parvus. Secundum sumitur a motus qualitate; unde pulsus celer, mediocris, tardus. Tertium est respectu quietis; unde pulsus creber, mediocris, rarus. Quartum respectu facultatis vitalis; unde pulsus vehemens, digitum tangentis propellens, mediocris, languidus. Quintum respectu arteriae; unde pulsus durus, mediocris, mollis.
units.tr: There are five primary kinds of simple pulse. First, there is the quantity of expansion: with respect to this, the body of the artery is moved in every extent, long, broad and deep, or the reverse, whence arise a large, a medium and a small pulse. Second, the pulse is taken from the quality of motion, whence a quick, a medium and a slow pulse. Third, it is taken with respect to rest, whence a frequent, a medium and a rare pulse. Fourth, with respect to the vital faculty, whence a strong pulse, one that pushes away the finger touching it, a medium pulse, and a weak pulse. Fifth, with respect to the artery, whence a hard, a medium and a soft pulse.

units.la: Sunt ergo quindecim pulsuum simplicium differentiae, quae arteriam se attollentem semper comitantur. Pulsus calidus, aut frigidus, inutiles sunt Medico ad praedicendum dum, pulsus vacuus, plenus, gravis, levis, cognosci nequeunt ; proinde à nobis negligentur. Quod de pulsibus dicitur, subjecta figura illustrat. 1. celer. | 2. moder | 3. lang. 1. creb. | 2. mod. | 3. Rarus 1. vehe. | 2. mod. | 3. tardus 1. moll. | 2. mod. | 3. durus 1. mag. | 2. moderi | 3. Parvus
units.tr: There are therefore fifteen differences of simple pulses, which always accompany the artery as it rises. A warm or cold pulse is useless to the physician for prognosis, and a empty, full, heavy or light pulse cannot be recognised; therefore we pass them over. What has been said of the pulses is illustrated by the figure below: (1) quick, (2) moderate, (3) slow; (1) frequent, (2) moderate, (3) rare; (1) strong, (2) moderate, (3) weak; (1) soft, (2) moderate, (3) hard; (1) large, (2) moderate, (3) small.

units.la: Pulsus compositi dicuntur, qui ex simplicibus constant ; quorum licet plurimæ sint differentiæ, singulę tamen ex quinque speciebus simplicibus componuntur, exempli causa, magnus, celer, creber, vehemēs, mollis, vel mediocris, mediocris, mediocris cris, vehemens, mediocris; qui pulsus est quadratus, convenitq; homini temperatissimo. Observa tantum quosdam pulsus esse incomparabiles, ut loquuntur; quemadmodum pulsus magnus & durus, qui nunquam, aut rarissimè conjunguntur; idē de molli & vehementi judicium esto.
units.tr: Compound pulses are those that consist of simple ones. Although there are very many of these differences, each is composed of one of the five simple species, for example large, quick, frequent, strong, soft, or medium, medium, medium, strong, medium. This pulse is "square," and it suits a man of the most balanced temperament. Note only that some pulses are, as they say, incompatible: for example a large and hard pulse, which are never or very rarely combined; the same judgement should be made of soft and strong.

units.la: Relationes pulsuum, sunt ordo, æqualitas, rythmus. Quicunque pulsus neque magnitudinem, neque celeritatem, crebritatem, vehementiā, nec denique mollitiem mutarunt, verum in his omnibus perseverant; dicuntur æquales: qui vero in omnibus immutati sunt, dicuntur absolutè inæquales: qui verò non in omnibus, sed in uno aut altero genere variantur, dicuntur inæquales secundum quid, ut magnitudine aut vehementiā inæquales. Jam æqualibus pulsibus, semper adjunctus ordo: at inæquales interdum sunt ordinati, interdum inordinati. Illi sunt qui in multis pulsationibus suam servant diversitatem: inordinati contra.
units.tr: The relations of pulses are order, equality and rhythm. Those pulses which have changed neither in magnitude, speed, frequency, strength, nor finally in softness, but persist in all these, are called equal; those which have changed in all respects are called absolutely unequal; those which vary not in all respects but in one or another kind are called unequal in a certain respect, as unequal in size or in strength. Now, order always accompanies equal pulses; unequal pulses are sometimes ordered, sometimes disordered. The former are those which keep their variation through many beats; the latter the reverse.

units.la: Verbi bi gratia ; sint octo pulsus vehemen-tes, nonus debilis; nonum istum sequantur octo denuo pulsus vehemen-tes; istos autem, nonus debilis, & ita deinceps; pulsus iste est inæqualis in vehementiâ, seu uno genere, at ordinatus ; quia nonus pulsus est debilis. Verum si diversitas varietur, ita ut indifferenter nunc octavus, nunc sextus sit debilis & languidus; pulsus talis non tantum est inæqualis, sed & inordinatus. Quod de vehementiâ dicitur, idem intelligendum de magnitudine, celeritate, crebritate &c. Ergo sunto decem pulsus crebri, undecimus rarus ; & rursum decem crebri, undecimus rarus; erit talis pulsus inæqualis in crebritate; quia undecimus pulsus est rarus; sed ordinatus tamen. inordinatus vero esset, si indifferenter tertius aut quintus esset rarus.
units.tr: For example: let there be eight strong pulses, then a ninth weak one; let these eight strong pulses follow that ninth weak one again, and so on. That pulse is unequal in strength, or in one kind, but ordered, because the ninth pulse is weak. But if the variation shifts, so that now the eighth, now the sixth, is indifferently weak and feeble, such a pulse is not only unequal but also disordered. What is said of strength applies equally to size, speed, frequency and so on. So let there be ten frequent pulses and an eleventh rare one, and again ten frequent and an eleventh rare; such a pulse will be unequal in frequency, because the eleventh pulse is rare, yet it is ordered. It would be disordered, however, if the third or the fifth were indifferently rare.

units.la: Rhytmus Galeni (nam Herophili non morantur medici) est qualitatum pulsus secundum distensionem & contractionem proportio. qualitates voco, celerileritatem, tarditatem, & utriusque mediocritatem. Proportio enim, non solum in quantitate, sed in qualitate habet locum. quomodo sanitas dicitur justa proportio calidi, frigidi, humidi, sicci. Quando ergo contractio & distensio sunt pares, oritur rhythmus æqualis: ut si distensio sit tarda, & contractio erit tarda. Sin distentio sit celer & contractio tarda, oritur rhythmus inæqualis.
units.tr: Rhythm, according to Galen (for the physicians do not dwell on Herophilus), is the proportion of the qualities of the pulse according to expansion and contraction. By qualities I mean speed, slowness and the mean of each. For proportion has a place not only in quantity but also in quality, as health is called the just proportion of warm, cold, moist and dry. When, therefore, contraction and expansion are equal, an equal rhythm arises: for example, if the expansion is slow, the contraction will also be slow. But if the expansion is quick and the contraction slow, an unequal rhythm arises.

units.la: Sed redeamus ad pulsus inæqualitatem; quæ duplex statuitur: vel enim est in pluribus; vocaturque systematica, vel collectia inæqualitas: interdum inæqualitas est in unâ pulsatione: quæ singularis dicitur. Quod ad systematicam attinet; illa duas habet species. Alii enim pulsus sunt æqualiter inæquales, alii inæqualiter. Æqualiter inæquales sunt, si secundus sit minor primo, tertius secundo, quartus tertio, & ita deinceps. Hic ille est pulsus qui vocatur Decurtatus, Myurus ab Avicennâ cauda soricina; quia magnitudin eius, semper ali-quid quid decedit. Quod si eousque minuatur pulsus ut deficiat, vocatur Myurus deficiens: sin autem maneat in eadem parvitate, ad quam sensim pervenit; caret nomine: sin in eâdem parvitate non maneat pulsus, sed ad pristinam magnitudinem, vel etiam maiorem, aut minorem redeat; pulsus dicitur Myurus reciprocus.
units.tr: But let us return to the inequality of the pulse, which is set down as twofold: for it is either in several pulses, and is called systematic, or collective inequality; or sometimes the inequality is in a single beat, and this is called singular. As regards the systematic kind, it has two species. For some pulses are unequal in an even manner, others in an uneven manner. They are unequal in an even manner if the second is smaller than the first, the third than the second, the fourth than the third, and so on. This is the pulse called Decurtatus, or Myurus (a "mouse's tail," as Avicenna calls it), because its size continually diminishes. If the pulse is so reduced that it fails altogether, it is called Myurus deficiens; but if it remains at the same smallness to which it has gradually come, it has no name; and if the pulse does not remain at the same smallness but returns to its former size, or even becomes greater or smaller, it is called Myurus reciprocus.

units.la: Quod ad inæqualitatem singularem, seu quæ in uno pulsu cernitur, attinet; ea est primò duplex: vel enim est in una parte arteriæ, respondente uno digito: vel in pluribus partibus, respondentibus pluribus digitis. Si in unâ parte; tres existunt differentiæ. Nam primò motus interrumpitur mediâ quiete, vocaturque intermittens in uno pulsu. Secundò motu est continens, transit tamen celeritate in tarditatem, & contra; dicitur verò latinis Medicis impar citatus. Tertiò, pulsus retrocedit, redit tamen; estque pulsus Dicrotus sive bis pulsans: Pulsus bis pulsans, est etiam bis feriens; sed non contra. Nam caprizans bis ferit, non est tamen Dicrotus. hic enim est unicus tantum pulsus : lege Galenum lib. 1. de pulsuum differentiis. Sin inæqualitas sit in uno quidem pulsu, verum diversis arteriæ partibus ; multæ orientur differentiæ. Interdum motus pulsusque continui sunt ; interdum interrupti, quas quidem differentias, quia innominatæ sunt, omittam lubens.
units.tr: As for the singular inequality, that is, the kind seen in a single pulse, it is first of all twofold: for it is either in one part of the artery, corresponding to one finger, or in several parts, corresponding to several fingers. If it is in one part, there are three differences. First, the motion is interrupted by a middle rest, and this is called intermittent within a single pulse. Second, the motion is continuous, but passes from speed into slowness, and the reverse; Latin physicians call this an unequal quick pulse. Third, the pulse recedes and yet returns; this is the Dicrotus pulse, or pulse beating twice. A pulse that beats twice also strikes twice, but not conversely; for the goat-leaping pulse strikes twice but is not Dicrotus, since it is only a single pulse. Read Galen, book 1, On the Differences of Pulses. But if the inequality is in a single pulse yet in different parts of the artery, many differences arise. Sometimes the motions and pulses are continuous, sometimes interrupted; these differences, since they have no names, I will gladly omit.

units.la: Præter simplices inæqualitates, sunt aliæ compositæ, quæ omnes, exceptis decem, carent nomine. Nomina autem sunt eiusmodi, pulsus undosus, vermiculans, formicans, capricans, serrans, spasmosus, vibratus, tremens, palpitans, hecticus. Undosus est in quo omnes partes arteriæ non attolluntur simul, sed initio prima pars arteriæ, deinde secunda, tum tertia, & quidem motu continuo, usque ad arteriæ finem, seu ægri pollicem. Accedit quarundam partium altitudo, quarundam humilitas, instar undarum se elevantium. Ab undoso non differt vermiculans, nisi secundum minus: & quantum undosus superat vermiculantem, tantò vermiculans formicantem; qui adeo est debilis, ut sæpe non obseruetur; est enim non solum minimus, sed & tardissimus & languidissimus. Caprizans est de genere intermittentium in uno pulsu, quos media quies interpellat. In hoc prima pars motus systoles vel diastoles est tarda, aut moderata; secunda autem pars celer. Obserua secundum motum non tantum debere esse celeriorem, sed & vehementiorem. nam quemadmodum capra, dum alteram adoritur, primò se effert, ac priusquam impetum perficiat, se retinet, & quasi desinens, altero tamen motu & celeriore & fortiore denuò ruit; similiter & hic pulsus. Serrans pulsus est in diuersis arteriæ partibus, in uno tamen pulsu. nam primus digitus sentit motum & tertius: verum secundus, & quartus, nequaquam. Spasmosus, seu retortus, in quo muta-to sito situ arteria attollitur sursum, & deorsum, à pollice, & ad pollicem ægroti; & quidem in altum. Huic similis est vibratus; nisi quod tensio sursum & deorsum hic sit minor, sed tamen eminentia maior. Pulsus tre- mens & palpitans, est in quo arteria tremit, & palpitat. Hecticus pulsus est, qui perpetuò sibi similis est, est- que perpetua arteriarum agitatio, sibi semper similis, cuiuscunque tan- dem sit speciei. nomen habet à febre hectică.
units.tr: Besides the simple inequalities there are other, compound ones, all of which, except ten, lack a name. The names are these: undulating, wormlike, ant-like, goat-leaping, sawing, convulsive, vibrating, trembling, palpitating, hectic. The undulating pulse is one in which all parts of the artery do not rise together, but at the beginning the first part of the artery, then the second, then the third, and indeed with continuous motion, as far as the end of the artery, or the patient's thumb. To this is added that some parts are raised high and some low, like waves rising up. The wormlike pulse differs from the undulating only by degree: and as the undulating exceeds the wormlike, so the wormlike exceeds the ant-like, which is so weak that it is often not observed; for it is not only very small but also very slow and very languid. The goat-leaping pulse belongs to the class of intermittent pulses within a single beat, which a middle rest interrupts. In this, the first part of the motion, of systole or diastole, is slow or moderate, but the second part is quick. Observe that the second motion must be not only quicker but also stronger; for just as a goat, when it attacks another, first rises up and, before completing its thrust, holds itself back, and as if ceasing, yet with a second motion both quicker and stronger rushes down again, so also does this pulse. The sawing pulse occurs in different parts of the artery, yet within one beat; for the first finger feels the motion and the third, but the second and fourth not at all. The convulsive, or twisted, pulse is one in which, the position of the artery having changed, it rises upward and downward, from the thumb and back to the patient's thumb; and indeed it rises high. Similar to this is the vibrating pulse, except that the upward and downward tension here is less, though the elevation is greater. The trembling and palpitating pulse is one in which the artery trembles and palpitates. The hectic pulse is one which is perpetually like itself, and is a perpetual agitation of the arteries, always similar to itself, of whatever species it finally is; it takes its name from hectic fever.

units.la: Causa pulsus efficiens, est vis vitalis cordi insidens, ab eoque in arterias diffusa. Instrumentum est arteria. Finis est necessitas & usus; temperies nimirum caloris vitalis.
units.tr: The efficient cause of the pulse is the vital power residing in the heart and diffused from it into the arteries. The instrument is the artery. The end is necessity and use, namely the temperament of the vital heat.

units.la: Varietas pulsus oritur à causa continente; quæ triplex est, facultas, instrumentum, & usus, seu necessitas. quæ si bene habent, pulsus in omni genere erit moderatus: sin mutetur causa continens, pulsus quoque mutabitur. Si ergo usus fuerit auctus, nimirum calor præter naturā intensus, sus, facultas valida, arteria obse- quens; generabitur pulsus magnus. Si magnitudo non suffecerit; accedit celeritas. Si ne hæc quidem; crebi- tas, succedit. Ob contrarias causas fiunt pulsus parvi.Celer pulsus fit aut ob usum auctum, aut penuriam spiri- tus vitalis; ob quas causas pulsus fit creber, seu frequens. Vehemens pul- sus fit à robore facultatis; ita tamen ut usus & instrumentū respondeant. Languidus à contrariâ causâ. Pulsus duri causa, est arteriæ durities; sicut eiusdem mollities, causa est pulsus mollis. Pulsus dicroti causa, est in- æqualis cordis, & arteriarum dispo- sitio: nam quædam partes tantum ca- lent, quædam præterea fuligine ob- sidentur. Pars enim tantum calida di- stendit, at altera calida, & fuligino- sa, contrahit eodem tempore: & hæc quidem ad expulsionem fuliginum, illa verò ad refrigerium. Fit ergo di- stensio, & contractio diversimodè, pro huius, aut illius partis victoria. Pulsus undosus, vermiculans, formicans, differunt tantum secundum magis & minus; proinde tales habebunt causas; nimirum debilitatem facultatis, vel humorum in arteriis copiam, aut alioqui instrumenti mollitiem. Undosus enim quia maior est reliquis & celerior, ab humorum copia fieri certum est; reliqui à facultate debili. Caprizantis causa est facultas valida, impedita tamen; aut humorum copia, ut compressione arteriarum. Serrantis causa, est facultas onerata, usus auctus, instrumentum durum. Pulsus convulsivi causa, est spasmus membrorum. Vibratus pulsus, tres agnoscit causas; facultatem validam, usum auctum, & instrumentum durum. Quaecunque febrem hecticam inducunt, pulsum quoque hecticum efficiunt. Myuri causam agnoscunt facultatem debilem, sicut & Myuri reciproci. Observandum porro, variari pulsum pro conditione rerum non naturalium, sexus, aetatis, loci, &c. Quod Avicenna ex hominum pulsu eorum patriam cognoscere pore potuerit, ut quidam produnt ; logi sunt. Si tria verba addidero : finem faciam. Supponendum hic, non tantum distensionem arteriæ, sed & contractionem à digito percipi posse. Finis contractionis & initium distensionis percipi nequeunt : contra utraque quies perceptibilis est.
units.tr: The variety of the pulse arises from its containing cause, which is threefold: the faculty, the instrument, and the use or necessity. If these are in good condition, the pulse will be moderate in every kind; but if the containing cause changes, the pulse will change too. If then the use is increased, that is, the heat is intense beyond nature, the faculty strong, and the artery compliant, a large pulse will be produced. If its size does not suffice, speed is added; if not even this, frequency follows. Small pulses arise from contrary causes. A quick pulse arises either from increased use or from a lack of vital spirit, and for these causes the pulse becomes frequent or repeated. A vehement pulse arises from the vigour of the faculty, provided that use and instrument correspond; a languid pulse arises from the contrary cause. The cause of a hard pulse is hardness of the artery, just as the cause of a soft pulse is its softness. The cause of the dicrotic pulse is an unequal disposition of the heart and arteries: for some parts are only hot, while others are also clogged with soot. The hot part alone dilates, while the other, both hot and sooty, contracts at the same time; the one for expelling the soot, the other for cooling. Dilation and contraction therefore occur in different ways, according to the victory of this or that part. The undulating, worm-like and ant-like pulses differ only in degree; accordingly they will have the same causes, namely weakness of the faculty, an abundance of humours in the arteries, or otherwise a softness of the instrument. For the undulating pulse, being larger and quicker than the others, is certainly produced by an abundance of humours; the others by a weak faculty. The cause of the goat-leaping pulse is a strong faculty that is nevertheless impeded, or an abundance of humours, such as compression of the arteries.
