The cause of the saw-toothed pulse is a burdened faculty, increased use, and a hard instrument. The cause of the convulsive pulse is spasm of the limbs. The vibrating pulse acknowledges three causes: a strong faculty, increased use, and a hard instrument. Whatever induces hectic fever also produces the hectic pulse. The causes of the myurus pulse are a weak faculty, as also in the reciprocal myurus. It is further to be observed that the pulse varies according to the conditions of the non-natural things, sex, age, place, and so on. That Avicenna could recognise a man's homeland from his pulse, as some report, is idle talk. If I add three more words, I shall make an end. It must be supposed here that not only the dilation of the artery but also its contraction can be perceived by the finger. The end of a contraction and the beginning of a dilation cannot be perceived; on the contrary, both kinds of rest can be perceived.

units.la: CAP. V. De Vrinis.
units.tr: CHAP. V. Of Urines.

units.la: SIgnum ab urinâ sumptum est manifestum pulsu. Est autem urina, excrementum serosum sanguinis, genitum ex superflua portione, liquidorum assumptorum, & ab excrementitiâ bile tinctum, quod renes attractum ad vesicam demittunt. Jam antea monui, serum esse sanguinis vehiculum: sanguis enim crassus, penetrare nequit & subire tenues venas, nisi sero copioso dilueretur. Proinde sanguinis naturam, nec non hepar, lienem, renes, vesicam, optimè manifestat urina. Quæ non omni tempore est colligenda; verum mane, peractâ concoctione, ctione[?], in matulâ vitreâ, pellucidâ, albâ, tenui. colligenda inquam, non post crapulam, aut assumptione medicamentorum eam tingentium, aut alio modo afficientium: nec tamen diu servanda, quæ ultra quinque aut sex horas servatur corrumpitur, & putrescit;adeò ut nihil significet. Vbi verò aliquandiu resederit,& refrixerit,inspicienda erit;non tamen in radiis solaribus, sed extra eos in aëre lucido.
units.tr: A sign taken from the urine is clearly tied to the pulse. Now, urine is a serous excrement of the blood, produced from the surplus portion of the liquids taken in, tinged with excrementitious bile, which the kidneys draw off and send down to the bladder. I have already pointed out that serum is the vehicle of the blood, for thick blood cannot penetrate or pass through the fine veins unless it is diluted with a copious serum. Therefore urine clearly reveals the nature of the blood, and also of the liver, spleen, kidneys and bladder. It should not be collected at every hour, but in the morning, after concoction is complete, in a clear, transparent, white, thin glass flask. I say it should be collected, not after a drinking bout, nor after taking medicines that tint it or otherwise affect it. Nor should it be kept for long: urine kept more than five or six hours spoils and putrefies, so that it signifies nothing. But when it has settled for some time and cooled, it must be examined, not in the rays of the sun but outside them, in clear air.

units.la: In uriua sex considerant Medici, consistentiam, seu modum substantiæ, perspicuitatem, quantitatem, odorem, colorem, & [illegible, ~8 letters] contenta; quæ singula consideranda sunt seorsum. Si modus substantiæ consideretur; urina alia crassa, alia tenuis, alia mediocris. Urina interdum transparens, interdum obscura & opaca, ut eam permeare nequeat visus. Ratione quantitatis, vel multa, vel pauca, ac proinde interdum respondet potui, interdum non. Odor urinæ propriè nullus est; aut si est, fœtidus est; nisi forsan medicadicamenti alicuius permistione sua- vem odorem spiret. Vrinę color mul- tiplex est, albus, (quo pertinent cry- stallinus) aqueus, lacteus, glaucus, charopus, pilis camelorum similis. Tum subspiceus, spiceus, pallidus, subrufus, subflavus, rufus, flavus, ru- ber. Tertiò est color viridis, ærugi- nosus, prasseus, ceruleus, venetus, li- vidus, niger. Postremò in urinâ confi- derantur contenta; nimirum hyposta- sis, enæorema, nubes, bullæ, ramenta, squammæ, pili, arenæ, pinguedo, pus, humores &c.
units.tr: Physicians consider six things in urine: its consistency, or the state of its substance, its transparency, its quantity, its odour, its colour, and [illegible] its contents. Each of these must be considered separately. If the state of the substance is considered, some urine is thick, some thin, some of middling consistency. Urine is sometimes transparent, sometimes dark and opaque, so that the sight cannot pass through it. As to quantity, it is sometimes abundant, sometimes scanty, and so sometimes corresponds to the drink taken, sometimes not. Urine has no proper odour; or if it has one, it is foul, unless perhaps by mixing in some medicine it breathes out a sweet smell. The colour of urine is manifold: white (to which belongs the crystalline), watery, milky, grey-green, the colour of camel's hair. Then sub-spiceous, spice-coloured, pale, reddish-tinged, yellowish-tinged, red, yellow, ruddy. Thirdly there is green, verdigris-coloured, leek-green, sky-blue, Venetian, livid, black. Lastly in urine are considered the contents: namely the hypostasis, the enaeorema, the cloud, bubbles, flakes, scales, hairs, sands, fat, pus, humours, and so on.

units.la: Sed quia nemo urinam ægrorum cognoscere potest, ignorata sanorum, de hac, tanquam regula alterius, age- mus primò. Sanorum, bono corpo- ris habitu præditorum urina, subfla- va, aut flava est, talis manens, qualis mingitur; cuius quantitas potulento- rum quantitati respondet, mediocris substantiæ, odore nequaquam gravi, sæpe sine contentis, interdum adest hypostasis alba, levis, æqualis, pyra- midalis in fundo matulæ, sine aliis excreexcrementis. Huiusmodi itaq; urina signum est bonæ concoctionis. Negandum tamen non est, etiam in sanis urinam à jam descripta recedere, ob varias & multiplices causas.
units.tr: But since no one can know the urine of the sick unless he knows the urine of the healthy, we shall treat first of the healthy, using it as the rule for the other. The urine of healthy people, who have a good state of body, is yellowish or yellow, remaining as it is when passed; its quantity corresponds to the quantity of drink, its substance is of middling consistency, its odour by no means strong, often without contents; sometimes there is a white, light, even, pyramidal hypostasis at the bottom of the flask, without other excrements. Urine of this kind is therefore a sign of good concoction. Yet it must not be denied that even in healthy people urine may depart from this description, for various and manifold causes.

units.la: Ergò urina mediocris substantiæ bonam hepatis concoctionem significat; justo autem crassior, vel tenuior, concoctionem malam arguit. Vrinam tenuem efficit liberalior potus, vel obstructio aliqua viscerum; modo crassities sit ex admistione substantię alienę: nam si natura sua, & substantię modo crassa sit, nulla obstructio eam extenuare valet. In morbis acutis urina est tenuis, ex sententiâ Medicorum, ob facultatis concoctricis debilitatem; unde cruditatem arguit. Quæ si diutius perseveret, virēsque fuerint debiles, mors: alioqui si vires non adeò sint debiles, abscessus in partibus inferioribus metuendus erit; in crisibus recidiva. Crassa urina fit, aut modo substantiæ, aut aliarum rerum permistione. In febrium initiis, huiusmodi urina est signum dedebilitatis, & pugnæ naturæ cum morbo; nisi præcesserit tenuis, tum vero concoctionis est signum. Vrina crassa, interdum est perspicua, & transparens; interdum turbulenta. Crassa, & perspicua, si sit candida, creditur esse ut plurimum ex permissione pituitæ, signumque est cruditatis; si reliqua signa bene se habeant, salutem, aut longum morbum portendit. Sin morbus sit acutus, appareat autem quarto die huiusmodi urina; die septimo morietur æger.
units.tr: Therefore urine of middling substance signifies good concoction of the liver; but urine that is too thick or too thin indicates poor concoction. A more generous drink, or some obstruction of the viscera, makes urine thin; thickness only arises from the admixture of foreign matter, for if it is thick by its own nature and substance, no obstruction can make it thin. In acute diseases the urine is thin, according to the opinion of physicians, because of the weakness of the faculty of concoction, and so it indicates crudity. If this persists for longer, and the strength is weak, it means death; otherwise, if the strength is not so weak, an abscess in the lower parts is to be feared; in crises, a relapse. Urine becomes thick either from the nature of its substance or from the mixing in of other things. At the beginning of fevers, urine of this kind is a sign of weakness, and of nature struggling with the disease; unless it was preceded by thin urine, in which case it is a sign of concoction. Thick urine is sometimes clear and transparent, sometimes turbid. If it is thick and transparent, and white, it is believed to arise for the most part from an admixture of phlegm, and is a sign of crudity; if the other signs are good, it portends health, or a long illness. But if the disease is acute and urine of this kind appears on the fourth day, the patient will die on the seventh day.

units.la: Vrina crassa & turbulenta, quam calculi renum, aut vesicæ excrementa non effecerunt, nec frigus externum induxit, est ob humorum crudorum copiam. Turbulenta urina est triplex. Prima clara mingitur, postea verò crassescit. Secunda crassa mingitur, postea verò subsidet. Tertia crassa mingitur, crassaque permanet. Estque hæc urina verè turbida, & confusa, sine ullis contentis, nec ignis calore dissolvitur. Prima urina est turbulentarum optima; significat enim natunaturam incipere concoctionem. Secunda signum est secretionis, & attenuationis. Postrema est pessima, indicatque humorum fermentationem, copiam, perturbationem, virum debilitatem, dolorem praeterea capitis, aut praesentem aut imminentem.
units.tr: Urine that is thick and turbid, which neither kidney stones nor bladder excrements have produced, and which external cold has not brought on, comes from a copious supply of crude humours. Turbid urine is of three kinds. The first is passed clear, but afterwards thickens. The second is passed thick, but afterwards settles. The third is passed thick and remains thick. This last is truly turbid and confused, without any contents, and is not dissolved by the heat of fire. The first kind is the best of the turbid urines, for it signifies that nature is beginning concoction. The second is a sign of secretion and thinning. The last is the worst, and indicates fermentation of the humours, their abundance, disturbance, and weakness of the strength, and besides, pain in the head, either present or threatening.

units.la: Vrina omnis debet respondere potui; nam si ille multus est, & haec non multo minor esse debet, sin paucus, & haec quoque pauca. Nam copiosa est mala; nisi forsan sit critica; designat enim magnam colliquationem succorum, & corporis; quemadmodum in febribus ardentibus videre est. interdum retentricem facultatem jecoris & ventriculi debilitatam. interdum etiam intemperiem calidam renum; sicut in Diabete. Pauca urina redditur, vel ob potus penuriam, vel renum & huiusmodi viscerum obstructionem, aut debilitatem facultatis expultricis, aut evacuationem per alias vias, aut etiam consumptionem a vehementi calore. Magnus urinae foetor comes est putredinis, (si eum non contraxerit ex assūptis potulentis, aut ulcere partiū, per quas transit) signumq; est malum in morbis acutis ; nisi forsan die critico urina copiosè excernatur.
units.tr: All urine ought to correspond to the drink: if the drink is copious, the urine too ought to be not much less; if scanty, the urine too should be scanty. For abundant urine is bad, unless perhaps it is critical; it signifies a great melting away of the juices and of the body, as may be seen in burning fevers; sometimes it signifies that the retentive faculty of the liver and stomach is weakened, sometimes also a hot disorder of the kidneys, as in diabetes. Scanty urine is passed either from lack of drink, or from obstruction of the kidneys and such viscera, or from weakness of the expulsive faculty, or from evacuation by other channels, or even from consumption by vehement heat. A strong foul smell of urine accompanies putrefaction (unless it was contracted from drinks taken, or from an ulcer of the parts through which it passes), and it is a bad sign in acute diseases, unless perhaps on a critical day the urine is passed copiously.

units.la: Omnis urinę color, est ex admistione alieni humoris; bilis scilicet aut alterius succi; nam sola coctio, aut alteratio urinā non tingit. proinde flava sanorum urina, est ex admistione bilis naturalis serum imbuentis & tingentis. Quāto itaq; urina candidior, tanto minus inest bilis; cruditateq; indicat, aut obstructiones: nisi forsam alio ut in caput, rapiatur; quemadmodū in Phrenitide & febribus ardētibus fieri amat; proinde malū est signum. Ita in lętero urina alba diu perseverans hydropē minatur. Vrina alba, crassaq; significat pituitæ copiam. Vrina pinguis, phtisin & colliquationem pinguedinis. Vrina subspicea meliorem concoctionem indicat, quam subalba. Quanto bilis, quā tingitur, urina, intensiorem habet calorē ; tanto majorem viscerum ardorem arguit. Subrubra, & tenuis argumentum est crudi di & periculosi morbi : sin vero hæc eadem subrubra, fuerit crassa, simileq; habuerit sedimentum, longũ morbum, at periculi expertem portendit. Vrina admodum rubra claraq; sequitur febres ardentes, & hepatis intemperiem calidam. Rubra & crassa, aut sanguinis multitudinem, aut bilis vitellinæ admistionem designat. Hæc diu perseverans in morbo acuto, aut mortem, aut inflammationem renum minatur : sin verò turbida manserit, hepatis inflammationem & non raro schirrũ ostendit. Vrina nigricãs, si impositum linteũ colore citrino tingat, habeatq; citrinam spumam, significat icterũ ex obstructione vesicæ fellis; aut si sit alba, seu parũ rubra, maneatq; icterus; hydrops in propinquo est.
units.tr: Every colour of urine comes from the admixture of some foreign humour, namely bile or another juice; for concoction or alteration alone does not tinge urine. Therefore the yellow urine of healthy people comes from the admixture of natural bile, which imbues and tinges the serum. Hence the whiter the urine, the less bile is in it, and this indicates crudity or obstructions, unless perhaps the matter is drawn elsewhere, as into the head, which it is wont to do in phrenitis and burning fevers; so it is then a bad sign. Thus in jaundice, white urine persisting for a long time threatens dropsy. White and thick urine signifies a copious phlegm. Fatty urine signifies phthisis and a melting away of fat. Sub-spiceous urine indicates better concoction than sub-white. The more bile that tinges the urine, the more intense the heat it has, and the greater the burning of the viscera it indicates. Sub-reddish and thin is a sign of a crude and dangerous disease; but if this same sub-reddish urine is thick, and has a similar sediment, it portends a long illness, yet one free of danger. Very red and clear urine follows burning fevers and a hot disorder of the liver. Red and thick urine designates either a multitude of blood or an admixture of yolk-coloured bile. If this persists in an acute disease, it threatens either death or inflammation of the kidneys; but if it remains turbid, it shows inflammation of the liver and not infrequently a scirrhus. Blackish urine, if a linen cloth placed in it is tinged citron-yellow and has a citron-coloured froth, signifies jaundice from obstruction of the gall of the bladder; or if it is white, or only slightly red, and the jaundice persists, dropsy is near.

units.la: Transeamus ad urinas cruentas; quæ si fiant à sanguinis copiâ, die critico, cum ægri tolerantiâ, bonæ sunt; significant enim facultatem expultricem vigere: hæc enim materiam morbificam in febribus per vesicam expellit. Cruentæ evadunt urinę in nephreticis ex erosione venarum. Vrina craffea est signum sanguinis tosti, & eiusdem putredinis. Viridis est signum bilis æruginosæ, vel confi-milis, estque judicium magni incen-dii, interdum & convulsionis. Color venetus melancholiam arguit: & u-rina veneta crassa, frigoris magni est comes, quæ si ad nigrorem vergat, caloris extinctionem significare creditur; quanquam nigror urinæ magnum alioqui incendium arguit. Non omnis urina nigra est mala; quod multis exemplis probatur in Epidemicis; eius enim mictione multi liberantur à melancholicis affectibus.
units.tr: Let us pass on to bloody urines. If these arise from an abundance of blood, on a critical day, with the patient able to bear it, they are good; for they signify that the expulsive faculty is strong, since in fevers it expels the morbid matter through the bladder. Bloody urines occur in kidney disease from erosion of the veins. Urine like sooty water is a sign of scorched blood and of the same putrefaction. Green is a sign of verdigris-like or similar bile, and is a judgment of a great burning, and sometimes of convulsion. Venetian colour indicates melancholy; and thick Venetian urine is the companion of great cold, which, if it tends towards blackness, is believed to signify the extinction of heat; although blackness of urine otherwise indicates a great burning. Not every black urine is bad; this is proved by many examples in the Epidemics, for many are freed from melancholic affections by passing it.

units.la: Verum tempus est contenta urinæ considerare. Vrina in matulâ contenta, ad aëris similitudinem, dividitur in tres regiones; supremam, mediam, & infimam. In primâ est nubes; in secundâ suspensum; in tertiâ & infimâ, seu matulæ fundo, est sedimentum, ὑπόστασις <bl>dicta</bl>. De cuius materia, & modo magna est contentio. Nam Fernelius putat, non malè, esse crassiocrassiorem urinæ portionem, & quasi secem; non tantum in sanis, sed & ægris. Alii dicunt sanorum hypostasin esse reliquias tertiæ concoctionis in venis. At male habentium, sicut & neutrorum, esse materiæ morbificæ portionem: alii aliter. Quicquid sit, sanorum hypostasis & contenta, sunt regula aliarum urinarum. Contenta itaque in urinis ægrorum quanto sunt similiora contentis sanorum, tanto meliora; quanto vero dissimiliora, tanto deteriora. Hypostasis ergo alba, levis, & æqualis, arguit in ægris bonam concoctionem. Sin suspensum sit album, leve, & æquale; indicium est concoctionis debilioris; ac proinde maioris cruditatis, quam in superiore. Melius tamen est nubecula, quæ tenue est coctionis initium. Ergo nubecula gradus est ad suspensum; sicut ad hypostasin. Quæ si laudabilis sit, perfectæ concoctionis est signum. Si ergò nullum sit contenum, hoc est nubes, nec suspensum,
units.tr: Now it is time to consider the contents of the urine. The urine in the flask divides, like the air, into three regions: upper, middle and lower. In the first is the cloud; in the second, the suspended matter; in the third and lowest, that is, at the bottom of the flask, is the sediment, called hypostasis [ὑπόστασις]. About its material and nature there is great dispute. Fernelius thinks, not without reason, that it is the thicker portion of the urine, as it were its dregs, not only in the sick but also in the healthy. Others say that the hypostasis of the healthy is the remnant of the third concoction in the veins, but that in the ill, as in those who are neither, it is a portion of morbific matter; others hold different views. Whatever the case, the hypostasis and contents of healthy people are the standard for other urines. Therefore, the more the contents of the urine of the sick resemble the contents of the healthy, the better they are; the more they differ, the worse. So a white, light and even hypostasis indicates good concoction in the sick. But if the suspended matter is white, light and even, it is a sign of weaker concoction and therefore of greater crudity than in the upper region. Yet a little cloud is better, since it is the beginning of thin concoction. The cloud is thus a step towards the suspended matter, as the suspended matter is a step towards the hypostasis. If the cloud is praiseworthy, it is a sign of perfect concoction. If there is then no content at all, neither cloud, nor suspended matter,

units.la: nec fedimentum in urinâ ; plerum-que arguit naturam non esse aggref-fam concoctionem ; at si interdum appareant, rursumque evanescant naturæ & morbi certamen innuunt. Quod si in morbis nulla appareant contenta,ut quandoque accidit; cru-ditatis magnæ , aut corruptionis hu-morum est argumentum.quod & ac-cidit in viscerum debilitate. inflam-matione , aut obstructione. Si præ-cesserint magnæ evacuationes , hu-mores excrementitios expurgantes destituitur urina contentis. Quod in sanis contentorum defectus ab ob-structione fiat;non est admittendum illi enim sæpè non gignunt. Multa contenta in ægris fiunt à validâ fa-cultate alteratrice ; quæ in febrium initiis & augmento copiam humo-rũ designant ; in declinatione auten-si appareant ; modo nullum pravum interveniat signum; salutem & secu-ritatem denunciant. Pus sæpe in urì-nâ subsidens, mentitur bonam hypo-stasin;distinguitur tamen,quia purulenta urina non tantum fœtet, sed & abscessum in visceribus supponit. Apparet interdum in urina pinguedo; quam ex adipis liquatione fieri, ante dixi, in febribus magnis: nam magnus calor non tantum solvit adipem, sed & ipsam carnem; unde fiunt hypostases ervinæ, similes farinæ hordeaceæ. Sin partes ipsæ solidæ dissolvantur; urina erit laminea, furfuracea, pultacea. Pullæ urinarum sunt ab incluso spiritu, & flatu.
units.tr: nor sediment in the urine, this mostly indicates that nature has not undertaken a vigorous concoction; but if such contents sometimes appear and again vanish, they point to a struggle between nature and disease. But if no contents appear in diseases, as sometimes happens, it is a sign of great crudity or corruption of the humours, which also occurs in weakness of the viscera, inflammation or obstruction. If great evacuations have preceded, purging the excrementitious humours, the urine is left without contents. That the lack of contents in the healthy comes from obstruction is not to be admitted, for they often do not produce them. Many contents in the sick are produced by a strong altering faculty; these, at the beginning and increase of fevers, indicate an abundance of humours; if they appear in the decline, provided no bad sign intervenes, they announce health and safety. Pus settling often in urine feigns a good hypostasis; it is distinguished, however, because purulent urine not only stinks but also suggests an abscess in the viscera. Greasiness sometimes appears in urine, which I said before comes from the melting of fat in great fevers: for great heat dissolves not only fat but the flesh itself, whence arise lentil-like hypostases, similar to barley meal. But if the solid parts themselves dissolve, the urine will be scaly, bran-like or poultice-like. The bubbles in urines come from enclosed spirit and wind.

units.la: CAP. VI. De Præsagiis.
units.tr: CAP. VI. Of Prognoses.

units.la: DEventum tandem ad Medicinæ partem, tum nobilissimam, tum difficillimam; futurorum nimirum circa ægrum prædictionem. Morbo enim, & causa, locoque affecto cognitis, præsagitio, & prædictio superunt. Præsagitio nil aliud est, quam prænotio, & scientia futurorum in humano corpore, ex manifestis signis. Horum enunciatio, est prædictio; nam prænotio in mente tantum est. Signa hoc loco vocamus tantum prognostica.
units.tr: Having at last come to the part of medicine that is both the noblest and the most difficult, namely the prediction of future events concerning the patient. For once the disease, its cause and the affected place are known, prognosis and prediction follow. Prognosis is nothing other than foreknowledge and knowledge of future events in the human body, drawn from manifest signs. The declaration of these is prediction; for foreknowledge exists only in the mind. Here we call the signs simply prognostics.

units.la: Circa ægrum tria sunt præcognoscenda; primò, quò morbus erumpet ad salutem, an vero mortem. secundò quo tempore: postremò quomodo Unde & signa sunt triplicia; primò salutis & mortis: secundò concoctionis & cruditatis; tertiò decretoria. Sumuntur autem huiusmodi signa causis proximis; morbo & facultate non ab affectibus, qui non sunt. Comparandi itaque sunt morbus & natura, considerandumque uter superet. Nam si morbus sit facultate superior, morietur æger: sin contra, vivet.
units.tr: Three things must be known in advance concerning the patient: first, whether the disease will end in health or in death; second, at what time; and last, in what manner. Accordingly the signs are also threefold: first, those of health and death; second, those of concoction and crudity; third, those that are decisive. Such signs are taken from the proximate causes, namely the disease and the faculty, not from the affections, which are not causes. The disease and nature must therefore be compared, and it must be considered which prevails. For if the disease is stronger than the faculty, the patient will die; but if the contrary, he will live.

units.la: In morbo quinque examinand[?] veniunt. primum eius idea; secundum magnitudo; tertium mos; quartum motus; & demum exitus. quæ singula suis cognoscuntur signis. Morbi speciem & ideam, symptomata patefaciunt; sicut & eiusdem magnitudinem. Nam parvus morbus prava habet symptomata; magnus magna magna. Mos morbi, cognoscitur ex benignitate, & malignitate symptomatum. Omnis enim morbi malignitas (hæc vitæ furtim quasi insidiatur) periculi plena est. Motus causæ morbificæ, sunt quatuor illa tempora, in quæ duratio morbi dividitur; nimirum principium, augmentum, status declinatio. Verum ex omnibus his temporibus, status (in quo magna naturæ & morbi pugna) maxime cognosci debet; non tantum ad curationem, sed etiam præsagitionem.
units.tr: Five things in a disease come to be examined: first its kind, second its magnitude, third its manner, fourth its motion, and finally its outcome. Each of these is known by its own signs. The symptoms reveal the species and kind of the disease, and likewise its magnitude: a small disease has bad symptoms, a great one great symptoms. The manner of the disease is known from the mildness or malignity of its symptoms. For all malignity in a disease, which lies in wait against life almost by stealth, is full of danger. The motions of the morbific cause are the four periods into which the course of a disease is divided: beginning, increase, state, and decline. Of all these periods, the state, in which nature and disease wage their great struggle, must above all be recognised, not only for treatment but also for prognosis.

units.la: Tendit autem huc morbus admodū variè; interdum tardè, interdum celeriter; interdum æqualiter, interdum inæqualiter; nonnunquā constanter, & ordinatè, nonnunquā contra. Morbi celeritatem aut tarditatem, ostendit eiusdem species. Apoplexia enim citò ad statum venit, quartana intermittens tardè. Idē facit symptomatū incrementum: prout enim illa crescunt, morbi brevitas, & longitudo manifestatur. Idem faciet accessionum natura: si enim posterior accessio sio priore sit longior, & vehemen-tior, citiusque recurrat; morbus citò admodum ad statum veniet. Sin con-tra se res habeat, ita ut posterior ac-cessio sit priore brevior, benignior, tardiusque redeat; morbus declinat, vigorque & status superati sunt. At-que hęc quidem intelligenda sunt de morbo periodos habente; quibus si careat, ad symptomatum incremen-tum decurrendum est. hæc enim si celeriter augeantur, brevi status ex-pectandus: Quod dico, evidens est in morbis à causis calidis, qui citò moventur. Sin causa sit frigida; con-trarium fiet. Huc referuntur anni tempus, regio, ætas, natura ægri &c. Iuvenis enim, in regione calida, æſta-te, si ægrotet; ut plurimum morbus celerem habebit statum. An tempora morborum, æqualiter & inæquali-ter (nimirum an principium sit ve-lox, augmentum tardum vel contra constanter, ordinatè; an vero contra disces non tantum ex propriis symp-tomatis, sed & supervenientibus ac-cidencidentibus. Tempora morborū (quæ in benignis morbis semper sunt quatuor, in malignis nulla est declinatio) non circumscribitur dierum numero: nam sæpe morborum principia nos latent; cognoscuntur non tantum ex symptomatum incremento, sed etiam causarum motione. Quod ad principium attinet; multipliciter accipi solet. nam & primus insultus morbi, & tres primi dies, & totum tempus, quo materia cruda est; principium dicitur. Propriè tamen principium hic est, cum symptomata sunt leviora. Augmentum, in quo hæc augentur. Status est,cum est vehemens pugna naturæ, & morbi; in quo maximè sæviunt symptomata. Declinatio autem est, quando symptomata mitescunt. Atque hoc primo modo, cognoscuntur tempora. Cognoscuntur præterea ex motione causarum morbificarum. nam cum natura conetur coquere perfectè, & alterare materiam, principiū morbi est illud tempus, quo causa morbifica, sive materiaria est adhuc cruda. Augmentum in quo apparent notæ concoctionis. Vigor in quo concoctio est perfecta. Declinatio excipit concoctionem.
units.tr: A disease tends in many ways: sometimes slowly, sometimes quickly; sometimes evenly, sometimes unevenly; sometimes steadily and in order, sometimes otherwise. The species of the disease shows whether it is quick or slow: apoplexy quickly reaches its state, quartan intermittent fever slowly. The increase of the symptoms does the same; as they grow, the brevity or length of the disease becomes clear. The nature of the paroxysms will do the same: if a later paroxysm is longer and more violent than the earlier one and returns more quickly, the disease will reach its state very soon. But if the matter is otherwise, so that the later paroxysm is shorter and milder and returns more slowly, the disease is declining, and its vigour and state are overcome. These things are to be understood of a disease that has periods; if it lacks them, one must follow the increase of the symptoms, for if these grow quickly, the state is to be expected soon. What I say is evident in diseases from hot causes, which move quickly; if the cause is cold, the contrary will happen. To this belong the season of the year, the region, the age, the nature of the patient, and so on. A young man in a hot region, in summer, if he falls ill, will for the most part have a disease with a swift state. Whether the times of diseases are even or uneven (that is, whether the beginning is rapid and the increase slow, or the reverse; whether they proceed steadily and in order, or otherwise), one will learn not only from the proper symptoms but also from those that supervene and accompany them. The times of diseases (which in benign diseases are always four, while in malignant ones there is no decline) are not bounded by a number of days, for the beginnings of diseases often escape us; they are known not only from the increase of the symptoms but also from the motion of the causes. As regards the beginning, the word is commonly taken in several senses: the first onset of the disease, the first three days, and the whole time during which the matter is still crude, are all called the beginning. Properly, however, the beginning is when the symptoms are milder. The increase is that in which they grow. The state is when there is a violent struggle between nature and disease, and the symptoms rage most fiercely. The decline is when the symptoms grow milder. This is the first way in which the periods are known. They are also known from the motion of the morbific causes: since nature strives to concoct and alter the matter perfectly, the beginning of the disease is the time in which the morbific or material cause is still crude. The increase is that in which the marks of concoction appear. The vigour is that in which concoction is complete. The decline follows concoction.

units.la: Quintum in morbis observabile, & quo tota præsagii doctrina est directa, & morbi exitus; an scilicet victurus sit æger, an vero moriturus; tum quo tempore; postremo subitone, an paulatim. Signa, quibus ægri status cognoscitur, sunt functiones, excrementa, & nonnulla ad ęgri corpus pertinentia. Functiones ostendunt facultatum robur, & constantiam: Huiusmodi facultates principes, tres sunt, Naturalis, Vitalis, Animalis. harum potissima est vitalis, quæ ex pulsu cognoscitur: frequentes enim & graves lipothymiæ eius debilitatem testantur. Idem de anima-li judicandum. Nam visio, & audi-tio subito debilitatæ, signa sunt gra-vis morbi. Eadem est ratio sensuum internorum, & facultatum princi-pum, nec non facultatis motricis: malum enim est excrementa præter natunaturam supprimi, aut respirationem redditam esse difficiliorem. Robur virtutis naturalis cognoscitur ex co-ctione, & cruditate excrementorum; quæ quanto similiora sunt excremen-tis fanorum, tanto sunt similiora, o-ftenduntque robur facultatis naturalis: quanto autem dissimiliora, tanto eiusdem debilitatem magis arguunt. Verum quia unâ excretione non solvuntur omnes morbi, hinc diversorum excrementorum diversæ existunt significationes. Habitum enim totius corporis, indicant sudores: ventris constitutionem, dejectiones: at urina genus venosum, & partes eas, quas transit indicat. Eadem & aliarum ratio. In quibus omnibus observandus odor, color, copia &c. sudor enim fœtidus, frigidus, circa solum caput erumpens, peffimum signum est: ille enim est signum magnæ putredinis: hic vero, aut mortis, aut morbi prorogationis. Contra, fi die critico, apparentibus signis concoctionis, sudor erumpat uniuniversalis, calidus, continuus, bonum est signum. Quod de sudore dico, intelligendum itidem est de alvi excrementis, aliisque aliarum partium; nam quanto sanorum similiora sunt, tanto meliora. In quibus omnibus consideranda sunt notæ cruditatis, & coctionis, tum an tempestive fiant, an secus? tertio an cito, an tardè? quarto an constanter? postremo an cum ægri damno, an salute? Quæ à laborantis corpore desumuntur signa non sunt contemnenda. nam exempli causa, nasus acutus, oculi concavi, cæteraque Hippocraticam dictam faciem constituentia in malis sunt. Idem de involuntariis lachrimis, pravo ægri decubitu statuendum. Ex horum signorum, quæ prognostica dicuntur, cognitione, & eorum inter se comparatione eventus, morbi præscitur. Diximus illa duo esse, morbum, & naturam. Ad morbum pertinent non solum symptomata, sed & causæ, si eas habet: ad naturam omnia auxilia, tam naturalia, quam artificia-
units.tr: The fifth thing to be observed in diseases, and the one to which the whole doctrine of prognosis is directed, is the outcome of the disease: whether the patient will live or die, at what time, and lastly whether suddenly or gradually. The signs by which the state of the patient is known are the functions, the excretions, and certain features of the patient's body. The functions show the strength and steadiness of the faculties. The principal faculties are three: natural, vital, and animal. The chief of these is the vital, which is known from the pulse, for frequent and grave fainting attests its weakness. The same is to be judged of the animal faculty: sight and hearing suddenly weakened are signs of a grave disease. The same reasoning holds for the internal senses and the chief faculties, and also for the motive faculty; for it is bad when excretions are suppressed contrary to nature, or when breathing has become more difficult. The strength of the natural virtue is known from the concoction and crudity of the excretions. The more these resemble the excretions of healthy people, the more they show the strength of the natural faculty; the more they differ, the more they argue its weakness. But since not all diseases are resolved by one excretion, different excretions have different meanings. Sweats indicate the habit of the whole body; the stools indicate the constitution of the belly; urine indicates the venous kind and the parts through which it passes. The same holds of the others. In all of these one must observe the odour, colour, quantity, and so on. A foul, cold sweat breaking out only about the head is the worst sign, for it is a sign of great putrefaction, and either of death or of a prolonged disease. On the contrary, if on a critical day, with the signs of concoction appearing, a sweat breaks out all over the body, warm and continuous, it is a good sign. What I say of sweat must likewise be understood of the excretions of the bowels and of other parts: the more they resemble those of the healthy, the better. In all of these the marks of crudity and concoction must be considered: whether they occur at the proper time or not; third, whether quickly or slowly; fourth, whether constantly; and last, whether with harm to the patient or with his recovery. Signs taken from the body of the sufferer are not to be despised. For example, a sharp nose, hollow eyes, and the other features that make up the so-called Hippocratic face are bad signs. The same is to be judged of involuntary tears and of a bad posture of the patient in bed. From knowledge of these signs, which are called prognostics, and from comparing them with one another, the outcome of the disease is foreseen. We have said that there are two things, the disease and nature. To the disease belong not only the symptoms but also the causes, if it has any; to nature belong all aids, both natural and artificial.

units.la: [Marginal notes, right edge, largely cut off and too faint to read reliably; fragments visible include "Instit. M", "ficialia", "(tanquam", "randas", "Erquia", "Commode", "pruden", "Medicina", "Ms.", "Nec deper", "ratione".] ficialia. Ergo morbus cum natura (tanquam duo athletæ) est comparandus, videndumq; uter potentior. Et quia medicus, minister est naturæ, observare debet, an natura sola morbum debellare possit; quod si fiat, spectator tantum erit. Sin minus; subvenire debet commodè. Commodè dico; nam si vires penitus sint prostratæ, frustra medicina adhibetur. Nec enim sine signis, & naturæ ductu contra morbum pugnabit prudens medicus: nec etiam fuit iis quæ præter rationem apparent bona; nec desperabit si præter rationem mala apparebunt. Signorum in prædicendo non est eadem dignitas: signa enim quædam quibusdam sunt maiora, quædam præstantiora & dignniora. Magnitudo innotescit ex comparatione facultatis, vel morbi, cum aliis eiusdem generis. Quanto enim facultas similior est naturali, tanto deterius & maius etiam est signum. & quia vita pendet à facultate vitali; signa, quæ eam patefaciunt, dignissinissima judicantur. Ergo ut de morbi exitu, & modo prædicere possis, confer inter se morbum, & facultatem. morbi enim species, & magnitudo, eius exitum facile declarant. Nam morbi quidam sua natura sunt lethales, ut vulnus cordis. quidam ut plurimum, sicut pestis. quidam medio modo se habet. quia nec lethales sunt, nec tamen facilè curantur; ut elephantiasis. Sunt nonnulli periculi expertes, ut vulnus carnosum manus, aut febris quartana intermittens. Periculum auget, aut minuit morbi longitudo, præcipuè in morbis acutis. Cæterum malignitas in morbis semper est suspecta: nam sæpè contingit, apparentibus concoctionis in urinis signis, ægrum subitò de medio tolli. Quod tamen cautum medicum non fallit: nam malignitas prodit se in pulsu, qui parvus est; aut succedit animi deliquium &c. Videndum præterea, an morbus sit simplex, an verò compositus: horum enim signa non sunt confundenda, sed seorsum distinstinguenda. in quibus omnibus, ut verbo absolvam, vires conferendæ cum morbi magnitudine sunt, & eiusdem statu.
units.tr: ...artificial. Therefore the disease must be compared with nature, as two athletes, and it must be seen which is the stronger. And since the physician is the servant of nature, he ought to observe whether nature alone can overcome the disease; if so, he will be merely a spectator. If not, he ought to help appropriately. I say appropriately, for if the powers are utterly prostrated, medicine is applied in vain. Nor will a prudent physician fight against the disease without signs and without the guidance of nature; nor should he rejoice at good things that appear contrary to reason, nor despair if bad things appear contrary to reason. Signs do not all have the same weight in prediction: some are greater than others, and some are more excellent and more worthy. The magnitude becomes known from comparing the faculty, or the disease, with others of the same kind. For the more the faculty resembles the natural one, the worse and greater the sign is too. And since life depends on the vital faculty, the signs that reveal it are judged most worthy. Therefore, to predict the outcome and manner of the disease, compare the disease and the faculty with each other, for the kind and magnitude of the disease readily declare its outcome. Some diseases are lethal by their nature, like a wound of the heart; some for the most part, like the plague; some hold a middle course, being neither lethal nor easily cured, like elephantiasis. Some are free of danger, like a fleshy wound of the hand or quartan intermittent fever. The length of a disease increases or lessens the danger, especially in acute diseases. Moreover, malignity in diseases is always to be suspected, for it often happens that, while signs of concoction appear in the urine, the patient is suddenly taken from the midst. A cautious physician, however, is not deceived by this, for malignity betrays itself in the pulse, which is small, or a fainting of the spirits follows, and so on. It must also be considered whether the disease is simple or compound, for their signs are not to be confused but distinguished separately. In all these things, to sum up in a word, the strength must be compared with the magnitude of the disease and its state.

units.la: CAP. VII. De Crisi.
units.tr: CAP. VII. Concerning Crisis.

units.la: REliquum est, (nam de eventu morbi dictum est) ut de modo eventus agamus ; hoc est, solveturne morbus subitò,an verò paulatim. Subitus eventus, conjunctus cum naturæ pugna, est crisis : sin verò nulla sit pugna, non est crisis, sed repentina mors;ut in magna Apoplexia cernere licet. Hoc idem contingit in accessionum principiis, vigore, & declinatione particulari. Quanquam Crisis multipliciter usurpetur ; tamen proprie est subita mutatio in morbis, vel ad salutem, vel ad mortem, cum pugnâ & perturbatione. Per excellentiam tamen illa mutatio quæ ad salutē ducit, Crisis dici solet. Hæc fit die critico, in morbi statu & vigore, à facultate naturali, materiâ morbificâ expellente. Dico à facultate naturali & quidem sola; ut excludam evacuationes factas à medicamentis. Talis tres requirit conditiones; quarum prima est, ut sit fida, liberans ægrum à morbo: ac proinde nulla materia, recidivam factura superest. Secundo ut materia expellatur ex corpore, non verò de parte in partem transferatur. Tertiò ut prius judicata sit & bono die decretorio eveniat. Prænunciant futuram crisin deliria, vertigo, capitis dolor &c. aliæque perturbationes; quæ Medicum terrere non debent, quia tantum sunt signa, à quibus perturbatio incipit. Efficit crisin non ars, aut medicamentum, sed natura, seu facultas naturalis, cuius est expellere id quod noxium est: expelli autem debet materia, non quovis morbi tempore, verum in fine vigoris, cum materia est cocta. Dico cocta materia; quia crisis non habet locum in morbis non humoralibus. Sin crisis mala sit, in augmento plerunque jugulat; nam summum vigorem rem nunquam superat. Materiæ excretio semper est manifesta; nisi forsan in pueris; in quibus ob pororum laxitatem, materia insensibiliter expellitur. At si materia transferatur ad partem aliquam ignobilem; non liberatur ęger, sed novus morbus gignitur; proinde non est perfecta crisis, materiæ translatio.
units.tr: It remains (since we have already spoken of the outcome of the disease) to treat of the manner of the outcome, that is, whether the disease ends suddenly or gradually. A sudden outcome, joined with a struggle of nature, is a crisis; but if there is no struggle, it is not a crisis but sudden death, as can be seen in a severe apoplexy. The same happens at the beginnings, the height and the particular decline of the paroxysms. Although crisis is used in many senses, properly it is a sudden change in diseases, either to health or to death, with struggle and disturbance. By preeminence, however, the change that leads to health is usually called crisis. It occurs on a critical day, in the state and height of the disease, when the natural faculty expels the morbific matter. I say the natural faculty, and that alone, to exclude evacuations brought about by medicines. A true crisis requires three conditions. The first is that it be sound, freeing the patient from the disease, so that no matter remains that will produce a relapse. Second, the matter must be expelled from the body, not merely transferred from one part to another. Third, it must be judged beforehand and occur on a good decretory day. Delirium, vertigo, headache and other disturbances foretell an approaching crisis; these should not frighten the physician, since they are only signs from which the disturbance begins. Crisis is effected not by art or medicine but by nature, or the natural faculty, whose task is to expel what is harmful. The matter must be expelled, however, not at just any time of the disease but at the end of its height, when the matter has been concocted. I say concocted, because crisis has no place in non-humoral diseases. If a crisis is bad, it usually kills during the increase, for the disease never overcomes its greatest strength. The excretion of matter is always evident, except perhaps in children, in whom, because of the looseness of their pores, the matter is expelled imperceptibly. But if the matter is transferred to some ignoble part, the patient is not freed, but a new disease is generated; therefore a transfer of matter is not a perfect crisis.

units.la: Porrò maiores nostri observarunt, non quovis die fieri crises bonas (quanquam quidam ex Hippocrate contrarium doceant) sed septimo, decimo quarto, vigesimo. Quorum tamen dierum non est eadem dignitas. nam 7. & 14. nobilissimi sunt; iis enim plurimæ fiunt bonæ crises. Post 20 diē crises sunt imperfectiores, unde & pauciores dies critici numerantur, quam in prioribus tribus septimanis; à primo nimirum die 20. post 40. diem, (quia morbi, absoluta crisi non terminantur, sed vel decubitu materiæ, vel solutione simplici) usque ad 60. omnes intermedii dies omittuntur. 60. excipit 80. 100. 120. un-
units.tr: Furthermore, our forebears observed that good crises do not occur on just any day (although some, following Hippocrates, teach the contrary), but on the seventh, the fourteenth and the twentieth. Yet these days do not have equal dignity: the seventh and the fourteenth are the most noble, for most good crises occur on them. After the twentieth day the crises are more imperfect, which is why fewer critical days are counted than in the first three weeks. From the first day after the twentieth up to the fortieth day (because diseases do not end with a complete crisis but either by a settling of matter or by simple resolution), all the intervening days are passed over; the sixtieth is followed by 80, 100, 120, whence-

units.la: unde horum dierum incertitudo maximè apparet. Diebus criticis suì attribuuntur indices, qui die critico futuram crisin prænunciant. hoc modo: 4. est index 7. & 11. 14. 17. 20. nam dies critici integris septimanis definiuntur, sicut indices dimidiatis. Iam verò ratio supputandi septimanas, & dies criticos supra modum est incerta. prima enim, & secunda septimana, à novo incipiunt principio. tertia verò ab ultimo die secundæ septimanæ: ita ut 14. dies sit finis secundæ septimanæ & tertiæ initium. ultimus vero dies tertiæ septimanæ est 20, non 21, si scholæ Hippocraticæ decretis statur: illo enim die meliores fieri crises, experientia testatur. Sed quare hoc potius die, quam alia fiat crisis, quæritur. Quidam putant causam esse revolutionem corporum cœlestium, imprimis lunæ; quæ morbis brevibus imperare creditur, sicut sol longis. sed hoc non potest fieri, nisi corpus cœleste moveat nostrum corpus; nam Crisis fit à facultate irritatâ. Qui numeris multum tribuunt, confugiunt ad diei septimi, aliorumque similium dignitatẽ: queç (nam quantitas non est actiua) nulla est: alii aliter Philosophantur. Rectius illi sentiunt qui causas proximas examinant; facultatem nimirum & morbum. Facultas enim non expellit nisi irritetur à materiâ: pendet ergò dierum criticorum ratio à proportione facultatis agentis, & materiæ resistentis. quod in omnibus evacuationibus fieri amat: hac enim de causa, certis horis fæces alvi excernuntur, & urina redditur. Quæ de diebus criticis diximus, intelligenda sunt in morbis continuis, non intermittentibus; in quibus accessiones numerantur, non verò dies. hinc septimus circuitus est terminus tertianæ intermittentis, sicut septimus dies, continuæ.
units.tr: hence the uncertainty of these days is most evident. Indices are assigned to the critical days, which foretell by the critical day that a crisis is coming, in this way: 4 is the index of 7; and 11, 14, 17, 20 are likewise indices, for critical days are defined by whole weeks, and indices by half-weeks. Now the reckoning of the weeks and critical days is beyond measure uncertain. The first and second weeks begin from a new starting point, but the third from the last day of the second week, so that the fourteenth day is both the end of the second week and the beginning of the third. The last day of the third week is the twentieth, not the twenty-first, if one abides by the decrees of the Hippocratic school, for experience testifies that crises are better on that day. But why a crisis happens on this day rather than another is a question. Some think the cause is the revolution of the heavenly bodies, chiefly the moon, which is believed to govern short diseases as the sun governs long ones. But this cannot happen unless a heavenly body moves our body, for crisis arises from an aroused faculty. Those who attribute much to numbers take refuge in the dignity of the seventh day and of other such days; but since quantity is not active, this has no force. Others philosophize otherwise. Those are more correct who examine the proximate causes, namely the faculty and the disease. For the faculty does not expel unless it is stirred by the matter; the reckoning of critical days therefore depends on the proportion between the acting faculty and the resisting matter, which in all evacuations is wont to happen in this way: for this reason, at certain hours the faeces of the bowels are excreted and urine is passed. What we have said about critical days must be understood of continuous diseases, not intermittent ones, in which paroxysms are counted rather than days. Hence the seventh cycle is the terminus of tertian intermittent fever, just as the seventh day is that of a continuous fever.

units.la: CAP. VII. Quomodo sit futura Crisis.
units.tr: CAP. VII. How the Crisis Will Come About.

units.la: QUomodo sit solvendus morbus, subitone, an paulatim, ex morbi æstimatur magnitudine, (quo referuntur: mos & morbi species) facta eius cum viribus comparatione. An verò citò, an tarde, motus imprimis docebit. Cui adjunguntur quæcunque morbum vel accelerant, vel tardant; ut temperamentum, ætas, regio. si enim sit morbus vehemens, vires robustæ, ætas juvenilis &c. morbus erit brevis: sin contra longus. nam morbi acuti, aut subitò cum pugna ad vitam, vel mortem terminantur; aut ad mortem sine pugna, si vires sint debiles. Mors itaque cum crisi & pugna, postulat vires debiliores morbo, non tamē omnino debiles & prostratas. At mortis tempus ex statu deprehenditur, & morbi motu. Morbus lethalis, cum validus est & celer, hominem derepente necat: sin nec vehemens, nec celer paulatim. Contra se res habet in minime lethalibus: nam natura valida subitò sanare solet, imbecilla paulatim. An crisis sit futura ad salutem vel mortem, colligi potest ex comparatione morbi cum naturâ. ita ut non negligatur urinarum concoctio, ætas, temperamentum, &c. Est enim concoctio, signum instantis bonę criseos, quæ semper est in statu: quo elapso, nemo vi morbi perit; sed vel errore, vel alia causa. Iam verò crisis, ante statũ facta, mala est; quia irritatione naturæ à morbi magnitudine fit. Quando natura dominatur materiæ, motus in ægris sunt determinati. sin vires deficiant, nullus motuũ ordo; unde prædictio sæpè est fallax, & incerta. Morbi omnes salutares solvuntur paulatim, vel subitò. Causa solutionis interdum est sola natura; ea enim levem continui solutionem curat sine medicamento: interdum est sola ars; ut in luxato digito videre est: interdum ars cum natura conspirat; ut in graviorum morborum curatione tione appareat. At crisis omnis fit à sola naturâ. Ea autem convenire debet naturæ morbi. ardens enim febris solvitur vel sanguinis è naribus fluxu, vel sudore post rigorem, nonnunquam alvi fluxu, & vomitu. Locus affectus non est prætereundus. nam si gibba hepatis pars afficiatur, natura per ureteres materiam expellit morbificam. Considerandum tertiò est temperamentum, ætas, regio, tempus. juvenes enim calidi, vere ægrotantes, liberantur sanguinis è naribus profluvio. Quartò sexus inspiciendus est: nam mulieres liberantur à magnis morbis sanguinis ex utero profluvio. Postremò consuetudo est observanda; ut in hæmorrhoidibus videre est: graves enim lienis affectus, transmissio ad hæmorrhoides sanguine, fælicissimè curantur. Instare crisin ex propriis signis hoc modo cognoscesi enim sit febris ardens, immineatque hæmorrhagia, caput graviter dolet, & pulsat, nares pruriunt, oculis observantur splensplendores, lachrymæ oboriuntur involuntariæ &c. at si crisis vomitu terminetur, gravis præcedit capitis dolor, visus est hebes, vertigo, morsus orificii ventriculi, labri inferioris agitatio &c. atque hoc modo terminantur sæpè febres intermittentes: sin verò sudor expectatur, cognoscMes ex suppressione urinæ, & fæcum, præter rationem, conjuncta cum rigore; partes exteriores magis rubent, & calent: quo modo judicantur febres continuæ. Instare crisin per alvi dejectionē, cognoscês ex aliarum evacuationum suppressione, si nempe earum notæ non appareant; inprimis autem, si retineatur urina, sitque dolor ventris &c. Per urinas fieri discis ex suppressione alvi, præter rationem. Ex similibus denique signis judicandum de excretione, tum per uterum, tum per hæmorrhoides. Verùm si nulla adsint huiusmodi signa, judicabitur morbus ex transmissione humoris in partem ignoignobilem per vias patentes & rectas. Nam transmissio humoris à parte ignobili in nobilem, metastasis vulgò dicta, pernitiosa admodum, nec crisis propriè dicitur. Partes ignobiles, recipientes aliorum membrorum excrementa, sunt glandulæ, cutis, articuli &c. Idem hîc observandū quod supra, huiusmodi transmissionem criticam, (diadosin vocant Medici) debere fieri à naturâ nec à morbo, nec medicamento irritata. Quibus autē in partibus sit metuenda materiæ translatio, docebunt accidentia eas partes circumstantia; rubor nimirum, dolor, distensio. si humorum indolem contempleris, crassi, & frigidi ad partes inferiores magis abscedunt: ad superiores vero tenues, & calidi.
units.tr: How the disease will be resolved, suddenly or gradually, is judged from the magnitude of the disease (to which belong the custom and the species of the disease), with its strength compared to the patient's powers. Whether it will come quickly or slowly, the movement of the disease will chiefly show. To this are added whatever either hastens or delays the disease, such as temperament, age, and region. If the disease is violent, the powers robust, and the age youthful, the disease will be brief; but if the reverse, long. For acute diseases either end quickly, with a struggle, in life or death, or end in death without a struggle, if the powers are weak. Death with crisis and struggle therefore requires powers weaker than the disease, yet not wholly weak and prostrate. The time of death, however, is discerned from the state and the movement of the disease. A deadly disease, when it is strong and swift, kills the man suddenly; but if it is neither violent nor swift, it kills gradually. It is otherwise with those that are least deadly: for a vigorous nature usually heals suddenly, a feeble one gradually. Whether the crisis will be toward salvation or death can be gathered from the comparison of the disease with the nature, so that the concoction of the urine, age, temperament, and so on are not neglected. For concoction is the sign of an impending good crisis, which is always at a fixed state; once that has passed, no one perishes by the force of the disease, but through error or some other cause. Now, a crisis that occurs before the fixed state is bad, because it is brought about by the irritation of nature caused by the magnitude of the disease. When nature dominates the matter, the movements in the sick are regular; but if the powers fail, there is no order of movements, whence the prediction is often fallacious and uncertain. All salutary diseases are resolved gradually or suddenly. The cause of the resolution is sometimes nature alone, for she cures a slight continuous resolution without medicine; sometimes art alone, as may be seen in a dislocated finger; sometimes art and nature conspire together, as appears in the cure of more serious diseases. But every crisis comes from nature alone. This, moreover, ought to agree with the nature of the disease: for an burning fever is resolved either by a flux of blood from the nostrils, or by sweat after a shivering, sometimes by a flux of the bowels and by vomiting. The part affected must not be passed over: for if the convex part of the liver is affected, nature expels the morbific matter through the ureters. In the third place, temperament, age, region, and season must be considered. For young men, being hot and truly sick, are relieved by a flow of blood from the nostrils. Fourthly, the sex must be examined: for women are relieved of great diseases by a flow of blood from the womb. Lastly, custom is to be observed, as may be seen in haemorrhoids: for grave affections of the spleen, with transmission of the blood to the haemorrhoids, are most happily cured. The impending crisis is recognised from its own signs in this way: if the fever is burning and a haemorrhage threatens, the head aches severely and throbs, the nostrils itch, splendours are observed in the eyes, tears well up involuntarily, and so on. But if the crisis is to end in vomiting, a heavy pain of the head precedes, the sight is dull, there is vertigo, a biting at the mouth of the stomach, agitation of the lower lip, and so on; and in this way intermittent fevers often end. But if sweat is awaited, one knows it from the suppression of urine and of the faeces beyond the usual, joined with a shivering; the outer parts grow redder and warmer: by which manner continuous fevers are judged. A crisis by evacuation of the bowels is impending when one recognises it from the suppression of the other evacuations, namely if their signs do not appear; especially if the urine is retained and there is pain in the belly, and so on. You may learn that the excretion occurs through the urine from the suppression of the bowels beyond the usual. Finally, one should judge in a similar way from similar signs concerning excretion, both through the womb and through the haemorrhoids. But if no such signs are present, the disease will be judged by the transmission of the humour into an ignoble part by open and straight passages. For the transmission of the humour from an ignoble part into a noble one, commonly called metastasis, is very pernicious, and is not properly called a crisis. The ignoble parts, which receive the excrements of other members, are the glands, skin, joints, and so on. The same thing is to be observed here as above: that such a critical transmission (which physicians call diadosis) ought to be made by nature, and not irritated by the disease or by medicine. In which parts the translation of matter is to be feared, the accompanying symptoms of those parts will show: namely redness, pain, and distension. If you consider the quality of the humours, the thick and cold ones tend more to the lower parts, but the thin and hot ones to the upper.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: De futura crisis tempore.
units.tr: On the time of the coming crisis.

units.la: TEmpus futuræ crisis cognoscēs ex longitudine morbi, eiusdemque statu. quo enim morbus brevior. eo propinquior status; in quo bona crisis semper contingit. Cognosci autem statum ex morbi natura, & symptomatum incrementis, jam di-ximus antea: quibus adjunguntur ætas, regio, tempus, anni &c. sin morbus intermittat, ex accessionum incremento, & magnitudine, aliisque adjunctis. Hoc idem certius consta-bit ex observatione dierum criticorum, & viribus ægri. quæ si validæ fuerint, irritenturq; ab humoris morbifici irritatione crisin anticipabunt. Præstantissimum futuræ crisis signū ex urinarum concoctione haberi solet. Morbus peracutus subitam habet crisin; die nimirum septimo, indicato tamen à quarto. si igitur primo die signa apparent bona, quarto die aut citius morbus finietur: synochus exempli causa: crisi tum terminatur: at verò simplici solutione, si morbus sit parvus: tertiana continua magna tertio die expediri solet. At si primis duobus diebus nulla concoctionis appareant signa, verum quarto apto appareat in urinis nebula rubra, aut aliud aliquid; crisis fiet die septimo, nisi peccatu aliquod intervenerit. Sin autem morbus nec sit adeo magnus, nec velox; differtur crisis in 9. diem: sin septimo die primum appareant in urinis concoctionis signa, undecimo aut decimo quarto ad summum die fiet crisis. Eadem est ratio aliorum quaternariorum, & septenariorum. Ergo si morbus sit funestus, iisdem diebus criticis, quarto, septimo, aut simili morietur æger. Non semel monui concoctionis indicium esse urinam, nam in acutis morbis; urinæ albæ tenues, sunt pessimæ: sicut tenues, rubræ, in statu apparentes, non bonæ. Crisis quæ die non bono fit, conjuncta tamen cum aliis bonis signis, recidivam minatur; infida enim est. at si mala conjungantur signa, mors in propinquo. Tentpus salutis, aut mortis cognoscitur ex comparatione virium cum morbo, eiusdemque statu. Nam si natura & morbus viribus sint partes, longior temtempore opus est ad alterutrius victoriam: at si impares sint, hoc est si morbus superaverit naturam, aut contra; cita erit victoria. Quicunque curantur morbi, quatuor illa tempora universalia pertranseunt: qui vero non sanantur, postremum tempus nimirum declinationem, non attingunt: Saepe enim in ipso augmento mors contingit. ubi natura morbo longè est inferior, in ipso principio, sine crisi, mors evenire solet. Si statum morbus superarit, nihil est periculi; nam in declinatione non contingit mors. Ergo si observaveris, quantum morbus naturam superet, & quo tempore æger pessimè se habeat; quando accessio recurrit, praedices mortis tempus. In lethali enim morbo, quia vires admodum sunt debiles, mors citò advenit. Sin autem vires non adeò sint debiles; quo die accessio recurrit, eo morietur. At si vires paulo validiores fuerint; differtur mors ad unum, vel alterum diem. Horam mortis discès; si observaveris tempus particularis alicu-ius exacerbationis, quo maximè ęger affligitur: tum enim, quia maximè languet, morietur: languoris indicium est pulsus debilitas, animi deli-quium, difficultas respirandi, &c.
units.tr: Knowing the time of the coming crisis from the length of the disease and its state: the shorter the disease, the nearer its state, and it is in that state that a favourable crisis always occurs. We have already said earlier how the state is known, from the nature of the disease and the increase of the symptoms; to these are added age, region, season, the year, and so on. If the disease intermits, the state is known from the increase and magnitude of the paroxysms and other accompanying circumstances. The same thing is established more certainly by observing the critical days and the strength of the patient: if these are vigorous and are roused by the irritation of the morbid humour, they will anticipate the crisis. The most excellent sign of the coming crisis is usually taken from the concoction of the urine. A very acute disease has a sudden crisis, namely on the seventh day, though it is indicated from the fourth. So if on the first day signs appear that are good, the illness will end on the fourth day or sooner: a synochus, for example, is then terminated by crisis, but by simple solution if the disease is slight; a large tertian continua is usually dispatched on the third day. But if no signs of concoction appear on the first two days, yet on the fourth day a red cloud or something else appears in the urine, the crisis will come on the seventh day, unless some error intervenes. But if the disease is neither very large nor swift, the crisis is put off to the ninth day; and if the first signs of concoction appear in the urine on the seventh day, the crisis will come on the eleventh or at the latest the fourteenth day. The reasoning is the same for the other quaternaries and septenaries. Therefore, if the disease is deadly, the patient will die on the same critical days, the fourth, seventh, or a similar one. I have more than once pointed out that the urine is the indication of concoction: in acute diseases, thin white urine is the worst, just as thin red urine appearing in the state is not good. A crisis that comes on an unfavourable day, though joined with other good signs, threatens a relapse, for it is unreliable; but if bad signs are joined, death is near. The time of recovery or death is known from comparing the strength with the disease and its state. For if nature and the disease are evenly matched, a longer time is needed for the victory of either; but if they are unequal, that is, if the disease has overcome nature or the reverse, the victory will be swift. All diseases that are cured pass through those four universal periods; but those that are not cured do not reach the last period, namely the decline: death often comes in the very increase. Where nature is far inferior to the disease, death usually comes at the very beginning, without crisis. If the disease has overcome the state, there is no danger, for death does not occur in the decline. Therefore, if you observe how far the disease surpasses nature, and at what time the patient is at his worst, you can foretell the time of death when the paroxysm returns. In a lethal disease, since the strength is very weak, death comes quickly; but if the strength is not so weak, the patient dies on the day the paroxysm returns. But if the strength is a little stronger, death is put off by one or two days. You will learn the hour of death if you observe the time of a particular exacerbation by which the patient is most troubled: for then, since he is most exhausted, he will die; the sign of exhaustion is weakness of the pulse, fainting, difficulty in breathing, and so on.

units.la: MEDICARVM LIBER V. De Medendi Methodo.
units.tr: MEDICARVM LIBER V. De Medendi Methodo.

units.la: CAP. I. De Indicatione.
units.tr: CAP. I. De Indicatione.

units.la: CUm Medicina circa corpus ægrum maximè versetur, ut morbus nimirum profligetur, & natura conservetur; cognitis morbo, causa, locoque affecto, nihil superesse videtur aliud, quam medicamenti idonei & alimenti inventio. illo morbus corrumpitur, hoc facultas conservatur. Hoc fieri nequit, ignoratis iis, quæ secundum & præter naturam homini accidunt. Proinde Medicus, naturæ minister, nunquam huiusmodi scopos attinget, ignoratis iis, quę ante à nobis sunt dicta. Itaque Empirici,
units.tr: Since medicine is chiefly concerned with the sick body, so that the disease may be overthrown and nature preserved, once the disease, its cause and the affected place are known, nothing seems to remain but the discovery of a suitable medicine and of nourishment. By the one the disease is corrupted; by the other the faculty is preserved. This cannot be done unless we know those things which happen to man according to nature and beyond nature. Therefore the physician, the minister of nature, will never reach such goals if he ignores those things which we have treated before. Thus the Empirics and the Methodists

units.la: pirici, Methodicique hic vehemen- tér errant. illi enim neglectis causis, solâ experientiâ & analogismo ad sa- lubria eligenda, & insalubria evitan- da contenti sunt: at hi neglectâ expe- rientiâ, rejectisque causis, & faculta- tibus, solam indicationem à morbo, & evidentibus communitatibus sum- ptam, ad curationem sufficere arbi- trantur. Dogmatici, & rationales Medici, rationi experientiam adjun- gunt; confiderantq; non tantum cau- sas evidentes, sed & abditas, non neglectis partibus, locis affectis, eo- rumque signis. Ratio enim & expe- rientia se mutuo juvant; pulchrum enim est, judicium rationis ab expe- rientiâ confirmari. proinde dogma- tici his duobus fulcris experientiâ in singularibus, & ratione in universali- bus quasi nixi, multo felicius & ac- curatius curant.
units.tr: err here greatly. For the former, neglecting causes, are content with experience alone and analogy for choosing wholesome things and avoiding unwholesome ones; while the latter, neglecting experience and rejecting causes and faculties, think that the indication taken from the disease and its evident accompaniments suffices for the cure. The Dogmatic and rational physicians join experience to reason; and they consider not only the evident causes but also the hidden ones, not neglecting the parts, the affected places and their signs. For reason and experience help each other; for it is a fine thing that the judgement of reason be confirmed by experience. Accordingly the dogmatists, leaning as it were on these two supports, experience in particulars and reason in universals, cure far more happily and accurately.

units.la: Medendi methodus est ratio inve- niendi certa cuique morbo remedia, sani- tatis gratiâ, per convenientes indicatio- nes. Ratio hæc procedit à communibus, & generalibus indicationibus, ad speciales, & proprias: nam non curatur homo in genere, sed Socrates, & Plato. Scopus itaque omnium operationum est morbi depulsio, & sanitatis introductio. Verum si vires penitus sunt viȼę, à prudente Medico nihil est tentandum: sin autem constent, de mediis quibus morbus depelli potest, consultandum. Considerandum ergo primum, quid agendum; alterandum, evacuandum, an reficiendum. Deinde quibus remediis; refrigerantibus, an pituitam, bilemque evacuantibus; solidis, an liquidis. Tertiò quantum agendum; multumne, an parum. Quartò quomodo; an sensim an verò confertim. Quintò quando; in principione morbi, an vero statu. Postremò, quo ordine & via.
units.tr: The method of healing is a sure reasoning for discovering remedies for each disease, for the sake of health, through suitable indications. This reasoning proceeds from common and general indications to special and proper ones; for a man is not cured in general, but Socrates and Plato are. Therefore the aim of all operations is the driving out of disease and the introduction of health. But if the strength is wholly spent, the prudent physician must attempt nothing; but if it remains, one must consider by what means the disease can be driven out. First, then, one must consider what is to be done: whether to alter, to evacuate, or to restore. Then by what remedies: cooling, or those that evacuate phlegm and bile; solid or liquid. Thirdly, how much is to be done: much or little. Fourthly, how: gradually or all at once. Fifthly, when: at the beginning of the disease or in its state. Lastly, in what order and by what way.

units.la: Indicatio est agendi insinuatio; sive ratio dirigendi actionem, seu comprehensio juvantis, junčta comprehensioni eius, cui conferre dicitur, sine experientiâ, & manifestâ ratiocinatione. Indicatio omnis ex nis ex scopo nascitur; nam scopus, est curationis indicatio; sicut indicatio, est agedi insinuatio. Indicatio omnis est indicantis ad indicatum relatio. Indicans est aliquid in corpore, aut conservandum, aut corrumpendum; cuius gratia aliquid fieri debet: sicut morbus indicat sui corruptionem, & facultas conservationem. Indicatum est illud, quod indicanti prodest, eique aliquo modo congruit; ut venæ sectio tollit febre ardentem. Proinde indicatum omne est aut simile, aut contrarium. Contraria tollunt morbum, similia autem facultatem conservant. Ex quibus colligitur; indicare esse manifestare quid conveniat.
units.tr: An indication is the insinuation of an action; or the reasoning that directs the action, or the grasping of what helps, joined to the grasping of that to which it is said to contribute, without experience and without manifest reasoning. Every indication arises from the aim; for the aim is the indication of the cure, just as an indication is the insinuation of an action. Every indication is the relation of the indicating to the indicated. The indicans is something in the body that must either be conserved or corrupted, for whose sake something ought to be done: thus disease indicates its own corruption, and the faculty its conservation. The indicatum is that which benefits the indicating thing and in some way agrees with it; as bloodletting removes a burning fever. Therefore every indicated thing is either similar or contrary. Contraries remove disease, while similars preserve the faculty. From these it is gathered that to indicate is to make manifest what is fitting.

units.la: Cum curatio debeatur morbo, præservatio causæ, conservatio facultati: totidem erunt in Medicina scopi, curare, præservare, & conservare. Sed quia non omnes morbi causam habent; Medici duos scopos proponunt, facultatem, & morbum. Hunc quidem corrumpendum; illam autem conservandam. Secundum sicut fit cut fit per similia, ita primum per contraria. Iam verò non sufficit scire morbum calidum esse frigidis curandum, quod plebem non latet; sed quomodo, quando, quo, refrigeratio fit instituenda: quod fieri nequit, ignoratis temperamento, partibus, facultatibus &c. à quibus non tam indicatio, quam coindicatio sumitur.
units.tr: Since the cure is owed to the disease, the prevention to the cause, and the conservation to the faculty, there will be as many aims in medicine: to cure, to prevent, and to conserve. But since not all diseases have a cause, physicians propose two aims, the faculty and the disease: the one to be corrupted, the other to be conserved. The second is effected by similars, as the first is by contraries. Now it is not enough to know that a hot disease is to be treated with cold things, which the common people do not fail to know; but how, when, and where cooling is to be instituted: which cannot be done unless the temperament, the parts, the faculties and so on are known, from which not so much an indication as a co-indication is taken.

units.la: Primę indicationes tres tantum sunt, totidemque indicantia; morbus, causa, (si ea est) facultas, quæ primò quid agendum sit insinuant. Ætas, temperamentum, sexus, consuetudo, coindicant, id est, ostendunt quantum, quomodo, sit agendum. nam coindicantia non per se, sed per aliud indicant. Exempli causa; cacochymia primò indicat evacuationem, coindicant vires robustæ, consuetudo. Contra indicans est quod per se primò impedit. Correpugnans quod secundariò impedit. Facultas enim victum indicat; ætas, temperamentum, coindicant, morbi vehementia contra indicat; symptomata verò correpugnant.
units.tr: There are only three primary indications, and as many indicating things: the disease, the cause (if there is one), and the faculty, which first insinuate what is to be done. Age, temperament, sex and habit are co-indicating, that is, they show how much and in what way something is to be done; for co-indicating things do not indicate through themselves but through something else. For example, cacochymia first indicates evacuation, while strong strength and habit co-indicate. A contra-indicating thing is that which first and of itself hinders; a counter-opposing thing is that which hinders secondarily. For the faculty indicates nourishment; age and temperament co-indicate; the vehemence of the disease contra-indicates; but the symptoms counter-oppose.

units.la: Cum verò indicationes sunt contrariæ, præferenda ea est, quæ magis urget. Exempli causa, in statu acutarum febrium, si magna sit virium debilitas, facultas indicat victum, contraindicat vehementia morbi; quia verò vires sunt conservandæ, ante omnia cibandus est æger, nec permittendus ob inediam deficere. Verum si morbus sit in fieri, ut dicunt, non autem facto esse, causæ habenda est ratio, jungendaque curatio præservationi: nam sicut illa morbum, ita hæc causam innuit. Cum itaque morbus sit sanitati contrarius; prima maximè communis indicatio curativa est ipsa contrarietas; quæ à morbo sumitur: indicationes sumptæ à parte affectâ, ætate, consuetudine, sunt magis particulares; determinant tamen curationis modum, & mensuram. quam nemo ritè intelliget, ignoratis temperamento, corporisque natura: nam quanto morbus magis à naturâ recesserit, intentioribus & vehementioribus remediis (hæc vero sunt ro sunt contraria) indiget. Si ergo quis febricitet; quantum sit refrige-randum, indicat temperamentum naturale, ad quod medicamentis frigidis est reducendus; non neglecta magnitudine morbi & situ partis. Ubi ergo cognoveris quousque refrigerandum sit, remedia accommodata sunt investiganda, eorumque dosis instituenda. & quanquam inexplicabilis sit mensura remediorum in singularibus, nec scientia aliqua comprehensibilis; artificiosa tamen conjectura, usurpanda venit: haec nititur ratione, & experientia. Sicut morbus remedium indicat; ita modum utendi indicant vires, & situs partis affectae. Tempus utendi praescribunt morbi tempora; sicut locum, & vias, corporis figura, & partium situs. Verum quid primo, secundove agen-dum, indicat quod maxime urget. Indicationes a parte affecta sumptae, sunt magni momenti, consid-erantur enim eius temperamentum, sensus, figura, situs, & actio laesa. Temperamento adjunge sexum, ætatem, consuetudinem, vitæ institutum &c. Gravius siquidē ægrotat cuius temperamento, consuetudini, ætati morbus est dissimilis, quam similis. Ergo si frigidus temperamento incidat in febrem; periculosius ægrotat, quam calidus, frigidioraque requirit medicamenta. Idem de ætate judica. Si enim senex febricitet, frigidiora poscit remedia, quam juvenis. Eadem est partium conditio. os enim fractū validiora exsiccantia postulat, quam cutis scissa. Sin actionem spectes; videndum, ea ne privata sit & uni parti inserviens: tum enim audaciūs alterandum, laxandum etiam: sin autem actio sit publica, ut cordis, cerebri; tum eadem timidiūs facienda sunt. nec tamen simul, sed per intervalla, parsque corroboranda est benignis medicamentis. Figura partis adeò est conspicua, ut plebem non lateat. Quivis enim novit, maiora emplastra adhibenda esse ventriculo quam lieni; & ventriculum purgari tum supra, tū infra; pectus autem supra tantū. Idem de situ statuendum, nam si superficies corporis sit violata; levioribus medicamentis est utendum, quam si pars corporis profunda. Ita ad purgandum ventriculum opus est debilioribus, quam ad uterum. Si sensum consideres; quanto is acutior, tanto benignioribus, minusq; acribus utendum est remediis. Ergo si intestina malè habeant, validiora exigunt, quam ventriculus; hic enim acribus medicamentis (est enim acerrimi sensus) irritatur. In quibus observandum semper, ut reducatur æger ad illud temperamentum, quod habuit, cum in morbum incideret. Intemperies quælibet poscit contraria in eodem gradu medicamenta.
