Cæterum si foveatur ab aliquā causā, ea prius est auferenda: nunquā enim curabitur morbus (à quo prima indicatio sumitur) manente causā antecedente: quod dum fit, tutius multò est calefacere, quam refrigerare: sicut humectare, quam exsiccare. Calida enim, aut humida intemperies, facilius curatur, quam frigida, aut sicca: siccitas enim, & frigus, sunt inimica vitæ. Eadem est indicationis ratio in morbis malę compositionis, & solutione continui. Nam meatuum dilatatio indicat astringentia; obstructio, aperientia; solutio continui, unientia. Compositorum morborum, compositæ sunt indicationes: singulisque sua remedia sunt præscribenda. Contingit interdum duos morbos ita esse connexos, ut unius curatio, sit etiam alterius: nam curata inflammatione pleuræ, febris cessat. Idem de peripneumoniâ similibusque judicandum. Interdum secus evenit; ut si pars inflammata sit cum ulcere cavo. nam seorsum & prius inflammatio est sedanda, cuius ablatio nihil commune habet cum consolidatione ulceris.
units.tr: When indications are contrary, that one is to be preferred which presses more. For example, in the state of acute fevers, if there is great weakness of strength, the faculty indicates food, and the vehemence of the disease contra-indicates; but since the strength must be preserved, above all the patient must be fed, and must not be allowed to fail from lack of food. Yet if the disease is in becoming, as they say, and not yet in being, regard must be had to the cause, and cure must be joined with prevention: for as the one points to the disease, so the other points to the cause. Since therefore disease is contrary to health, the first and most common curative indication is that very contrariety, which is taken from the disease. Indications taken from the affected part, age, and habit are more particular; yet they determine the manner and measure of the cure, which no one will rightly understand without knowledge of the temperament and nature of the body: for the further the disease has departed from nature, the more it needs intenser and more vehement remedies (these are the contraries). If therefore someone has fever, the natural temperament indicates how far he must be cooled, to which he must be brought back by cooling medicines, without neglecting the magnitude of the disease and the situation of the part. When therefore you have discovered how far cooling must go, suitable remedies are to be sought and their doses arranged. And although the measure of remedies in particular cases is inexplicable and comprehensible by no science, an artful conjecture must nevertheless be employed; this rests on reason and experience. As the disease indicates the remedy, so the strength and the situation of the affected part indicate the manner of using it. The times of the disease prescribe the time of use, as the body's figure and the situation of its parts prescribe the place and the ways. But what is to be done first or second is indicated by what presses most. Indications taken from the affected part are of great moment, for its temperament, sense, figure, situation and disturbed action are considered. To the temperament add sex, age, habit, way of life and so on. For one whose temperament, habit or age is unlike the disease suffers more gravely than one for whom it is like. Therefore if a cold-tempered man falls into fever, he is sicker and more dangerously than a hot one, and requires colder remedies. Judge the same of age: if an old man has fever, he asks for colder remedies than a young man. The condition of the parts is the same: a broken bone demands stronger drying remedies than a torn skin. But if you regard the action, it must be seen whether it is private and serves a single part; for then one may alter and even relax more boldly; but if the action is public, as that of the heart or brain, then the same things must be done more cautiously, and not all at once but at intervals, and the weakened part must be strengthened with gentle medicines. The figure of a part is so conspicuous that it is not hidden from the common people. Anyone knows that larger plasters are to be applied to the stomach than to the spleen, and that the stomach is purged both above and below, but the chest only above. The same is to be determined for situation: if the surface of the body is violated, lighter medicines must be used than if the part is deep. Thus weaker things are needed to purge the stomach than the womb. If you consider sense: the sharper it is, the gentler and less acrid the remedies must be. Therefore if the intestines are ill, they demand stronger ones than the stomach; for the stomach is irritated by sharp medicines (for its sense is most acute). In all these things it must always be observed that the patient is brought back to that temperament which he had when he fell into the disease. Any intemperance requires contrary remedies of the same degree. Moreover, if it is nourished by some cause, that cause must first be removed: for a disease (from which the first indication is taken) will never be cured while the antecedent cause remains. While this is being done, it is much safer to warm than to cool, as to moisten than to dry. For a hot or moist intemperance is more easily cured than a cold or dry one: dryness and cold are enemies of life. The same reasoning of indication holds in diseases of bad composition and in solution of continuity. For dilation of the passages indicates astringents, obstruction indicates opening remedies, and solution of continuity indicates uniting ones. For compound diseases the indications are compound, and a remedy must be prescribed for each. It sometimes happens that two diseases are so connected that the cure of one is also the cure of the other: for when pleurisy is cured, the fever ceases. The same is to be judged of peripneumony and similar things. Sometimes it turns out otherwise, as when an inflamed part has a hollow ulcer: for the inflammation must be calmed separately and first, and its removal has nothing in common with the consolidation of the ulcer.

units.la: CAP. II. De indicatione praservativa, & conservativa.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. On the preservative and conservative indication.

units.la: INDICATIO praeservativa sumitur à causâ morbi antecedente, quam continentem diximus vocari. Causa morbi formalis est ipse morbus, qui curationem exigit, de quâ superiori capite. Antecedens est prava corporis dispositio; plethora nimirum, aut cacochymia. Quae si adeo manifeste actiones non laedant, sunt causae tantum antecedentes, conjunctae cum neutra corporis dispositione: sin vero manifeste actiones laedant, (quod sine morbo fieri nequit) causae fiunt morborum continentes: ex quibus oriuntur indicationes praesevativae: ad causas antecedentes referunt multi calculos, vermes, &c. Indicatio hinc sumpta est multiplex, pro varietate causarum: earum enim consideratur, quantitas, qualitas, locus, motus, substantia. Si enim est aliquid toto genere praeter naturam in corpore, pore, ut calculus, lumbricus; indicat sui ablationem. sin vapor, aut flatus, discussionem insensibilem. si sanguis justo sit frigidior; indicat calefaciens proportionatum: sin crassus sit, medicamentum attenuans; sin malignus, refrenans, aut evacuans; & ita deinceps. Jam si deficiat sanguis, indicat alimentum instaurans: sin redundet, evacuans. Et quia varia est redundantia; nimirum bilis, pituitæ &c. singuli humores indicant convenientia remedia, rhabarbarum, agaricum &c. Si locum consideres; is est vel prima regio corporis, vel secunda, tertia, aut pars corporis ut pulmo; quæ omnia suas privatas habent indicationes. Et sicut sanguis qualitate peccans indicat purgationem: ita quantitate si peccet, indicat phlebotomiam. Hæc enim duo, plethora, & cacochymia, indicant semper sectionem venæ, & evacuationem. & si cacochymia sit primæ regionis; indicat evacuationem esse instituendam aut vomitu, aut dejectione. sin in habitu corporis; sudoribus, & ita deinceps.
units.tr: The preservative indication is taken from the antecedent cause of the disease, which we have said is called the containing cause. The formal cause of the disease is the disease itself, which demands treatment, as discussed in the previous chapter. The antecedent cause is a faulty disposition of the body, namely plethora or cacochymia. If these do not manifestly harm the functions, they are merely antecedent causes, joined to neither bodily disposition; but if they manifestly harm the functions (which cannot happen without disease), they become containing causes of disease, from which the preservative indications arise. Many refer calculi, worms, and the like to antecedent causes. The indication taken from these is manifold, according to the variety of causes; for their quantity, quality, place, motion and substance are considered. If something wholly foreign to nature is in the body, such as a stone or a worm, it indicates its removal. If it is wind or vapour, it indicates dispersal without being felt. If the blood is too cold, it indicates a suitable warming agent; if it is thick, an attenuating medicine; if it is malignant, a restraining or evacuating one; and so on. If the blood is deficient, it indicates restorative nourishment; if it is in excess, evacuation. And since redundancy takes various forms, namely of bile, phlegm and so on, each humour indicates its own suitable remedy: rhubarb, agaric and so on. If you consider the place, it is either the first region of the body, or the second, or the third, or a part of the body such as the lungs; and all of these have their own particular indications. Just as blood that sins in quality indicates purging, so if it sins in quantity it indicates phlebotomy. For these two, plethora and cacochymia, always indicate the opening of a vein and evacuation. And if the cacochymia is in the first region, it indicates that evacuation should be carried out either by vomiting or by stool; if it is in the habit of the body, by sweats, and so on.

units.la: Iam si materia moveatur, pro eius motus varietate, variat indicatio. Nam si materia feratur ad os ventriculi, sed imperfectè; vomitus præscribendus. sin motus sit immodicus; indicat remedium compescens eum. ut in fluxu sanguinis per nares videre est. Et quia humores fluunt ab unâ parte corporis in aliam, gignuntque inflammationes; considerandæ sunt partes mittentes, recipientes, & viæ per quas fit motus. Pars mittens indicat revulsionem; recipiens astrictionem, derivationem. ipsæ deniq; viæ medicamentū exigunt intercipiens, &c. Revulsio (est autem tractio humoris fluentis ad locum oppositum affectæ parti) fit phlebotomiâ, scarificatione, frictionibus, vinculis dolorificis, & quidem in principio. Astrictio partis affectæ, fit medicamentis repellentibus; crassis nimirum, frigidis, terreisque: hæc enim & huiusmodi partem affectam corroboroborant. Eadem est viarum ratio. Sicut motu peccat humor, ita quiete. Nam si sanguis non fluat per uterū, aut hæmorrhoides; incitandus est medicamentis calefacientibus, attenuantibus &c. sin sit parti impactus; indicat ablationem per ipsam partem, aut sensibiliter aut insensibiliter.
units.tr: Again, if the matter is moving, the indication varies with the variety of its motion. For if the matter is carried towards the mouth of the stomach, but imperfectly, a vomit should be prescribed; if the motion is excessive, it indicates a remedy to check it, as may be seen in a flux of blood through the nostrils. And since humours flow from one part of the body into another and give rise to inflammations, one must consider the parts sending, the parts receiving, and the channels through which the motion occurs. The sending part indicates revulsion; the receiving part, astriction and derivation; the channels themselves require an intercepting medicine, and so on. Revulsion (which is the drawing of a flowing humour to a place opposite the affected part) is effected by phlebotomy, scarification, friction, painful bindings, and indeed at the beginning. Astriction of the affected part is effected by repelling medicines, namely thick, cold and earthy ones; for these and such like strengthen the affected part. The reasoning is the same for the channels. Just as a humour sins by motion, so it sins by rest: for if blood does not flow through the uterus or the haemorrhoids, it must be stimulated by warming, attenuating medicines and so on. If it has become lodged in a part, it indicates removal through that same part, either sensibly or insensibly.

units.la: Purgationis tempus volunt Medici esse, cum materia esse cocta; nisi forsan turgens statim est educenda. Quantitatem prescribunt morbi magnitudo, & facultas. Magnus morbus conjunctus robustis viribus indicat magnam evacuationem. Contraria est indicatio, si cum morbi magnitudine conjuncta sit uirium debilitas. Et ita quidem se res habet in ordinariâ legitimâq; curatione; quæ primò aufert causas morborum, tum morbos: quibus sublatis, statim evanescunt symptomata; quæ si vehementia sint, ut dolor magnus, vigiliæ, à quibus imminet vitæ periculum; iis primò occurrendum neglecto morbo, & causa; sed hic curandi modus, modus, quanquam sæpè necessarius illegitimus tamen est, & extraordinarius.
units.tr: Physicians hold that the time for purging is when the matter has been concocted, unless perhaps the swelling requires it to be drawn off at once. The magnitude of the disease and the strength of the patient prescribe the quantity. A great disease joined with robust strength indicates a large evacuation; the indication is the opposite if weakness of strength is joined with the magnitude of the disease. And indeed matters stand thus in ordinary and lawful treatment, which first removes the causes of diseases, then the diseases themselves; once these are removed, the symptoms immediately vanish. But if the symptoms are violent, such as great pain or sleeplessness, from which danger to life threatens, these must be met first, neglecting the disease and its cause; yet this mode of treatment, although often necessary, is nonetheless irregular and extraordinary.

units.la: Indicatio conservativa semper debetur facultati; quæ est conservanda similibus, seu victu, & alimento reficientibus. In victu instituendo quatuor considerantur. Primum est forma victus; hoc maior aut minor, quam postulant vires, aut æqualis. Nam in victu pleno, plus reponitur substantiæ, quam est a morbo ablatum. In tenui plus substantiæ aufertur a morbo, quam reponitur a cibo. In victu æquali tantum reponitur, quantum aufertur. Forma victus est instituenda prout vires postulant, & morbus permittit. Norma victus in ægris est extremus morbi vigor; quo tempore tenuissimo victu est utendum, in comparatione ad alia tempora; nisi sit inflammatio conjuncta. Sicut in pleuritide, quo in morbo minus in principio, quam statu est edendum. Secundum est victus materia, crassa, tenuis, mediocris.
units.tr: The conservative indication is always owed to the faculty, which is to be preserved by things that restore, namely by diet and nourishment. In setting up a diet four things are considered. The first is the form of diet: this is either greater or less than the strength requires, or equal to it. For in a full diet more substance is restored than the disease has taken away; in a thin diet more substance is taken away by the disease than is restored by food; in an equal diet only as much is restored as is taken away. The form of diet is to be arranged according as the strength requires and the disease permits. The norm of diet in the sick is the extreme vigour of the disease; at that time the most slender diet is to be used, compared with other times, unless an inflammation is joined to it, as in pleurisy, in which disease less should be eaten at the beginning than at the height of the illness. The second is the matter of the diet: thick, thin or moderate.

units.la: Nam spiritus si deficiunt, requirunt alimentum spirituosum: sin partes solidæ sint instaurandæ, ut in Phthisi; alimentum indicatur crassum & solidum, ut caro vitulina. Tertium in victu observandum, est eiusdem qualitas, ut scilicet alimentum simile sit naturæ, & contrarium morbo, eiusdemque causæ. Quartum est modus: hoc est an multum, an parum sit dandum; an sæpe, an raro. Quæ indicantur à virium magnitudine, & indigentia; nam si vires sint debiles, & magna est indigentia; parum & sæpè est nutriendum: sin indigentia non sit magna, sed copia sit boni succi in corpore; parum & raro. in quibus semper habenda est ratio temporis, ætatis, &c. Postremum, est tempus opportunum; hoc est illud, quo minus à morbo gravatur æger: ut in intermittentibus febribus est declinatio: aut aliàs hora consueta in sanitate.
units.tr: For if the spirits are deficient, they require spirituous nourishment; but if the solid parts are to be restored, as in phthisis, thick and solid nourishment is indicated, such as veal. The third thing to be observed in diet is its quality, namely that the nourishment should be similar to the nature and contrary to the disease and its cause. The fourth is the manner: that is, whether much or little is to be given, and whether often or rarely. These are indicated by the magnitude of the strength and the need; for if the strength is weak and the need great, one should nourish little and often; but if the need is not great, yet there is an abundance of good juice in the body, little and rarely. In all these the regard for time, age and so on must always be had. Last is the opportune time, that is, the time at which the patient is least burdened by the disease: as in intermittent fevers, the remission; or otherwise the customary hour of health.

units.la: CAP. III. De Medicamentis in genere.
units.tr: CAP. III. Of Medicines in general.

units.la: MEdicamenta propriè dicuntur, quæ corpus humanū alterant, sed non corrumpunt : Venenum, quòd utrunque facit : Alimentum, quod in naturam corporis perfectè converti potest. Sicut huius natura est pati ; (nam alimenta alterantia sunt etiam medicamentosa, ut lactuca, acetosa) ita contra medicamenti & veneni est agere. Alimenti cum corpore nostro est aliqua similitudo, interdum maior, interdum minor. Venenum, & medicamentum, contrariantur : magis tamen venenum, quam medicamentum : quanquam medicamentum, si nimium sit potens, etiam vires dissolvit, mortemque accersit, ut opium ; quod tamen iustâ quantitate sumatur, prodest vehementer. Tantum observa, quod alterius speciei, exempli causa humanæ, est venenum ; alteri speciei, ut caninæ, esse potest alimentum.
units.tr: Medicines are properly those things which alter the human body without corrupting it. Poison does both. Food is that which can be wholly converted into the nature of the body. Just as it is the nature of food to be acted upon (for nourishing foods are also medicinal, such as lettuce and sorrel), so it is the nature of medicine and poison to act. Food has some likeness to our body, sometimes greater, sometimes less. Poison and medicine are contrary, though poison more so than medicine. Yet a medicine, if it is too potent, also dissolves the strength and brings on death, as opium does; taken in the right quantity, however, it benefits greatly. Only observe that what is poison for one species, for example humans, can be food for another, such as dogs.

units.la: Medicamentū agit in nostrum corpus, non tantum formâ substantiali, sed & qualitatibus eam consequentibus, quemadmodum & elementa. Qualitates hæ sunt proximæ alterandi causæ: iis enim proximè corpus humanum afficitur. Hæc dicuntur in medicamentis esse potentiâ, & virtute non actu. Quod tamen commodè est intelligendum: nec enim calor piperis dicitur potentiâ inesse quasi noster ventriculus eum generet; sed quia sopitus non prius agit quàm à nostro calore leviter alteretur. Atque hinc fit, quod glacies dicitur actu frigida, & ignis actu calidus: quia ad manifestandas operationes, non egent aliquâ præviâ corporis nostri alteratione. Ergo noster calor, nullas medicamento vires impertit. Huius temperies exigitur a corpus humanum, quod est regula & mensura. omne enim, quod corpus humanum temperatum calefacit, calidum dicitur. Idem judicium est in reliquis qualitatibus. Videndum tamen
units.tr: A medicine acts upon our body not only through its substantial form but also through the qualities that follow that form, as the elements do. These qualities are the nearest causes of alteration, since the human body is affected most directly by them. They are said to be in medicines potentially and by virtue, not actually. This must be understood properly. The heat of pepper is not said to be in it potentially as if our stomach generated it; rather, it is dormant and acts only once it is slightly altered by our heat. Hence ice is said to be actually cold and fire actually hot, because to manifest their operations they need no prior alteration of our body. Therefore our heat confers no powers on a medicine. Its temperament is measured against the human body, which is the rule and measure: whatever warms a body that is tempered is called hot. The same judgment holds for the other qualities. Yet it must be considered

units.la: tamen, an per se huiusmodi effectus producant, an vero per accidens. Illud per se calefacit, quod immediate, nullius alterius rei interventu hoc facit, ut piper. Quod autem calefacit interventu alterius, per accidens calefacit: sicut vestes; quae non calefaciunt imprimendo calorem, sed caloris spirituum effluxuum impediendo, & reprimendo. Nunquam enim unum contrarium alterum generat, sed corrumpit. ergo si quidpiam calefaciendo refrigeret; per se calefacit, per accidens vero refrigerat. sin refrigerando calefaciat, per se refrigerat; per accidens autem calefacit.
units.tr: whether such effects are produced per se or only per accidens. That warms per se which does so immediately, without the intervention of anything else, as pepper does. But that which warms through the intervention of another thing warms per accidens, as clothes do. Clothes do not warm by imparting heat, but by impeding and restraining the outflow of the body's heat-bearing spirits. For one contrary never generates the other; it destroys it. Therefore, if something cools by warming, it warms per se and cools per accidens; but if by cooling it warms, it cools per se and warms per accidens.

units.la: Distinguuntur qualitates, in occultas, & manifestas. Haec dicuntur non tantum primae, sed quae primas immediate consequuntur, ut mollities, durities, caeteraeque temperamentum comitantes. De occultis dubitatur. quidam omnino eas negant, aiuntque omnes actiones a manifestis fieri qualitatibus: quidam admittunt, afferuntque a forma sub-stanstantiali proximè manare, sicut vis stupefaciendi in opio. hæc occulta qualitas, non sensu, non ratione, sed solâ experientiâ deprehendi creditur; & quanquam à temperamento non immediatè fluat, supponit tamen debitũ commodûq; temperamentũ
units.tr: Qualities are distinguished into occult and manifest. These are said to be not only the first qualities but also those that immediately follow the first, such as softness, hardness, and the others that accompany temperament. There is doubt about the occult ones. Some deny them altogether and say that all actions arise from manifest qualities. Others admit them and maintain that they flow immediately from the substantial form, as the power of stupefying does in opium. This occult quality is believed to be detected not by sense or reason but by experience alone; and although it does not flow immediately from the temperament, it nonetheless presupposes a due and suitable temperament.

units.la: CAP. IV. De medicamentorum facultatibus in genere.
units.tr: CAP. IV. Of the faculties of medicines in general.

units.la: MEdicamenta alia simplicia sunt alia composita. Illa dicuntur quæ natura fiunt, nec arti quicquam debent, quemadmodum lactuca, mandragora: quæ quidem non sunt corpora penitus simplicia, omnisque compositionis expertia;(revera enim lactuca est composita, non tantum ex materia & forma, sed etiam ex elementis:) sed dicuntur talia comparatè, ad composita nimirum, quę arte & industriâ humanâ fiunt; ut theriaca, diaphœnicum. De simplicibus primò agendum.
units.tr: Medicines are either simple or compound. Those are called simple which are produced by nature and owe nothing to art, such as lettuce and mandrake. These are not absolutely simple bodies, free of all composition (for lettuce is indeed compound, not only of matter and form but also of the elements); they are called simple only in comparison, that is, in relation to compounds, which are made by art and human industry, such as theriac and diaphoenicon. We must first treat of simples.

units.la: Diximus medicamentum simplex conconstare calido, frigido, humido, sicco. cuius temperies exigitur ad corpus humanum temperatissimū. Temperatum illud dicitur, quod corpus humanum, nec calefacit, humectat; aut quod corporis humani temperati calorem, frigus, nec auget, nec minuit, sed conservat tantum, & quoad sensum simile videtur: ac proinde in qualitatibus hîc est magna nobiscum similitudo: quod si accedat porrò substantiæ similitudo, erit alimentum. Intemperatum est, quod corpori humano admotum, eius frigus, aut humiditatem auget. Temperatum medicamentum est regula intemperati. Temperatum interdum est omnibus qualitatibus, interdum unâ, alterâve. illius exemplum est cera, huius est lini semen, quod licet calefaciat, siccitate tamen & humiditate temperatum est. Quicquid ergo auget nostrum calorem, dicitur calidum: quod humiditatē, humidum: eodem est similium ratio. Tale est quadruplex; calidum, frigidū, humidum, siccum. sed quia alia aliis sunt calidiora, oriuntur quatuor gradus medicamentorum. Primus gradus dicitur recessus primus à corpore temperato. Quòd ergo est primo gradu calidum, aut siccum, obscurè tantum corpus humanum alterat. quod secundo gradu, manifestè alterat, sed sine noxâ. tertius gradus, est tertius à temperato corpore recessus. Medicamentum ergo tale, corpus humanum vehementer alterat. Ultimus recessus, & summus, est quartus gradus, quo corpus humanum non tantum alteratur, sed & corrumpitur.
units.tr: We have said that a simple medicine consists of hot, cold, moist and dry. Its temperament is required to be most temperate for the human body. A medicine is called temperate when it neither heats nor moistens the human body, or when it neither increases nor diminishes the heat or cold of a temperate human body but merely preserves it, and seems similar to the senses. Accordingly, in qualities there is great likeness between such a medicine and ourselves; if further likeness of substance is added, it will be food. A medicine is intemperate when, applied to the human body, it increases its cold or its moisture. A temperate medicine is the rule for an intemperate one. Sometimes a medicine is temperate in all its qualities, sometimes in one or two of them: an example of the former is wax, of the latter is linseed, which, although it warms, is tempered by its dryness and moisture. Whatever increases our heat is called hot; whatever increases moisture, moist; and the reasoning is the same for the rest. There are thus four kinds: hot, cold, moist and dry. But because some are hotter than others, four degrees of medicines arise. The first degree is called the first recession from the temperate body. Therefore what is hot or dry in the first degree alters the human body only obscurely. What is in the second degree alters it manifestly, but without harm. The third degree is the third recession from the temperate body; such a medicine alters the human body vehemently. The last and highest recession is the fourth degree, by which the human body is not only altered but also corrupted.

units.la: Hi sunt generales medicamentorum simplicium ordines in qualitatibus primis, ad quas exiguntur secundæ. Medici longo usu edocti, singulos gradus dividunt in tres mansiones, principium, medium, & finem: observarunt enim, non omnia primo gradu frigida, æqualiter refrigerare; & hinc factum est, ut latitudinem illam, hoc quo diximus modo, partiti fuerint. Nam quæ in principio pri-mi grami gradus, non adeo conspicuè alte-rant,sed in medio evidentius,in fine autem evidentissimè. Varietas gra-duum est magis conspicua in qualita-tibus tam actívis, quam passivis. Hæ enim remissè agunt, nec perfectè at-tingunt quartum gradum.Si modum substantiæ in medicamentis spectes ; quædam sunt essentiæ tenuis,quæ fa-cilè in tenues partes resolvuntur : quædam substantiæ crassæ,quæ diffi-culter solvuntur, nec penetrant cor-poris nostri partes : quædam sunt mediocris,quæ medío se habent mo-do. Aliter Philosophi ac Medici sen-tiunt de secundis qualitatibus,& fa-cultatibus. Illi enim omnes eas vo-cant secundas,quæ sequuntur prima-rum inter se actionem ; ut odorem, saporem , colorem &c. qui quidem vim agendi habent in propria senso-ria, non verò in aliam corporis par-tem;nam sapor afficit solam linguam, odor processus mammillares. Hi eas solas,quæ viribus primarum qualita-tum agunt. Dicuntur autem activæ, quia subjectum, iis præditum, aptum est ut certo & determinato modo in corpus nostrum agat. Huiusmodi qualitates sunt variæ; emolliens, indurans, intendens, relaxans, condensans, rarefaciens, incrassans, attenuans, attrahens, repellens, dolorem leniens, irritans &c. quæ non sunt accipienda, quasi mollities, durities, tenuitas, vim habeant agendi; sed quod vis extenuandi, & emolliendi, in medicamentis procedit à qualitatibus activis pro modo materiæ. Actiones enim hæ secundæ sequuntur primarum actiones: nam calidum medicamentum primò calefacit; postea, si tenuis sit essentiæ, attenuat, rarefacit, discutit. Unde constat, actiones secundarum qualitatum oriri à medicamentorum temperamentis. Si itaque quidpiam est in corpore durum præter naturam; indicat medicamentum, non molle, sed emolliens: si quid verò crassum; non tenue, sed attenuans. Sunt itaq; secundæ qualitates, peculiares dispositiones nes primarum in materiâ. Tertiæ facultates sunt, quæ determinatum membrum respiciunt, aut alioqui determinatam materiam. Agunt hæ qualitates non modo occulto, sed evidente; detergendo nimirum, aperiendo &c. Respiciunt interdum contenta in corpore, ut medicamenta semen excitantia, aut urinas moventia, calculos frangentia: interdum ipsa membra, unde medicamenta cephalica, cardiaca &c. quia manifesta qualitate tales partes afficiunt. Omnes hæ qualitates evidentes promanant à primis medicamentorum facultatibus pro materiæ dispositione.
units.tr: These are the general orders of simple medicines in the primary qualities, from which the secondary qualities are derived. Physicians, taught by long experience, divide each degree into three stages: beginning, middle and end. For they have observed that not all things cold in the first degree cool equally; and hence they divided that breadth, in the manner we have described. For those things which are at the beginning of the first degree act less conspicuously, in the middle more evidently, and at the end most evidently. The variety of degrees is more conspicuous in qualities both active and passive. For these act feebly and do not perfectly reach the fourth degree. If you consider the nature of the substance in medicines, some are of a thin essence, which are easily resolved into thin parts; some are of a thick substance, which are dissolved with difficulty and do not penetrate the parts of our body; some are of a middling kind, which hold a middle position. Philosophers and physicians think differently about secondary qualities and faculties. The former call secondary all those qualities which follow upon the mutual action of the primary ones, such as odour, savour, colour, etc.; these have power to act only on their own sense organs, and not on another part of the body, for savour affects only the tongue, and odour the mammillary processes. The physicians, however, call secondary only those which act by the powers of the primary qualities. These are said to be active, because the subject endowed with them is apt to act upon our body in a certain and determined way. Such qualities are various: softening, hardening, tightening, relaxing, condensing, rarefying, thickening, thinning, attracting, repelling, easing pain, irritating, etc. These are not to be understood as if softness, hardness or thinness had the power of acting; rather, the power of thinning and softening in medicines proceeds from active qualities according to the mode of the matter. For these secondary actions follow the actions of the primary qualities: a hot medicine first warms; afterwards, if it is of thin essence, it thins, rarefies and disperses. Hence it is clear that the actions of secondary qualities arise from the temperaments of medicines. Thus, if something in the body is hard beyond nature, the medicine indicated is not a softening one but an emollient one; if something is thick, not a thinning one but an attenuating one. Secondary qualities, then, are peculiar dispositions of the primary ones in matter. Tertiary faculties are those which regard a determinate member, or otherwise a determinate matter. These qualities act not only by a hidden but by an evident means: namely by cleansing, opening, etc. Sometimes they regard the contents of the body, as medicines which excite semen, move urine, or break stones; sometimes the members themselves, whence cephalic, cardiac medicines, etc., because they affect such parts by a manifest quality. All these evident qualities proceed from the primary faculties of medicines according to the disposition of the matter.

units.la: Nam materia interdum est crassa, interdum tenuis, interdum mediocris; pro quâ varietate medicamentum actiones suas variat. nam calor aut frigus in materia densâ aliter agunt, quam in tenui. Medicamentum tenuis substantiæ, si sit simul calidum, ut feniculum, validè attenuat, discusit, aperit.
units.tr: For the matter is sometimes thick, sometimes thin, sometimes middling; and according to this variety the medicine varies its actions. For heat or cold acts differently in dense matter than in thin. A medicine of thin substance, if at the same time it is hot, such as fennel, greatly thins, disperses and opens.

units.la: Quartæ medicamentorum facultates à temperamento non oriuntur, si optimis creditur Medicis, verùm à formâ substantiali: nec agunt manifestâ qualitate, sed occultâ. sicut in medicamentis electivè purgantibus videre est, & in venenis, & alexipharmacis.
units.tr: The fourth faculties of medicines do not arise from temperament, if we believe the best physicians, but from the substantial form; and they act not by a manifest quality but by a hidden one, as may be seen in medicines that purge by selective action, and in poisons and alexipharmics.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: De Facultatibus medicamentorum in specie.
units.tr: On the Faculties of Medicines in Particular.

units.la: OMissis primis medicamentorũ facultatibus, reliquas ordine persequamur. Medicamentum indurans est quod corpus minus aptum reddit, ut tactui cedat: non quidem dissolvendo tenues partes, aut eas exprimendo, sed manente humido naturali, corpus ineptum reddit ut cedat tactui. Tale est frigidum & humidum, sine evidente adstrictione, ut portulaca, lenticula palustris. Emolliens contra calidum esse debet, non tamen ultra secundum gradum, in passivis qualitatibus temperatum; sine tamen partium crassitie, ut semen lini, Althæa. Sed quia multa emolemollientia discutiunt, & calefaciunt, ut medullæ; fit ut cum relaxantibus confundantur. Intendens est triplex. Primum exsiccans, cum calor humorem consumit. Secundum congelans, cum frigus humorem exprimit, aut concrescere facit. Tertium est replens ex humorum affluxu. Huius contrarium relaxans, triplex quoque est; humectans, calefaciens, evacuans. Quæ exsiccatione intenduntur, humectantibus relaxantur; talia sunt viola, malua recens. Quæ frigore; relaxantur calidis, & emollientibus; ut anetho; meliloto. Quæ intenduntur humoris repletione, relaxantur evacuatione, eaque sensibili, vel insensibili. Materia in habitu corporis, emollientibus, rarefacientibus, discutientibus, insensibiliter discutitur. Quod si insensibiliter fieri nequit, tum materia est præparanda maturantibus pus &c. Quanquam hæc ita se habent, proprie relaxantia sunt quæ rarefaciunt, & attenuant, diaphoretica vulgò dicta: me-dicadicamenta scilicet humores in halitus dissolventia. talia sunt tenuis substantiæ; calida tamen non ultra tertium gradum. Hæc enim penetrando, crassa, solidaque attenuant, porosaque reddunt. Horum alia, aliis sunt potentiora. huius generis sunt camomilla, melilotus. Quæ modicè rarefaciunt, cutemque contemperant, Anodyna dicuntur, & quidem proprie. Dico proprie; nam alias omne quod dolorem quoquo modo sedat, anodynum dicitur: & hoc modo narcoticum ut opium est anodynum; quia sensum doloris aufert. Ita quicquid causam doloris corrumpit anodynum censetur. nam si dolor sit à calore, qui frigore corrumpitur, medicamentum frigidum est anodynum. at, ut dixi, proprie anodyna sunt paregorica, quæ rarefaciendo, causam doloris demulcent. Contra, densantia & incrassantia sunt, quæ poros cogunt, & humores addensant. talia sunt frigida, crassarumque partium, ut plantago, myrtus, quæ modicè astringunt. Referuntur huc admodum refrigerantia, papaver, mandragora ; nam & hæc condensant. Ad rarefacientia pertinent attrahentia, quæ humores ad cutem attrahunt manifesto calore;ut sinapi, euphorbium. quæ quantò calidiora, tantò validus attrahunt : quo pertinent dropaces, sinapismi, phænigmi. Horum contraria repellentia, frigida sunt, crassarumque partium ; huiusmodi enim humores ad interiora trudunt, ut hyoscyamus. Distingue inter medicamentum repellens & astringens. Astringere enim, est humores cogere, membrumque firmare; quod faciunt nonnulla calida ; ut spica, aloë.quanquam non sit negandum valide adstringentia,esse etiam repellentia : talia sunt frigida, substantiæque terrestris, ut galla, acacia. Quæ minus validè adstringunt, ut santali, corroborantibus accensetur.Quicquid est,hæc duo admodum inter se similia sunt; sicut oblinentia, incrassantia,& oppilantia. Astringere enim re enim communiter dicitur, quicquid cogit, roborat, intendit, condensat, humores incrassat, repellit, refrenat: proprie vero, quod venarum orificia adstringit, & contrahit, sensibilesque evacuationes cohibet. Tale autem est naturae terrestris; ut medicamenta austera, & acerba: haec enim venarum orificia claudunt; sicut quae aperiunt, calida & mordacia existere, necesse est; ut coepa, allium. Quibus similia sunt extergentia, & deobstruentia. illa superficiem corporis, & externos meatus expurgant; haec autem internas cavitates, utraque calida sunt, & ex parte mordacia; qualia sunt amara & nitrosa. Quae extenuant medicamenta & incidunt, eiusdem farinae sunt, cum deobstruentibus; nisi quod interdum sint frigida, ut acetum.Lubricans est, quod vias inaequales laevigat; adeo ut humores nequeant adhaerere: quale est pingue & lentum medicamentum, modicum habens calorem; ut malua althaea, prunum'. Abluens est, quod superficiem partium expurgat; non oblinendo, sed sordes diluendo. Est autem naturæ aqueæ, minusque calidæ; ut serum lactis, jus mercurialis. Detergens potentius est abluente; altius enim penetrat, subitque tenuiores meatus, & sordes educit: calidum tamen est; ut centaureum minus; mel. Hisce tribus medicamentorum generibus, supra memoratis, quæ alvum manifesta qualitate evacuant, nonnulli addunt comprimentia (de quibus admodum dubitatur) quæ vasa contrahendo, humores contentos exprimunt; ut tamarindi. Emplastica medicamenta sunt, quæ tenues humores incrassant, suaque tenacitate meatus infarciunt sine adstrictione. Quorum alia terrea, & sicca sunt, sine manifesto calore, aut frigore, ut tutia, terra samia: alia terrea, & aquea simul; nempe lenta, & viscida; ut cera lota. Sanguis Draconis, & alumen magis adstringentibus annumerantur; coarctant enim vias. Suppuratoria medicamencamenta sunt, quæ humores extra va-sa corruptos in pus convertunt. Talia sunt similia corpori nostro; eius enim calorem nec augent, nec mi-nuunt, sed eodem statu conservant; suntque temperata, sed emplastica; ut liliorum radix. Medicamenta sarcotica non dicuntur, quod carnem generent; (carnis enim generatio, sicut & puris, naturæ est opus) sed quod humores in carnis generatione exsiccant simul, & tergent; sine morsu tamen. Nam in carnis generatione, est duplex excrementum: unum tenue, alterum crassum: ulcus verò ut sanetur, utroque liberari debet; nam & exsiccandum est, & sordes auferendæ. Talia sunt farina fabarum, sarcocolla. His opponuntur edentia medicamenta, quæ callos, verrucas, absumunt; quæ igneæ sunt substantiæ pyroticisque accensetur. Tale est vitriolum, ærugo, alumen ustum. Sub pyroticis multa continentur admodum inter se similia: idem enim calor, pro materiæ varietate, varios affectus inducit. Ergo rubrificantia, calore suo humorem ad cutem trahunt, eamq; rubore inficiunt; non tamen excedunt. unde nonnulli sub attrahentibus ea comprehendunt. Sunt quidem talia admodum calida, sed tenuium partium, ut sinapi. Secundò sunt vesicatoria, quæ humores non tantū ad cutim evocant, sed & pustulas faciunt. Hæc, ut superiorâ, calida sunt, sed partium crassiorum; ut mel anacardinum. Septica altius penetrant, carnemque tenuem colliquant. proinde calidiora superioribus & crassiora, ut arsenicum. Postremo, huius generis sunt escharotica, pyroticorum vehementissima. Hæc ad ferri candentis similitudinem cutim exurunt: unde & crassa, & mordacia existere necesse est; ut calx viva. Epulotica medicamenta sunt, quæ repleti ulceris summam carnem in cicatricem indurant; ut cerussa. Talia sicca sunt, & crassæ substantiæ, sine manifesto calore, & frigore, atque adeò morsu. Glutinantia postremò sunt, quæ cruenti vulneris labia uniunt, ut plantago, verbena. Huiusmodi constant crassâ substantiâ, quæ desiccant sine morsu, & calore; proinde terrea sunt, & ex parte viscida.
units.tr: Having dealt with the primary faculties of medicines, let us go through the rest in order. An indurating medicine is one that makes a body less pliant so that it yields less to the touch. It does this not by dissolving the fine parts or squeezing them out, but by leaving the natural moisture in place while rendering the body unyielding to touch. Cold and moist medicines do this without obvious astringency, such as purslane and marsh duckweed. An emollient ought to be warm, though not beyond the second degree in passive qualities, and tempered; yet without thickening the parts, as linseed and marshmallow. But because many emollients also disperse and warm, as marrow does, they are sometimes confused with relaxants. Intensives are of three kinds. The first is drying, when heat consumes the moisture. The second is congealing, when cold squeezes out the moisture or makes it coagulate. The third is filling, from an influx of humours. The opposite of these, the relaxants, is also threefold: moistening, warming, and evacuating. Those things that are intensified by drying are relaxed by moistening agents, such as violet and fresh mallow. Those intensified by cold are relaxed by warm and emollient things, such as dill and melilot. Those intensified by a repletion of humour are relaxed by evacuation, which is either perceptible or imperceptible. Matter within the habit of the body is dispersed imperceptibly by emollients, rarefiers, and discutients. If this cannot be done imperceptibly, the matter must then be prepared with maturatives to produce pus, and so on. Although these things stand thus, strictly speaking the relaxants are those that rarefy and thin, commonly called diaphoretics, that is, medicines that dissolve humours into vapours. Such are of a subtle substance, yet warm, though not beyond the third degree. For by penetrating they thin what is thick and solid, and make it porous. Some of these are stronger than others; of this kind are chamomile and melilot. Those that rarefy moderately and temper the skin are called anodynes, and properly so. I say properly, for otherwise anything that in any way allays pain is called an anodyne, and in this way opium, a narcotic, is an anodyne, because it removes the sense of pain. Thus whatever corrupts the cause of pain is judged an anodyne. For if the pain comes from heat, which is corrupted by cold, then a cold medicine is an anodyne. But, as I have said, strictly speaking the anodynes are the paregorics, which by rarefying soothe the cause of pain. On the other hand, the condensing and thickening agents are those that constrict the pores and thicken the humours. Such are cold medicines of thick parts, such as plantain and myrtle, which astringe moderately. Here also belong the strongly refrigerant medicines, poppy and mandrake, for these too condense. Among the rarefiers belong the attractives, which draw humours to the skin by manifest heat, such as mustard and spurge. The more warm they are, the more powerfully they draw; to this class belong the drawing plasters, mustard plasters, and phoenigmi. Their opposites, the repellents, are cold and of thick parts, for they thrust such humours inwards, as henbane does. Distinguish between a repellent and an astringent medicine. For to astringe is to compel the humours and firm up the limb, which some warm things do, such as spikenard and aloe. Although one should not deny that strongly astringent things are also repellent, such as cold substances of earthy nature, like gallnut and acacia. Those that astringe less strongly, such as sandalwood, are counted among the corroborants. Whatever the case, these two are very similar to each other, as are the obliterants, thickeners, and obstruents. For in common usage, to astringe means whatever compels, strengthens, tightens, condenses, thickens humours, repels, or restrains. Properly, however, it means what constricts and contracts the orifices of the veins and checks perceptible evacuations. Such are medicines of an earthy nature, like austere and sour ones, for these close the orifices of the veins; just as those that open them must of necessity be warm and biting, such as onion and garlic. Similar to these are the detergents and the deobstruents. The former cleanse the surface of the body and the external passages; the latter cleanse the internal cavities. Both are warm and in part biting, like bitter and nitrous things. Medicines that thin and cut are of the same sort as the deobstruents, except that sometimes they are cold, like vinegar. The lubricant is what smooths uneven passages so that humours cannot cling; such is a fatty and viscous medicine with moderate warmth, like marshmallow and plum. The abstergent is what cleanses the surface of the parts, not by coating them but by dissolving the filth. It is of a watery nature and less warm, like whey and mercurialis broth. The detergent is more powerful than the abstergent; for it penetrates more deeply, passes into finer passages, and draws out filth. Yet it is warm, like lesser centaury and honey. To these three kinds of medicines mentioned above, which evacuate the bowels by a manifest quality, some add the compressives (about which there is much doubt), which by contracting the vessels squeeze out the contained humours, such as tamarind. Emplastic medicines are those which thicken thin humours and stuff the passages with their tenacity, without astringing. Of these, some are earthy and dry without manifest heat or cold, such as tutty and Samian earth; others are earthy and watery at once, namely slow and viscid, such as washed wax. Dragon's blood and alum are rather counted among the astringents, for they constrict the passages. Suppurative medicines are those that convert humours corrupted outside the vessels into pus. Such are similar to our body; for they neither increase nor diminish its heat, but keep it in the same state, and they are tempered but emplastic, like the root of lilies. Medicines are not called sarcotic because they generate flesh (for the generation of flesh, like that of pus, is the work of nature), but because they dry and cleanse the humours at the same time as flesh is being generated, yet without biting. For in the generation of flesh there are two excrements: one thin, the other thick. For an ulcer to be healed, both must be removed, for it must be dried and the filth carried away. Such are bean meal and sarcocolla. Opposed to these are the eating medicines, which consume calluses and warts; these are of a fiery substance and are counted among the pyrotics. Such are vitriol, verdigris, and burnt alum. Under the pyrotics are contained many things very similar to one another, for the same heat, according to the variety of matter, induces various effects. Therefore the reddening agents, by their heat, draw humours to the skin and stain it with redness, but do not go further. For this reason some include these among the attractives. Indeed they are very hot, but of subtle parts, like mustard. Secondly, there are the vesicatories, which not only draw humours to the skin but also raise blisters. These, like the former, are warm, but of thicker parts, such as anacardium honey. Septics penetrate more deeply and liquefy the thin flesh; therefore they are hotter and thicker than the former, such as arsenic. Lastly, of this kind are the escharotics, the most vehement of the pyrotics. These burn the skin as if with a red-hot iron; hence they must of necessity be thick and biting, such as quicklime. Epulotics are medicines that harden the surface flesh of a full ulcer into a scar, such as white lead. Such are dry, of thick substance, without manifest heat or cold, and so without biting. Lastly, the glutinants are those that join the lips of a bleeding wound, such as plantain and vervain. These consist of a thick substance that dries without biting or heat; therefore they are earthy and in part viscid.

units.la: Atque hæc de secundis medicamentorum facultatibus; ad tertias pergamus.
units.tr: And so much for the secondary faculties of medicaments; let us proceed to the tertiary ones.

units.la: Διuρητικὰ seu urinas moventia sunt, quæ serum ita præparant, ut copiosè & facilè ad renes feratur, non tamen obstructiones aperiendo. Talia medicamenta sunt tenuium partium, calida tamen, & sicca: hæc enim non tantum sanguinem extenuant, sed & fundunt, ut daucus, seseli, semina calida vulgò dicta, quæ validè urinas movent, vasaque urinaria expurgant, calculos etiam frangunt manifestâ qualitate; ut radices eryngii, graminis. Huiusmodi medicamenta sunt temperatè calida & humida.
units.tr: Diuretics [Διουρητικὰ], or urine-moving agents, are those which prepare the serum so that it is carried to the kidneys copiously and easily, yet without opening obstructions. Such medicaments are of thin parts, yet warm and dry; for these not only thin the blood but also cause it to flow, like wild carrot, seseli, and the so-called warm seeds, which powerfully move the urine and cleanse the urinary vessels; they also break stones by a manifest quality, like the roots of eryngo and couch grass. Medicaments of this kind are moderately warm and moist.

units.la: Franguntur calculi occultâ proprietate, qualis est in sanguine hyrcino. no. Non negandum tamen, & alia admodum calida, ut vitrum combu-ftum, cantharides, calculum diffol-vere, abradendo eum, & in pulve-rem redigendo.
units.tr: Stones are broken up by a hidden property, as is found in goat's blood. Yet it must not be denied that some very hot substances, such as burnt glass and cantharides, dissolve the stone by wearing it away and reducing it to powder.

units.la: Quæ menses movent, propriè sunt medicamenta obstructiones uteri a-perientia, & abstergentia, sangui-nemque eo deducentia: calida nimi-rum admodum, non tamen substan-tiæ tenuis, sed nonnihil crassæ & sic-cæ; ut sabina, pulegium. Hisce simi-lia sunt, quæ lac & semē promovent. Deducunt enim sanguinem ad mam-mas, & testes. Non sunt tamen tam calida & sicca: hoc enim modo eru-ca semen excitat, & fœniculum vi-ride lac.
units.tr: Medicines that bring on the menses are properly those that open obstructions of the womb, cleanse, and draw blood towards it. They are indeed very hot, but not thin in substance; they are somewhat thick and dry, such as savin and pennyroyal. Similar to these are those that promote milk and semen. For they draw blood towards the breasts and the testicles. They are not, however, as hot and dry as these: in this way rocket stimulates semen, and green fennel stimulates milk.

units.la: Generatio lactis, sicut & semi-nis, fit ex optimis alimentis, na-turæ opera. illorum tamen pro-vacatio & deductio ad convenien-tia membra, medicamentorum vi contingit sæpe.
units.tr: The generation of milk, as also of semen, comes about from the best nourishment by the work of nature. Yet their diversion and drawing to the appropriate parts often occurs by the power of medicines.

units.la: Bechica & sputū moventia, duûm sunt generū, alia enim crassam & vis-cidam cidam pituitam incîdunt, & exte-nuant ; sed sine vehementi calore,ut hyssopus. alia pituitam tenuem in-crassant leviter,& leniunt; ut nux pi-nea, amygdala, tragacantha. Huc pertinent errhina,quæ tennem pitui-tam, circa meninges delitescentem, expurgant per nares;talia calida sunt; & acria, incîdunt enim, & abster-gunt.
units.tr: Cough-relieving and expectorant medicines are of two kinds. Some cut and thin thick, viscid phlegm, but without strong heat, as hyssop does. Others thicken thin phlegm slightly and soothe it, as pine nut, almond, and tragacanth do. To this class belong the errhines, which purge through the nostrils the thin phlegm lying hidden about the membranes of the brain; these are hot and sharp, for they cut and wipe away.

units.la: Sunt & medicamenta partes cor-roborantia,manifesta aliqua qualita-te ; eas nimirum adstringendo, ne spiritus dissipentur;qualia sunt hepa-tica, & cardiaca. Illorum exempla sunt agrimonia: horum,rosa, marga-rita.
units.tr: There are also medicines that strengthen the parts, having some manifest quality; namely, by binding them so that the spirits are not dissipated. Such are the hepatics and cardiacs. Examples of these are agrimony; of the latter, rose and pearl.

units.la: Cardiacis adnumerantur, quæ te-tros spiritus discutiunt, ut viola ; aut bonos reficiunt,ut cinnamomi aqua ; aut deniq; venenū debellátia,ut the-riacalia, & bezoardica vulgò dicta.
units.tr: Among the cardiacs are counted those that disperse foul spirits, such as violet; or restore good ones, such as cinnamon water; or finally those that combat poison, such as what are commonly called theriacs and bezoars.

units.la: Diximus esse quartas medicamen-torū facultates, consequentes imme-diatè formā substantialē rei,non au-tem temperamentum. Hæc afficiunt nostrum corpus,non tantùm manifestè, sed & occulta ratione. Agunt in nostrum corpus dupliciter, vel movendo localiter aliquid in eo, aut simpliciter tantùm alterando,ut theriaca. Quædam enim retinent aliquid quod ex corpore exiturum erat, ut lapis ætites brachio alligatus, conceptum retinet. Alia attrahunt;sicut scorpius, morsui à se facto impositus, venenum attrahere dicitur,similitudine substantiæ. idem faciunt & alexiteria quædam. Quædam trahunt ad se aliquid, aut, ut aliis placet,incitant facultatem ad expulsionem; ut medicamenta electivè trahentia ex corpore, aut certa corporis parte, determinatum humorem; ut senna, rhabarb. agaricus.quę licet habeant primas & secundas medicamentorum in se facultates, iis tamen non trahunt determinatum humorem, sed quarta ista occulta, & specifica.
units.tr: We have said that there are fourth faculties of medicines, following immediately from the substantial form of a thing, and not from its temperament. These affect our body not only manifestly but also by a hidden manner. They act upon our body in two ways: either by moving something in it locally, or simply by altering it, as theriac does. For some retain something that was about to leave the body; thus the eagle-stone, bound to the arm, retains the conceived fetus. Others attract: the scorpion, placed upon the bite it made, is said to draw out the poison by likeness of substance; certain antidotes do the same. Some draw something to themselves or, as others prefer, stir up the faculty for expulsion; such as medicines that draw a determinate humour selectively out of the body or a certain part of it, as senna, rhubarb, and agaric do. Although these have the first and second faculties of medicines in themselves, they do not draw the determinate humour by these, but by that fourth, hidden and specific faculty.

units.la: Ad horum censum pertinent Venena, Antidota, eaque medicamenta quæ determinatam partem respiciunt. Quanquam omnia venena immediatè cor oppugnent ; non tamen eodem modo hoc faciunt. Quædam enim sunt calida, quædā frigida, nonnulla sicca ; nulla tamen destituuntur occulta proprietate, quæ conspirat cum manifesta. at serpentum venena, occulta tantum proprietate vires conficiunt. His opponuntur alexiteria propriè dicta, quæ venenum aut frangunt, alterantque, ut theriaca ; aut evocant, ut scorpius morsui suo impositus.
units.tr: To this class belong poisons, antidotes, and those medicines that are directed to a determinate part. Although all poisons assail the heart immediately, they do not do so in the same way. For some are hot, some cold, some dry; yet none is lacking a hidden property, which works together with the manifest one. But the poisons of serpents achieve their force by a hidden property alone. Opposed to these are the alexipharmics properly so called, which either break and alter the poison, as theriac does, or draw it out, as the scorpion placed upon its own bite does.

units.la: Postremò, quæ respiciunt determinatam partem medicamenta, hoc faciunt occulta sympathia, vel antipathia. illo modo salvia capiti conducit ; pulmo vulpis, pulmonibus hoc, cantharides nocent vesicæ. quæ dixi de medicamentorum facultatibus, vulgò à medicis fere recipiuntur. negandum tamen non est multa esse, quæ receptam sententiam dubiam reddere possunt, de quibus alii.
units.tr: Lastly, medicines that are directed to a determinate part do so by a hidden sympathy or antipathy. In that way sage is useful for the head; fox lung for the lungs; cantharides harm the bladder. What I have said about the faculties of medicines is commonly accepted by physicians almost universally. Yet it must not be denied that there are many things which can make the accepted opinion doubtful, about which others have written.

units.la: CAP. VI. Modus explorandi vires medicamentorum.
units.tr: CAP. VI. The method of testing the powers of medicines.

units.la: MEdicamentorum facultates eç, quæ tota substantia,ut loquuntur, agunt, experientia sola cognoscuntur. Verum primæ, & secundæ, non experientia tantum,sed & ratione. sed sine experientia vires nunquam dextrè cognoscentur.tutius est experientia niti, sine ratione, quam contra. Notum est ex Philosopho, accidentia rerum deducere in earum cognitionem. Cum verò in medicamentis varia sint accidentia,colores, odores, gravitas, levitas: nulla tamen æquè commodè,& certè deducunt in cognitionem temperamentorum quam sapores. Quorum materia est pars terrestris sicca, diluta tamen humore aqueo: unde destiguuntur sapores, ex varia mistione humidi cum sicco, à calore facta. Nec sapor est qualitas secunda, orta ex actione caloris in sicco terreo, aqua perfuso.
units.tr: The powers of medicines which act by their whole substance, as they say, are known by experience alone. The primary and secondary qualities, however, are known not by experience only but also by reason. Yet without experience the powers will never be known correctly; it is safer to rely on experience without reason than the reverse. It is known from the Philosopher that the accidents of things lead us to knowledge of them. Now in medicines there are various accidents: colours, odours, weight, lightness. But none leads so conveniently and surely to knowledge of their temperaments as taste. Its material is a dry earthy part, diluted however with watery moisture; from the varied mixture of moist with dry, produced by heat, the tastes are derived. Nor is taste a secondary quality arising from the action of heat on dry earth soaked in water.

units.la: Saporum alii calidi sunt, seu caloris dominiū sequuntur, ut acer, amarus, salsus. alii frigidi, ut acidus, austerus, acerbus, alii temperati, ut dulcis, pinguis, insipidus, si modo sapor dicendus. Acris qualis in pipere, & cæpa deprehenditur, linguam cum calore penetrat, inflammat, mordet. Huius generatio est ex sicco terreo, humido permixto, à calore attenuato adeo, ut partes effervescant: partes dico terrestres & aqueas. Ergo acria medicamenta, sunt calida, sicca, tenuium partium: habent autem vim rarefaciendi, attenuandi, discutiendi. Amarus, qualis in colocynthide, linguam detergit, abradit, exasperatque, cuius causa est vehemens calor humorem consumens: estque medicamentum amarum, calidum, siccum, substantiæ terrestris, ad similitudinem fuliginis aut cineris. minus penetrat, & rarefacit, quam acre: incidit tamen, detergit, meatus aperit. Huic vicinus est salsus, genitus ex sicco terreo, copioso humore perfuso, fusò, à calore humorem quidem affante, non tamen consumente, sed potius cogente cum parte terrestri. Proinde salsa, sunt substantiæ quasi mediæ, nec plane aqueæ, nec terreæ: unde exsiccant, absorbent, incîdunt; quæ indicant esse naturæ magis crassæ, quam tenuis.
units.tr: Some tastes are hot, or follow the dominance of heat, such as sharp, bitter and salty. Others are cold, such as sour, astringent and harsh; others are temperate, such as sweet, fatty and insipid, if indeed it can be called a taste. A sharp taste, such as is found in pepper and onion, penetrates the tongue with heat, inflames and bites. It is generated from dry earth mixed with moisture, attenuated by heat to such a degree that the parts effervesce; I mean the earthy and watery parts. Therefore sharp medicines are hot, dry, and of fine parts; they have the power of rarefying, attenuating and dispersing. A bitter taste, such as is found in colocynth, cleanses, scrapes and roughens the tongue, and its cause is a vehement heat consuming the moisture; and a bitter medicine is hot, dry, of an earthy substance, like soot or ash. It penetrates and rarefies less than a sharp one; nevertheless it cuts, cleanses and opens passages. Next to this is the salty taste, produced from dry earth soaked with abundant moisture, poured out, by a heat which indeed makes the moisture thin but does not consume it, rather binds it together with the earthy part. Accordingly salty substances are as it were intermediate, neither wholly watery nor wholly earthy; hence they dry, absorb and cut, which indicates that they are of a nature more gross than thin.

units.la: Hi sunt sapores calidi, sequentes nimirum caloris dominium.
units.tr: These are the hot tastes, namely those following the dominance of heat.

units.la: Frigidi sapores sunt totidem, quorum duo priores admodum sunt similes; austerus & acerbus; uterque enim adstringit. Verum acerbus (qualis galla immatura) linguā contrahit, & exasperat, & quidem validè, at austerus (qualis in malo cydonio) eadem præstat, sed moderatè. Utriusque causa, est debilis calor, qui non sufficienter attenuat, & permiscet partes terrestres cum aqueis, verum sinit illas his dominari. quanquam in austero maior sit attenuatio & permixtio humidi cum sicco, quam in acerbo. Medicamenta ergò austera, & acerba, crassa sunt, & terrestris naturæ; frigida tamen, & sicca: unde fluxiones sistunt, viasque claudunt. magis acerba, minus austera.
units.tr: There are as many cold tastes, of which the first two are very similar: astringent and harsh; for both bind. But the harsh taste (such as that of an unripe gall) draws and roughens the tongue, and indeed strongly, whereas the astringent (such as that of a quince) does the same but moderately. The cause of both is a weak heat, which does not sufficiently attenuate and mix the earthy parts with the watery, but allows the former to dominate; though in the astringent the attenuation and mixture of moist with dry is greater than in the harsh. Therefore astringent and harsh medicines are thick and of earthy nature, yet cold and dry; hence they check flows and close passages. More harsh, less astringent.

units.la: Acidus sapor, qualis in oxalide, linguam sine caloris sensu, altè, facilèque penetrat. Oritur ex sicco terreo, tenui, sed copioso tamen humore perfuso, à calore attenuante, non tamen perfectè elaborante, qui priusquam terminum assequatur defiecit. Medicamenta ergo acida, tenuis sunt substantiæ, refrigerant, exsiccant: incîdunt tamen, & aperiunt moderatè humorum ferociam contemperant; foris admota repellunt.
units.tr: The sour taste, such as that of sorrel, penetrates the tongue deeply and easily, without any sense of heat. It arises from dry earth, thin but nevertheless soaked with abundant moisture, by a heat that attenuates but does not perfectly work it, which fails before it reaches its end. Sour medicines are therefore of thin substance; they cool and dry. Yet they cut and open moderately, temper the fierceness of humours, and when applied externally they repel.

units.la: Atque hi sunt sapores extremi, sequuntur medii, dulcis, & pinguis. Ille est in saccharo, qui cum jucunditate linguam oblinit, & replet: hic est in oleo maturo, linguamque oblinit cum lentore, sed sine evidente suavitate. Oriuntur à calore temperato & proportionato, ab optima concoctione, & determinatione hune humidi cum sicco.
units.tr: These are the extreme tastes; the middle ones follow, sweet and fatty. The sweet taste is in sugar, which coats and fills the tongue with pleasantness; the fatty is in ripe oil, which coats the tongue with viscosity but without evident sweetness. They arise from a temperate and proportionate heat, from optimal concoction, and from the due proportion of moist with dry.

units.la: Huiusmodi itaque medicamenta, simillima sunt alimentis. Humor rerum dulcium, est aqueus, sicut in humiditate, & siccitate; unde maturant, leniunt, emolliunt, relaxant, sed magis pinguia.
units.tr: Medicines of this kind are therefore very like foods. The moisture of sweet things is watery, as in humidity and dryness; hence they ripen, soothe, soften and relax, but the fatty ones more so.

units.la: Insipidus sapor, non est sapor; nec enim aqua, aut aliud elementum purum sapidum est. nam sapor suppo-nit elementorum miftionem.quæ autem obscurum habent saporem, insipida dicuntur, ut cucurbita, cæteraque obscurè dulcia. Causa est materia crassa, humore aqueo leviter perfusa, fine manifesto calore.
units.tr: Insipid taste is not a taste; for neither water nor any other pure element is savoury, since taste presupposes a mixture of the elements. Those which have an obscure taste are called insipid, such as gourd and other obscurely sweet things. The cause is thick matter lightly soaked in watery moisture, without manifest heat.

units.la: Notandum porrò, cum pleraque omnia medicamenta varietate partium constent, sinceros sapores raro habere, sed mixtos & confusos; qui nihilominus mixtas vires indicant. denominantur tamen ab hoc aut illo sapore, qui reliquos superat, & dominatur. Quod dico, manifestum est in aceto;quod non tantū acidum est, sed & acre. ita mel non tantum dulce, sed & acre, ita absynthium.
units.tr: It should further be noted that, since nearly all medicines consist of a variety of parts, they rarely have pure tastes, but mixed and confused ones; these nevertheless indicate mixed powers. They are nonetheless named from this or that taste which surpasses the rest and dominates. What I say is plain in vinegar, which is not only sour but also sharp. So honey is not only sweet but also sharp, and so is wormwood.

units.la: Et hęc quidem est ratio explorandi medicamenta ex saporibus: cui tamen experientia adjungenda, alioqui falleris. Nam cichorium lingua sentit amarum, ratio judicat calidū, & tamen experientia ostendit esse frigidum. Idem quidam produnt de opio, esse nimirum frigidum, multum aliis reclamantibus; nec injuria. Quod ad occultas vires attinet, ex solâ experientiâ cognoscuntur, non ratione, ut dictum est.
units.tr: This is indeed the method of testing medicines by their tastes; yet experience must be added to it, otherwise you will be deceived. For chicory the tongue perceives as bitter, reason judges it hot, and yet experience shows it to be cold. Some report the same of opium, that it is cold, though many object, and not without reason. As for hidden powers, they are known from experience alone, not from reason, as has been said.

units.la: CAP. VII. De Medicamentorum compositione.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. On the composition of medicines.

units.la: SI medicamenta simplicia nostris usibus semper convenirent, non opus esset alio confugere. sed quia hoc non contingit, quod à natura desideratur, cogimur arte supplere. Nam scopus φαρμακοποιίας est idoneum medicamentum efficere in eos usus, quos indicatio curativa poscit; niminimirum ut citò, tutò, jucundè curetur æger. Compositum medicamentum dicitur in ordine ad simplex; tale non fit natura, sed arte, ex simplicium conjunctione; conjuncta enim facessunt in unam formam,ut mithridatium. Potissima causa componendi medicamenta, est morborum,causarumque,nec non symptomatum diversitas. Quilibet enim affectus remedium postulat, simplex morbus medicamentum tale, compositus autem compositum exigit medicamentum.Finge jecur non tantum inflammatum,sed & obstructum,certe medicamentum conveniens utriq; usui inservire debet: aliud enim indicat morbus , aliud causa sive obstructio. Quid ? quod pars affecta , ægrique natura imponunt sæpe necessitatem componendi medicamenta. principi enim laboranti parti,nunquam applicantur sola relaxantia,ne robur membri dissolvatur;verum laxantibus admiscentur adstringentia. Accedit, si pars sit in profundo sita, nec alterari possit à medicamento, tum illi dandum est vehiculum, quod tenuitate sua penetrans, eò deducat medicamentum. hoc modo in doloribus capitis acetum additur oleo rosaceo. Sunt & aliæ causæ, nimirum temperamentum, conformatio partis, sensus, ægrique natura. Accedit minus apta medicamenti simplicis qualitas, quæ intentioni nostræ interdum est necessaria; verù affectui non proportionata ; vel quia nimis remissa, vel intensa, vel alioqui maligna: unde oritur necessitas adjungendi aliud simplex. Exempli causa, vis purgatrix agarici excitatur zinzibere, vis rhabarbari spica: malignitas scammonii, corrigitur tragacantha. Sunt quidem aliæ plurimæ causæ, verum hæ præcipuæ judicantur.
units.tr: If simple medicines were always suited to our needs, there would be no need to resort to anything else. But since what nature requires does not always happen, we are forced to make up the difference by art. For the aim of pharmacopoeia [φαρμακοποιίας] is to produce a medicine fit for the uses that the curative indication calls for, namely that the patient may be cured quickly, safely and pleasantly. A compound medicine is so called in relation to a simple one. Such a medicine is not produced by nature but by art, from the combining of simples, since the combined ingredients merge into one form, as in mithridate. The chief reason for compounding medicines is the diversity of diseases, their causes, and also of their symptoms. Every affection calls for its own remedy: a simple disease needs a simple medicine, and a compound one requires a compound medicine. Suppose the liver is not only inflamed but also obstructed. The medicine that suits this must serve both needs, for the disease indicates one thing and the cause, or the obstruction, another. Moreover, the affected part and the patient's constitution often impose the necessity of compounding. For example, in a part that is already weakened, purgatives are never applied alone, lest the strength of the limb be dissolved; instead, astringents are mixed in with the laxatives. Again, if the part lies deep and cannot be altered by the medicine, a vehicle must be given that, by its thinness, penetrates and conveys the medicine there. In this way, for headaches, vinegar is added to rose oil. There are also other causes, namely the temperament, the structure of the part, the sensation, and the nature of the patient. Further, there is the less suitable quality of a simple medicine, which at times is necessary for our purpose but not proportionate to the affection, either because it is too weak, or too strong, or otherwise harmful; from this arises the need to add another simple. For example, the purgative power of agaric is roused by ginger, that of rhubarb by spikenard, and the malignity of scammony is corrected by tragacanth. There are indeed many other causes, but these are judged the principal ones.

units.la: Ut autem medicamentum ritè componas, non tantum requiritur simplicium cognitio, verum etiam morbi, causæ, partisque affectæ. In compositione res ita habet, primò est basis (per similitudinem dicta) hoc est, illud simplex, quod est profligando morbo accommodissimum, & quò cetera in tali compositione respiciunt. Sicut affectus alii simplices sunt, alii compositi, ita bases; alia enim est simplex, alia composita. illa est quæ unū præstat usum, sive componatur ex pluribus simplicibus eiusdem facultatis, sive ex uno tantum, ut aloë in hierapicra. hæc quæ diversos & multiplices respicit usus, constatque pluribus simplicibus, diversa facultate prædictis, unde fiunt medicamenta πολύχρηστα. Basis plerumque compositum denominat, & ex eius viribus judicandum est de tota compositione.
units.tr: To compound a medicine properly, however, one needs knowledge not only of the simples but also of the disease, its causes, and the affected part. In compounding the matter stands thus: first there is the base (so called by way of comparison), that is, the simple which is most suited to overcoming the disease, and to which the other ingredients in such a compound refer. Just as the affections are some simple and some compound, so bases are of two kinds: one is simple, the other compound. The simple base is the one that serves a single use, whether it is made up of several simples of the same faculty or of only one, as aloe in hierapicra. The compound base is the one that regards diverse and manifold uses, and consists of several simples endowed with different faculties; from these come medicines that are of many uses [πολύχρηστα]. The base generally gives its name to the compound, and from its powers the whole compound must be judged.

units.la: Solet basis variari pro morborum temporibus, & symptomatum vehementia. unde alia basis est in principio morbi, alia in statu. neque hoc tantum, sed vires ægri, consuetudo, pars affecta basin variant. Variatur basis pro qualitate & quantitate cæterorum componentium, ei ministrantium. Incumbit medico, reddere mere medicamentum morbo, partique affectæ accommodatum;quod in basis temperatione consistit. Si enim eius vis ignava est, acui debet:si maligna & vehemens, temperari debet benignioribus, quibus conciliatur suavis odor, sapor : quæ ut fieri possint, requiritur aliquid ad formam idoneam conciliandam ; liquores nimirum, decocta, syrupi, oleum, cera. & ut verbo absolvam, in compositione præter basin tria debent considerari, corrigentia, dirigentia ad partem affectam, & demum conservantia, saccharum nimirum aut mel. Basis quantitas est metienda ex eius vehementia. nam si valida sit, ut scammonium, eius minor debet esse in compositione quantitas : sin debilis, ut cassia, paulo maior: sin autem mediocris, ut agaricus, media debet sumi quantitas. quod tamen non est semper invariabile,nam ægri natura, morbus, parsque affecta &c. ut dixi variare cogunt.
units.tr: The base is usually varied according to the stages of the disease and the severity of the symptoms; hence one base is used at the beginning of a disease and another at its height. Not only this, but the strength of the patient, habit, and the affected part also vary the base. The base also varies according to the quality and quantity of the other ingredients that serve it. It is the physician's task to make the medicine altogether suited to the disease and to the affected part, and this consists in the tempering of the base. For if its power is sluggish, it must be sharpened; if it is harmful and violent, it must be tempered with milder ingredients, by which a pleasant smell and taste are imparted. To make this possible, something is needed to give it a suitable form, namely liquids, decoctions, syrups, oil, and wax. And, to sum up, in compounding, besides the base, three things must be considered: correctives, directives towards the affected part, and finally preservatives, namely sugar or honey. The quantity of the base is to be measured by its violence. For if it is strong, like scammony, its quantity in the compound should be smaller; if weak, like cassia, slightly larger; if moderate, like agaric, a medium quantity should be taken. This, however, is not always invariable, for the nature of the patient, the disease, the affected part, and so on, force variation, as I have said.

units.la: Basis composita pro componen-tium tium conditione, variari solet multipliciter, secundum qualitates primas, secundas &c. exempli causa secundum primas, quando in simplici non datur gradus quem cupimus, sed aut remissior, aut intensior. Cupio calidum in secundo gradu, nec datur simplex conveniens, cogor addere aliud simplex: sed hoc opus hic labor, in proportione invenienda; de eâ enim dubitatur; rectius ii sentiunt, qui gradus alterantium ex effectibus sensui manifestis constituunt: nimirum ut gradus æquales constituantur, hoc enim modo temperatum medicamentum, habebit æquales partes caloris, frigoris, humiditatis, & siccitatis. Nempe si summus in temperatis gradus sit sex, tres erunt gradus caloris, & totidem frigoris. in intemperatis, tantum unius contrarii corrumpi debet, quantum alterius generari. Ergo calidum in primo est, quod uno gradu superat temperatum; in secundo, quod duobus superat, & ita deinceps. Frigidum in secundo
units.tr: A compound base is commonly varied in many ways according to the condition of its ingredients, in accordance with the first qualities, the second qualities, and so on. For example, according to the first qualities, when among the simples there is not the degree we desire, but one that is either weaker or stronger. If I want heat in the second degree and no suitable simple is available, I am compelled to add another simple. But this is the labour here, in finding the proportion, for about it there is dispute. Those who establish the degrees of altering qualities from effects manifest to the senses think more correctly: namely, that equal degrees are set up, for in this way a temperate medicine will have equal parts of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. Indeed, if the highest degree in temperates is six, there will be three degrees of heat and as many of cold. In intemperates, only as much of one contrary must be corrupted as of the other is generated. Therefore, that which is hot in the first degree is that which exceeds the temperate by one degree; that which is hot in the second exceeds it by two, and so on. Cold in the second degree

units.la: Note: the marginal notes on the left edge are too faint and cut off to be read reliably. cundo, habet suos caloris gradus; qui tamen non denominant subjectum, quia iis respondent contrarii calidi. Dicitur tamen absolutè frigidum in secundo, quia duobus gradibus superrat, hoc est, habet tres partes frigoris & unam caloris, jam vero uni caloris parti, respondet alia frigoris. at supersunt duæ partes frigidæ, quibus calidæ non respondent, hæ vero subjectum denominant.
