Quæ ratio est in gradibus, eadem est in singulorum mansionibus. nam calidum in prima mansione primi gradus, habet caloris partes 26/1, frigoris 21/6, & ita deinceps. Ex quibus constat errare vehementer Alchindum, de quo vide Averrois colliget. lib. 5. c. 58.
units.tr: ...degree, has its own degrees of heat; these, however, do not name the subject, because they correspond to the contrary hot qualities. Yet it is called cold absolutely in the second degree, because it exceeds by two degrees; that is, it has three parts of cold and one of heat. Now, one part of heat corresponds to one part of cold, but two parts of cold remain to which no heat corresponds, and these name the subject. The same reasoning applies to the degrees as to the mansions of each: for heat in the first mansion of the first degree has 26/1 parts of heat and 21/6 of cold, and so on. From these things it is clear how greatly Alkindus errs, on whom see Averroes' Colliget, book 5, chapter 58.

units.la: In compositione ergo quando plura simplicia eiusdem sunt facultatis, & gradus, compositum erit eiusdem & facultatis, & gradus. verum si plura sint eiusdem quidem facultatis sed non gradus, quemadmodum piper calidum in tertio, & spica in primo, tum spica remittit calorem piperis, & hoc spicæ frigus, oritur- que medicamentum calidum in se- cundo. sin plura simplicia contrariæ facultatis, sed eiusdem gradus, ut ro- sa, & spica, oritur compositum tem- peratum. Quæ est ratio in primis qualitatibus, eadem est in secundis, & tertiis.
units.tr: Therefore, in a compound, when several simples are of the same faculty and degree, the compound will be of the same faculty and degree. But if there are several of the same faculty but not of the same degree, as pepper, hot in the third degree, and spikenard in the first, then spikenard moderates the heat of the pepper, and the cold of the spikenard is moderated by it, and the result is a medicine hot in the second degree. But if several simples are of contrary faculty yet of the same degree, as rose and spikenard, the result is a temperate compound. What holds for the first qualities holds equally for the second and third.

units.la: Quod ad purgantia attinet, diver- simodè ea miscentur: nam interdum, similia similibus : ut vehementia ve- hementibus miscentur. interdum quę miscentur dissimilia sunt, ut medio- cria vehementibus, aut lenientibus. Si similia similibus misceantur, alte- rum autem alterius actionem pro- movet, vide ut compositi quantitas non excedat justam singulorum do- sin. nam quantum additur ab altera parte, tantum alteri demendum. ut si miscere velis rhabarbarum cum aga- rico, compositum non debet excede- re duas drachmas, quæ utriusque se- orsim est dosis. Observa tantum ut illius simplicis plus in compositio- nem veniat, cuius maximus est usus,
units.tr: As regards purgatives, they are mixed in different ways: sometimes like with like, as violent with violent; sometimes the things mixed are unlike, as mild with violent, or with softening agents. If like is mixed with like, and one promotes the action of the other, take care that the quantity of the compound does not exceed the just dose of each. For as much as is added from one side, so much must be taken away from the other. For example, if you wish to mix rhubarb with agaric, the compound ought not to exceed two drachms, which is the separate dose of each. Only take care that more of that simple enters the compound whose use is greatest,

units.la: & necessitas ad curandum morbum præsentem. sin lenientia mediocri-bus, aut vehementibus misceantur, compositi dosis non erit minor,quam singulorum seorsim.sin valida adjun-gantur mediocribus ; ad ea acuenda minui debet dosis vehementium, re-licta mediocrium usitata.
units.tr: and which is necessary for curing the present disease. But if softening agents are mixed with moderate or violent ones, the dose of the compound will be no less than the separate doses of each. If strong ones are added to moderate ones, the dose of the violent ones must be reduced to sharpen them, while the usual dose of the moderate ones is kept.

units.la: Porro quia basis est compositi medicamenti quasi anima , eius ad reli-qua ingredientia proportio diligen-ter est consideranda , nec unquam commitendum ut vehementia mag-na copia basi adjungantur.ergo basis vehemens,minorem exigit quantita-tem , debilis vero maiorem : verum corrigentia,quæ vel augent , vel mi-nuunt vim basis,in minore, quam ea, sumi oportet. at quæ corrigunt basis maligunitatem , proprietate. aliqua æquare eam debent. Quod ad diri-gentia attinet;si basis magna sit quã-titas (ut in medicamentis debilibus) dirigentium minor debet esse quan-titas.sin basis sit vehemens,ac proin-de parvæ quantitatis,ut colocynthis; dirigentium quantitas æquare debent basin. Dirigentia siquidem debilia sunt, nec ad partem affectam exigua dosi, basin deducere possunt. De formis medicamentorum agere superfluum videtur; eæ enim omnibus sunt notæ, sicut & differentiæ, ut pilulæ, emplastra, linctus &c.
units.tr: Moreover, since the base is, as it were, the soul of the compound medicine, its proportion to the other ingredients must be carefully considered, and it must never be allowed that large amounts of violent ingredients be added to the base. Therefore a violent base requires a smaller quantity, and a weak base a larger; but correctives, which either increase or diminish the power of the base, ought to be taken in smaller quantity than the base. But those which correct the malignity of the base should match it in property. As for directives: if the quantity of the base is large (as in weak medicines), the quantity of the directives should be smaller; but if the base is violent, and therefore of small quantity, as colocynth, the quantity of the directives should equal the base. For directives are weak, and cannot convey the base to the affected part in a small dose. It seems superfluous to treat of the forms of medicines, for these are known to everyone, as are their differences, such as pills, plasters, linctuses and so on.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: De Purgatione.
units.tr: On Purgation.

units.la: VT purgatio recte intelligatur, sciendum corpus humanum in tres regiones dividi. Prima harum, quæ sentina corporis dicitur, à gulâ ad mediam hepatis partem extenditur. Secunda est à medio hepatis ad tenues partium venas. Tertia regio comprehendit venas capillares, necnon corporis habitum. si humores sola quantitate in vasis peccant, phlebotomia evacuantur; sicut cacochymia eorundem cathartico; sin humores in corporis habitu contineantur, sudoribus, & insensibili perspiratu discutiuntur. Hæc tria genera evacuatiocuationum sunt universalia, quia totum corpus purgatur. nam quæ ab hac, aut illa evacuant, purgationes sunt particulares, ut diuretica, bechica.
units.tr: So that purgation may be rightly understood, it must be known that the human body is divided into three regions. The first of these, which is called the sink of the body, extends from the throat to the middle of the liver. The second is from the middle of the liver to the fine veins of the parts. The third region comprises the capillary veins, and also the habit of the body. If the humours sin only in quantity within the vessels, they are evacuated by phlebotomy; likewise, when there is cacochymia of the same humours, they are evacuated by a cathartic; but if the humours are contained in the habit of the body, they are dispersed by sweats and insensible perspiration. These three kinds of evacuation are universal, because the whole body is purged. Those evacuations, however, which discharge from this or that part are particular purgations, such as diuretics and bechics.

units.la: Est autem Purgatio evacuatio humoris, qualitate peccantis, sive per superiora, sive inferiora, medicamenti vi facta.
units.tr: Purgation, moreover, is the evacuation of a humour that sins in its quality, whether upwards or downwards, effected by the power of a medicine.

units.la: Purgatio indicatur à cacochymia, si vires ferant, cæteraq; consentiant. Quod autem expurgat, & humorem expellit, est facultas naturalis irritata à pharmaco: nam purgantibus non esse vim trahendi humorem, sed irritandi tantum facultatem multi non improbabiliter asserunt. Medicamenta hoc efficientia, qualitate ut loquuntur occulta (hæc illa sunt quæ determinatum tantum humorē trahere creduntur) καθαρτικὰ dicuntur. At quæ manifesta, ut lubricantia, detergentia, ὑπαγωγικὰ communiter vocantur. Vis illa peculiaris, qua medicamenta hunc, aut illum humorem purgant, specifica est; sequiturque formam substantialem, & ab ea nascitur. citur : quanquam nihil impedit corrupta forma manere in misto. Videmus enim scammonium, quantumvis corruptum, vim purgandi non amittere ; idem in rhabarbaro tosto videre est.
units.tr: Purgation is indicated by cacochymia, if the strength allows and the other circumstances agree. What expels the humour and purges is a natural faculty roused by the drug: for many assert, not without reason, that purgatives do not have a power of drawing the humour, but only of stirring up the faculty. Medicines that do this by a quality they call occult (these are those which are believed to draw only one determinate humour) are called katharktika. Those which act by evident qualities, such as lubricants and detergents, are commonly called hypagogika. That peculiar power by which medicines purge this or that humour is specific; it follows from the substantial form and arises from it, although nothing prevents a corrupted form from remaining in the mixture. For we see that scammony, however corrupted, does not lose its power of purging; the same may be seen in roasted rhubarb.

units.la: Dubitant multi, nec injuria, an medicamentum aliquod, hunc aut illum tantum humorem purget: an indifferenter quosvis. & certè pauca sunt, quæ unum tantum trahunt, si experientiæ creditur. Quidquid est, medicamenta pro varietate humorum peccantium sunt quadruplicia: chylagoga, melanagoga, phlegmagoga, hydragoga.
units.tr: Many doubt, and not without reason, whether some medicine purges only this or that humour, or whether it purges any indifferently. And certainly there are few which draw only one, if we trust experience. Whatever the case, medicines are fourfold according to the variety of the humours that sin: chylagogues, melanagogues, phlegmagogues, and hydragogues.

units.la: Est & alia eorum divisio, nam quædam vomitu hoc præstant, quædam dejectione, quædam vehementer, quædam blandè, nonnulla medio modo. Blandè per inferiora purgant bilem, manna, tamarindi, cassia. mediocriter rhabarbarum, & aloë. vehementer scammonium: eadem est cæterorum ratio. Vomitum leviter provocant aqua hordei, syrupus acetosus; tosus; potentius succus raphani, decoctum radicum betonicæ; validissimè radices hellebori albi, antimonium. Observatum est à majoribus medicamenta quædam, quamvis determinatum humorem purgent, magis tamen ab unâ parte, quam aliâ: nam agaricus & colocynthis quamvis pituitam purgent, magis tamen à capite trahunt, rhabarbarum à jecore, hermodactyli ab articulis. nisi mavis dicere, humorem purgandum in ijs partibus magis turgere; quod in capite est manifestum. Ex his alijsque simplicibus purgantibus variæ compositiones emergunt. nam sunt quædã composita, quæ ore sumuntur quædam per anum immittuntur; tum quædam sunt liquida, quædam solida. In omni purgatione prima indicatio sumitur à causâ morbificâ, seu cocochymiâ; deinde à viribus ægri, quatenus eam aut permittunt, aut impediunt: quibus adjunguntur pars affecta &c. Humores ergo vitiosi qui à natura superari nequeunt, expellendi pellēndi sunt. non ergo debetur purgatio sanis, sed aut ægris, aut neutris, quanquam nihil impedit, sanum corpus purgari leniente, & blando pharmaco, quale est manna, cassia. Ætas media optimè purgationē fert ; nam senilis, & infantilis ob debilitatem ægrè. quanquam blandè purgantia & senes & infantes ferre possint, magis tamen illi. Sed si infans admodum sit cacochymus, nihil impedit nutrici aliquid mediocriter purgans propinari, ejus enim vires lacti imprimentur, aut infanti ipsi suppositorium, aut aliquid lene per os dari potest. Si sexum spectes, viri magis idonei sunt fœminis. at si his fluant menses medicamentum non convenit. Gravidæ difficulter purgantur; si tamē faciendum est, fiat à mense quarto ad septimū, teste Hippocrate 1.4. nam primis, & postremis mensibus, ligamenta facilius rumpuntur. Si corpora spectes; temperata purgationes maxime ferunt; at sicca, frigida, macilenta, laxa, minus. sicut qui animo facilè linquuntur, ac qui levi de causa vomunt. Omnes tamen purgandi si vires validæ sint, & necessitas urgeat.Regio temperata,tempus vernum, & autumnale, purgationibus valde conveniunt. Aëris constitutio, justo calidior, vires corporis exhaurit. Vnde sub cane, & ante canem difficiliores sunt purgationes.at frigidus aër corpora densat, & humores cogit.Eæ purgationes censentur bonæ, quibus talia educuntur, qualia debent: hoc enim modo naturaliberatur,& facile fert hujusmodi purgationes.
units.tr: There is also another division of them: for some accomplish this by vomiting, some by stool; some act vehemently, some gently, and some in a middle way. Gently by the lower passages purge bile: manna, tamarinds, cassia. Moderately rhubarb and aloe; vehemently scammony; the rule is the same for the rest. Vomiting is lightly provoked by barley water and sour syrup, roasted; more powerfully by juice of radish and decoction of the roots of betony; most strongly by the roots of white hellebore and antimony. It has been observed by our elders that certain medicines, although they purge a determinate humour, nevertheless act more on one part than another: for agaric and colocynth, though they purge phlegm, nevertheless draw more from the head; rhubarb from the liver; hermodactyls from the joints. Unless you prefer to say that the humour to be purged swells more in those parts, which is evident in the head. From these and other simple purgatives various compounds arise: for some compounds are taken by mouth, some are introduced through the anus; further, some are liquid, some solid. In every purgation the first indication is taken from the morbific cause, or cacochymia; then from the strength of the patient, insofar as it either permits or hinders it; to which are added the affected part, etc. Vitiated humours, therefore, which cannot be overcome by nature, must be expelled. Purgation is therefore not owed to the healthy, but to the sick or to neither; although nothing prevents a healthy body from being purged by a mild and gentle drug, such as manna or cassia. Middle age bears purgation best; for old age and infancy, on account of weakness, bear it with difficulty. Although old people and infants can bear gently purging medicines, it is nevertheless more so for the former. But if an infant is very cacochymic, nothing prevents a moderately purging medicine being given to the nurse, for her strength is imparted to the milk, or a suppository may be given to the infant itself, or something mild may be given by mouth. If you regard sex, men are more suitable than women; but if menses flow in women, a medicine is not suitable. Pregnant women are purged with difficulty; if nevertheless it must be done, let it be done from the fourth to the seventh month, as Hippocrates teaches in book 4; for in the first and last months the ligaments are more easily broken. If you regard bodies: temperate bodies bear purgations best; but dry, cold, emaciated and lax bodies bear them less well, as do those who faint easily in spirit, and those who vomit for a slight cause. Yet all may be purged if their strength is sound and necessity presses. A temperate region and the spring and autumn seasons are very suitable for purgations. A constitution of air that is too hot drains the strength of the body; hence purgations are more difficult under the dog-star and before the dog-star. But cold air thickens bodies and binds the humours. Those purgations are considered good by which such things are expelled as ought to be; for in this way nature is freed, and it bears purgations of this kind easily.

units.la: Cæterum de humoris conditione, qualis ea debeat esse, dubitatur.Hippocrates enim humores crudos purgari non vult,nisi turgeant; proinde crudi primò sunt coquendi, tum purgandi. Crudus humor est duplex; alius est infra sanguinem, qui justam concoctionem non est assequutus, ut pituita. alius supra sanguinem; utraque nimirum bilis.Quod ad pituitam attinet; si ea sit sanguis inchoatus, purgari non magis debet, quam ipse sanguis. crudus enim est relinquendus naturæ ad coctionem, & corporis nutritionem : at jam coctus, cum sit sanguis, expelli non debet, nisi peccet quantitate, ut in plethora; at utraque bilis, & pituita excrementitia naturaliter alioqui se habentes, quoad qualitatem coqui ulterius non debent, habent enim, terminum à natura præscriptum: hujusmodi enim humores cum sint excrementitij, corpus nostrum alere nequeunt: proinde si abundent, sine coctione sunt educendi : at si putrescere incipiant (nam cruditas eorum est putredo) in venis, quanquam eorum substantia non possit reddi corpori alendo utilis; tamen quoad qualitates, eæ possunt fieri benigniores, naturæque nostræ similiores, proinde non prius educēdi veniunt, quam putredo fuerit evicta. Ergò hujusmodi humores in principio morbi, cum sint crudi, educi non debent. Expectanda itaque est concoctio, quæ utilia, ab inutilibus seperat. At si turgeant, minenturque in nobiliora viscera impetum, educendi sunt statim in principio. Alij contra differunt, negantque hujusmodi coctionem esse expectandam. Nam quid facit coctio? Refrenat inquis putredinem. Quid? humorne malus in corpore relinquetur, & ubi melior evaserit expelletur? Hoc quidem inauditum est. Tum coctio ista, humores incrassat, coctique fiunt crassiores, difficiliusque expelluntur. at crudi cum tenues sint multo facilius movebuntur; crudi ergo debebant expelli, & in principio morbi. Nam quid necesse est, tamdiu ægrum torquere, concoctionem expectando, quem posses statim morbo liberare? At dices, in principio si hoc fiat, interpellabitur crisis; hæc est causa quare tam paucæ hodie conspiciuntur crises. Quid hoc ad rem? melius est enim humorem peccantem statim educere, quam permittere ejus cum natura pugnam, cujus eventus admodum modum sit incertus. Certè Galeni ratio ad Aphorismum, eget divinatore. Ait enim si coctionem expectes, naturam habebis adjutricem. Ergo ita statuunt; in principio morbi, etiamsi materia non turgeat, educendam tamen benigno & commodo cathartico; caeterum si viae sint obstructione aliqua impeditae, aut humores viscidi; non prius purgandum, quam materia fuerit attenuata, & viae expeditae. In hac materiae praeparatione, & vasorum apertione, totam coctionem positam esse contendunt; negantque omnes evacuationes symptomaticas (multae enim sunt) esse vituperandas, verum quae solo tempore sunt symptomaticae, anticipantes nimirum coctionem, utilissimae esse possunt.
units.tr: Moreover, it is doubted what the condition of the humour ought to be. For Hippocrates does not wish raw humours to be purged unless they swell; therefore raw humours must first be concocted, and then purged. A raw humour is of two kinds: one lies below the blood, which has not attained due concoction, such as phlegm; the other lies above the blood, namely both kinds of bile. As far as phlegm is concerned: if it is blood begun, it ought no more to be purged than the blood itself; for it is raw and must be left to nature for concoction and the nourishment of the body; but when already concocted, since it is blood, it must not be expelled unless it sins in quantity, as in plethora. But both bile and excrementitious phlegm, naturally otherwise disposed, ought not to be further concocted in quality, for they have a term prescribed by nature; such humours, being excrementitious, cannot nourish our body; therefore, if they abound, they are to be led out without concoction. But if they begin to putrefy (for their rawness is putrefaction) in the veins, although their substance cannot be made useful to the nourishing body, nevertheless as to their qualities they can become more benign and more similar to our nature; therefore they are not to be led out until the putrefaction has been overcome. Therefore humours of this kind, at the beginning of a disease, since they are raw, ought not to be led out. Concoction, which separates the useful from the useless, is therefore to be awaited. But if they swell and threaten an impetus upon the more noble viscera, they must be led out at once at the beginning. Others, on the contrary, differ, and deny that such concoction is to be awaited. For what does concoction do? It restrains putrefaction, you say. What then? Will the bad humour be left in the body, and expelled only when it has become better? This indeed is unheard of. Then, that concoction thickens the humours, and when concocted they become thicker and are expelled with more difficulty; but raw humours, since they are thin, will be moved much more easily; raw humours therefore ought to be expelled, and at the beginning of the disease. For why is it necessary to torment the patient so long, awaiting concoction, when you could free him from the disease at once? But you will say that if this is done at the beginning, the crisis will be interrupted; this is the reason why so few crises are seen today. What has this to do with the matter? It is better, indeed, to lead out the sinning humour at once than to permit its struggle with nature, the outcome of which is quite uncertain. Surely Galen's reasoning on the Aphorism needs a diviner. For he says that if you await concoction, you will have nature as a helper. Therefore they establish thus: at the beginning of the disease, even if the matter does not swell, it is nevertheless to be led out by a benign and convenient cathartic; but if the passages are impeded by some obstruction, or the humours are viscid, purgation is not to be done before the matter has been attenuated and the passages cleared. They contend that all the concoction lies in this preparation of the matter and opening of the vessels; and they deny that all symptomatic evacuations (for they are many) are to be blamed, but that those which are symptomatic only in time, anticipating concoction, can be most useful.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: De dosi medicamenti purgantis.
units.tr: On the dose of a purgative medicine.

units.la: SI ullibi opus est artificiosa conjectura, in purgationibus certè (quae exacta scientia comprehendi nequenequeunt) opus est, propter varietatē non modo morborum, sed & corporis humani constitutionem. Nam quanquam humor indicet medicamentum, ejus tamen dosis, & vis, ex situ humoris in corpore & ægri viribus pendet. Vnde factum, ut corpus humanum divisum sit in tres regiones, quemadmodum diximus: nam si in tertia regione abundet humor noxius, validioribus opus est purgantibus, quam si in primâ turgeret regione. Medicamenta benedicta, seu leniter purgantia, exhibentur fere unciarum pondere: Validissima autē granorum; mediocria drachmarum. Eadem ratio dosis observatur in vomitorijs; in quibus semper habenda est ratio virium; pro quarum varietate, medicamentorum doses augentur, & minuuntur. Vitandæ tamen nimis magnæ, parvæque evacuationes: illæ enim tormina excitant, humores perturbant, hæmulto majora damna corpori inferunt, convulsiones nimirum incurabiles, aliaque symptomata.
units.tr: If skilled judgement is needed anywhere, it certainly is in purging, which cannot be grasped by exact knowledge, because of the variety not only of diseases but also of the constitution of the human body. For although the humour indicates the medicine, its dose and strength depend on the position of the humour in the body and on the patient's strength. Hence the human body is divided into three regions, as we have said: if the harmful humour abounds in the third region, stronger purgatives are needed than if it swells in the first region. Gentle or mildly purging medicines are usually given in doses of about an ounce; the most powerful are given in grains, and medium ones in drachms. The same principle of dosage applies to emetics, in which the patient's strength must always be taken into account; the doses of the medicines are increased or decreased according to the variety of strength. Yet evacuations that are too large or too small should be avoided, for the former excite gripings, disturb the humours, and do far greater damage to the body, namely incurable convulsions and other symptoms.

units.la: Purgatio nunquam est judicanda ex humorum copia, sed si talia evacuentur, qualia debent, humor nimirum peccans, & æger facilè toleret. Purgationum quædam una vice totam educunt materiam, quæ perfectæ dicuntur: aliæ pluribus vicibus, in corporibus nimirum debilibus. nam quanquam humorum sit copia, quia tamen vires debiles sunt, repetenda est purgatio, nec tota materia simul educenda, ne vires concidant. Legitimum ordinem remediorum administrandorum, indicat causarum ordo; ita tamen ut ante oculos habeamus id, quod maximè urget. Semper itaque est primò tollenda consequētium causa. ex quibus facilè est determinare an phlebotomia sit purgationi præferenda, an contra. Nam si magna sit necessitas mittendi sanguinem, quæ moram non patitur, ut in inflammationibus partium, certè purgatio est postponenda. at si prima regio sit impura, morbus autem ferat moram, postponenda est phlebotomia, mia, ne crudus & putridus humor, à vasis ex haustis attrahantur. Humor itaque vitiosus in ventriculo, primisque venis, statim est educendus, nisi forsan sit viscidus; tum enim est incidendus & præparandus. at corruptus, quacunque sit regione corporis, est pariter educendus. humorem putrescentem in vasis, etiamsi viæ sint liberæ, statim expurgare non expedit, sed expectandum est tempus oportunum, cum nimirum in urina apparent concoctionum signa; nisi forsan turgeat. tum quoque statim educendus, & quanquam humorum expectanda sit concoctio, nihil impedit, etiam in principio, minorativam dari purgationem, quo natura copia levata facilius coquere possit quod superest. In purgatione cavendus est morbi paroxismus, nisi forsan sit febris quartana, aut alia similis conjuncta cum virium robore: hic enim, materia crassa, viscidaque ægrè admodum cedit; proinde nihil obest purgare eo tempore quo movetur, tum enim facilius detrahitur materia noxia. In alijs morbis, paroxifmis destitutis, eligendæ sunt horæ matutinæ. tum enim pharmacum est fumendum jeiuno ventriculo, & fi fortefuerit, dormiendum paululum, post surgendum. sin debile, vitandus somnus: hoc enim modo facilius in actu deducitur medicamentum. At quibus vijs educendus fit humor, docebit locus affectus, aut humoris inclinatio. Nam fi caput est male affectum à gravante materia; per os, nares, educitur. sin totum corpus, per intestina commodissimè evacuatur. sin ventriculus, vicinæque regiones laborent; per superiora feliciter evomitur. Cave tamen patiaris humorem fluere ad partem affectam; nam fi caput vehementer laboret, ascendant verò ifthuc ex alijs partibus vapores, tum non vomitu (nisi laboret ventriculus) sed per inferiora, revellenda est materia. Quicquid est, alij alijs evacuationibus sunt magis idonei, nec ad vomitum incitandus qui difficulter ferre potest. Talis est phti-ficus, aut angustum habens pectus: nam revera, licet vomitus à multis inveteratis affectibus liberet eos, quibus purgatio non profuit, tamen est nimis violentus, & minus naturalis. VndeHippocrates supra robustos, infra debiles purgari vult. si sympto-mata evanescant, redeat appetentia, somnus, aliaquè tum demum utilem esse purgationem cognosces liquidò.
units.tr: A purgation is never to be judged by the quantity of humours evacuated, but by whether those evacuated are of the right kind, namely the humour that is at fault, and whether the patient tolerates it easily. Some purgatives draw off the whole matter at one time, and these are called complete; others are given several times, especially in weak bodies. For although there is an abundance of humours, because the strength is weak the purgation must be repeated, and the whole matter must not be removed at once, lest the strength collapse. The order of the causes indicates the proper order of administering remedies, yet so that we keep before our eyes what presses most. Therefore the cause of the consequences must always be removed first. From this it is easy to determine whether phlebotomy is to be preferred to purging or the reverse. For if there is great necessity to let blood, one that brooks no delay, as in inflammations of parts, then purging must be postponed. But if the first region is impure and the disease allows of delay, phlebotomy is to be postponed, lest the raw and putrid humour be drawn from the swallowed contents into the vessels. Therefore a vitiated humour in the stomach and the first veins must be drawn off at once, unless perhaps it is viscous; for then it must be cut and prepared first. A corrupt humour, however, wherever it is in the body, must likewise be drawn off. A putrefying humour in the vessels, even if the passages are open, should not be purged at once; instead the suitable time must be awaited, namely when signs of concoction appear in the urine, unless perhaps it swells. Then too it must be drawn off at once; and although the concoction of the humours is to be awaited, nothing prevents a mildly purgative dose being given even at the beginning, so that, with the bulk lightened, nature can more easily concoct what remains. During purging the paroxysm of the disease must be avoided, unless perhaps it is a quartan fever or some similar one combined with robust strength; for in these the matter is thick and viscous and yields with great difficulty, so there is no harm in purging at the time when it is moving, since the harmful matter is then drawn off more easily. In other diseases, when there are no paroxysms, morning hours should be chosen. The medicine is then to be taken on an empty stomach, and if the strength is good, a little sleep may be taken afterwards and then one rises. If the strength is weak, sleep is to be avoided, for in this way the medicine is more easily carried into action. By what passages the humour is to be drawn off, the site of the affection or the tendency of the humour will show. For if the head is badly affected by a burdensome matter, it is drawn off through the mouth and nostrils. If the whole body, it is most conveniently evacuated through the intestines. If the stomach and neighbouring regions suffer, it is happily vomited up through the upper passages. Take care, however, not to allow the humour to flow towards the affected part; for if the head suffers violently while vapours rise there from other parts, the matter must be drawn away not by vomiting (unless the stomach is affected) but downwards. Whatever the case, some evacuations suit some patients better than others, and one should not induce vomiting in someone who can hardly bear it. Such is the consumptive, or the person with a narrow chest; for indeed, although vomiting relieves many long-standing affections in which purging has not helped, it is too violent and less natural. Hence Hippocrates wishes the robust to be purged from above and the weak from below. If the symptoms fade, and appetite and sleep return, you will clearly recognise that purging has then at last been useful.

units.la: CAP. X. De Phlebotomia.
units.tr: CHAPTER X. On Phlebotomy.

units.la: SIcut purgatio est magnum remedium, & evacuatio universalis; ita phlebotomia. Verùm illa respicit certos humores qualitate peccantes, hęc eorum quantitatem, omnemque humorem indifferenter ex venis elicit, primo quidem ex venis proximis, secundario ex remotioribus, quia omnes sunt inter se continuæ. Hoc præstat purgationi, quod pro arbitrio sisti potest, quod in purgatione fieri nequit. Eius tres sunt præcipui scopi; magnus nimirum morbus, ætas florens, & demum virium róbur. Quod non est ita accipiendum, quasi omnis magnus morbus phlebotomiam exigat, cum purgatio sit etiam in magno morbo, sed is demum, qui à plethora oritur. Omnis ergo talis morbus, sive præsens, sive imminens, phlebotomiam indicat. Nã plethora est venosi generis affectio, à redundantiâ sanguinis, secundario habitus corporis; minuitur promptè venæ sectione: & quãquam in sanis integraque valetudine præditis sæpe infit, diu tamen consistere nequit; humores enim aut putrescunt, aut fluxiones concitant, aut aliquod aliud damnum inferunt. Morbus magnus à phlebotomia indicatus, non tantum est is, qui essentia & natura talis, sed & qui ob præstantiam partis est magnus: nam parva inflammatio ignobilis partis à sanguine orta, non poscit semper phlebotomiam; cum leviore remedio facile curari possit. at si eadem sit in parte nobili, jecore, liene, venæ sectionem requirit; non quidem gratia sui, seu ob affectus magnitudinem, sed, ut dixi ob partis præstantiam.
units.tr: Just as purging is a great remedy and a universal evacuation, so is phlebotomy. But the former concerns certain humours that sin in quality, whereas the latter concerns their quantity, and draws out any humour indifferently from the veins, first from the nearby veins and secondarily from the more distant ones, because all are continuous with one another. Phlebotomy has this advantage over purging, that it can be stopped at will, which cannot be done in purging. It has three principal aims: a great disease, a flourishing age, and finally the strength of the patient's vigour. This is not to be understood as meaning that every great disease calls for phlebotomy, since purging is also used in a great disease; but it is the disease that arises from plethora. Every such disease, whether present or threatening, therefore indicates phlebotomy. For plethora is an affection of the venous kind, arising from a redundance of blood, a condition of the body's habit; it is quickly relieved by opening a vein. And although it often arises in healthy people of sound constitution, it cannot long persist, for the humours either putrefy, or provoke fluxions, or inflict some other harm. A great disease that calls for phlebotomy is not only one that is great in its essence and nature, but also one that is great because of the excellence of the part affected. For a slight inflammation of an ignoble part arising from blood does not always demand phlebotomy, since it can easily be cured with a milder remedy. But if the same occurs in a noble part, such as the liver or spleen, it requires opening of a vein; not indeed for its own sake, or because of the magnitude of the affection, but, as I have said, because of the excellence of the part.

units.la: Venæ sectio, quanquam videtur, non est tamen simplex remedium, sed multiplex. usurpatur enim ad refrigerandum; quod facit minuendo sanguinem; caloris fontem: eo enim sublato necesse est corpus frigescere. Nonnunquam sistimus sanguinem fluentem, ut initio inflammationum in pleuritide, phrenitide. ubi locum habet revulsio; quæ est humorum fluentium in contrariam partem aversio, ut eorum impetus sistatur. Contrarietas est respectu originis fluxionis; cum scilicet humor fluens revocatur ad eam partem à quâ fluxit, nisi quid impediat; aut certe in partem proximam; ut si à capite descendant humores in latus.
units.tr: Although it seems simple, opening a vein is not a single remedy but a manifold one. It is used for cooling, which it does by diminishing the blood, the source of heat; for when this is removed the body must grow cold. Sometimes we stop blood that is flowing, as at the beginning of inflammations in pleurisy or phrenitis, where revulsion has its place. Revulsion is the turning away of flowing humours into the opposite part, so that their onrush is checked. The opposition is with respect to the origin of the fluxion: namely, when the flowing humour is called back to the part from which it flowed, unless something hinders this; or at least to a neighbouring part, as when humours descend from the head to the side.

units.la: Secatur ejusdem lateris vena, qua humor inde descendens quasi revocatur ad suum fontem, aut certe intercipitur. Ita cauteria adhibentur capiti, cum inde cadunt humores in pulmones. Cæterum si origo fluxionis ignoretur, revellendum est ad distantissimas partes; sic enim retrahuntur humores ab omnibus partibus, quæ mittere possunt. Maximè videndum, ut vena secetur, quæ societatem habet proximam, & communionem cum parte affecta; alioqui nihil juverit revulsio. nam laborante latere dextro, oppositi sectio nihil juvat; quandoquidem non est proxima communio venarum, sed remota; quo modo omnes venæ communicant. at laborante crure altero, alterum secatur, propter proximam communionem ab eâdem venâ cavâ. Quicquid sit, cum humores fluere incipiunt in partem, revellendi sunt ad originem suam. nam partim impacti, nõ possunt sectione extrahi; ut post cõstabit. Ergo in angina, peripneumonia, lethargo &c. statim revelli debet materia. neq; hoc tãtùm, sed si metus sit fluxionis, ut in vulneratis, idem præsidium est adhibendum.
units.tr: The vein of the same side is opened, by which the humour descending from there is, as it were, called back to its source, or at least intercepted. So cauteries are applied to the head when humours fall from there into the lungs. Otherwise, if the origin of the fluxion is unknown, the revulsion must be made to the most distant parts; for in this way the humours are drawn back from all the parts that can send them. Above all care must be taken that the vein be opened which has close connection and communication with the affected part; otherwise the revulsion will do no good. For when the right side is affected, opening a vein on the opposite side does no good, since the communication of the veins there is not close but remote, although all the veins communicate with one another. But when one leg is affected, the other is opened, because of the close communication from the same vena cava. However it may be, when humours begin to flow into a part, they must be revulsed to their origin; for once they have become lodged, they cannot be drawn out by bleeding, as will be established later. Therefore in quinsy, peripneumonia, lethargy, and so on, the matter must be revulsed at once. And not only this, but if there is fear of a fluxion, as in the wounded, the same safeguard must be applied.

units.la: Derivatio est humorum, in venis partis affecta contentorum, per vicina aversio. Hæc non respiciunt humores fluentes, sed, ut dixi, contentos & quiescentes, non autem parti impactos, aut in corporis habitum effusos. Vt si inflammatio sit inguinis sinistri, secta vena poplitis dextri pedis, derivat ad latus sanguinem. Sectio hæc non habet locum in principio inflammationum, sed postea; ut humor nimirum venarum evacuetur. at si humor est parti impactus, inde educi nequit revulsione, aut derivatione, sed medicamentis localibus. Plenitudo totius corporis commodissimè evacuatur, secta interiore vena cubiti dextri lateris, quæ à vena cava, & jecore, validissimè trahit. maximè si corpus turget sanguine laudabili, aut alioqui bilioso: nam si abundet melancholia, contrarij lateris in cubito vena secari debet. Basilica secta evacuat totum corpus, maximè verò partes infra collum. nimis commodè idé fit salvatella pertusa. partes supra claviculas sitas expeditissimè liberat humera-ria, seu cephalica : idem fit in funicu-lo, sed tardius. Vena communis ex basilica & cephalica, quæ mediana dicitur, circa mediam flexuram sita (quam Arabes venã nigram vocant) à superioribus pariter, & inferiori-bus revellit. Si affectus aliquis sit in partibus infra renes, cruris vena secta eum tollit expeditè. Renes ipsi inflammati, melius curantur secta vena cubiti, quam partium inferiorum. Nam promptius discendunt humores quam ascendunt. Qua de causa fluxus menstruorum, & hæmorrhoi-dum sistitur secta cubiti vena. Verum si menses subsistant, provocantur, secta saphena, aut vena poplitis. Arteriæ, propter periculum, non facilè secantur.
units.tr: Derivation is the diversion, through neighbouring parts, of humours contained in the veins of an affected part. These rules do not concern humours that are flowing, but, as I said, humours that are contained and at rest, not those lodged in the part or poured out through the body's habit. For example, if there is an inflammation of the left groin, opening the vein of the popliteal region of the right foot draws the blood to the other side. This bleeding has no place at the beginning of inflammations but later on, so that the humour in the veins is evacuated. But if the humour has lodged in the part, it cannot be drawn out by revulsion or derivation, but only by local remedies. Fullness of the whole body is most conveniently evacuated by opening the inner vein of the right arm at the elbow, which draws most strongly from the vena cava and the liver, especially if the body is swollen with sound blood or with bile; but if melancholy abounds, the vein at the elbow of the opposite side should be opened. Opening the basilic vein evacuates the whole body, but chiefly the parts below the neck. The saphena opened in the pierced form does this quite conveniently. The humeral or cephalic vein most quickly frees the parts situated above the collarbones; the same happens with the funicular vein, but more slowly. The common vein formed from the basilic and cephalic, which is called the median, lying near the middle bend of the arm (which the Arabs call the black vein), draws away from both upper and lower parts alike. If some affection is in the parts below the kidneys, opening the vein of the leg quickly removes it. Inflamed kidneys themselves are better treated by opening the vein of the elbow than that of the lower parts, for humours descend more readily than they ascend. For this reason a flux of the menses or of the haemorrhoids is stopped by opening the vein of the elbow. But if the menses are suppressed, they are provoked by opening the saphena or the vein of the popliteal region. Arteries are not easily opened, because of the danger.

units.la: Hæ sunt præcipuæ venæ, quarum in sectionibus est usus ad sanguinem vacuandum.
units.tr: These are the principal veins whose opening is used for evacuating blood.

units.la: Videndum tamen ne vires sint languidæ, aut dissolutæ; quo in casu, cum sanguis sit vitæ thesaurus, nihil ejus demendum est. at si vires consistent in corpore valido, tum copiosè auferri potest.
units.tr: Care must be taken, however, that the strength is not weak or broken down; in that case, since blood is the treasury of life, none of it should be taken away. But if the strength holds up in a sound body, then a large amount may be drawn off.

units.la: Si ætates spectes; media ætas est validissima, in ea enim vires omnes sunt constantissimæ, fertque magnas sanguinis evacuationes. Ætas decrepita contra se habens, copiosam sanguinis evacuationem non fert. Ætas puerilis ante annum decimum quartum, valida quidem est; sed quia mollis & humida est, non fert sectionem; satis enim sponte evacuatur & dissipatur insensibiliter. His tamen non obstantibus, si vires ferant, & morbus exigat in quacunque ætate, nisi forsan lactans & sit, tentanda sectio est. Notum est exemplum filij Abumeron Avenzoaris, curati venæ sectione, cum adhuc trimus esset. vide Averroëm 7 colli: cap.3.
units.tr: If you consider age: middle age is the most robust, for in it all the powers are most steady, and it bears large evacuations of blood. Decrepit age, on the other hand, does not bear a copious evacuation of blood. Childhood, before the fourteenth year, is indeed vigorous, but because it is soft and moist it does not bear bleeding; for it is evacuated and dissipated sufficiently of its own accord, and imperceptibly. Nevertheless, notwithstanding these things, if the strength bears it and the disease demands it at any age, unless perhaps the child is still nursing, bleeding should be tried. The example of the son of Abumeron Avenzoar, cured by opening a vein when he was still three years old, is well known. See Averroes, Colliget, book 7, chapter 3.

units.la: Si sexum pectes, viri facilius tolerant venæ sectionem, quam mulieres, robustiores enim sunt.
units.tr: If you consider sex: men more easily tolerate opening of a vein than women, for they are more robust.

units.la: Inter anni tempora ver est commodissimum, quia maximè temperatum: tum: ad quod proximè accedit autumnus ; sequitur æstas, quæ aptior sectioni venæ est , quam hyems. ita faciendum est, si tempus eligendum venit: at ubi necesse est,omni tempore est molienda sectio.
units.tr: Among the seasons of the year, spring is the most suitable, because it is most temperate; next to it comes autumn; then summer, which is more apt for opening a vein than winter. This is how it should be done if a time has to be chosen; but where necessity demands, the bleeding must be undertaken at any time.

units.la: CAP. XI. Quantum sanguinis detrahendum.
units.tr: CHAP. XI. How much blood is to be taken away.

units.la: QVicunque tutam evacuationem sanguinis missione moliris,confer diligenter magnitudinem morbi cum viribus, alioqui præcipitabis ægrum. Sicut enim vires aliæ sunt robustæ , aliæ prostratæ , aliæ mediocres:ita phlebotomia alia magna,quæ materiam totam, aut maximam partem aufert. alia parva , quæ parum, aut nihil demit. Proinde inutilis censenda. media est quidem utilis, quia materiam aufert ; sed imperfecta, quia magnam partem humorum adhuc relinquit in venis. Vires robustæ perfectam evacuationem, at dejectæ & prostratæ nullam sanguinis detractionem ctionem sustinent. mediocres quidem imperfectam, at non inutilem. Morbus itaque extremus, conjunctus cum virium robore, plenam integramque detractionem tolerat. verum si morbus parvus sit, sintque vires robustæ, plena evacuatio non est tam necessaria, sed infra subsistere tutius videtur. at si vites sint debiles, sed non exhaustæ, sitque morbus magnus, expedit sanguinem per vires minuere, viresque interea reficere. Quanto itaque morbus est acutior, quia urget, tanto liberalius sanguis est fundendus; modo ferant vires. Chronicus verò, quia diu durat, minorem evacuationem exigit. sed an præcautionis gratia, dum metuitur à plenitudine morbis, integris adhuc viribus, ad animi deliquium ducendus sit sanguis, quod majores facere consueverunt; dubitatur. Multos novimus deficere animo, viso semel scalpello: nonnullos una aut altera uncia effusa, protinus labascere. contra, nonulli non deficiunt, etiamsi, plus
units.tr: Whoever sets about a safe evacuation of blood by bleeding should carefully compare the magnitude of the disease with the strength, or else you will throw the patient headlong. For just as strengths differ, some robust, some broken down, some middling, so bleedings differ: one large, which removes the whole or the greater part of the matter; another small, which takes away little or nothing. Therefore the small bleeding should be judged useless. The middling one is indeed useful, because it removes some of the matter; but it is incomplete, because it leaves a large part of the humours still in the veins. Robust strengths bear a complete evacuation, but those cast down and prostrated bear no withdrawal of blood at all. The middling bear an incomplete one, but not a useless one. So an extreme disease, joined with robust strength, bears a full and entire withdrawal. But if the disease is slight and the strength robust, a full evacuation is not so necessary, and it seems safer to stop short of it. But if the strengths are weak, yet not exhausted, and the disease is great, it is expedient to diminish the blood in proportion to the strength, and meanwhile to restore the strength. Therefore the more acute the disease, because it presses, the more freely the blood should be poured out, provided the strength bears it. A chronic disease, however, because it lasts long, demands a smaller evacuation. But whether, as a precaution, while there is fear of fullness from the disease, with the strength still intact, the blood should be drawn to the point of fainting, which the ancients were accustomed to do, is doubtful. We have known many who faint at the mere sight of the lancet, and some who, after one or two ounces have flowed out, immediately grow faint; on the other hand, some do not faint even if

units.la: s plus justo auferatur. Animi ergo deliquium fallax erit mensura. Adhibenda itaque meo judicio artificiosa conjectura, quæ habetur ex conferentia, & tolerantia ægri.
units.tr: more than is right is taken away. A fainting fit, therefore, will be a deceptive measure. Therefore, in my judgement, an artful conjecture must be applied, which is drawn from the comparison and the tolerance of the patient.

units.la: Evacuatio confert, quæ manifestè morbificam causam minuit : sin eadem viribus non sit molesta, toleratur. Æstimatur tolerantia ex omnibus viribus : maximè tamen vitalibus, si Galeno creditur, quibus adde temperamentum, ætatem, cæteraque. Si una sectione omnibus indicantibus est satisfactum, repetenda non est : sin minus, repetenda venit, ubi enim vires periclitantur, revulsiones, derivationesque sunt partiendæ. Si ipsum tempus spectes, sitque electio ejus concessa, quod fit in præservatione ; cum morbus non urget, ver præfertur, ut dixi. Hora esto matutina, una aut altera post somnum consuetum. Vide tamen ut concoctio pridiana sit expedita, & prima regio, in qua sunt intestina, levata sit excrementis : periculum alioqui suberit, berit, ne inanitæ venæ humores excrementitios attrahant. At in magnis morbis, inprimis ijs qui oriuntur à sanguinis fluxu, ut pleuritis, statim quavis diei & noctis hora, neglecta præparatione, sanguis est demendus. In mora enim est magnum periculum; est enim magna necessitas, & vires constant. In principio itaque febrium ardentium sectio est instituenda. Idem fit in revulsione, partibus nimirum inflammatis.
units.tr: An evacuation is beneficial if it clearly diminishes the morbific cause; but if it is not troublesome to the strength, it is tolerated. Tolerance is estimated from all the strengths, but chiefly the vital ones, if Galen is to be believed; to these add the temperament, age, and the rest. If the one bleeding has satisfied all the indications, it need not be repeated; but if not, it must be repeated, for where the strengths are in peril, revulsions and derivations must be used instead. If you consider the time itself, and the choice of it is granted, as happens in prevention, when the disease is not pressing, spring is preferred, as I have said. Let the hour be the morning, one or two hours after the customary sleep. See, however, that the digestion of the previous day is complete and that the first region, in which the intestines lie, is relieved of excrement; otherwise there will be danger that the emptied veins will draw in excremental humours. But in great diseases, especially those that arise from a flux of blood, such as pleurisy, blood must be taken at once, at whatever hour of the day or night, with preparation neglected; for delay carries great danger, since the necessity is great and the strength holds. Therefore at the beginning of burning fevers the bleeding is to be undertaken. The same holds for revulsion, namely in inflamed parts.

units.la: Derivatio revulsionem sequitur. at si sanguinem parti impactum discutere, aut putrefacere nolis sed elicere, decurrendum erit ad minora præsidia; hirudines nimirum, cucurbitulas, scarificationem.
units.tr: Derivation follows revulsion. But if you do not wish to disperse or putrefy blood lodged in a part, but to draw it out, you must have recourse to lesser remedies: leeches, cupping-glasses, and scarification.

units.la: Hirudines bonæ (nec enim omnes conveniunt) aqua purissima, eaque sæpius mutata, eousque lavandæ sunt, donec omnem virulentiam & malignitatem deponant; tum partibus admotæ, (quibus trifidum vulnus infligunt) relinquendæ, dum sanguine turgidæ, sponte cadant. Multum sanguinis guinis proliciunt, inprimis verò, melancholici.
units.tr: Good leeches (for not all suit) must be washed in the purest water, changed often, until they lay aside all their virulence and malignity; then, applied to the parts (into which they inflict a three-cleft wound), they are to be left until, swollen with blood, they fall off of their own accord. They draw off a great deal of blood, especially in melancholics.

units.la: Scarificatio tantò liberalius sanguinem vacuat, quanto altius scalpellum adigitur. tum enim non solum humorem parti inhærentem, sed longius etiam sanguinem revellit. Hujus præsidij, est usus in brachijs, cruribusque humore turgentibus: convenit cutaneis affectibus, morsibus venenatis, alijsque.
units.tr: Scarification empties blood the more freely the deeper the lancet is driven in. For then it draws away not only the humour clinging to the part but also the blood farther off. This remedy is used in arms and legs swollen with humour; it suits cutaneous affections, venomous bites, and others.

units.la: Si scarificationi succedat cucurbitula cum flamma, liberalior erit evacuatio. Nam sine ea parum sanguinis detrahitur. Cucurbitulæ siccæ insensibiliter evacuant, flatusque discutiunt, ut in colico affectu videre est. impositæ ventriculo vomitũ sistunt, & singultum. at mammis, menstrua. revellunt etiam ab internis partibus ad externas. Cave tamen admoveas parti inflammatæ, aut ijs utaris ante revulsionem cum eâ est opus.
units.tr: If cupping with flame follows scarification, the evacuation will be more copious; for without it little blood is withdrawn. Dry cupping-glasses evacuate imperceptibly and dispel wind, as can be seen in colic. Applied to the stomach they stop vomiting and hiccups; applied to the breasts, the menses. They also draw from internal parts to external ones. Take care, however, not to apply them to an inflamed part, or to use them before revulsion is needed there.

units.la: INSTITVTIONVM MEDICARVM LIBER VI, De VICTVS RATIONE.
units.tr: Book VI of the Medical Institutions, On the Management of Diet

units.la: CAP. I. De Alimento.
units.tr: CHAP. I. On Food.

units.la: POstrema hæc est medicinæ pars, communis ægro cum sano. Ratio enim victus est necessaria non tantum ad sanitatem restituendam, sed & præsentem conservandam. Consistit autem in legitimo usu sex rerum non naturalium, sine quibus non vivitur. Res non naturales ideo dicuntur, quia nec secundum naturam humano corpori insunt, ut facultates, temperamenta; nec tamen præter naturam, ut morbus, & symptoma. sed medio modo se habent. nam si ijs bene utaris prosunt; sin minus, nocent. hujusmodi sunt aër, cibus, potus, motus, tus, quies, excreta, retenta, somnus, vigilia, perturbationes, seu animi affectus. Qui victus rationem omnem, & diætam in sola ciborum administratione ponunt, nimis eam contrahunt, & in angustum cogunt. Animati corporis substantia dissolvitur, & carpitur perpetuo à calore infito; nisi verò cibo utili reficeretur, interiret protinus vivens. proinde ut conservetur, reponi & instaurari debet id, quod deperijt. hoc, ut duxi, fit alimento. Ea de causa corpori inest appetitus alimenti, & facultates illud commutantes, de quibus supra. Quanquam sanguis in venis, & qui in partibus extra vasa concrescit ros, propriè alimentum sit (hæc enim apta sunt proximè in substantiam nostram facessere) tamē alimentum hoc loco usurpatur, quod nullam mutationem, aut alterationem in nostro corpore perpessum est; ut panis, vinum. quod quanquam ex elementis constat, non tamen debet nimis esse dissimile nostro corpori; ut lapis, quia non coqueretur; sed aliquo modo simile. Hoc est, cibus sumendus non debet nimium contrariari corpori nostro, tum enim esset medicamentum, cujus est agere in corpus, & non pati, sicut contra alimenti est pati magis. Alimentum ergo converti debet in humanam naturam, ut substantiæ fluxus reparetur. nam potus siccitatem partium, & æstum tantum temperat, nisi idem sit potus, & cibus simul. Alimentum omne debet esse animatum, aut ab animato fluxisse, ut lac, vinum. nam inanimatum si esset, nutrire non posset ob contrarietatem. Sumi ergo potest ex omni genere animalium, & stirpium.
units.tr: This is the last part of medicine, common to the sick and the healthy. The management of diet is necessary not only to restore health but also to preserve the health one has. It consists in the proper use of the six non-natural things, without which no one can live. They are called non-natural because they are not part of the human body by nature, as faculties and temperaments are, nor are they against nature, as disease and symptom are. They stand in a middle position: if we use them well they benefit us, and if not, they harm us. Such things are air, food, drink, motion and rest, sleep and waking, the excreta and retained matter, and the passions or affections of the mind. Those who place the whole management of diet and regimen in the mere administration of food narrow it too much and confine it within too small a compass. The substance of a living body is dissolved and consumed continually by the innate heat; unless it were restored by useful food, the living creature would die at once. Therefore, so that it may be preserved, what has been lost must be replaced and renewed. As I have said, this is done by nourishment. For this reason the body has an appetite for food, and the faculties that change it, as discussed above. Although blood in the veins, and the dew that congeals in the parts outside the vessels, are properly food (for these are fitted to pass most directly into our substance), nevertheless in this place "food" is taken to mean what has undergone no change or alteration in our body, such as bread and wine. Although this consists of the elements, it ought not to be too unlike our body, as a stone is not, since it would not be digested; but it should be in some way similar. That is, the food we take should not be too contrary to our body, for then it would be a medicine, whose function is to act upon the body and not to be acted upon, whereas the function of food is rather to be acted upon. Food, therefore, ought to be turned into human nature, so that the loss of substance may be made good. For drink only tempers the dryness of the parts and their heat, unless the same thing is both drink and food. All food should be alive, or come from something alive, such as milk and wine; for if it were not alive it could not nourish, because of its contrariety. Food may therefore be taken from every kind of animal and plant.

units.la: Distingui debet alimentum simplex à medicamentoso. illud enim tantum vires reparat, nec morbum ejusque causam respicit: hoc verò præterquam quod vires reparat, morbo etiam resistit, ut endivia, acetosa in febricitante.
units.tr: Simple food must be distinguished from medicinal food. The former only restores strength and takes no account of the disease or its cause; the latter, besides restoring strength, also resists the disease, as endive and sorrel do in a feverish patient.

units.la: Ad medicamentosa alimenta pertinent tinent omnia obsonia; alimenta item refrigerantia, calefacientia, incrassantia &c. Carnes, piscesque raro excedunt in qualitatibus primis activis, nisi condiantur aromatibus. nam quę illis qualitatibus excedunt. sunt herbæ & vegetabilia, ut vinum, cæpa, allium.
units.tr: All relishes belong among the medicinal foods, as do foods that cool, warm, thicken and so on. Meats and fish rarely exceed in the primary active qualities unless they are seasoned with spices; for those foods which do exceed in these qualities are herbs and vegetables, such as wine, onions and garlic.

units.la: Veram ciborum temperiem in qualitatibus primis, optimè venaberis ex saporibus; de quibus supra.
units.tr: You will best discover the true temperament of foods in the primary qualities from their tastes, which were discussed above.

units.la: Alimentum attenuans, succum tenuem præbet, ut panis triticeus fermentatus in clibano coctus, perca, aliique pisces saxatiles aceto conditi, pipiones, pulli gallinacei, turdi. Idem faciunt aromata, plurimæque herbæ earumque partes, & semina; ut hyssopus, menta, origanum, petroselinum, apium, semina calida &c. vinum album tenue. Incrassans sanguinem viscidum, crassumque gignit, ut oriza, lentes, fabæ, panis triticeus, secalinus non fermentatus, placentæ, lac caseosum, ova dura, caro porcina, bubula, cervina, omnefque carnes infumatæ, anguillæ, castaneæ, vina rubra, crassa.
units.tr: Attenuating food gives a thin juice, such as wheaten bread leavened and baked in an oven, perch and other rock fish pickled in vinegar, pigeons, young chickens, thrushes. Spices do the same, and most herbs and their parts and seeds, such as hyssop, mint, marjoram, parsley, celery, warm seeds and so on; also thin white wine. Thickening food generates viscid and thick blood, such as rice, lentils, beans, wheaten bread, unleavened rye bread, cakes, cheese made from curds, hard eggs, pork, beef, venison, all smoked meats, eels, chestnuts, and thick red wines.

units.la: Qui valetudini consultum vult, alimento nec incrassante nimis, nec contra nimis attenuante uti debet. tale est panis triticeus, mediocriter fermentatus, & in clibano coctus, caro gallinarum, columbarum, phasianorum, vitulina, vervecina, aliorumque castratorum, potissimum juniorum. pisces marini (inprimis saxatiles, qui in magnis promontorijs degunt) ova recentia tremula, vina fulva, duscia, ficus, uvæ passæ, amydalæ dulces.
units.tr: Anyone who wishes to look after his health should use food that neither thickens too much nor, on the other hand, attenuates too much. Such are wheaten bread moderately leavened and baked in an oven, the flesh of hens, pigeons, pheasants, veal, mutton and other castrated animals, especially young ones; sea fish (above all rock fish, which live near great headlands); fresh, trembling eggs; tawny wines; dates, figs, raisins and sweet almonds.

units.la: Quæcunque alimenta solidioris sunt substantiæ, plus nutriunt; ut panis ex puro tritico bene fermentatus, caro animalium castratorum, vervecis, caponis &c. cancrorum item caro, & astacorum. at quæ substantiæ sunt minus solidæ, ut sorbitiones, panis hordeaceus, tum olera pleraque, aviculæ montanæ, vinum aquosum, minus nutriunt.
units.tr: Foods of a more solid substance nourish more; such as bread made of pure wheat and well leavened, the flesh of castrated animals, mutton, capons and so on; likewise the flesh of crabs and crayfish. But foods of less solid substance, such as broths, barley bread, most vegetables, small mountain birds, and watery wine, nourish less.

units.la: Alimenta comparata cum humano ventriventriculo, vel sunt facilis, vel difficilis concoctionis. Difficulter coquuntur panes fermenti expertes, caro cervina, arietina, bubula, infumata, pisces indurati quocunque modo. & ut verbo dicam, quæcunque nimis sunt terrestria. At panis probè fermentatus, ova tremula, lactuca, spinachia &c. facilis sunt concoctionis. Fructus horarij, cerasa, mala persica, melones, facile corrumpuntur propter aquositatem. pyra verò, mala cydonia, reliquaq; nimis crassæ substantiæ, difficulter corrumpuntur.
units.tr: Foods, compared with the human stomach, are either easy or difficult to digest. Breads without leaven, venison, lamb, beef, smoked meat, and fish hardened in any way are digested with difficulty; and, to say it in a word, whatever is too earthy. But well-leavened bread, soft eggs, lettuce, spinach and so on are easy to digest. Seasonal fruits, cherries, peaches and melons, spoil easily because of their watery nature; pears, quinces and other fruits of too thick a substance spoil with difficulty.

units.la: Dividi solent alimenta à medicis in boni, & mali succi, hoc est, quædam generant laudabilem sanguinē, quædam non. Laudabilem succum generant panis triticeus bene fermentatus, coctusque in clibano, ova recentia, carnes animalium castratorum &c. perca, merula, multique pisces, exceptis ijs qui in paludibus & stagnis vivunt. at carnes animalium non castratorum, tum vulpinum, asinorum, aviumq; carnivorarum malum sanguisanguinem generant. Huc quoque referri possunt fructus horarij. Operosum nimis esset hic omnes ciborum differentias persequi. Omnis alimenti finis est nutritio, seu reparatio deperditæ substantiæ. Indicatur itaque victus, à substantia nostri corporis conservanda. quanquam per accidens in ægro nihil impedit quominus resistat causæ morbificæ, & morbo. Per accidens dico; quia morbus non indicat victum sed medicamentum.nam morbus indicat sui corruptionem, sicut facultas conservationem.
units.tr: Physicians usually divide foods into those of good and of bad juice; that is, some generate praiseworthy blood and some do not. Well-leavened wheaten bread baked in an oven, fresh eggs, the flesh of castrated animals and so on generate praiseworthy juice; as do perch, blackbirds and many fish, except those that live in marshes and ponds. But the flesh of uncastrated animals, also fox, donkey and carnivorous birds, generates bad blood. Seasonal fruits may also be referred to this group. It would be too laborious to pursue all the differences of foods here. The whole purpose of food is nourishment, or the restoration of lost substance. Diet is therefore indicated by the need to preserve the substance of our body, although in the sick, by accident, nothing hinders it from resisting the morbific cause and the disease. I say "by accident," because disease does not indicate diet but medicine; for disease indicates its own corruption, just as the faculty indicates preservation.

units.la: CAP. II. De Forma Victus, & Quantitate.
units.tr: CHAP. II. On the Form and Quantity of Diet.

units.la: TRiplex victus ratio considerari potest; crassa, tenuis, & media. Crassa, auget substantiam nostram, plusque reponit, quam calor consumpsit. Tenuis minuit. Media tantum reponit, quantum calor abstulit. proinde nec auget nec minuit. Si cui tamen lubet minutius dividere, victus crassus,
units.tr: A diet may be considered in three ways: thick, thin, and middling. A thick diet increases our substance and restores more than the heat has consumed. A thin diet diminishes it. A middling diet restores only as much as the heat has taken away, and so neither increases nor diminishes. If anyone prefers to divide more finely, the thick diet,
