Victus enim crassus, est vel simpliciter talis, vel exactè ple- nus; idem de tenui judicandum; nisi quod plura inferiora membra sub se contineat. Est enim tenuis simplici- ter,tenuis exquisitè,tenuissimus sim- pliciter,tenuissimus exquisitè: sed hi postremi diu exoleverunt, quia ad inediam revocantur: eorum tamen loco aquam hordei, aut melicraton exhibemus.
units.tr: the thick diet, like the thin, can be subdivided further. For a thick diet is either thick in the simple sense or exactly full; the same judgement applies to a thin diet, except that it contains more lower grades beneath it. Thus there is thin in the simple sense, thin exactly, thinnest in the simple sense, and thinnest exactly. But these last have long since fallen out of use, since they amount to starvation; in their place we give barley water or melicraton [μελίκρατον].

units.la: In idonea victus forma constitu- enda, considerandæ sunt vires, ali- mentum indicantes. Hæ enim non tantum genus formamque alimenti, sed & quantitatem modumque præ- scribunt: inæqualiter tamen. Sano- rum enim vires aut augendæ veni- unt, aut eodem statu conservandæ. Quo enim majores sunt, eo plenius nutrire convenit; quo minores, eo parcius. In ægris vires cum morbo caufaq; morbifica conferendæ sunt, videndumque an permittat, vel pro- hibeat morbus, aut causa ejusdem, quod vires insinuant. Nam in his non permittit morbus ut plenior victus instituatur; distraheretur enim natura à coctione materiæ morbificæ, nec hoc tantum, sed plethora, aut cacochymia augerentur. Ergo in morbis chronicis vires eodem statu sunt conservandæ, mediâ victus formâ. in acutis verò nonnihil debilitari ad statum usque permittuntur, tenui victu. Quo enim acutior est morbus & symptomata vigent, eo tenuiori victu utendum. quo minus acutus, pleniore, ut diuturnæ coctioni sufficiat natura. Ergo in morbis extremè acutis (hi 4. die judicantur) exactè tenuissimus victus instituendus est, ne natura avocetur à pugna contra morbum. In ægris enim norma victus est status morbi, quo tempore gravissima urgent symptomata. Vires considerandæ non solum sunt, præsentes, sed & futuræ; dandumque aliquid ætati, consuetudini &c. ætas enim puerilis, temperatura calida, habitusque corporis rarus, liberalius cibare cogunt, ac plenius quam morbo expedit. Virium est prima dignitas, ad quas confervandas, victus instituitur: si ergo praecesserint vigiliæ, aut evacuatio copiosa, procedendum est ad pleniorem victum; tum enim incertū est, an cum tenui admodum victu ad statum perdurare possit æger. At si debilitas virium non sit ab evacuatione, vigiliisque dissolventibus, sed ob copiam crudorum humorum, vehementiamque symptomatum, victus minuendus est, non augendus; nec enim vires tum dissolvuntur, sed opprimentur. Quando itaque ægri vires dissolutæ victum indicant, si morbus non urget, is plenior est instituendus. At si vires non urgeant (non urgent, si non sint dissolutæ) sed morbus extremè peracutus, tenuissimus victus est instituendus. In parvo morbo, constantibus viribus, quia nec ille, nec hæ urgent, medius convenit victus, quicquid est, potior semper est ratio ejus habenda, quod magis urget. Verum, quemadquemadmodum dixi, quia virium est prima cura & dignitas, si declinandum est ad extremorum alterutrum, potius ad excessum, quam defectum hoc faciendum est. Morbi vigor & status æstimandus est ex symptomatum vehementia. Nam quidam morbi, ut pleuritis, peripneumonia, statim vigent, habentque gravissima symptomata, quæ incipiente humorum coctione, leniuntur. alij morbi leniter incipiunt, augenturque paulatim, quemadmodum febres continuæ pleræque omnes; in quibus symptomata in principio non vigent, verum cum humorum completur concoctio. In illis ergò, quia in principio vigent symptomata, statim etiam tenuissimus victus est præscribendus; in his non item: nam in principio plenior victus est instituendus, in vigore autem tenuis admodum. Porrò homo sanus & suæ spontis, cibis satiari non debet, nec ad labores esse piger: nec eam ciborum copiam ingeret, quæ ventrem sit gravatura. quo vero quis minus exercetur, par-cius edendum. quò magis autem, liberalius edendum: in quibus omni-bus habenda est consuetudinis ratio.
units.tr: In constituting a suitable form of diet, one must consider the strength, which indicates the nourishment. For strength prescribes not only the kind and form of food but also its quantity and manner, though not in the same way in each case. In the healthy, strength must either be increased or kept in the same state. The greater the strength, the fuller the nourishment should be; the smaller, the more sparing. In the sick, strength must be weighed against the disease and its cause, and it must be seen whether the disease, or its cause, permits or forbids what the strength suggests. For in these the disease does not permit a fuller diet to be instituted, since nature would be distracted from concocting the morbid matter; and not only that, but plethora or cacochymia would be increased. Therefore in chronic diseases the strength must be kept in the same state, with a middling form of diet. In acute diseases, however, it is allowed to be somewhat weakened down to its present state, by a thin diet. For the more acute the disease and the more vigorous the symptoms, the thinner the diet must be; the less acute, the fuller, so that nature is equal to the long concoction. Therefore in extremely acute diseases (these are judged on the fourth day) the strictly thinnest diet must be instituted, lest nature be diverted from the struggle against the disease. For in the sick the rule of diet is the state of the disease, at the time when the most grievous symptoms press. The strength must be considered not only as it is present but also as it will be in future, and some allowance must be made for age, habit, and so on. For childhood age, a warm temperament, and a loose habit of body compel us to feed more liberally, and more fully than is expedient for the disease. The first concern is strength, and it is for preserving this that diet is instituted. If therefore wakefulness or copious evacuation has gone before, one must proceed to a fuller diet, since it is then uncertain whether the patient can keep up his state on a very thin diet. But if the weakness of strength arises not from evacuation and dissolving wakefulness but from a copious supply of crude humours and the violence of the symptoms, the diet must be diminished, not increased; for then the strength is not dissolved but oppressed. Therefore, when the sick person's dissolved strength indicates a diet, if the disease does not press, a fuller one is to be instituted. But if the strength is not pressed (it is not pressed if it has not dissolved), but the disease is extremely peracute, the thinnest diet must be instituted. In a mild disease, with strength holding steady, since neither presses, a middling diet is appropriate; whatever the case, the reason that presses more must always be given the greater weight. Yet, as I have said, since the first care and dignity lies with strength, if one must lean toward one of the extremes, it should be toward excess rather than deficiency. The vigour and state of the disease must be estimated from the violence of the symptoms. For some diseases, such as pleurisy and peripneumonia, are vigorous from the start and have the gravest symptoms, which abate as the concoction of the humours begins. Other diseases begin mildly and increase gradually, as nearly all continued fevers do; in these the symptoms are not vigorous at the beginning, but only when the concoction of the humours is complete. In the former, since the symptoms are vigorous from the start, the thinnest diet is to be prescribed at once; in the latter this is not so, for at the beginning a fuller diet is to be instituted, and a very thin one at the height of the illness. Furthermore, a healthy man in his own right ought not to be sated with food, nor be lazy for labours; nor should he take in such an abundance of food as will weigh down the stomach. The less a man exercises, the more sparingly he should eat; the more he exercises, the more liberally he may eat. In all these matters regard must be had to custom.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: De Alimentorum qualitate.
units.tr: On the Quality of Foods.

units.la: QValitas alimenti in sanis æsti-matur ex temperamento, ætate, alijsque adjunctis; regione nimi-rum, & anni temporibus. adverten-dum tamen, si regio, cœlique condi-tio temperatæ sint, temperatum si-milemque victum indicare: verum si intemperatæ sint contraria. Non ita se res habet in temperamento & ætate. Nam temperamentum, licet justo calidius sit, ac proinde intem-peratum, non statim indicat contra-ria; nisi reducere velis, ac commuta-re; tum enim ad contrarium victum est decurrendum. verum si conserva-re vis, similibus est utendum. Ita puer quanquam humidus sit, non ex-siccandus, sed eodem statu conser-vandus. Consuetudini multum est dandum, inprimis in morbis; nam ejus eadem est cum natura indicatio; nam homo, alioqui siccus, si diu assueverit humidis, non amplius manebit siccus, sed humidus evadet. Quid? quod consueta alimenta, deterioris licet notæ, jucundiora tamen sunt. Qui crudos humores coacervare solent, uti debent alimentis attenuantibus. Hæc enim incidunt, obstructionesque aperiunt; at, qui firmo est corpore, quique optimè digerit, medium victum inter incrassantem & attenuantem eligere debet, cavendo semper ab alimentis pravi succi. In ægrorum victu instituendo, habenda ratio est morbi, temperamenti, quibus nonnulli addunt consuetudinem; quæ tamen meo judicio reducitur ad temperamentum. Morbus enim semper indicat contrarium victum; nam febris, intemperies nimirum calida, & sicca, indicat humidum, frigidumque victum; temperamentum (quod conservari debet) similem. At si pugnent gnent morbus & temperamentum in indicando, ut si biliosus febricitet, certè non est alimentis calidis fovendus, ad servandum temperamentum,hoc enim modo intenderetur febris, corrumpereturque tandem temperamentum, sed aut frigidum, aut temperatum cibum dare expedit. In quibus nunquam negligenda consuetudo; sicut nec denegandus cibus deterioris notæ, si vehementius appetatur: talis enim plerumque melius coquitur. Quod ad tempus attinet; ita habeto: sani edant tempore consueto: nisi forsan tum cibus prius sumptus, nondum sit concoctus,nec exoneratus ventriculus. Consuetum tempus aut antevertere,aut alioqui protrahere, consultum non est. illud enim facit humorum cruditatem: hoc ventriculum replet pravis humoribus. Sin animus est horam mutare,sensim hoc fiat, non subito. ægris cibus dandus tum,cum minus à morbo gravantur. Proinde si morbus careat typo, ut hydrops; retinenda est hora, in sani-tate consueta. Sin typos habeat, ut febris continua tertiana; eligatur hora minoris afflictionis. In inter-mittente, eligendum declinationis tempus, aut quod longissimè abest à paroxismo: nam paroxismus, quan-tum fieri potest, declinandus est.
units.tr: The quality of food in the healthy is judged from temperament, age, and other circumstances: namely, region and the seasons of the year. It must be noted, however, that if the region and the condition of the sky are temperate, they indicate a temperate and similar diet, but if they are intemperate, they indicate the opposite. It is not so with temperament and age. For temperament, although it may be warmer than is just, and therefore intemperate, does not at once indicate the opposite, unless you wish to reduce and change it; for then one must have recourse to the contrary diet. But if you wish to preserve it, one must use similar things. Thus a child, although moist, is not to be dried out, but kept in the same state. Much must be given to custom, especially in illnesses; for its indication is the same as that of nature. For a man who is otherwise dry, if he has long been accustomed to moist things, will no longer remain dry but will become moist. What of it, that customary foods, though of poorer quality, are nonetheless more pleasant? Those who are accustomed to heap up crude humours must use attenuating foods, for these cut through and open obstructions; but one who has a firm body and digests best should choose a middle diet between thickening and attenuating foods, always taking care to avoid foods of bad juice. In arranging the diet of the sick, account must be taken of the illness and of the temperament, to which some add custom; yet in my judgement this is reduced to temperament. For illness always indicates the contrary diet: for fever, namely a hot and dry intemperance, indicates a moist and cold diet; temperament (which ought to be preserved) indicates a similar one. But if illness and temperament conflict in their indications, as when a bilious patient has a fever, certainly he is not to be nourished with hot foods in order to preserve the temperament, for in this way the fever would be increased and the temperament at last corrupted; it is expedient instead to give cold or temperate food. In such cases custom must never be neglected; nor should food of poorer quality be denied if it is desired more vehemently, for such food is usually digested better. As to time, hold to this: the healthy should eat at the customary hour, unless perhaps the food previously taken has not yet been digested, nor the stomach emptied. To bring forward or otherwise postpone the customary time is not advisable; the former produces crudity of humours, the latter fills the stomach with bad humours. But if one intends to change the hour, let it be done gradually, not suddenly. Food is to be given to the sick when they are least burdened by the illness. Therefore, if the illness lacks a typical course, as dropsy does, the hour customary in health is to be kept; but if it has a typical course, as a continuous tertian fever, the hour of least affliction is to be chosen. In intermittent fever, the time of decline should be chosen, or that which is furthest from the paroxysm, for the paroxysm is to be avoided as far as possible.

units.la: Si modum cibandi quæris; nimi-rum rarone, an sæpe sit edendum, parúmne, an multum; in sanis negotium totum pendet ex viribus & indigentia: ita tamen ut concedatur aliquid ætati, consuetudini &c. declinando semper nimis anxiam victus rationem ex mente Celsi. In ægris semper vires conferendæ sunt cum morbo. nam robustæ, copiosum victum indicant; debiles contra paucum; mediocres vero mediocrem. Si vires alioqui robustæ conjunctæ sint cum plethora, tum quia abundat intus nutrimentum, raro, & paucis est nutriendus æger. sed si vires quidem constent, sit autem humorum aut defectus, aut corruptio, sæpe mulmultumque est edendum; modo nihil impediat. Impediunt non raro, paroxismus, & symptomata, quo in casu saepe dandus cibus, sed parum. Si vires sint debiles, sitque copia humorum, raro dandum est alimentum, & paucum. Sin debilitas virium conjungatur cum humorum inopia aut malignitate, parum saepeque exhibere decet cibum.
units.tr: If you ask about the manner of feeding, namely whether one should eat rarely or often, little or much: in the healthy the whole matter depends on their strength and need, yet so that something is conceded to age, custom, and so on, always avoiding an overly anxious regimen of diet, following the mind of Celsus. In the sick, strength must always be weighed against the illness: for robust strength indicates a copious diet, weak strength a sparing one, and moderate strength a moderate one. If strength is otherwise robust and joined with plethora, then, since nourishment abounds within, the sick person should be nourished rarely and in small amounts. But if strength is sound yet there is either a deficiency or a corruption of humours, one should eat often and much, provided nothing hinders. Often a paroxysm and symptoms do hinder, in which case food should often be given, but in small quantity. If strength is weak but there is an abundance of humours, food should be given rarely and in small amounts. If weakness of strength is joined with a lack or malignancy of humours, it is fitting to give food in small amounts and often.

units.la: Sed tempora consideremus. Aestate, quia calor ambiens dissipat vires, parcius, sed crebrius est edendum. Hyeme vero, quia sanorum corpora sunt robustiora propter externum frigus, eorum dissolutionem impediens, liberalius edere convenit; non tamen saepe. Sed in aegris aliter statuendum videtur; nam licet hyeme corpora validiora sint, morbus tamen est consideranduss. Nam vis naturalis in aegro non tam bene coquit, quam in sano; propterea aegri hyeme parcius cibandi, quam aestate; nam hyeme minus corpora dissolvuntur.
units.tr: But let us consider the seasons. In summer, because the surrounding heat dissipates strength, one should eat more sparingly but more frequently. In winter, however, since the bodies of the healthy are more robust on account of the external cold, which prevents their dissolution, it is fitting to eat more generously, yet not often. In the sick, however, the matter seems to be decided otherwise; for although bodies are stronger in winter, the illness must nonetheless be considered. For the natural power in the sick does not digest as well as in the healthy; therefore the sick are to be fed more sparingly in winter than in summer, since in winter bodies dissolve less.

units.la: At vere medio (quia tum ægri sunt plethorici, aut ad eam constitutionem proximè accedunt) parum, & raro exhibendum. si vires autumno sint constantes; multum, sæpèque edendum esse censent plerique; sin contra debiles fuerint, parum & sæpè.
units.tr: In mid-spring (because the sick are then plethoric, or come very near to that condition) little should be given, and rarely. If strength is steady in autumn, most people judge that much should be eaten, and often; but if strength has been weak, little and often.

units.la: Eadem est regionum, & ætatum ratio: nam certè in regione calida non est tam liberaliter edendum, quam frigida: proinde in calidis nati regionibus, cum ad frigidas pervenerunt liberalius edunt. Nec enim Hispanus in patria tantum edere potest, quantum in Germania, aut Britannia. Idem de ætate judica; nam juvenes, quia eorum corpora dissolvuntur magis, magis cibandi sunt, quam senes.
units.tr: The same is true of regions and ages: for certainly in a hot region one should not eat as liberally as in a cold one; therefore those born in hot regions, when they come to cold ones, eat more liberally. For a Spaniard cannot eat in his homeland as much as in Germany or Britain. Judge the same of age: for young people, because their bodies dissolve more, must be fed more than the old.

units.la: Quærunt medici, utrum prandium liberalius debeat esse cæna, an contra. Certe, qui firmo est corpore & sano, melius est plus in cæna sumere, quam in prandio, non solum quia plus temporis est inter cænam & prandium, quam inter hoc, illam. sed quia noctu melior fit concoctio, tu enim quiescimus: at quiete melius coquitur cibus.nam motus magis facit ad distributionem,quam coctionem. verum qui catarrhis obnoxius est, quandoquidem somnus caput replet vaporibus, parcius in tali casu cænandum est. Potus qui tantum est potus(nam vinum & cervisia potens etiam nutriunt) respondere debet siti naturali. Proinde constantibus viribus, si necesse sit, quocunq; tempore liberalis est concedendus. At si vires sint debiles, parcus esto,sed creber. Hic attende, potus non tantum sitim sedat, sed & alimenti est vehiculum quasi. Nam coctio prima in ventriculo est elixatio, quæ sine humore peragi nequit. Dum itaque edimus, respondere debet alimentorum copiæ, si multum editur, multum etiam est bibendum; non tamen simul, verum per intervalla. & quia alimentum, potus interventu, per venas distribuitur,qui eas angustas habent,
units.tr: Physicians ask whether the midday meal ought to be more generous than the evening meal, or the reverse. Certainly, for one who is firm of body and healthy, it is better to take more at supper than at dinner, not only because there is more time between supper and the following dinner than between the latter and the former, but because digestion is better at night, for we are then at rest; and food is digested better in quiet, for motion contributes more to distribution than to concoction. But one who is prone to catarrhs, since sleep fills the head with vapours, should eat more sparingly at supper in such a case. Drink, which is only drink (for wine and strong beer also nourish), should answer to natural thirst. Therefore, when strength is steady, it may be granted liberally at any time, if need be. But if strength is weak, be sparing, yet frequent. Here note that drink not only quenches thirst but is, as it were, a vehicle for food. For the first concoction in the stomach is a softening, which cannot be carried out without moisture. Therefore, as we eat, the drink should correspond to the quantity of food: if much is eaten, much is also to be drunk; yet not all at once, but at intervals. And since food, by means of drink, is distributed through the veins, those who have narrow veins

units.la: R plus bibant, qui vero amplas, paulò minus.
units.tr: should drink more, but those who have wide ones, a little less.

units.la: CAP. VI. De Caeteris rebus non naturalibus.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI. Of the other non-natural things.

units.la: EXequamur reliqua non naturalia, initio facto ab aëre; qui substantia, purus, tenuisque esse debet, caeterum qualitate, & temperamento, varius. Nam homo sanus potissimum eligere debet temperatum; at æger, morbo contrarium. Proinde febricitans vivat in aëre frigido, contra hydropicus in calido. nam quoad ejus substantiam, puritatem dico, ea esse debet ægro cum sano communis. Loca uliginosa, palustria, & cadaveribus obsita fugienda sunt. in ijs siquidem aërem putrescere necesse est. contra loca sicca, montosa, ventisque obnoxia, salubriora habentur. Quod si vivat quispiam in aëre parum salubri, corrigi debet non solum intemperies, sed & malignitas aceto, odoribus, fumo rerum convenientium.
units.tr: Let us now go through the remaining non-natural things, beginning with the air. Air should be pure, thin in substance, and otherwise varied in quality and temperament. A healthy person should choose air that is mostly temperate, while a sick person should choose the opposite of his illness. So a feverish patient should live in cold air, and a dropsical patient in warm air. As for its substance, that is, its purity, the same standard must apply to the sick as to the healthy. Marshy, swampy places and places full of corpses must be avoided, since air there must necessarily putrefy. By contrast, dry, mountainous places exposed to the winds are considered healthier. If someone must live in air that is not very healthy, not only the temperature but also the harmful quality must be corrected with vinegar, fragrances, and suitable smoke.

units.la: Ad sanitatem conservandam multum facit motus, nam corpus roborat, excrementa dissolvit, cibum distribuit. Quod intelligi debet de moderato exercitio; nam magni labores corpus reddunt biliosum, & tenue. Exercendum corpus, donec in tumorem, & molem elevetur, floridumque evadat, nec non donec sudor calidus copiosè erumpat. cessandum cum sudor minuitur, & corporis moles contrahitur. Tempus maximè oportunum est ante cibos, peracta concoctione, depositis alui, & vesicæ excrementis, pleno ventre hoc facere inconsultum est; nam alimentum adhuc crudum distribuitur, humoresque funduntur. Cæterum qui temperamento est calido, & sicco, parcius exerceri debet, quam qui frigido, humidove, aut alioqui temperato.
units.tr: Motion contributes much to preserving health: it strengthens the body, dissolves excrements, and distributes food. This must be understood of moderate exercise, for great labours make the body bilious and thin. The body should be exercised until it swells and grows in bulk and becomes flushed, and until warm sweat breaks out copiously. One should stop when the sweat lessens and the bulk of the body contracts. The most suitable time is before meals, once digestion is finished and the bowels and bladder have been emptied. To do this on a full stomach is ill-advised, for the food is still raw and is being distributed, and the humours are being poured out. Moreover, one with a hot and dry temperament should exercise more sparingly than one who is cold, moist, or otherwise temperate.

units.la: Sequuntur excreta, & retenta, quorum diligentissimam curam habere debet sanus juxta & æger. Cum in omni concoctione suum sit excrementum; si retineatur diutius, necesse est in corpore contentum tandem putrescere, morbumque procreare, proinde sanitatis studiosus providere debet, ut mature expellatur. Similiter laeditur sanitas, si expellantur humores qui retineri alioqui debent, nisi peccent copia, & quantitate; tum enim, quia fluxiones concitant, minuendi sunt, sicut de plethora diximus antea. Idem est judicium & sanguinis menstrui, haemorrhoidum, lactis, seminis; quae etsi sola quantitate peccent, expelli tamen debent; alioqui sunt promptissimae morborum causae.
units.tr: Next come the excretions and retentions, which both the healthy and the sick must take the most careful heed of. Since every digestion produces its own excrement, if it is retained too long, what is contained in the body must eventually putrefy and produce disease. Therefore one who studies health should take care that it is expelled in good time. Health is likewise harmed if humours that ought otherwise to be retained are expelled, unless they are at fault in quantity or amount; for then, since they provoke fluxions, they must be diminished, as we said earlier concerning plethora. The same judgement applies to menstrual blood, haemorrhoids, milk, and semen. Even if these sin only in quantity, they must nevertheless be expelled; otherwise they are the most ready causes of diseases.

units.la: Quod dico conspicuum est in femine; nam diutius retentum, quod a castis viduis, puellisque fit, plurima inducit symptomata. corrumpitur enim, affectumque parit hystericum. Moderatus veneris usus corpus reddit vegetum & alacre; immoderatus vires exhaurit, corpus refrigerat, nervosque debilitat &c. Ætas veneri aptissima est juvenilis & virilis. eam maximè ferunt temperati, aut alioqui calidi, humidique, sicci enim frigidique ea læduntur. Inter anni tempora præfertur ver; post hyems, tum autumnus; quanquam quidam putent non improbabiliter, autumnum hyemi præferendum. Æstate quantum fieri potest abstinendum, inprimis diebus canicularibus. nam tum corpora sunt admodum debilia. Caeterum hora maximè ideonea est matutina; tum enim ventriculus est vacuus. pleno stomacho hoc facere est noxium; motus enim crudum chylum ex ventriculo præcipitat.
units.tr: What I say is plain in the case of semen; for when it is retained too long, as happens with chaste widows and girls, it brings on many symptoms. It is corrupted and gives rise to hysterical affections. Moderate sexual intercourse makes the body vigorous and lively; immoderate intercourse exhausts the strength, chills the body, weakens the nerves, and so on. The most suitable age for intercourse is youth and manhood. Temperate people, or those who are otherwise hot and moist, bear it best; dry and cold people are harmed by it. Among the seasons of the year, spring is preferred, then winter, then autumn; although some think, not unreasonably, that autumn should be preferred to winter. In summer one should abstain as far as possible, especially in the dog days, for then bodies are very weak. The most suitable hour is in the morning, for then the stomach is empty. To do it on a full stomach is harmful, for motion throws raw chyle out of the stomach.

units.la: Somni & vigiliæ ratio non est negligenda. Vigilia consistit in functioneanimali, quâ alimentum distribuitur, excrementumque expellitur; somnus ad concoctionem magis facit, & retentionem. in utroque modus est tenendus. Vigiliæ enim nimiæ corpus exsiccant, virésque exhauriunt. ita somnus justo major, nimium humectat, calorem obruit, excrementa crementa gignit. Tempus idoneum est nocturnum, (ipsæ tenebræ tum invitant) non statim à cæna sed paulo post, interposita levi deambulatiuncula. Dormiendum est, quamdiu in ventriculo & hepate est alimentum, quod spatium creditur esse septem horarum in homine sano: jacendum est super alterutrum latus, non tergum, nisi quis assuetus fuerit: illo enim modo melior fit concoctio. Cæterum si quis laboret morbo calido, somnus justo longior est concedendus, nisi sit visceris alicujus inflammatio, quam somnus auget. at si morbus sit frigidus, humidusque, somnus esto parcior, nam ut dixi somnus humectat. In paroxysmo febrili vigilandum, quia calor magis ad interiora cogitur.
units.tr: The regulation of sleep and waking must not be neglected. Waking consists in the animal function by which food is distributed and excrement is expelled; sleep contributes more to digestion and retention. A measure must be kept in both. For excessive waking dries up the body and exhausts the strength; sleep that is longer than is right moistens too much, overwhelms the heat, and generates excrements. The suitable time is night (the darkness itself then invites us), not straight after supper but a little later, with a light stroll taken in between. One should sleep as long as food remains in the stomach and liver, which in a healthy person is believed to be a period of seven hours. One should lie on either side, not on the back, unless one is accustomed to it, for in that position digestion is better. But if someone suffers from a hot disease, longer sleep should be allowed, unless there is inflammation of some organ, which sleep increases. But if the disease is cold and moist, sleep should be more sparing, for, as I said, sleep moistens. During a febrile paroxysm one should stay awake, because the heat is driven more inward.

units.la: Tandem animi perturbationes ad tuendam, aut destruendam sanitatem, plurimum possunt. Eæ enim concitant sanguinem in omnem partem. Proinde si vehementiores fuerint, non modo morbum, sed & mortem tem inducunt. ita timor magnus interficit, ita gaudium. Hoc non facit ira, quia medio modo corpus alterat; hoc est, nec spiritus evocat subitò, nec etiam intus cogit; unde immediatè neminem tollere creditur. horum omnium legitimus debet esse modus in homine sano. Ergo calidus fugiat iram, & immodicum gaudium. contra frigidus, eosdem affectus provocet, melancholicus tristitiam fugiat.
units.tr: Finally, the passions of the mind have very great power either to preserve or to destroy health. For they stir the blood in every direction. Therefore, if they are too violent, they induce not only disease but even death. Great fear kills, and so does joy. Anger does not do this, because it alters the body in a middling way; that is, it neither suddenly calls forth the spirits nor drives them inward, and so it is believed not to carry anyone off immediately. A lawful measure of all these passions ought to be kept in a healthy person. Therefore the hot-tempered person should avoid anger and immoderate joy; the cold-tempered person, on the other hand, should arouse these same feelings, and the melancholic person should avoid sadness.
